findings.title: Tool adapter registration tightly coupled at module load
findings.description: All tool adapters are registered in a static ADAPTERS dict populated at module import time. New adapters must be manually imported and added to ADAPTERS before they can be used. No dynamic registration or plugin discovery mechanism exists.
findings.impact: Tool system is not extensible without modifying the tools module. Adding new tools requires code changes to a central registry. This creates coupling between the tool system and the orchestrator, making it difficult to add tools dynamically or third-party tools.
findings.remediation: Implement a plugin architecture with dynamic discovery (e.g., scanning a tools/ directory) or a registration function that allows tools to self-register. Define a clear ToolAdapter protocol/interface.
references: DEVELOPMENT.md lines 66-72 (Adding a new tool section)
skill/scripts/run_tools.py:88-91 (select_adapters accepts an injected adapters dict)

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Every factual assertion in the claim body checks out. skill/scripts/tools/__init__.py is 31 lines: eleven module-level `from scripts.tools.X import YAdapter` statements followed by a literal ADAPTERS dict whose 16 values are adapter instances constructed at import time (including six `LegacySarifAdapter('<name>')` instances). I grepped the whole repo for ADAPTERS and found no entry point, setuptools plugin hook, importlib/pkgutil scan, or directory walk that could register an adapter — every consumer does a direct `from scripts.tools import ADAPTERS` (skill/scripts/run_tools.py:12, skill/scripts/ingest_tools.py:52, skill/scripts/_run_adapter.py:12) and looks up by key (ingest_tools.py:58 routes by output-file basename, printing 'no adapter registered' otherwise). DEVELOPMENT.md:66-72 confirms the manual procedure verbatim: 'Register it in skill/scripts/tools/__init__.py under ADAPTERS'. The coupling is in fact slightly worse than described: run_tools.py:23-29 keeps two further hand-maintained sets, PHASE1_ADAPTERS and PHASE2_ADAPTERS, that a new adapter must also be added to for selection to reach it, and DEVELOPMENT.md's checklist does not mention that step. Two corrections to the write-up. (1) The remediation's 'Define a clear ToolAdapter protocol/interface' is already done — skill/scripts/tools/base.py:51-62 defines `class ToolAdapter(Protocol)` with name, prefix, is_applicable, invoke, parse; only the discovery half of the remediation is outstanding. (2) The impact's 'coupling between the tool system and the orchestrator' is imprecise: orchestrator.py never imports ADAPTERS; the coupling is to run_tools/ingest_tools/_run_adapter, and run_tools.select_adapters(target, adapters=None) at line 88-91 already provides a substitution seam (`adapters = adapters or ADAPTERS`) that tests use, alongside runtime mutation of the dict (tests/test_run_tools.py:114,178,204). I also consider the MEDIUM severity unsupported: this is a design-choice observation with no failure mode, no incorrect behaviour, and no stated third-party-plugin requirement, in a deliberately stdlib-only skill where the registry is a 31-line file; LOW/INFO would match the evidence. Confidence LIKELY rather than CERTAIN reflects those characterization defects, not doubt about the underlying code facts, which are certain.

findings.title: Inconsistent security posture between production and test Docker images
findings.description: The production panopticon-tools image runs as non-root user 'scanner' (Dockerfile line 110: USER scanner), but the panopticon-fixtures test image runs as root (Dockerfile.fixtures lines 54-55: 'The fixtures image runs as root because it installs language toolchains'). This creates different security models and permission behaviors between the two environments.
findings.impact: Testing and production environments have different security constraints. Root access in fixtures allows unrestricted operations that would fail in production. This could mask issues that only appear when running with reduced privileges. Security testing is not representative of production execution context.
findings.remediation: Either: (1) Run fixtures image as the same non-root user as production, using sudo for privileged operations during build, or (2) Document that fixtures is development-only and intentionally uses root for test convenience, with clear separation from the production image contract.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning:
The factual assertions check out. Dockerfile:103-110 creates `scanner` (uid 1000) and ends with `USER scanner` / `WORKDIR /src`; skill/scripts/run_tools.py:130-131 and :156-167 build `docker run --rm -v <target>:/src:ro ... panopticon-tools` with no `--user` override, so production scans genuinely execute as the unprivileged `scanner`. Dockerfile.fixtures:4-6 does `FROM panopticon-tools:latest` then `USER root` and never switches back, so every layer and the runtime CMD run as root; skill/scripts/run_fixture_tests.py:52 and :79-86 likewise invoke `docker run` with no `--user`, so the adapter integration tests execute as root. The divergence is therefore real and confirmed at the cited lines.

The claim's 'masks issues' impact is not hypothetical — I found two concrete instances in the same files. (1) Dockerfile:72-76 unzips OWASP dependency-check into /opt as root, so /opt/dependency-check and its default `data/` directory are root-owned; skill/scripts/tools/dependency_check.py:21-35 builds the command with only `--scan/--format/--out` and never passes `--data`, so the tool falls back to the root-owned home directory for its H2 database. That is writable in the fixtures image (root) and not writable under `USER scanner`. (2) Dockerfile:17-18 populates the ruby-advisory-db under /root/.local/share, and Dockerfile:106-108 copies it to /home/scanner; because the fixtures image runs as root with HOME=/root, tests/tools/test_ruby_integration.py:30-41 exercises the /root copy and can never detect a broken or stale scanner-user copy. A third, smaller instance: CARGO_HOME is /usr/local/cargo during build (Dockerfile:79) but rebound to /home/scanner/.cargo at Dockerfile:109. The masking is compounded because the integration tests downgrade non-zero exit codes to skips (test_ruby_integration.py:25-26, 38-39), so a permission failure would surface as a silent skip rather than a red test.

Two qualifications that argue the severity is lower than MEDIUM. First, the claim quotes Dockerfile.fixtures:54-55 as evidence of the defect, but those lines are in fact the documentation the claim's own remediation option (2) asks for ('runs as root because it installs language toolchains and writes build artifacts during image build. It is intended for local test use only'), reinforced by DEVELOPMENT.md:74-83. So half the proposed remediation already exists. Second, the fixtures image is never published — .github/workflows/docker-publish.yml only builds and pushes the production Dockerfile to ghcr.io, and Dockerfile.fixtures has no workflow — so the root posture is not itself an exposed attack surface. The finding is a test-fidelity gap, not a deployed privilege problem, and it should be recharacterized that way (and the run_fixture_tests.py `docker run` calls given `--user 1000` plus a read-only fixture mount) rather than framed as a security-posture inconsistency.

findings.title: Mutable build-time dependencies in test fixtures
findings.description: The Dockerfile.fixtures clones public repositories using mutable branch references (e.g., 'main', 'v2023.8') without pinning to specific commit SHAs. These branches can change over time, potentially causing non-deterministic container builds. Lines 34-37 use 'echo ... || echo skipped' pattern to tolerate missing dependencies.
findings.impact: Build reproducibility is not guaranteed. The same Dockerfile.fixtures invocation could produce different containers on different dates. Tests may pass/fail based on upstream repository state changes rather than panopticon code changes. Long-term archival of test results may become unreliable.
findings.remediation: Pin repository clones to specific commit SHAs instead of branch names. Implement a process to regularly update the SHAs and tag the image with dates (already done for tagging: 'docker tag panopticon-fixtures:latest panopticon-fixtures:YYYY-MM-DD').
references: DEVELOPMENT.md lines 76-83 (Local scanner fixture suite section)

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Verified directly in /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/Dockerfile.fixtures. Line 25 `ARG RAILS_GOAT_REF=main` and line 31 `ARG ASP_GOAT_REF=main` are mutable branch names; line 28 `ARG WEB_GOAT_REF=v2023.8` is a tag (stable in practice, still re-pushable). All three are consumed by `git clone --depth 1 --branch ${REF}` on lines 26, 29, 32, so a rebuild on a different date pulls whatever those refs point to then. The tolerate-failure pattern is real: lines 35-37 each end in `|| echo "... skipped"`, so a broken upstream produces a silently degraded image rather than a failed build (the claim cites 34-37; line 34 is the comment, the RUNs are 35-37 -- trivial off-by-one, not material). Non-determinism is in fact broader than the claim states: line 9 `apt-get install` is unpinned, line 16 pipes an unpinned remote installer (`curl -sfL https://dot.net/v1/dotnet-install.sh | bash`), and line 48 `pip install pytest` is unpinned; only line 20 `cargo install cargo-audit --version 0.22.2` is version-pinned. The reproducibility impact reaches the tests: tests/tools/test_ruby_integration.py and test_csharp_integration.py assert `self.assertTrue(findings, ...)` against the cloned upstream trees, so upstream content changes can flip results independently of panopticon code. Two scope caveats that argue the impact statement is somewhat overstated (but do not falsify the claim): (1) no CI workflow builds this Dockerfile -- .github/workflows/docker-publish.yml builds only ./Dockerfile, and security.yml builds panopticon-tools -- so this is local-only test infrastructure, and (2) skill/scripts/run_fixture_tests.py:38-44 `build_image()` passes no `--build-arg`, so the defaults on lines 25/28/31 are always what is used. Also note the stated remediation is not literally applicable: `git clone --depth 1 --branch <SHA>` does not accept a raw commit SHA; SHA pinning requires clone + `git fetch origin <sha>` + `git checkout <sha>` (or `--revision` on very recent git).

findings.title: Fixture image builds from unpinned mutable git branches of third-party repositories and executes their build tooling
findings.description: `RAILS_GOAT_REF` (line 25) and `ASP_GOAT_REF` (line 31) default to the mutable branch `main`, unlike `WEB_GOAT_REF=v2023.8` (line 28), which is correctly pinned to a tag. `ASP_GOAT_REF` clones `Soham7-dev/AspGoat.git` — a single-maintainer personal repository, not an official OWASP project. The image then executes each project's own build/dependency tooling against the cloned code: `bundle install` (line 35), `./mvnw clean compile`/`mvn clean compile` (line 36), and `dotnet restore && dotnet build` (line 37) — all of which can execute arbitrary code via Gemfile hooks, Maven plugin goals, or NuGet package install/build scripts.
findings.impact: Any commit merged to `main` of RailsGoat or AspGoat is silently pulled and built the next time this image is rebuilt, with no diff review by this project's maintainers. Because the subsequent build steps execute arbitrary code from that fetched project (bundler/Maven/NuGet), an upstream compromise of either mutable branch is a direct code-execution vector on whichever host builds `Dockerfile.fixtures`.
findings.remediation: Pin `RAILS_GOAT_REF` and `ASP_GOAT_REF` to specific commit SHAs, matching the already-pinned `WEB_GOAT_REF` pattern, and bump them deliberately (per the documented monthly rebuild cadence in DEVELOPMENT.md). Prefer an OWASP-org-maintained AspGoat equivalent over a single-maintainer personal fork if one exists.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Every code-level assertion in this claim checks out against /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/Dockerfile.fixtures. Line 25 `ARG RAILS_GOAT_REF=main` and line 31 `ARG ASP_GOAT_REF=main` default to the mutable `main` branch, while line 28 `ARG WEB_GOAT_REF=v2023.8` is pinned to a tag -- the asymmetry the claim describes is exactly present. Line 32 clones `https://github.com/Soham7-dev/AspGoat.git`, a personal-namespace repository rather than an OWASP-org one (tests/fixtures/manifest.json:20 records the same source). The build then executes that fetched code's own tooling as root (line 6 `USER root`): line 35 `bundle install` (evaluates the upstream Gemfile/gemspec as Ruby and compiles native extensions -- ruby-dev and build-essential are installed at line 10), line 36 `./mvnw clean compile ... || mvn clean compile` (this is stronger than the claim states: `./mvnw` is a shell script checked into the cloned repo, executed directly, before any Maven plugin goals run), and line 37 `dotnet restore && dotnet build` (MSBuild targets and NuGet install/build scripts). So an upstream compromise of either mutable branch does yield code execution on the build host, and no maintainer diff review sits in that path. Two independent facts moderate the severity without falsifying the claim: this image is never built by CI (.github/workflows/docker-publish.yml builds only ./Dockerfile; no workflow references Dockerfile.fixtures), so the blast radius is a developer workstation that opted into `docker build -f Dockerfile.fixtures` per DEVELOPMENT.md:78; and the same file already accepts an equivalent-trust vector at line 16, `curl -sfL https://dot.net/v1/dotnet-install.sh | bash`, which pinning the git refs would not address. Confidence is LIKELY rather than CERTAIN only because one sub-assertion -- that Soham7-dev/AspGoat is single-maintainer -- is about an external repository's governance and cannot be verified from this checkout; the verifiable part is that the namespace is a personal account, not OWASP. Remediation note: `--branch` with `--depth 1` does not take a raw commit SHA, so SHA pinning requires switching to clone + `git fetch origin <sha>` + checkout.

findings.title: Model policy hardcoded and duplicated across dispatch and resolver
findings.description: Claude model assignments (scout=haiku, lens_sweep=haiku, panel_review=sonnet, advisor=opus) are hardcoded in dispatch.py EMIT_MODEL_POLICY dict. These are duplicated again in model_resolver.py _CLAUDE_FALLBACK dict. While model-profiles.yml provides an escape hatch, the hardcoded defaults are spread across multiple files, creating maintenance burden and confusion about the source of truth.
findings.impact: Model selection logic is duplicated across three locations (dispatch.py, model_resolver.py, model-profiles.yml). Changes to model assignments must be made in multiple places. The relationship between these sources is not clearly documented. Inconsistencies could arise if only some locations are updated.
findings.remediation: Consolidate model selection into a single source of truth, either: (1) Make model-profiles.yml the authoritative source and remove hardcoded fallbacks, or (2) Generate the Python fallbacks from the YAML at build time. Document which source takes precedence in the code.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The factual core of the claim is verified. The claude role->model mapping (scout=haiku, lens_sweep=haiku, panel_review=sonnet, advisor=opus) literally appears in three places: (1) /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/dispatch.py:87-88 `EMIT_MODEL_POLICY = {"claude": {"scout": "haiku", "lens_sweep": "haiku", "panel_review": "sonnet", "advisor": "opus"}}`, consumed at dispatch.py:123 when writing registered agent frontmatter; (2) /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/model_resolver.py:51-56 `_CLAUDE_FALLBACK`, consumed at model_resolver.py:70; (3) /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/reference/model-profiles.yml:19-27 (`hosts.claude`). All three currently agree, so there is no live inconsistency, but they can drift independently: model-profiles.yml is authoritative only for per-run dispatch-plan `model` fields (model_resolver.resolve_model precedence 1-4), while EMIT_MODEL_POLICY alone decides the `model:` line persisted into ~/.claude/agents/panopticon-*.md — and for a registered/enforced agent that persisted frontmatter is what the host actually applies. Editing the YAML claude block therefore silently fails to change registered agent models, which is exactly the drift risk the claim describes. Two sub-assertions are overstated and I am calling them out rather than letting them carry the verdict: (a) the separation is deliberate and partly documented — dispatch.py:85-86 states 'Emission is deterministic policy — ambient PANOPTICON_MODEL_* overrides apply to per-run dispatch plans, never to persisted registrations', and this is pinned by tests/test_dispatch.py:482-488 (`test_emission_ignores_ambient_model_env_overrides`); model_resolver.resolve_model's docstring (lines 98-103) documents the 4-level precedence explicitly; (b) the claim's own remediation option (1) 'remove hardcoded fallbacks' would break the documented graceful-degradation path when PyYAML is absent (model_resolver.py:17-21). So this is a real but maintainability-only duplication; MEDIUM severity looks high — the defensible fix is to have emit_host_agents read the profile's host defaults with overrides suppressed, keeping the hardcoded dict only as the no-PyYAML fallback. Confirmed as a duplication/maintainability finding, not as a functional bug.

findings.title: Panel names require manual synchronization in regex pattern
findings.description: Valid panels are defined in VALID_PANELS set at line 34, but the GROUP_RE regex at lines 455-457 hardcodes the list of panel names as an OR-pattern. When new panels are added (e.g., 'architecture' in version 3.0.0), both locations must be updated manually. There is no single source of truth.
findings.impact: Adding new panels requires code changes in two places: the VALID_PANELS set and the GROUP_RE regex. Failure to update both could cause parsing errors or findings to be silently dropped. The synchronization requirement is not documented.

references: DEVELOPMENT.md line 116 (Version 3.0.0 introduced architecture, database, redteam panels)

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The structural claim is factually correct. `VALID_PANELS` at skill/scripts/synthesize.py:34 enumerates {code, test, security, architecture, database, redteam}, and `GROUP_RE` at lines 455-457 re-enumerates the identical set inline as `(?:code|test|security|architecture|database|redteam)`. There is no derivation between them, and grep confirms GROUP_RE is defined exactly once with no generated pattern. The duplication is in fact broader than the claim states: PANEL_ORDER (synthesize.py:35), html_report._PANEL_ORDER (skill/scripts/html_report.py:197), and orchestrator.compute_group_panels (skill/scripts/orchestrator.py:99-116, which appends each of the six names by hand and is what feeds panel names into dispatch.build_plan's out_file templates at skill/scripts/dispatch.py:256,281) all restate the list. findings.title: Packaging version (3.0.0) is two major versions behind the runtime/doc version (4.2.0)
findings.description: pyproject.toml declares `version = "3.0.0"`, but `skill/SKILL.md`'s frontmatter declares `metadata.version: "4.2.0"` (line 14), DEVELOPMENT.md states "Current version: 4.2.0" (line 8) with a full History section through 4.2.0, and `skill/scripts/synthesize.py:682` independently hardcodes `"version": "4.2.0"` in the emitted report meta. CHANGELOG.md's newest entry is still `## 3.0.0 — Multi-model reviewer dispatch` (line 3) and never documents the 4.0.0 (epistemics core), 4.1.0 (Claude Code port), or 4.2.0 (tool-policy enforcement) releases that DEVELOPMENT.md's own History section describes in detail. DEVELOPMENT.md's "Versioning" section explicitly lists the files that must be bumped together (SKILL.md metadata.version, synthesize.build_report's meta.version, evidence.write_verify_queue's payload version) but never mentions pyproject.toml or CHANGELOG.md — the release process structurally omits two of the project's canonical version surfaces.
findings.impact: Anyone inspecting packaging metadata (`pip show panopticon`, a future PyPI listing, SBOM/dependency-scanner output) sees version 3.0.0 for code that is actually 4.2.0, which can mislead consumers about the feature set/security posture, break version-gated automation, and leaves CHANGELOG.md an inaccurate record for anyone auditing what changed since 3.0.0.
findings.remediation: Add pyproject.toml and CHANGELOG.md to the version-bump checklist in DEVELOPMENT.md's Versioning section; bump pyproject.toml's `version` to 4.2.0 now and backfill CHANGELOG.md entries for 4.0.0/4.1.0/4.2.0 (the content already exists in DEVELOPMENT.md's History section and can be ported over).

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Every discrete factual assertion in this claim checks out against the files. pyproject.toml:3 is `version = "3.0.0"`. skill/SKILL.md:14 is `version: "4.2.0"` under the `metadata:` key. DEVELOPMENT.md:8 is `**Current version: 4.2.0** (semver — see Versioning below).` and its History section (starting line 91) runs `**4.2.0** (current) — tool-policy enforcement`, then 4.1.0, 4.0.0, and 3.0.0 entries. skill/scripts/synthesize.py:682 independently hardcodes `"version": "4.2.0"` in build_report's meta. CHANGELOG.md:3 is `## 3.0.0 — Multi-model reviewer dispatch` and it is the newest entry — the only other heading is `## Earlier releases` at line 15 pointing back to DEVELOPMENT.md 'through 2.2.1', so 4.0.0/4.1.0/4.2.0 are genuinely undocumented in the changelog. Most load-bearing, DEVELOPMENT.md's Versioning section (lines 85-89) reads `Bump \`SKILL.md\` \`metadata.version\`, \`synthesize.build_report\`'s \`meta.version\`, and \`evidence.write_verify_queue\`'s payload \`version\` together.` — exactly three surfaces, with no mention of pyproject.toml or CHANGELOG.md. The claim's structural point (the documented release checklist omits two canonical version surfaces) is therefore correct, and it is the strongest of the three claims in this batch because it identifies the process cause rather than only the symptom. I also found a fourth omitted surface the claim missed: skill/scripts/citations.py:153 hardcodes `"User-Agent": "panopticon/3.0.0"`, also absent from the checklist and also stale. Two accuracy notes for the auditor. The title says 'two major versions behind'; 3.0.0 to 4.2.0 is one major version (plus two minors), so the title overstates the gap. And the impact is currently hypothetical rather than live: pyproject.toml has no [build-system] table and I found no packaging/publish workflow or `pip install panopticon` instruction anywhere in the repo, so `pip show panopticon` / a PyPI listing / SBOM output are not paths that exist today (the claim does hedge with 'a future PyPI listing'). findings.title: Project version out of sync with implementation
findings.description: pyproject.toml declares version "3.0.0" but the actual current version is "4.2.0" as specified in skill/SKILL.md, skill/scripts/evidence.py, skill/scripts/synthesize.py, and all test expectations. This mismatch causes version strings in reports and HTTP headers (User-Agent) to be inconsistent.
findings.impact: Version mismatch can cause confusion in reporting, CI/CD pipelines may fail version checks, and downstream tools consuming the version string will receive incorrect information.
findings.remediation: Update pyproject.toml line 3 to `version = "4.2.0"` to match the versions declared in skill/SKILL.md (line 14), skill/scripts/evidence.py (line 126), and skill/scripts/synthesize.py (line 682).

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The core factual assertion is verifiable and true. /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/pyproject.toml line 3 is exactly `version = "3.0.0"`, while skill/SKILL.md line 14 is `  version: "4.2.0"` under `metadata:`, skill/scripts/synthesize.py line 682 hardcodes `"version": "4.2.0"` inside build_report's returned `meta` dict, skill/scripts/evidence.py line 126 hardcodes `"version": "4.2.0"` in write_verify_queue's payload, and DEVELOPMENT.md line 8 says `**Current version: 4.2.0**`. So the version drift is real, and every line reference in the claim resolves exactly as stated. Two corrections that the auditor should carry forward. (1) The stated causal mechanism is wrong: pyproject.toml's version is never read at runtime. I grepped the whole repo for importlib.metadata / pkg_resources / __version__ and found no consumer; the report version comes from synthesize.py's own literal and the EPSS User-Agent comes from a third independent literal at skill/scripts/citations.py:153 (`req = urllib.request.Request(url, headers={"User-Agent": "panopticon/3.0.0"})`). So pyproject.toml does not 'cause' the report/User-Agent strings to be inconsistent; there are simply four unsynchronized literals. The end state the claim describes (inconsistent version surfaces, User-Agent among them) is nevertheless accurate. (2) 'all test expectations' say 4.2.0 is not quite right: tests/test_synthesize.py:1194,1479, tests/test_schema.py:170 and tests/test_verify_queue.py:115 assert 4.2.0, but tests/test_citations.py:167 asserts `"panopticon/3.0.0"` and tests/test_html_report.py:38 uses `"version": "3.0.0"` as fixture data — a remediator bumping the User-Agent must update test_citations.py:167 or CI will fail. Severity HIGH is not supported by anything I could verify: pyproject.toml has no [build-system] table, no packaging/publish workflow exists (.github/workflows/ci.yml and security.yml only set python-version for the runner), and no CI step reads the project version, so nothing can currently 'fail version checks'. This is documentation/release-hygiene drift, i.e. LOW. Confirmed on the facts, with the mechanism and severity overstated.

findings.remediation: Bump `[project].version` in pyproject.toml to match `skill/SKILL.md`'s `metadata.version` (4.2.0) as part of the release process, and add a checklist note (in DEVELOPMENT.md's Versioning section) that pyproject.toml is one of the files to bump together with SKILL.md/synthesize.py/evidence.py.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Verified independently of the other two claims in this batch. pyproject.toml:3 is `version = "3.0.0"`; DEVELOPMENT.md:8 is `**Current version: 4.2.0** (semver — see Versioning below).`; skill/SKILL.md frontmatter carries `metadata:` / `  version: "4.2.0"` at line 14. The claim's appeal to prior-art also checks out: docs/superpowers/2026-08-04-self-scan-report.json lines 953-956 contain a finding titled 'Hardcoded User-Agent version string is stale relative to the project's actual current version' whose description explicitly states "pyproject.toml's `[project].version` is also `3.0.0`, so this literal was likely copied from there and never updated as the two drifted" — so this is indeed a previously-known, still-unfixed inconsistency. I confirmed the underlying literal still exists at skill/scripts/citations.py:153. Corrections. First, 'two major versions behind' is wrong: 3.0.0 to 4.2.0 is one major version behind. Second, the impact ('pip, dependency scanners, badges, release tooling see an incorrect version') is not currently realizable: pyproject.toml contains only [project], [project.urls] and [tool.ruff] tables — there is no [build-system], no packages/setuptools configuration, no publish workflow, and no `pip install panopticon` instruction anywhere in the repo, so nothing installs or resolves this package today. findings.title: CODEOWNERS assigns owners to /scripts/ and /reference/ paths that don't exist; rules are permanently dead
findings.description: CODEOWNERS line 7 (`/scripts/run_tools.py`), line 8 (`/scripts/tools/`), and line 11 (`/reference/`) target paths that do not exist at the repo root. The actual locations, confirmed against the on-disk tree and README's repository-layout table, are `skill/scripts/run_tools.py`, `skill/scripts/tools/`, and `skill/reference/`. GitHub's CODEOWNERS matching is path-relative to the repo root, so these three rules never match any real file and are silently inert (only `/.github/` and `/Dockerfile`, lines 5-6, are correctly scoped).
findings.impact: The intended granular review-ownership for CI/security tooling scripts (scanner adapters under `skill/scripts/tools/`) and reference data (`skill/reference/security-checklists.md`, `cwe-catalog.json`, `report-schema.json`) is not enforced. Currently masked because the sole global owner (`* @psyberone`) happens to be the same person as the specific rules, but the moment a second maintainer/team is added expecting these paths to route review to a specific owner, changes to the actual scanner-adapter or schema files will receive no targeted review requirement.
findings.remediation: Fix the paths to `/skill/scripts/run_tools.py`, `/skill/scripts/tools/`, and `/skill/reference/` (add a leading `/skill` segment), and add a regression check (e.g., a test asserting every CODEOWNERS path glob matches at least one tracked file).

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Verified line by line against /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/CODEOWNERS. Line 7 is `/scripts/run_tools.py @psyberone`, line 8 is `/scripts/tools/ @psyberone`, line 11 is `/reference/ @psyberone`. None of these root-anchored paths exist: glob `scripts/*` yields only `scripts/file_issues.py`, and globs `reference*` / `reference/**` yield nothing. The actual locations are `skill/scripts/run_tools.py`, `skill/scripts/tools/` (base.py plus 12 scanner adapters and sarif_utils.py), and `skill/reference/` (report-schema.json, scope-profile-schema.json, cwe-catalog.json, security-checklists.md, model-profiles.yml, code-review-groups.example.yml) — exactly the three files/dirs the claim names. README.md lines 76-83 ('Repository layout') and DEVELOPMENT.md lines 21-43 and 68-69 both document the `skill/`-rooted layout, corroborating the claim's cross-references. No .gitmodules exists, so `skill/` is an ordinary directory in this repo and its contents are repo-root-relative paths under `skill/...`; CODEOWNERS globs anchored with a leading `/` therefore cannot match them. The claim's parenthetical that only lines 5-6 are correctly scoped is also accurate: `/.github/` and `/Dockerfile` both exist at the root. The masking argument is correct as stated — line 2's `* @psyberone` already assigns the same sole owner to every path, so effective ownership is unchanged today and the defect only bites when a second maintainer/team is added; the claim states this honestly rather than overselling present-day impact, which is why MEDIUM is defensible-but-generous (this is latent dead config, arguably LOW). I also verified the remediation's premise that no regression check exists: grep for CODEOWNERS across the tree finds no test or script that validates the patterns (the only test hit, tests/test_orchestrator.py:421-428, is an unrelated tempdir fixture asserting dotfile-scan exclusion, and grep under skill/ returns nothing). Supporting context for why the paths went stale: CHANGELOG.md 3.0.0 lines 6-13 still describes the pre-move layout (`scripts/model_resolver.py`, `scripts/dispatch.py`, `agents/`) and records CODEOWNERS being added in that same release — i.e., the file was written for the old root layout and never updated after the move into skill/. CWE-1059 is a poor category fit (it is about insufficient technical documentation, not dead config) and is absent from the repo's bundled skill/reference/cwe-catalog.json, so I could not verify it from context; that does not change the verdict.

findings.title: CONTRIBUTING.md's test/lint instructions omit dependency installation and diverge from CI
findings.description: CONTRIBUTING.md step 5 (lines 11-15) tells contributors to run `python -m pytest tests/ -q` and `python -m ruff check skill/scripts/ tests/` with no preceding install step. CI's test job (`.github/workflows/ci.yml` lines 36-39) installs `pytest ruff pyyaml jsonschema` and the lint job (lines 18-21) installs `ruff` before running the equivalent commands. pyproject.toml declares no `[project.optional-dependencies]`/dev extra, so a contributor following CONTRIBUTING.md verbatim on a clean environment has no documented way to get pytest/ruff/pyyaml/jsonschema installed.
findings.impact: Onboarding friction — a contributor following the documented workflow hits `ModuleNotFoundError` for pytest/ruff, or gets a local test run that silently differs from CI (e.g., yaml/jsonschema-gated code paths behaving differently) without realizing the local run isn't equivalent to what CI actually exercises.
findings.remediation: Add an explicit `pip install pytest ruff pyyaml jsonschema` step to CONTRIBUTING.md before step 5, or define a `dev`/`test` extra in pyproject.toml (`pip install -e .[dev]`) and reference that same extra from both CONTRIBUTING.md and ci.yml so the two can't drift.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Every element of the claim checks out. CONTRIBUTING.md lines 11-15 read: '5. Run the full test suite and lint locally:' then a bash block with `python -m pytest tests/ -q` and `python -m ruff check skill/scripts/ tests/`. Steps 1-4 above it contain no install/setup step, and the rest of the file (34 lines total, read in full) never mentions installing anything. .github/workflows/ci.yml lint job lines 18-21 run `pip install ruff`; test job lines 36-39 run `pip install pytest ruff pyyaml jsonschema` before the identical commands, so CI does provision what CONTRIBUTING.md assumes. pyproject.toml (28 lines, read in full) has no `[project.optional-dependencies]`, no `dependencies`, and no dev/test extra — only metadata plus `[tool.ruff]`. Glob for requirements*.txt / Makefile / tox.ini / setup.py / setup.cfg / noxfile.py / .pre-commit-config.yaml at the repo root returned only tests/fixtures/vulnerable-python/requirements.txt (an intentionally vulnerable fixture, not a dev manifest). README.md's 'Installation' section (line 15 onward) covers symlinking `skill/` into an agent's skills dir, not dev dependencies. The concrete consequence is verifiable: tests/test_schemas.py line 7 does `from jsonschema import validate` at module scope, so a jsonschema-less environment produces a pytest collection error rather than a clean run; and skill/scripts/model_resolver.py has a yaml-gated path that tests/test_model_resolver.py lines 51-82 explicitly exercise both with and without yaml (`test_missing_yaml_warns_and_falls_back`, `test_claude_fallback_matches_policy_without_yaml`), which is exactly the 'local run silently differs from CI' scenario the claim describes. findings.title: ci.yml is the only workflow with no explicit least-privilege `permissions:` block
findings.description: `.github/workflows/codeql.yml` (lines 15-18), `.github/workflows/docker-publish.yml` (lines 22-26), and `.github/workflows/security.yml` (lines 15-18) each declare an explicit `permissions:` block scoped to what the job needs. `.github/workflows/ci.yml` (lint + test jobs) declares no `permissions:` key at all, so both jobs run under the repository's default `GITHUB_TOKEN` permissions, which is a repo/org-level setting and can be broader than either job requires — both jobs only checkout code and run pip-installed ruff/pytest.
findings.impact: If the repo or org default token permissions are ever set to read/write (still GitHub's classic default for many repos), a compromised transitive dependency pulled in by `pip install ruff` / `pip install pytest ruff pyyaml jsonschema` during this workflow, or any other code executing in that job context, would run with a wider blast radius (e.g. push/tag ability) than necessary — inconsistent with the least-privilege posture already established in the other three workflows in this same directory.
findings.remediation: Add `permissions: contents: read` at the top of ci.yml (or per-job), matching the pattern already used in codeql.yml, security.yml, and docker-publish.yml.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Verified directly against all four workflow files in the repo. `.github/workflows/ci.yml` is 42 lines and contains no `permissions:` key at any level (no workflow-level block, none on the `lint` job at lines 10-23, none on the `test` job at lines 25-41). The three sibling workflows do declare explicit blocks exactly where the claim says: codeql.yml lines 15-18 (`actions: read`, `contents: read`, `security-events: write`), security.yml lines 15-18 (`contents: read`, `packages: read`, `security-events: write`), docker-publish.yml lines 22-26 (`contents: read`, `packages: write`, `attestations: write`, `id-token: write`). A repo-wide grep for `permissions:` returns hits only in those three files, so ci.yml is indeed the sole outlier. Both ci.yml jobs only checkout, set up Python, `pip install ruff` / `pip install pytest ruff pyyaml jsonschema`, and run ruff/pytest — no token-consuming step, so `contents: read` would suffice. Two qualifications on the impact framing: (1) the actual blast radius depends on the repository/organization 'Workflow permissions' default setting, which is not stored in the repo and cannot be read from here — if that default is already 'read-only' the practical exposure today is nil, and this is purely a defense-in-depth/consistency gap that survives any future org setting change; (2) the fix is trivial and matches an already-established in-repo pattern. The claim itself states the conditional ('can be broader than either job requires'), so it is not overstated. MEDIUM is on the generous side for what is a hardening gap rather than an exploitable defect; LOW would be defensible. CWE-276 (Incorrect Default Permissions) is an apt mapping for an omitted explicit permission scope falling back to a platform default.

findings.title: GitHub Actions step uses a mutable tag or branch reference. Tags and branch names can be silently repointed by the action owner, enabling supply-chain attacks — as seen in the trivy-action and kics-github-action compromises. Pin the reference to a full 40-character commit SHA instead, e.g. `uses: actions/checkout@8ade135a41bc03ea155e62e844d188df1ea18608`.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: yaml.github-actions.security.github-actions-mutable-action-tag.github-actions-mutable-action-tag

findings.impact: Tags are mutable refs; if any referenced action's repo/account is compromised and the tag re-pointed to malicious code, it executes with the workflow's permissions on the next run — including runs with `packages: write` + `id-token: write` (docker-publish.yml) or `security-events: write` (codeql.yml, security.yml). `.github/dependabot.yml` already tracks the `github-actions` ecosystem weekly, which would keep SHA pins current via automated PRs if pins were adopted.
findings.remediation: Pin every action reference to a full commit SHA with a trailing version comment (e.g. `actions/checkout@<sha> # v4.x.x`), per OpenSSF Scorecard's Pinned-Dependencies guidance; Dependabot will then propose SHA bumps automatically.

findings.title: docker-publish.yml's trigger `paths:` filter doesn't cover everything the Dockerfile COPYs into the published image
findings.description: `Dockerfile:53` does `COPY skill/scripts /opt/panopticon/scripts` — the entire `skill/scripts/` tree, including `synthesize.py`, `dispatch.py`, `citations.py`, `evidence.py`, `provenance.py`, `orchestrator.py`, `model_resolver.py`, `html_report.py`, and `depth_planner.py`. `docker-publish.yml`'s `paths:` filter (lines 6-12) only watches the workflow file, `Dockerfile`, `skill/scripts/tools/**`, `skill/scripts/_run_adapter.py`, `skill/scripts/ingest_tools.py`, and `skill/scripts/run_tools.py`.
findings.impact: A change to any unwatched file under `skill/scripts/` (e.g. a fix in `citations.py` or `synthesize.py`) gets baked into the next locally-built image but does NOT trigger a rebuild/republish of `ghcr.io/<repo>-tools`, so the published image silently drifts from what a fresh local `docker build` produces. `security.yml`'s `docker pull ${{ env.IMAGE }}` step (pulling `:latest`) will keep using the stale published copy until an unrelated watched-path change happens to trigger a republish, weakening the CI security gate's grounding.
findings.remediation: Widen the `paths:` filter to `skill/scripts/**` to match the Dockerfile's actual COPY scope, or narrow the Dockerfile's COPY to only the subset genuinely needed by the containerized adapters and keep the filter in lockstep with that subset.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning:
The literal mismatch is real and verified. `Dockerfile:53` is `COPY skill/scripts /opt/panopticon/scripts` (whole tree) with `ENV PYTHONPATH=/opt/panopticon` on line 54. `docker-publish.yml` lines 6-12 filter on only: the workflow file, `Dockerfile`, `skill/scripts/tools/**`, `skill/scripts/_run_adapter.py`, `skill/scripts/ingest_tools.py`, `skill/scripts/run_tools.py`. A glob of `skill/scripts/*.py` shows nine additional modules that are COPYed but unwatched: citations.py, depth_planner.py, orchestrator.py, provenance.py, model_resolver.py, run_fixture_tests.py, dispatch.py, evidence.py, html_report.py, synthesize.py. So edits to those do change what a fresh `docker build` produces without triggering a republish — the filter/COPY-scope divergence the claim describes exists.

HOWEVER, the claimed IMPACT is contradicted by the code and the severity should be downgraded to LOW/INFO. Two independent facts neutralize the runtime consequence: (1) `skill/scripts/run_tools.py` lines 159-167 bind-mount the checkout's own scripts directory over the image's copy on every adapter invocation — `docker.extend(["-v", "%s:/src:ro" % os.path.abspath(target), "-v", "%s:/opt/panopticon/scripts:ro" % scripts_dir, image, "python3", "/opt/panopticon/scripts/_run_adapter.py", tool])` where `scripts_dir = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))`. The in-image copy is shadowed at runtime, deliberately: `docs/superpowers/2026-08-03-calibration-fixmes.md:37-40` records this exact drift as a fixed defect ('Adapter code skew: containers ran image-baked code'). (2) `security.yml:51` runs `python skill/scripts/run_tools.py ...` and lines 55-71 import `scripts.ingest_tools` from the checked-out `skill/` tree, not from the image — so the CI gate's Python logic is always the PR's code. The only other container entrypoint is the legacy `TOOL_CMD` path (run_tools.py:130-131), which invokes tool binaries directly (`skill/scripts/tools/legacy_sarif.py:17-24`: semgrep/gitleaks/trivy/bandit/gosec) and touches no panopticon script. Net: the unwatched baked-in files are never executed in CI or in normal local runs; the drift is inert. Residual real risk is limited to someone running the published image manually without the bind mount, plus the general hygiene problem that image contents no longer correspond to any single commit. Confirming the defect, rejecting the stated 'weakens the CI security gate's grounding' rationale.

findings.title: Dockerfile pipes remote installer scripts to a shell without checksum/signature verification
findings.description: `Dockerfile:82` (`curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh -s -- -y --default-toolchain stable`) and `Dockerfile:86` (`curl -sfL https://dot.net/v1/dotnet-install.sh | bash -s -- --channel 8.0 --install-dir /usr/share/dotnet`) fetch and immediately execute remote shell scripts during the image build with no hash pin or signature check; `Dockerfile.fixtures:16` repeats the dotnet-install.sh pattern. Separately, the FindSecBugs plugin jar (`Dockerfile:67-69`, fetched via `search.maven.org/remotecontent?filepath=...`) is downloaded and later loaded onto SpotBugs's classpath with no checksum verification either.
findings.impact: If `sh.rustup.rs`, `dot.net`, or the Maven Central redirect endpoint were ever compromised (TLS pinning on the rustup fetch mitigates transport-level MITM but not an origin-side compromise), arbitrary code executes as root during the `panopticon-tools`/`panopticon-fixtures` image build; that image is subsequently published to `ghcr.io` and pulled by `security.yml` and any downstream consumer of the scanner image.
findings.remediation: Verify rustup/dotnet-install against a published checksum or switch to signed vendor packages where available (as already done for `trivy` via its apt repo); verify the FindSecBugs jar against the SHA published for that artifact/version on Maven Central, and prefer the direct `repo1.maven.org/maven2/...` path over the `search.maven.org/remotecontent` redirect endpoint.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Every cited line is verbatim accurate. Dockerfile:82 is `RUN curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh -s -- -y --default-toolchain stable` and Dockerfile:86 is `RUN curl -sfL https://dot.net/v1/dotnet-install.sh | bash -s -- --channel 8.0 --install-dir /usr/share/dotnet`; both pipe a remotely fetched script straight into a shell with no hash pin, signature check, or `--verify` step. Dockerfile.fixtures:16 repeats the identical dotnet-install.sh pattern (`curl -sfL https://dot.net/v1/dotnet-install.sh | bash -s -- --channel 8.0`). The FindSecBugs jar is fetched at Dockerfile:67-69 via `https://search.maven.org/remotecontent?filepath=com/h3xstream/findsecbugs/findsecbugs-plugin/${FINDSECBUGS_VERSION}/findsecbugs-plugin-${FINDSECBUGS_VERSION}.jar` into /opt/spotbugs/plugin/ with no checksum; SpotBugs loads plugins from that directory. The privilege claim holds: `USER scanner` first appears at Dockerfile:110, so lines 62-101 all execute as root. The exposure chain also holds: .github/workflows/docker-publish.yml pushes this image to `ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}-tools` on every push to main touching Dockerfile, and .github/workflows/security.yml:41-42 pulls `ghcr.io/...-tools:latest` and tags it `panopticon-tools`, which skill/scripts/run_tools.py then executes (run_tools.py:36,115 default image="panopticon-tools"). Two fairness notes that do not change the verdict: (a) docker-publish.yml does generate a build-provenance attestation (attest-build-provenance@v1), but that attests who built the image, not the integrity of the third-party inputs, so it is not a mitigation for CWE-494; (b) the same missing-integrity pattern extends beyond the four sites named — osv-scanner (Dockerfile:30), gitleaks (37), gosec (48), spotbugs tarball (62) and the dependency-check zip (73) are also fetched without checksums, so the claim if anything understates scope. Only trivy (41-43) uses a signed apt repo, exactly as the remediation notes. No pin/constraints file exists anywhere in the repo that would supply the missing verification.

findings.title: Unverified curl-pipe-to-shell installers execute remote code during panopticon-tools image build
findings.description: Dockerfile:82 pipes `curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs` directly into `sh` to install Rust, and Dockerfile:86 pipes `curl -sfL https://dot.net/v1/dotnet-install.sh` directly into `bash` to install the .NET SDK. TLS only authenticates the transport, not the content: neither invocation pins the installer script to a known-good commit/version or verifies a checksum/signature before executing it, so the build unconditionally trusts whatever the remote endpoint (or its CDN) returns at build time.
findings.impact: A compromise of either upstream distribution channel (maintainer account takeover, CDN/object-storage compromise, or a malicious release) lets an attacker execute arbitrary code with root privileges during every `docker build -t panopticon-tools .`. Because this image is subsequently published to `ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}-tools` by `.github/workflows/docker-publish.yml` and mounted read-only against arbitrary source trees by consumers (`docker run --rm -v "$PWD":/src:ro panopticon-tools ...`, Dockerfile:3), a single upstream compromise becomes a supply-chain backdoor that reaches every downstream repository the tool ever scans.
findings.remediation: Pin installer scripts to a specific release and verify a published checksum/signature before executing (e.g. download to a file, verify SHA256/GPG against a pinned known-good value, then `sh`/`bash` the local, verified copy instead of streaming curl output directly into the interpreter). rustup and the dotnet-install script both support offline/pinned installation flows that avoid the curl-pipe pattern.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Every factual element of the claim checks out against the code, at the exact cited lines. (1) Dockerfile:82 is verbatim `RUN curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh -s -- -y --default-toolchain stable` and Dockerfile:86 is verbatim `RUN curl -sfL https://dot.net/v1/dotnet-install.sh | bash -s -- --channel 8.0 --install-dir /usr/share/dotnet`. Both stream a remote script straight into an interpreter with no intermediate file, no checksum, and no signature check. (2) Neither is pinned: `sh.rustup.rs` is a mutable endpoint and both `--default-toolchain stable` and `--channel 8.0` are floating channels, so the content executed varies per build. (3) A repo-wide grep for `sha256|checksum|gpg --verify` across Dockerfiles returns nothing — the only gpg use is Dockerfile:41 `gpg --dearmor`, which is keyring format conversion for the trivy apt repo, not verification of these installers. Notably the trivy step is the one place the Dockerfile does establish signature-verified installation, which makes the absence at 82/86 a genuine inconsistency rather than a uniform project stance. (4) Root privilege at build time is confirmed: the `USER scanner` directive does not appear until Dockerfile:110, so lines 82 and 86 execute as root. (5) The distribution path the impact statement depends on is real and I traced it end to end: .github/workflows/docker-publish.yml:17,51-60 builds this Dockerfile and pushes to `ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}-tools` tagged `latest`; .github/workflows/security.yml:11,39-46 pulls `ghcr.io/<repo>-tools:latest` (mutable tag, no digest pin) and falls back to `docker build -t panopticon-tools .`; skill/scripts/run_tools.py:130-131 and :164-167 then invoke `docker run --rm -v <target>:/src:ro panopticon-tools ...`. So a build-time compromise does propagate to consumers. Two calibration notes for the auditor, neither of which defeats the finding. First, the runtime blast radius is narrower than 'reaches every downstream repository' implies: the container drops to uid 1000 (`USER scanner`, Dockerfile:110) and both mounts are `:ro`, so a backdoored tool cannot write to a consumer's source tree. It can still read and exfiltrate the full checkout (no `--network none` on the docker run), can read `NVD_API_KEY` when that env var is forwarded at run_tools.py:157-158, and controls the JSON/SARIF the host subsequently parses — so CVSS C:H is well supported while I:H rests on integrity of the image rather than of the scanned repo. Second, this is a latent trust-boundary weakness conditioned on a third-party compromise, not an independently reachable bug in this repo's own logic, which is exactly what CVSS AC:H already encodes; HIGH is defensible given the artifact is a security scanner redistributed to other repos, though a MEDIUM rating would also be reasonable. Scope gap worth recording: the identical unpinned dotnet-install curl-pipe also exists at Dockerfile.fixtures:16, and the sibling downloads at Dockerfile:30, 37, 48, 62, 68 and 73 are version-pinned but still have no checksum verification — same CWE-494 class, so the remediation should cover them rather than only lines 82 and 86. The cited CWEs (494 primary, 829 secondary) and OWASP A08:2021 are all apt. No CVE is asserted by the claim and none is verifiable from the repository, so I cite none.

findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker compromises the release/CDN infrastructure behind sh.rustup.rs or dot.net's install-script host. The next scheduled or manual `docker build`/CI run of `docker-publish.yml` fetches and executes the attacker's payload as root, planting a backdoor (e.g. a modified `semgrep`/`bandit` wrapper) in the image before it is published to GHCR. Every subsequent `docker run ... -v $PWD:/src:ro panopticon-tools` invocation by any consumer then executes the backdoored tool against that consumer's own source tree.

(1) Dockerfile:82 is verbatim `RUN curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh -s -- -y --default-toolchain stable` and Dockerfile:86 is verbatim `RUN curl -sfL https://dot.net/v1/dotnet-install.sh | bash -s -- --channel 8.0 --install-dir /usr/share/dotnet`. Both stream a remote script straight into an interpreter with no intermediate file, no checksum, and no signature check. (2) Neither is pinned: `sh.rustup.rs` is a mutable endpoint and both `--default-toolchain stable` and `--channel 8.0` are floating channels, so the content executed varies per build. (3) A repo-wide grep for `sha256|checksum|gpg --verify` across Dockerfiles returns nothing — the only gpg use is Dockerfile:41 `gpg --dearmor`, which is keyring format conversion for the trivy apt repo, not verification of these installers. Notably the trivy step is the one place the Dockerfile does establish signature-verified installation, which makes the absence at 82/86 a genuine inconsistency rather than a uniform project stance. (4) Root privilege at build time is confirmed: the `USER scanner` directive does not appear until Dockerfile:110, so lines 82 and 86 execute as root. (5) The distribution path the impact statement depends on is real and I traced it end to end: .github/workflows/docker-publish.yml:17,51-60 builds this Dockerfile and pushes to `ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}-tools` tagged `latest`; .github/workflows/security.yml:11,39-46 pulls `ghcr.io/<repo>-tools:latest` (mutable tag, no digest pin) and falls back to `docker build -t panopticon-tools .`; skill/scripts/run_tools.py:130-131 and :164-167 then invoke `docker run --rm -v <target>:/src:ro panopticon-tools ...`. So a build-time compromise does propagate to consumers. Two calibration notes for the auditor, neither of which defeats the finding. First, the runtime blast radius is narrower than 'reaches every downstream repository' implies: the container drops to uid 1000 (`USER scanner`, Dockerfile:110) and both mounts are `:ro`, so a backdoored tool cannot write to a consumer's source tree. It can still read and exfiltrate the full checkout (no `--network none` on the docker run), can read `NVD_API_KEY` when that env var is forwarded at run_tools.py:157-158, and controls the JSON/SARIF the host subsequently parses — so CVSS C:H is well supported while I:H rests on integrity of the image rather than of the scanned repo. Second, this is a latent trust-boundary weakness conditioned on a third-party compromise, not an independently reachable bug in this repo's own logic, which is exactly what CVSS AC:H already encodes; HIGH is defensible given the artifact is a security scanner redistributed to other repos, though a MEDIUM rating would also be reasonable. Scope gap worth recording: the identical unpinned dotnet-install curl-pipe also exists at Dockerfile.fixtures:16, and the sibling downloads at Dockerfile:30, 37, 48, 62, 68 and 73 are version-pinned but still have no checksum verification — same CWE-494 class, so the remediation should cover them rather than only lines 82 and 86. The cited CWEs (494 primary, 829 secondary) and OWASP A08:2021 are all apt. No CVE is asserted by the claim and none is verifiable from the repository, so I cite none.

findings.title: Most Dockerfile tool installs are unpinned, contradicting the documented monthly-rebuild reproducibility model
findings.description: DEVELOPMENT.md states the `panopticon-tools` image should be rebuilt on a "monthly cadence... so the scanner BINARIES and their rule/advisory databases age with the image," implying each build is a deliberate, versioned snapshot. However `pip install --no-cache-dir semgrep bandit bandit-sarif-formatter` (Dockerfile:14), `gem install --no-document brakeman bundler-audit` (line 17), `npm install -g eslint eslint-plugin-security @microsoft/eslint-formatter-sarif` (line 21), `pip install --no-cache-dir pip-audit` (line 24), `cargo install cargo-audit` (line 83, unpinned), and the `.NET SDK --channel 8.0` install (line 86, a floating channel not a fixed SDK version) all resolve to whatever is latest-on-registry at build time. This is inconsistent with `GITLEAKS_VERSION`, `GOSEC_VERSION`, `OSV_SCANNER_VERSION`, `SPOTBUGS_VERSION`, `FINDSECBUGS_VERSION`, and `DEPENDENCY_CHECK_VERSION`, all pinned via `ARG` in the same file — and with `Dockerfile.fixtures:20`'s `cargo install cargo-audit --version 0.22.2`, which pins the identical tool correctly.
findings.impact: Two builds of the same Dockerfile on different days can produce materially different scanner behavior (new/changed rules, different false-positive rates, or a compromised upstream release of e.g. `semgrep`/`eslint-plugin-security`) with no diff in this repo to explain why — undermining reproducibility and the ability to bisect a scan-result regression to a specific tool version.
findings.remediation: Pin the remaining tools the same way the others already are (`pip install semgrep==X bandit==Y`, `gem install brakeman -v X bundler-audit -v Y`, `npm install -g eslint@X eslint-plugin-security@Y`, `cargo install cargo-audit --version X`), and pin the .NET SDK to a specific version instead of a floating channel.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The factual core is fully verified. Unpinned installs: Dockerfile:14 `pip install --no-cache-dir semgrep bandit bandit-sarif-formatter`, :17 `gem install --no-document brakeman bundler-audit`, :21 `npm install -g eslint eslint-plugin-security @microsoft/eslint-formatter-sarif`, :24 `pip install --no-cache-dir pip-audit`, :83 `cargo install cargo-audit`, and :86 `dotnet-install.sh --channel 8.0` (a floating channel that resolves to the newest 8.0 SDK, not a fixed SDK version). Pinned in the same file: GITLEAKS_VERSION=8.18.4 (:6), GOSEC_VERSION=2.20.0 (:7), OSV_SCANNER_VERSION=1.8.2 (:27), SPOTBUGS_VERSION=4.8.6 (:61), FINDSECBUGS_VERSION=1.13.0 (:66), DEPENDENCY_CHECK_VERSION=10.0.3 (:72) — so the internal inconsistency is exactly as described, and Dockerfile.fixtures:20 does pin the identical cargo-audit tool (`--version 0.22.2`). I searched for any external pin source (requirements/constraints/lockfile) that would rescue these installs; the only requirements.txt in the repo is tests/fixtures/vulnerable-python/requirements.txt, a deliberately vulnerable fixture, so no such pinning exists. DEVELOPMENT.md:83 does contain the quoted cadence sentence for the panopticon-tools image. I mark confidence LIKELY rather than CERTAIN only because the doc's wording ('the scanner BINARIES and their rule/advisory databases age with the image') is a statement about staleness, not an explicit reproducibility guarantee — the claim's framing of it as a 'documented reproducibility model' is an interpretation. That interpretation is reasonable (the adjacent DEVELOPMENT.md:81 dated-snapshot tagging convention supports it) and, more importantly, the defect stands on its own without the doc: half the file pins and half does not, so two builds a month apart can carry materially different scanner rule sets with no repo diff. Two corroborating details: .github/workflows/docker-publish.yml uses `cache-from/cache-to: type=gha, mode=max`, so whether an unpinned layer refreshes depends on cache state rather than on any deliberate decision, which makes drift nondeterministic rather than merely periodic; and docs/superpowers/2026-08-03-calibration-fixmes.md:98-101 (F-CAL-7) shows the team previously addressed the tools-image aging problem with documentation only, never with pins.

findings.title: DEVELOPMENT.md's Architecture section under-describes the Dockerfile's actual tool set
findings.description: DEVELOPMENT.md lines 38-39 describe the Dockerfile as bundling "semgrep, gitleaks, trivy, bandit, brakeman, gosec, eslint" — the original tool set. The Dockerfile has since grown to also include `pip-audit`, `osv-scanner`, `bundler-audit`, `spotbugs`+`findsecbugs`, OWASP `dependency-check`, `cargo-audit`, and a Roslyn `SecurityCodeScan` analyzer for C#/.NET (confirmed against both the Dockerfile itself and the adapter registry under `skill/scripts/tools/`), none of which are mentioned in this summary line.
findings.impact: DEVELOPMENT.md is the repo's stated "durable design record" meant to give future work context without the original spec/plan docs; a reader relying on this line to scope the tool container's coverage will under-estimate it — Java, .NET, Rust, and Ruby dependency auditing are all silently missing from the description.
findings.remediation: Update the Dockerfile bullet in DEVELOPMENT.md's Architecture section to list the current full tool set, or replace the enumerated list with a pointer to `skill/scripts/tools/__init__.py`'s `ADAPTERS` registry as the single source of truth to avoid future drift.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Verified directly. /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/DEVELOPMENT.md lines 38-39 read: '`Dockerfile` — `panopticon-tools` image: semgrep, gitleaks, trivy, bandit, brakeman, gosec, eslint. Build once: `docker build -t panopticon-tools <this dir>`.' The actual Dockerfile installs substantially more than those seven: bundler-audit (line 17, `gem install --no-document brakeman bundler-audit`), pip-audit (line 24), osv-scanner v1.8.2 (lines 27-32), SpotBugs 4.8.6 + findsecbugs-plugin 1.13.0 (lines 61-69), OWASP dependency-check 10.0.3 (lines 72-76), Rust toolchain + cargo-audit (lines 78-83), the .NET 8 SDK (lines 85-89), and a SecurityCodeScan Roslyn analyzer injected via /Directory.Build.props (lines 93-101). The adapter registry in skill/scripts/tools/__init__.py corroborates this: ADAPTERS contains pip-audit, npm-audit, osv-scanner, eslint-security, brakeman, bundler-audit, spotbugs, dependency-check, cargo-audit, and roslyn-secguard in addition to the six LegacySarifAdapter entries. So the doc line under-describes the image by roughly seven tools, and the claim's specific enumeration is accurate (it even omits npm-audit, which is also registered — further support, not a contradiction). DEVELOPMENT.md self-describes at lines 4-6 as 'the durable design record that travels with the skill ... so future work has context', so the drift matters for the stated purpose. The Java/.NET/Rust/Ruby dependency-audit coverage really is invisible from this line. Severity LOW and category (documentation/architecture drift, CWE-1059 incomplete documentation) are reasonable. Note the same file already documents the intended single source of truth at lines 68-71 ('Register it in skill/scripts/tools/__init__.py under ADAPTERS' / 'add it to Dockerfile'), which is exactly the anchor the proposed remediation names.

findings.title: Quick start examples use nonexistent command-line flags
findings.description: README.md Quick start section (lines 61-70) documents command syntax using `--mode` flag (e.g., `kimi /panopticon --mode repo`, `kimi /panopticon --mode file --target src/auth.py`) which does not exist in skill/SKILL.md. The actual flags are `-f`/`--file`, `-d`/`--directory`, `-c`/`--changes`, `--pr`, `-e`/`--explore`, or no flag for whole-repo scan.
findings.impact: Users following the README documentation will receive command-line parsing errors or fail to invoke the skill correctly with the intended target scope.
findings.remediation: Correct the examples to use actual flags: (1) line 61: remove `--mode repo`; (2) line 67: change to `--file src/auth.py` and remove `--target`; (3) line 68: change `--mode changes` to `--changes` or `-c`; (4) line 69: remove `--mode pr` but keep `--pr 217`.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Verified directly. README.md lines 60-70 contain exactly the four invocations claimed: `kimi /panopticon --mode repo` (61), `kimi /panopticon --mode file --target src/auth.py` (67), `kimi /panopticon --mode changes` (68), `kimi /panopticon --mode pr --pr 217` (69). The cited authority, skill/SKILL.md lines 27-35 ('## Modes'), is accurate and defines an entirely different flag set: `-f`/`--file`, `-d`/`--directory`, `-g`/`--group`, `-c`/`--changes`, `--pr <n>`, `-e`/`--explore`, and '*(none)* — whole-repo scan'. A repo-wide grep for `--mode` returns only README.md:61,67,68,69 plus unrelated `--model-<role>` flags in skill/scripts/dispatch.py:365-367 and docs/superpowers/ plan docs; a repo-wide grep for `--target` returns only README.md:67 (skill invocation) plus legitimate uses of the separate `run_tools.py`/`synthesize.py` CLIs. DEVELOPMENT.md:61-64 independently corroborates the real contract ('/panopticon (`-f file`, `-d dir`, `-g "Group[Facet]"`, `-c` changes, `--pr N`, `-e` explore, or whole repo)'). skill/scripts/orchestrator.py:480-495 likewise exposes `--group/--directory/--file/--files/--changes,-c/--repo-scan` and no `--mode`. Two caveats that do not change the verdict but do bear on severity: (1) skill/SKILL.md frontmatter line 6-10 declares `arguments: target, mode, security, out`, so the argument *names* `mode`/`target` do appear at the host-metadata layer — but no script consumes that key (grep for 'arguments' in skill/scripts returns nothing) and the body defines no mapping for any `mode` value, so the README syntax is still unsupported by the operative contract; (2) `/panopticon` is a prompt-type skill interpreted by an LLM, not an argparse CLI, so the stated impact 'users will receive command-line parsing errors' is overstated — the realistic failure is ambiguous/incorrect scope selection, which argues for MEDIUM rather than HIGH. The documentation defect itself is real and the proposed remediation (lines 61/67/68/69) is correct.

findings.title: README.md Quick Start examples use a `--mode`/`--target` CLI syntax that no longer matches the documented flags
findings.description: README.md's Quick Start section shows `kimi /panopticon --mode repo`, `kimi /panopticon --mode file --target src/auth.py`, `kimi /panopticon --mode changes`, and `kimi /panopticon --mode pr --pr 217`. `skill/SKILL.md`'s "Modes" section (the current, authoritative flag contract) instead maps `-f <path>`/`--file <path>`, `-d <dir>`/`--directory <dir>`, `-g <name>`/`--group <name>`, `-c`/`--changes`, `--pr <n>`, and `-e`/`--explore` — there is no `--mode` or `--target` flag anywhere in the current skill contract (confirmed via repo-wide search; the only other `--mode`-shaped strings are inside historical design docs under `docs/superpowers/`).
findings.impact: A new user following the README's Quick Start verbatim will invoke a CLI syntax the skill doesn't actually implement, producing confusing behavior or an outright failure on first use — directly undermining the README's purpose as an onboarding entry point.
findings.remediation: Update the Quick Start examples to the current flag set, e.g. `kimi /panopticon` (whole repo), `kimi /panopticon -f src/auth.py`, `kimi /panopticon -c`, `kimi /panopticon --pr 217`, matching `skill/SKILL.md`'s Modes section exactly.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Independently verified. README.md:61,67,68,69 contain verbatim the four quoted invocations using `--mode`/`--target`. skill/SKILL.md:27-35 ('## Modes') is the operative flag contract and maps exactly the set the claim enumerates: `-f <path>`/`--file <path>`, `-d <dir>`/`--directory <dir>`, `-g <name>`/`--group <name>`, `-c`/`--changes`, `--pr <n>`, `-e`/`--explore`, and *(none)* for whole-repo — with no `--mode` and no `--target`. My own repo-wide greps reproduce the claim's search result with one small correction: `--mode`-shaped strings also occur in live code as `--model-lens-sweep`/`--model-panel-review`/`--model-advisor` at skill/scripts/dispatch.py:365-367, not only in docs/superpowers/; that does not affect the substance. DEVELOPMENT.md:61-64 and skill/scripts/orchestrator.py:480-495 independently corroborate the real flag set. The suggested replacements (`kimi /panopticon`, `-f src/auth.py`, `-c`, `--pr 217`) match SKILL.md's Modes section exactly. Two qualifications: (a) skill/SKILL.md frontmatter lines 6-10 do declare `arguments: target, mode, security, out`, so the claim's 'there is no `--mode` or `--target` flag anywhere in the current skill contract' is slightly too absolute at the frontmatter/host-metadata layer — however no script reads that key (grep for 'arguments' under skill/scripts returns nothing) and the body defines no semantics for any `mode` value, so the README examples remain unsupported; (b) since `/panopticon` is an LLM-interpreted prompt skill rather than an argparse CLI, 'outright failure on first use' is the pessimistic end of the range — silent scope misinterpretation is likelier. The CWE-1059 citation is unverified from this repository (not present in skill/reference/cwe-catalog.json) and is in any case decorative for a docs-drift issue.

findings.title: Inconsistent cargo-audit version between base and fixture Docker images
findings.description: Dockerfile (line 83) installs `cargo-audit` without specifying a version (`RUN cargo install cargo-audit`), while Dockerfile.fixtures (line 20) explicitly pins the version (`RUN cargo install cargo-audit --version 0.22.2`). Dockerfile.fixtures uses `FROM panopticon-tools:latest` (depends on Dockerfile), creating an inconsistency where the base image may have a different cargo-audit version than the fixture layer expects.
findings.impact: Different versions of cargo-audit in base vs fixture images can cause unexpected scanner behavior, inconsistent vulnerability detections, and test flakiness when fixture tests expect version 0.22.2 but the base image has a different version.
findings.remediation: Either: (1) Add `--version 0.22.2` to Dockerfile line 83 to match Dockerfile.fixtures, OR (2) Remove the version pin from Dockerfile.fixtures line 20 if using the latest version is acceptable. Option 1 is preferred for reproducibility.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The described inconsistency exists exactly as stated: Dockerfile:83 is `RUN cargo install cargo-audit` (no version) and Dockerfile.fixtures:20 is `RUN cargo install cargo-audit --version 0.22.2`, with Dockerfile.fixtures:4 being `FROM panopticon-tools:latest`, so the fixture image is built on top of the unpinned base. I confirm the divergence and that it is a genuine defect. Two corrections to the claim's reasoning that the auditor should carry forward. First, the stated impact — 'test flakiness when fixture tests expect version 0.22.2' — is not supported: I read every cargo-audit test path and none asserts a tool version. tests/tools/test_rust_integration.py only checks that findings exist and carry RUSTSEC citations, and skips on `rc not in (0, 1)`; tests/fixtures/manifest.json:24-30 names the adapter but no version; tests/tools/test_cargo_audit.py is a pure parser/argv unit test. So there is no test that 'expects 0.22.2'. Second, the mechanism is subtler and arguably worse than the claim describes. Dockerfile:79 sets CARGO_HOME=/usr/local/cargo for the base install and Dockerfile:81 puts /usr/local/cargo/bin on PATH, but Dockerfile:109 then overrides `ENV CARGO_HOME=/home/scanner/.cargo` in the final image. Dockerfile.fixtures inherits that ENV, so its pinned `cargo install cargo-audit --version 0.22.2` lands in /home/scanner/.cargo/bin — a directory that is NOT on PATH — while the base image's unpinned binary remains at /usr/local/cargo/bin/cargo-audit, which IS on PATH. The adapter invokes the tool as a cargo subcommand (skill/scripts/tools/cargo_audit.py:51, `["cargo", "audit", "--format", "json"]`), so which binary actually executes depends on cargo's external-subcommand resolution order between $CARGO_HOME/bin and $PATH. I could not settle that ordering from this repository alone and I am not permitted to execute anything, so either the pin silently has no effect (PATH wins, fixtures run the unpinned base version) or it wins via CARGO_HOME/bin and the two images legitimately differ. The claim is CONFIRMED on its stated substance — the versions are inconsistent and Dockerfile:83 should be pinned — but the remediation should also reconcile the CARGO_HOME/PATH mismatch, otherwise adding `--version 0.22.2` to one line may not change which binary runs. Note this finding is largely a single-tool instance of the broader unpinning issue; I judged it independently and it stands on its own text.

findings.short_title: Inconsistent cargo-audit version between base and fixture Docker images

evidence.reasoning: The described inconsistency exists exactly as stated: Dockerfile:83 is `RUN cargo install cargo-audit` (no version) and Dockerfile.fixtures:20 is `RUN cargo install cargo-audit --version 0.22.2`, with Dockerfile.fixtures:4 being `FROM panopticon-tools:latest`, so the fixture image is built on top of the unpinned base. I confirm the divergence and that it is a genuine defect. Two corrections to the claim's reasoning that the auditor should carry forward. First, the stated impact — 'test flakiness when fixture tests expect version 0.22.2' — is not supported: I read every cargo-audit test path and none asserts a tool version. tests/tools/test_rust_integration.py only checks that findings exist and carry RUSTSEC citations, and skips on `rc not in (0, 1)`; tests/fixtures/manifest.json:24-30 names the adapter but no version; tests/tools/test_cargo_audit.py is a pure parser/argv unit test. So there is no test that 'expects 0.22.2'. Second, the mechanism is subtler and arguably worse than the claim describes. Dockerfile:79 sets CARGO_HOME=/usr/local/cargo for the base install and Dockerfile:81 puts /usr/local/cargo/bin on PATH, but Dockerfile:109 then overrides `ENV CARGO_HOME=/home/scanner/.cargo` in the final image. Dockerfile.fixtures inherits that ENV, so its pinned `cargo install cargo-audit --version 0.22.2` lands in /home/scanner/.cargo/bin — a directory that is NOT on PATH — while the base image's unpinned binary remains at /usr/local/cargo/bin/cargo-audit, which IS on PATH. The adapter invokes the tool as a cargo subcommand (skill/scripts/tools/cargo_audit.py:51, `["cargo", "audit", "--format", "json"]`), so which binary actually executes depends on cargo's external-subcommand resolution order between $CARGO_HOME/bin and $PATH. I could not settle that ordering from this repository alone and I am not permitted to execute anything, so either the pin silently has no effect (PATH wins, fixtures run the unpinned base version) or it wins via CARGO_HOME/bin and the two images legitimately differ. The claim is CONFIRMED on its stated substance — the versions are inconsistent and Dockerfile:83 should be pinned — but the remediation should also reconcile the CARGO_HOME/PATH mismatch, otherwise adding `--version 0.22.2` to one line may not change which binary runs. Note this finding is largely a single-tool instance of the broader unpinning issue; I judged it independently and it stands on its own text.

findings.title: CHANGELOG.md is stale and its one entry doesn't match DEVELOPMENT.md's description of the same version
findings.description: CHANGELOG.md contains a single dated section, `## 3.0.0 — Multi-model reviewer dispatch`, listing role-based dispatch (`scout`/`lens_sweep`/`panel_review`/`advisor`), `model_resolver.py`, `depth_planner.py`, `dispatch.py`, and `synthesize.py` as 3.0.0 features, then says `## Earlier releases ... through 2.2.1`. But `DEVELOPMENT.md`'s own History section describes 3.0.0 as something different — "Kimi port: introduces architecture, database, and redteam panels; replaces the fixed 9-lens catalog...; rewrites orchestration for the Kimi Code agent platform" — and attributes the dispatch/model_resolver/synthesize features CHANGELOG.md lists under 3.0.0 to later entries (4.0.0/4.1.0/4.2.0) in that same file. CHANGELOG.md also never records 2.0.0, 2.1.0, 2.2.0, 2.2.1, 2.3.0, 4.0.0, 4.1.0, or 4.2.0 at all — those exist only as inline prose in DEVELOPMENT.md's History list, not in the changelog readers would normally consult.
findings.impact: A reader trusting the top-level CHANGELOG.md gets both an incorrect version number for the described feature set and a materially incomplete history (missing 8 of the project's ~9 documented releases), making CHANGELOG.md an unreliable source of truth that contradicts the more detailed DEVELOPMENT.md.
findings.remediation: Either retire CHANGELOG.md in favor of DEVELOPMENT.md's History section (and say so clearly, rather than pointing back to it as if it only covers "through 2.2.1"), or bring CHANGELOG.md's entries in sync with DEVELOPMENT.md — correcting the 3.0.0 entry's content/version label and backfilling the missing releases.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Verified directly against both files. /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/CHANGELOG.md is 18 lines total and contains exactly one release section, `## 3.0.0 — Multi-model reviewer dispatch` (lines 3-13), followed by `## Earlier releases` pointing at DEVELOPMENT.md 'for the detailed version history through 2.2.1' (line 17). DEVELOPMENT.md line 8 states `**Current version: 4.2.0**` and its History section (lines 91-149+) lists 4.2.0, 4.1.0, 2.0.0, 2.1.0, 2.2.0, 3.0.0, 4.0.0, 2.3.0, 2.2.1 — so the changelog's 'through 2.2.1' pointer is itself stale (DEVELOPMENT.md documents 2.3.0 and the whole 4.x line), and CHANGELOG.md records none of those 8 other releases. The direct contradiction the claim names is real: DEVELOPMENT.md line 116-118 describes 3.0.0 as 'Kimi port: introduces architecture, database, and redteam panels; replaces the fixed 9-lens catalog with a flexible lens model; rewrites orchestration for the Kimi Code agent platform', while CHANGELOG.md's 3.0.0 describes a different feature set (role-based dispatch, model_resolver.py, depth_planner.py, dispatch.py, synthesize.py advisor trigger, CI workflows, packaging files). Same version number, two materially different descriptions. One nuance where the claim overreaches: DEVELOPMENT.md does not clearly attribute the *introduction* of those features to 4.0.0/4.1.0/4.2.0 — 4.1.0 says reviewer dispatch 'moves to' rendered prompts (presupposing dispatch already existed) and 4.0.0 says verification 'moved out of synthesize', so the changelog's 3.0.0 label may have been accurate when written; the plan doc docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-01-multi-model-reviewer-dispatch.md line 1337 indeed sets `version: "3.0.0"`. That nuance does not rescue the file: the two docs still disagree about what 3.0.0 is, the changelog is 8 releases behind, and nothing in README.md or DEVELOPMENT.md references CHANGELOG.md (grep found no reference outside scan artifacts), so it is an orphaned, stale doc. Adjacent corroborating drift not in the claim: pyproject.toml line 3 still declares `version = "3.0.0"` while skill/SKILL.md line 14 declares `version: "4.2.0"`. MEDIUM severity is generous for a documentation-only inconsistency (LOW/INFO would fit the actual impact), but the factual assertions hold.
