findings.title: CODEOWNERS patterns for "CI / security tooling" and "Schemas and reference data" reference paths that don't exist in the repo
findings.description: CODEOWNERS assigns `@psyberone` to `/scripts/run_tools.py`, `/scripts/tools/`, and `/reference/` under the comments "CI / security tooling" and "Schemas and reference data". None of these paths exist at the repo root: the real files live at `skill/scripts/run_tools.py`, `skill/scripts/tools/`, and `skill/reference/` (confirmed via glob — a top-level `scripts/` dir exists but only contains an unrelated `scripts/file_issues.py`, and no top-level `reference/` directory exists at all). GitHub CODEOWNERS patterns are matched literally against repo-relative paths, so these three rules silently never match anything.
findings.impact: The stated intent — that changes to the security-tooling scripts and reference schemas require the named owner's review — is not actually enforced by CODEOWNERS for any real file in the repo, since the patterns never match. If branch protection relies on CODEOWNERS review for these paths, that review gate is silently absent for exactly the CI/security-tooling and schema files the comments say it protects.
findings.remediation: Update the patterns to the real paths: `/skill/scripts/run_tools.py`, `/skill/scripts/tools/`, and `/skill/reference/` (and consider `/skill/Dockerfile`-adjacent paths as well, verifying `/Dockerfile` at repo root is still correct, which it is).

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The factual core is verified exactly. /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/CODEOWNERS is 12 lines and contains, under '# CI / security tooling', `/scripts/run_tools.py @psyberone` (line 7) and `/scripts/tools/ @psyberone` (line 8), and under '# Schemas and reference data', `/reference/ @psyberone` (line 11). None of those three root-anchored paths exist. Glob for `scripts/*` returns only `scripts/file_issues.py`; glob for `reference*` and `reference/**` returns nothing (no root-level `reference` entry at all, symlink or otherwise). The real files are `skill/scripts/run_tools.py`, `skill/scripts/tools/` (14 adapter modules incl. base.py, osv_scanner.py, brakeman.py), and `skill/reference/` (report-schema.json, scope-profile-schema.json, cwe-catalog.json, security-checklists.md, model-profiles.yml, code-review-groups.example.yml). README.md lines 76-83 documents the layout as `skill/scripts/` and `skill/reference/`, with no top-level `scripts/` or `reference/` entries. There is no .gitmodules, so `skill/` is a plain tracked directory (not a submodule with its own root), and .gitignore does not exclude it. Since GitHub CODEOWNERS patterns with a leading `/` are anchored to the repository root, these three rules match no tracked file and are inert. The remediation's incidental assertions also check out: `/Dockerfile` exists at the repo root and `/.github/` exists (dependabot.yml, labels.yml, apply-labels.sh, workflows/{ci,codeql,security,docker-publish}.yml), so lines 5-6 are correctly scoped. CODEOWNERS at the repo root is the only CODEOWNERS in the tree (glob **/CODEOWNERS), so no other file supersedes it, and nothing in skill/ parses CODEOWNERS (grep found zero hits under skill/); the only other repo reference is an unrelated tempdir fixture at tests/test_orchestrator.py:421. CAVEAT ON IMPACT/SEVERITY, not on the finding: the impact paragraph's hedge ('If branch protection relies on CODEOWNERS review for these paths, that review gate is silently absent') is overstated. Line 2's `* @psyberone` already makes @psyberone the code owner of every file including everything under skill/, so a 'Require review from Code Owners' rule would still demand @psyberone's review on those files today. The real defect is dead/stale configuration whose documented intent is unenforced and which breaks the moment a second owner is added — which is why MEDIUM reads high for this; LOW is the better severity. The CWE-710 citation is a generic 'improper adherence to coding standards' stand-in and is not present in the repo's bundled skill/reference/cwe-catalog.json, so I could not verify it from the provided context; it does not affect the verdict.

findings.title: Ruff pydocstyle `convention = "google"` is dead configuration because the "D" rule set is never selected
findings.description: `[tool.ruff.lint]` sets `select = ["E", "F", "W"]` (line 23), which does not include Ruff's `D` (pydocstyle) rule prefix. `[tool.ruff.lint.pydocstyle]` then sets `convention = "google"` (line 27). Ruff only evaluates `pydocstyle`/`D`-prefixed checks when at least one `D` rule is present in `select`/`extend-select`; since none is, the `convention` setting has no observable effect on lint output — CI's `ruff check` will never flag a docstring for deviating from Google style.
findings.impact: The config reads as if the project enforces Google-style docstrings, misleading contributors and reviewers about what CI actually checks; docstrings can drift from the stated convention with zero lint signal, and the config itself is confusing dead weight.
findings.remediation: Either add `"D"` (or the specific `D1xx`/`D2xx` subset desired) to `select`/`extend-select` to actually enforce the Google docstring convention, or remove the `[tool.ruff.lint.pydocstyle]` block if docstring linting isn't currently wanted.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Verified directly. /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/pyproject.toml line 23 is `select = ["E", "F", "W"]` with `ignore = ["E401", "E501", "E701", "E702"]` (line 24), and there is no `extend-select` key anywhere in the file (the file is only 28 lines; I read it in full). Lines 26-27 are `[tool.ruff.lint.pydocstyle]` / `convention = "google"`. Ruff's `pydocstyle.convention` setting only has an effect on `D`-prefixed (pydocstyle) rules — it disables the subset of D rules incompatible with the chosen convention. With no D rule ever enabled, the setting has no observable effect on lint output. I checked for competing/overriding configuration and found none: a Glob for `**/*.toml` returned only `pyproject.toml` and `tests/fixtures/vulnerable-rust/Cargo.toml`, and a Glob for `.ruff.toml`, `ruff.toml`, `setup.cfg`, `tox.ini`, `.pre-commit-config.yaml` returned no files. A repo-wide grep for `ruff` shows the only invocations are `python -m ruff check skill/scripts/ tests/` (.github/workflows/ci.yml:23) and the same command in CONTRIBUTING.md:14 and README.md:93 — none pass `--select`/`--extend-select` on the command line, so nothing re-enables D at runtime. The project's own design docs corroborate the intended rule set as E/F/W only (docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-01-html-report.md:18 and others: 'ruff rules `E`, `F`, `W` with ignores ...'). So the pydocstyle block is inert configuration exactly as claimed. Severity LOW/style is appropriate: it is dead config with documentation-misleading effect, no runtime or security impact. CWE-561 (Dead Code) is an analogy rather than a precise fit for a config key, but it is not wrong enough to change the verdict.

findings.title: DEVELOPMENT.md's version History list is in neither ascending nor descending order
findings.description: The `History:` bullet list under `## Versioning` orders entries as 4.2.0, 4.1.0, 2.0.0, 2.1.0, 2.2.0, 3.0.0, 4.0.0, 2.3.0, 2.2.1 — not sorted by semver (ascending or descending) and not in evident chronological order either (e.g. 2.3.0 and 2.2.1 both carry 2026-07-23 dates yet appear after the unlabeled 4.x entries). Changelogs conventionally read either strictly newest-first or oldest-first so a reader can follow the project's actual progression.
findings.impact: A reader trying to reconstruct "what changed and when" from this list has to mentally re-sort nine entries; the jumbled order also makes it easy to miss that 3.0.0's description here (Kimi port) differs entirely from CHANGELOG.md's unrelated 3.0.0 entry (see STYLE-102), since the two aren't adjacent or cross-referenced.
findings.remediation: Re-order the History list strictly newest-first (or oldest-first) by semver, consistent with the "Current version" line at the top of the section.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Verified by reading DEVELOPMENT.md lines 85-164. The 'History:' bullet list begins at line 91 and its entries appear at lines 92 (4.2.0, marked '(current)'), 98 (4.1.0), 107 (2.0.0), 109 (2.1.0), 111 (2.2.0), 116 (3.0.0), 119 (4.0.0), 128 (2.3.0), and 143 (2.2.1) — exactly the nine-entry sequence 4.2.0, 4.1.0, 2.0.0, 2.1.0, 2.2.0, 3.0.0, 4.0.0, 2.3.0, 2.2.1 the claim describes. That is neither semver-ascending nor semver-descending: it starts newest-first for two entries, then restarts at the oldest and climbs to 4.0.0, then drops back to 2.3.0 and 2.2.1. The last entry's block runs to line 159, matching the claimed line range. The last two entries are also plainly out of place chronologically relative to the 4.x entries above them. One supporting detail in the description is imprecise and should not be relied on: the 2.3.0 and 2.2.1 bullets themselves carry no dates; the 2026-07-23 dates appear in the separate H3 section headings further down (lines 186 '### Self-scan round 2 (2026-07-23)', 201 '### From the baskin dogfood run (2026-07-23)', 212 "### From Panopticon's self-review (2026-07-23)"). The cross-reference to a 3.0.0 discrepancy does check out independently: CHANGELOG.md's only version heading is line 3 '## 3.0.0 — Multi-model reviewer dispatch', whereas DEVELOPMENT.md line 116 describes 3.0.0 as the 'Kimi port'. The core claim — the History list is in no consistent order — is factually correct, and LOW/style is the right weight.

findings.title: Gate logic is embedded as an inline Python heredoc in the workflow YAML instead of a reusable, tested script
findings.description: The "Ingest findings and gate on HIGH/CRITICAL" step runs a multi-line Python script inline via `python - <<'PY' ... PY` directly inside `security.yml` (importing `scripts.ingest_tools`, filtering by severity, and printing/exiting). Every other piece of non-trivial logic in this repository lives in a tested module under `skill/scripts/` (per DEVELOPMENT.md's Architecture section and CONTRIBUTING.md's testing expectations) with corresponding unit tests; this ~17-line gate script is the one exception, living untested and unversioned inside the workflow file, including an unexplained magic value (`f[:20]`, capping the printed HIGH/CRITICAL list at 20).
findings.impact: The gate logic can't be unit-tested, linted by ruff (it's YAML, not a `.py` file under `skill/scripts/`), or reused outside CI, breaking from the project's own stated convention and making it easier for the gate to silently regress without test coverage catching it.
findings.remediation: Extract the heredoc body into a small `skill/scripts/ci_gate.py` (or similar) module with a unit test, and have the workflow step simply invoke `python skill/scripts/ci_gate.py --tools-dir ${{ env.TOOLS_OUT }}`; name or comment the `20` truncation limit if kept.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Verified directly. `.github/workflows/security.yml` lines 53-71 contain the step 'Ingest findings and gate on HIGH/CRITICAL' whose body is `python - <<'PY' ... PY` — 16 lines of inline Python that mutate sys.path (`sys.path.insert(0, os.path.join(os.getcwd(), 'skill'))`), `import scripts.ingest_tools as it`, call `it.ingest_dir(os.environ['TOOLS_OUT'], 'ci', exclude_globs=['tests/fixtures/*'])`, filter `f.get('severity') in ('HIGH','CRITICAL')`, print `high[:20]`, and `sys.exit(1)`. The `20` at line 67 is an unexplained literal, as claimed. The convention the claim invokes is real: DEVELOPMENT.md's Architecture section (lines 20-43) enumerates every non-trivial piece of logic as a module under `skill/scripts/`; CONTRIBUTING.md line 27 states 'All changes should include tests'; and `.github/workflows/ci.yml` line 23 runs ruff only over `skill/scripts/ tests/`, so this YAML-embedded Python is neither linted nor unit-tested. I globbed `skill/scripts/*.py` — there is no `ci_gate.py` or equivalent — and grepped tests/ for any coverage of this gate; none exists (synthesize's `--fail-on` gate is a separate, report-level gate per DEVELOPMENT.md lines 62-63). The project has already treated inline CI Python as a defect in this same file: `docs/superpowers/2026-08-03-calibration-fixmes.md` lines 79-83 (F-CAL-2) says the fixture filter 'exists only as inline Python in .github/workflows/security.yml. Promote to a standard mechanism', which was done by adding `exclude_globs` to `ingest_dir` (skill/scripts/ingest_tools.py lines 40-50 document exactly that); the gate logic around it was left inline. Two small wording imprecisions that do not change the verdict: the code is version-controlled (the claim's 'unversioned' presumably means 'not a versioned module'), and within .github/ it is not literally the only heredoc — `.github/apply-labels.sh` line 21 also uses `python3 - <<'PY'`, though that is a helper shell script, not gate logic in workflow YAML. Within `.github/workflows/*.yml`, security.yml:55 is the only inline Python. LOW/style severity is appropriate; CWE-710 (improper adherence to coding standards) is a defensible but loose mapping.

findings.title: Known design vulnerability: unscoped write surface in agent framework (FIXME-6)
findings.description: FIXME-6 documents a known security issue where Claude Code agents with the Write tool have unrestricted write capabilities. Writing sub-orchestrators (agents managing group runner tasks) can write anywhere on the system because the Write tool grants unrestricted file access, not path-scoped access. This violates the principle of least privilege and creates a trust path vulnerability.
findings.impact: A malicious or compromised agent with Write capability could modify arbitrary files, escape the intended review scope (.panopticon/ directory), modify code, or corrupt build artifacts. Since sub-orchestrators are in the trust path for findings persistence, this represents a significant control gap.
findings.remediation: Implement path-scoped write restrictions through a PreToolUse hook that validates Write/Edit operations against an allowlist derived from dispatch plan output file paths. Add a third tool_policy_mode value ('enforced+scoped-write') to record when scoped write enforcement is in effect. The partial mitigations already in place (AGENT_FORBIDDEN_FIELDS strip, post-fan-out clean-tree check) are insufficient without out-of-band enforcement.
references: CWE-73: External Control of File Name or Path
CWE-78: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command
skill/scripts/dispatch.py:103-134 (emit_host_agents writes `tools:` only, no path scoping)
skill/reference/report-schema.json:28 (tool_policy_mode enum has no scoped-write value)
skill/agents/*.md:5-6 (all shipped roles are read-only; no Write role exists)

cwe.name: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command ('OS Command Injection')

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The cited text exists and says what the claim says it says. docs/superpowers/2026-08-04-run2-fixmes.md:81-99 (FIXME-6) states verbatim that the sub-orchestrator pattern requires an agent with `Write`, that 'Claude Code's agent frontmatter grants a *tool*, not a *path* — `Write` means write anywhere', and that 'That agent is in the trust path for findings persistence with no mechanical bound on what it can touch.' The claim's paraphrase of the mechanism, the trust-path framing, and the listed partial mitigations (AGENT_FORBIDDEN_FIELDS strip, post-fan-out clean-tree check) are all faithful. I independently corroborated the substance in the repo: (a) skill/scripts/dispatch.py:103-134 (`emit_host_agents`) writes host agent frontmatter as `tools: <allowed list>` only — the registration surface is a tool list with no path dimension, so a Write grant is inherently unscoped; (b) `PreToolUse` occurs nowhere in the repo except as the *proposed* fix at docs/superpowers/2026-08-04-run2-fixmes.md:95, and `.claude/settings.local.json` contains only an env var, no hooks — so the proposed out-of-band enforcement genuinely does not exist; (c) skill/reference/report-schema.json:28 enumerates `tool_policy_mode` as exactly [enforced, advisory, mixed], confirming there is no `enforced+scoped-write` posture to record; (d) the mitigations named are real — skill/scripts/synthesize.py:93 `AGENT_FORBIDDEN_FIELDS = ("source", "reinforced")` applied at load (line 125), and skill/SKILL.md:53,64 capture a `git status --porcelain` baseline before dispatch and compare it during validation. Two material corrections for the auditor, neither of which negates the claim. First, the risk is LATENT, not live: all four shipped reviewer templates (skill/agents/{advisor,scout,panel-review,lens-sweep}.md, each line 5-6) declare `allowed: [Read, Grep, Glob]` / `forbidden: [Bash, Edit, Write, Agent]`, and no `group_runner`/writing role exists anywhere in code — `group_runner` appears only at docs/superpowers/2026-08-04-run2-fixmes.md:76 as a proposed design. The writing sub-orchestrator was an ad-hoc general-purpose agent used in one run, and FIXME-6 is the authors' own forward-looking note about a pattern they intend to formalize. HIGH therefore overstates it; the source doc self-rates `severity:medium`, `evidence:unverified`, and MEDIUM is the defensible severity. Second, the citations are wrong: there is no OS command construction anywhere on this path, so CWE-78 and OWASP A03:2021-Injection do not apply and should be dropped. CWE-73 is only loosely applicable (nothing here is attacker-controlled path input); CWE-732 (incorrect permission assignment) or CWE-269 (improper privilege management) fit the least-privilege gap better. I confirm the finding's existence and technical substance, not its severity or its CWE mapping.

findings.title: Static-analysis tool binaries fetched from GitHub Releases / Maven Central without checksum or signature verification
findings.description: osv-scanner (lines 27-32), gitleaks (34-38), gosec (46-49), SpotBugs (61-65), FindSecBugs (66-69), and OWASP dependency-check (72-76) are each downloaded with a bare `curl -sfL ... | tar -xz` or `curl -sfL ... -o file` and then executed/installed with no comparison against a published `SHA256SUMS`/`.sig`/`.asc` file. This is inconsistent with the trivy install just above it (lines 40-44), which at least goes through an apt repo secured with a GPG-verified `[signed-by=...]` keyring.
findings.impact: A compromised release upload (maintainer account takeover, or attacker-controlled artifact substitution on any host in the download chain) for any of these six tools would ship an undetected malicious binary inside the publicly distributed `panopticon-tools` image, executed with the same repo-read access every scan invocation grants.
findings.remediation: Pin and verify SHA256 checksums for each downloaded release asset before use (all six upstream projects publish checksum files alongside their release archives); fail the build if verification fails.
references: Dockerfile:82,86 (rustup and dotnet-install piped to shell, unverified)

provenance.confirmation_reasoning:
Every downloaded artifact the claim names is verifiable at the cited lines, and none has an integrity check. osv-scanner (Dockerfile:28-32) curls a release binary straight to /usr/local/bin and chmod +x's it. gitleaks (35-38) pipes `curl -sfL <github release>.tar.gz | tar -xz -C /usr/local/bin`. gosec (47-49) does the same. SpotBugs (62-65) pipes a GitHub release tgz into `tar -xz -C /opt`. FindSecBugs (67-69) curls a jar from `search.maven.org/remotecontent?filepath=...` into the SpotBugs plugin directory. OWASP dependency-check (73-76) curls a release zip to /tmp and unzips it into /opt. Not one is compared against a SHA256SUMS, .sig, .asc, or cosign attestation. The claim's contrast with trivy is also accurate: Dockerfile:41-44 dearmors the Aqua public key into /usr/share/keyrings/trivy.gpg and pins the apt source with `[signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/trivy.gpg]`, so trivy's packages are signature-verified by apt. I grepped the whole repo for sha256/checksum/SHA256SUMS/checksums.txt/cosign/`gpg --verify`; the only hits are unrelated (an image digest in docker-publish.yml, report-rendering code, and fixture data). There is no build script or CI step performing verification.

The impact framing also holds up. .github/workflows/docker-publish.yml:35-60 logs into ghcr.io and pushes the built image as `latest`, so panopticon-tools is in fact publicly distributed, and .github/workflows/security.yml:39-46 pulls that published tag. skill/scripts/run_tools.py:130-131 and :156-167 mount the target repo at /src on every scan, so a trojaned binary would run with read access to whatever repo is under review — and DEVELOPMENT.md:55-56 records that `--network none` was deliberately dropped, so an implanted binary would also have outbound network. CWE-494 (Download of Code Without Integrity Check) and OWASP A08:2021 are the correct citations.

Two notes for the auditor. The claim actually undercounts: Dockerfile:82 (`curl --proto '=https' ... https://sh.rustup.rs | sh`) and Dockerfile:86 (`curl -sfL https://dot.net/v1/dotnet-install.sh | bash`) pipe remote shell scripts directly into an interpreter with no verification at all, which is a strictly larger exposure than the six artifacts listed, and Dockerfile.fixtures:16 repeats the dotnet pattern. Conversely, the threat description slightly overstates the network surface: all six URLs are HTTPS, so 'any host in the download chain' is not accurate — the realistic vectors are upstream account/release compromise or registry/CDN compromise. That nuance matters for the remediation, because upstream-published SHA256 files sit on the same platform as the artifacts and so do not defend against maintainer account takeover; pinning checksums verified once out-of-band (or verifying cosign/GPG signatures where the projects publish them) is the stronger fix. Neither note undermines the finding.

findings.title: Dockerfile.fixtures pipes dotnet-install.sh into bash without version pin or verification
findings.description: `RUN curl -sfL https://dot.net/v1/dotnet-install.sh | bash -s -- --channel 8.0` streams the .NET installer directly into a shell with no checksum/signature check, mirroring the pattern in the main Dockerfile (see NOVEL-101) but in the fixtures image, which builds and runs several other third-party project build systems as `root` (see NOVEL-104, NOVEL-108).
findings.impact: A compromise of the dot.net install-script host would give an attacker root code execution during every `docker build -f Dockerfile.fixtures ...`, on any contributor or CI machine that builds it.
findings.remediation: Download the script to a file, verify it against a pinned checksum, then execute the local copy — same remediation as NOVEL-101.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Every factual element checks out. `Dockerfile.fixtures:16` is verbatim `RUN curl -sfL https://dot.net/v1/dotnet-install.sh | bash -s -- --channel 8.0` — the remote script is streamed straight into `bash` with no download-to-file, no checksum, no signature, and no pinned script revision (`/v1/` is an API path, not a content pin; `--channel 8.0` pins the SDK channel, not the installer). The root-execution context is confirmed: `Dockerfile.fixtures:6` sets `USER root` (overriding the base image's `USER scanner` at `Dockerfile:110`) and no `USER` instruction follows, which the file's own comment at lines 54-55 acknowledges ('The fixtures image runs as root'). The cross-references in the description hold too: the identical pattern exists in the published base image at `Dockerfile:86`, and lines 35-37 of `Dockerfile.fixtures` execute three third-party build systems as root (`bundle install`, `./mvnw clean compile`, `dotnet restore && dotnet build`) against freshly cloned upstream repositories. So a compromise of the `dot.net` script host yields root code execution on any machine running `docker build -f Dockerfile.fixtures`. CWE-494 (download of code without integrity check) and A08:2021 are the right mappings. Two calibrating caveats for the auditor rather than grounds for rejection: (a) this image is never built in CI — no workflow references `Dockerfile.fixtures`; it is built only locally by `skill/scripts/run_fixture_tests.py:38-44` and by the documented manual command in `DEVELOPMENT.md:78`, so the blast radius is contributor workstations, not the release pipeline (unlike the same pattern in the root `Dockerfile`, which IS published to ghcr.io by `docker-publish.yml`); and (b) the surrounding lines already perform many unverified network installs at root (`apt-get install`, `gem install bundler`, `cargo install cargo-audit --version 0.22.2`, `pip install pytest`), so singling out this one line as MEDIUM while the peers go unflagged is inconsistent — the underlying risk is real but is a class-level supply-chain posture issue. I found no SECURITY.md and no documented risk-acceptance for the installer integrity gap (only for the root user).

The cross-references in the description hold too: the identical pattern exists in the published base image at `Dockerfile:86`, and lines 35-37 of `Dockerfile.fixtures` execute three third-party build systems as root (`bundle install`, `./mvnw clean compile`, `dotnet restore && dotnet build`) against freshly cloned upstream repositories. So a compromise of the `dot.net` script host yields root code execution on any machine running `docker build -f Dockerfile.fixtures`. CWE-494 (download of code without integrity check) and A08:2021 are the right mappings. Two calibrating caveats for the auditor rather than grounds for rejection: (a) this image is never built in CI — no workflow references `Dockerfile.fixtures`; it is built only locally by `skill/scripts/run_fixture_tests.py:38-44` and by the documented manual command in `DEVELOPMENT.md:78`, so the blast radius is contributor workstations, not the release pipeline (unlike the same pattern in the root `Dockerfile`, which IS published to ghcr.io by `docker-publish.yml`); and (b) the surrounding lines already perform many unverified network installs at root (`apt-get install`, `gem install bundler`, `cargo install cargo-audit --version 0.22.2`, `pip install pytest`), so singling out this one line as MEDIUM while the peers go unflagged is inconsistent — the underlying risk is real but is a class-level supply-chain posture issue. findings.title: Third-party GitHub Actions pinned to mutable tags in a workflow holding write-scoped tokens and attestation authority
findings.description: `docker-publish.yml` grants `packages: write`, `attestations: write`, and `id-token: write` (lines 22-26) and authenticates to GHCR with `secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN` (line 40), yet every third-party action it invokes is pinned to a mutable version tag rather than a full commit SHA: `actions/checkout@v4`, `docker/setup-buildx-action@v3`, `docker/login-action@v3`, `docker/metadata-action@v5`, `docker/build-push-action@v6`, and `actions/attest-build-provenance@v1`.
findings.impact: A tag re-point on any of these actions (maintainer account compromise or malicious release) would run with this workflow's write-scoped `GITHUB_TOKEN` and OIDC identity, allowing an attacker to push an arbitrary image to `ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}-tools` and obtain a legitimate-looking build-provenance attestation for it (lines 62-67) — undermining the exact supply-chain-integrity guarantee that attestation step is meant to provide.
findings.remediation: Pin every third-party action to a full-length commit SHA (with a version comment, e.g. `actions/checkout@<sha> # v4.x.x`) and use Dependabot/Renovate to bump them via reviewed PRs, per GitHub's Actions security-hardening guidance for workflows holding write-capable secrets.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning:
Every factual element checks out against `.github/workflows/docker-publish.yml`. Permissions at lines 22-26 are `contents: read`, `packages: write`, `attestations: write`, `id-token: write`. Line 40 authenticates to ghcr.io with `password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}`. All six `uses:` references are mutable major-version tags, not commit SHAs: `actions/checkout@v4` (30), `docker/setup-buildx-action@v3` (33), `docker/login-action@v3` (36), `docker/metadata-action@v5` (44), `docker/build-push-action@v6` (53), `actions/attest-build-provenance@v1` (63). The attestation step (62-67) uses `push-to-registry: true` with `subject-digest: ${{ steps.push.outputs.digest }}`, so a compromised action in the build chain could set the digest that gets a signed provenance statement — the escalation path described is coherent, and this is the highest-privilege workflow in the repo (the other three top out at `security-events: write`).

Two corrections that do not change the verdict: (a) `actions/checkout` and `actions/attest-build-provenance` are GitHub-owned first-party actions, not third-party, so 'every third-party action' is imprecise — the `docker/*` set is the genuine third-party (verified-publisher) exposure; (b) `.github/dependabot.yml` lines 13-21 already configure the `github-actions` ecosystem on a weekly schedule, so part of the stated remediation is in place. Dependabot does not mitigate tag re-pointing, though: with tag pins Dependabot has nothing to bump, and a silently moved `v3` tag is consumed without any PR. SHA pinning is what makes Dependabot the control the remediation describes, so the recommendation stands and is in fact the prerequisite that is missing. CWE-829 (Inclusion of Functionality from Untrusted Control Sphere) is the standard mapping for unpinned CI action references and is verifiable from the cited MITRE URL. No CVE claimed. MEDIUM is defensible given the write-scoped token plus attestation authority; a repo consuming only major-publisher actions could argue LOW.

findings.title: Scan container combines full read access to the target repository with unrestricted scan-time network egress
findings.description: The documented invocation (Dockerfile:3, `docker run --rm -v "$PWD":/src:ro panopticon-tools <tool> ...`) mounts the entire target repository read-only into the container. Per DEVELOPMENT.md:55-56, this is a deliberate design decision: 'Scan-time network is allowed (dropped `--network none`)... semgrep/trivy need to fetch rules/DB. Mount stays read-only + non-root.' Neither the Dockerfile nor `.github/workflows/security.yml` applies any egress restriction (DNS/IP allow-list, restricted proxy) to that network access.
findings.impact: Any tool in the image that phones home during a scan — either because it was tampered with upstream (see NOVEL-101/NOVEL-102) or because its own live rule/vulnerability feed (e.g. the semgrep registry, trivy's vulnerability DB) is itself compromised — has simultaneous read access to the entire mounted source tree and an unrestricted channel to exfiltrate it. Because `security.yml` runs this container against this repository's own pushes/PRs, and downstream adopters run it against their own (potentially proprietary/secret-containing) codebases per README.md's documented usage, this converts what the maintainers frame as a build-time integrity risk into a live source-code/secret exfiltration risk on every scan.
findings.remediation: Restore `--network none` for scan invocations where feasible by baking required rule/vulnerability databases into the image at build time instead of fetching them per-scan (already tracked as a backlog item — DEVELOPMENT.md's 'Later — features' section: 'Optional bake-at-build offline mode (trivy DB + semgrep rules) to restore `--network none`'), or at minimum restrict egress to an explicit allow-list of the specific rule/DB hosts each tool legitimately needs.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning:
Every factual element of the claim verifies, and I found additional evidence that strengthens it beyond what the claim asserts.

(1) The cited text is verbatim accurate. Dockerfile:3 reads `# Run:    docker run --rm -v "$PWD":/src:ro panopticon-tools <tool> ...`, and the image ends with `USER scanner` / `WORKDIR /src` (Dockerfile:110-111), so the whole target tree is readable at /src. DEVELOPMENT.md:55-56 reads exactly as quoted, including the deliberate `dropped --network none` decision, and DEVELOPMENT.md:231 confirms the backlog item the remediation points at.

(2) The claim's location (Dockerfile:1-4) is only the documentation of the invocation; the real enforcement point is `skill/scripts/run_tools.py`. I checked it and it corroborates rather than contradicts. Line 130-131 builds `["docker", "run", "--rm", "-v", "<abs target>:/src:ro", image] + cmd` and lines 156-167 build the adapter-dispatch variant — neither passes any `--network`, `--dns`, or proxy flag, so both run on Docker's default bridge with unrestricted egress. A repo-wide grep for `--network|network none|network=none` returns only the two DEVELOPMENT.md prose lines — there is no egress control anywhere in the codebase. `tests/test_run_tools.py:56-67` locks this in as intended behavior by asserting the exact argv with no network flag. `.github/workflows/security.yml` (triggers at lines 3-7; invocation at line 51, `python skill/scripts/run_tools.py --target . --out ... --deps`) adds no restriction either. So 'neither the Dockerfile nor security.yml applies any egress restriction' is correct, and so is the stronger statement that nothing in the repo does.

(3) The 'live feed at scan time' premise is real, not hypothetical. `skill/scripts/tools/legacy_sarif.py:18` invokes `semgrep scan --config auto`, which resolves rules from the semgrep registry over the network at scan time (and is the config mode that also reports scan metadata upstream); line 21 invokes `trivy fs`, which pulls/refreshes its vulnerability DB at scan time. These are exactly the two tools DEVELOPMENT.md names as the reason network was left on, so the exfiltration channel and the untrusted-input channel are the same channel, in the same container, as the read-only full-source mount.

(4) Two corroborating facts the claim did not mention, both of which make it harder to dismiss:
  - `skill/scripts/run_tools.py:157-158` injects a secret into that same unrestricted-egress container: `if os.environ.get("NVD_API_KEY"): docker.extend(["-e", "NVD_API_KEY"])`. The container therefore holds a credential in addition to the source tree.
  - The design rationale in DEVELOPMENT.md:55 ('SAST/SCA only parse code, never execute it') is factually false for at least one registered adapter. `skill/scripts/tools/roslyn_secguard.py:49-66` copies the target into a temp dir and runs `dotnet build tmp_target ...` via `run_tool`. `dotnet build` executes target-controlled MSBuild logic and restores NuGet packages from feeds the target configures. `roslyn-secguard` is in `PHASE2_ADAPTERS` (run_tools.py:26-29) and is auto-selected by applicability, so a hostile *target repo* gets code execution inside a container that simultaneously has the full source mount, unrestricted egress, and possibly NVD_API_KEY. Since `security.yml` fires on `pull_request` (line 6), fork-authored content is in scope for that path. This means the exposure does not even require the upstream-feed compromise the claim's exploit scenario posits.

(5) Minor corrections for the auditor, none of which change the verdict: the `location` should be retargeted to `skill/scripts/run_tools.py:130-131` and `:156-167` (the code that actually omits the restriction) with Dockerfile:3 and DEVELOPMENT.md:55-56 as supporting references. The README claim is directionally right but imprecise — README.md:96-108 documents `docker build -t panopticon-tools .` then `python skill/scripts/run_tools.py --target . --deps` rather than a raw `docker run`; that wrapper takes the identical unrestricted-egress path, so the substance holds. Finally the CVSS vector `AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:N/A:N` at 8.6 is miscalibrated for the claim as written: reaching the asserted impact requires prior compromise of an upstream rule/DB feed, which is not `PR:N/AC:L` from a network attacker's position. The finding is a genuine and defensible defense-in-depth / trust-boundary defect (the maintainers' own backlog agrees), but its scoring should be revisited — ironically the roslyn_secguard path in (4) is a better-grounded route to a high score than the one the claim argues.

findings.exploit_scenario: A malicious rule update is published to a live feed one of the bundled tools polls at scan time (e.g. a poisoned semgrep registry rule pack, or a compromised trivy vulnerability-DB mirror) — no prior compromise of the panopticon Dockerfile itself is required. The next `docker run --rm -v $PWD:/src:ro panopticon-tools semgrep ...` (locally, or via `security.yml` on every push/PR) executes the poisoned rule/update with full read access to the mounted repository and unrestricted outbound network access, allowing it to exfiltrate source code, embedded credentials, or `.env` files to an attacker-controlled endpoint before the scan even completes.

findings.title: Fixtures image never drops root privileges before running third-party build tooling
findings.description: Line 6 explicitly re-escalates to `USER root`, and the image never switches to an unprivileged user before its `CMD` (line 56) — unlike the parent `Dockerfile` it is `FROM` (line 4), which creates and switches to a `scanner` (uid 1000) user before its own entrypoint. Lines 54-55 acknowledge this in a comment ('runs as root because it installs language toolchains ... intended for local test use only'), but nothing in the repository enforces that boundary.
findings.impact: If this image is ever run in a less-trusted context than intended (a future CI job, a shared build agent, a hosted dev-container), a container-escape or privilege-escalation flaw in any of the several third-party build toolchains it executes (Maven/mvnw, Bundler, dotnet, cargo, all pulling further transitive dependencies) runs as root, removing the defense-in-depth layer the primary Dockerfile deliberately provides.
findings.remediation: Add a non-root `USER` step before the final `CMD`, mirroring the base image's `scanner` user, granting write access only to the specific build/output directories that require it; alternatively, add an explicit CI lint check that fails if `Dockerfile.fixtures` is ever referenced from a workflow file, to keep the documented 'local use only' boundary enforced rather than advisory.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Every factual assertion checks out. Dockerfile.fixtures line 4 is `FROM panopticon-tools:latest`; line 6 is `USER root`; there is no further USER instruction anywhere in the file, so the final `CMD ["python", "skill/scripts/run_fixture_tests.py"]` at line 56 executes as uid 0. The parent image does drop privileges: Dockerfile lines 103-110 create `useradd -m -u 1000 scanner`, chown the cargo/ruby-advisory-db dirs, and set `USER scanner` before WORKDIR /src / CMD. Lines 54-55 of Dockerfile.fixtures contain exactly the acknowledging comment quoted. The image does execute several third-party build toolchains that pull transitive dependencies (lines 35-37: `bundle install`, `./mvnw clean compile` / `mvn`, `dotnet restore && dotnet build`; line 42 `cargo build`), plus scanner adapters at test time. I also verified the 'nothing enforces the boundary' half: grep across .github/ found no reference to Dockerfile.fixtures or panopticon-fixtures in any workflow (only docker-publish.yml/security.yml, which build the primary `Dockerfile` / panopticon-tools), and the only invoker is skill/scripts/run_fixture_tests.py, whose `docker run` argv (lines 79-86) passes no `--user`, so the root CMD stands at runtime. Nothing lints or gates against a future workflow adding it. Two qualifications keep this at LIKELY rather than CERTAIN as a *bug*: (1) the risk is conditional and already explicitly accepted in-file and in the design docs (docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-02-local-scanner-fixture-suite-design.md line 21: 'independent of CI gates'), and the runtime attack surface is narrow — mounts are `:ro` (run_fixture_tests.py lines 82-83), no docker socket, and exploitation requires a container-escape flaw; (2) the proposed remediation is not drop-in as written: Dockerfile.fixtures line 17 sets `ENV PATH="/root/.dotnet:${PATH}"`, installing the .NET SDK under /root (line 16), so simply appending `USER scanner` would break the dotnet-dependent fixtures unless the SDK is relocated system-wide the way the base image does at Dockerfile lines 85-89. That is a remediation-detail correction, not grounds for rejection — the described condition (privileged runtime with only an advisory comment as the boundary, CWE-250) is real as written.

findings.title: No SECURITY.md backing the vulnerability-disclosure instruction
findings.description: CONTRIBUTING.md's 'Reporting security issues' section (lines 31-33) directs reporters to 'open a private security advisory rather than a public issue,' but the repository has no `SECURITY.md` (not present at the root among the reviewed files) specifying supported versions, a response SLA, a dedicated contact, or a PGP key, and nothing confirms GitHub's private-vulnerability-reporting feature is actually enabled on the repository.
findings.impact: A reporter following the stated instruction has no canonical, GitHub-surfaced entry point (the 'Security' tab reads from `SECURITY.md`, and it is what tooling such as OpenSSF Scorecard checks for) and no way to verify the advisory feature is turned on before disclosing a vulnerability, which can lead to accidental public disclosure or reports going unanswered.
findings.remediation: Add a `SECURITY.md` documenting the supported-version policy and disclosure process, and confirm 'Private vulnerability reporting' is enabled in the repository's Security settings.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: CONTRIBUTING.md lines 31-33 are exactly as quoted: '## Reporting security issues' / 'Please open a private security advisory rather than a public issue for vulnerabilities in the tool itself.' A repo-wide Glob for `**/SECURITY*` returned zero files — no SECURITY.md at the root, none in `.github/`, none in `docs/` (the three locations GitHub reads for the Security tab). Globbing `.github/**/*` confirms that directory holds only dependabot.yml, labels.yml, apply-labels.sh, and four workflows (ci, codeql, docker-publish, security) — no policy file. A case-insensitive grep for `SECURITY.md|security advisory|private vulnerability` across the repo matched only CONTRIBUTING.md line 33 plus two scanner-output artifacts under .panopticon.prev-20260803/, so nothing else in the tree documents supported versions, an SLA, a contact, or a key. The claim's second half — that nothing confirms GitHub's private-vulnerability-reporting toggle is enabled — is correct as stated: that setting lives in repository settings and is not representable in the checkout, and the claim asserts only that the repo does not confirm it, which is accurate rather than speculative. INFO severity is well calibrated: this is a missing-artifact/process gap, not an exploitable defect.

findings.title: TestRunTool test class is unreachable when test file is executed as script
findings.description: The `if __name__ == "__main__": unittest.main()` block (lines 40-41) is placed before the TestRunTool class definition (line 44), causing those tests to never be discovered or executed when test_base.py is run directly. When unittest.main() is invoked, the TestRunTool class has not yet been defined in the module namespace, so it cannot be discovered. These tests are only executed if the file is imported by a test runner like pytest, not if run as a standalone script.
findings.impact: TestRunTool tests implementing the F-CAL-1 requirement (that adapter failures with non-zero/non-one exit codes must log diagnostic stderr excerpts) are not reliably executed. This may lead to regressions in error diagnostics not being caught.
findings.remediation: Move the `if __name__ == "__main__": unittest.main()` block to the end of the test file, after all test class definitions (after line 89). This follows the standard Python test file pattern and ensures all test classes are defined before test discovery occurs.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Verified in /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/tests/tools/test_base.py. findings.title: Misplaced if __name__ == '__main__' guard between class definitions
findings.description: The if __name__ == '__main__' block (lines 40-41) is positioned between two test class definitions (TestBase and TestRunTool), rather than at the end of the file. This violates standard Python module structure where guard blocks should be at module level after all definitions.
findings.impact: Maintainers may be confused about module organization; the TestRunTool class is defined after a module guard that appears to conclude the module.
findings.remediation: Move the if __name__ == '__main__' block to the end of the file (after line 89) so it executes after all classes are defined.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Judged on its own evidence: /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/tests/tools/test_base.py has the `if __name__ == "__main__": unittest.main()` block at lines 40-41, sandwiched between `class TestBase` (line 10, methods through line 37) and `class TestRunTool` (line 44, methods through line 89, the last line of the file). The structural description is exactly as claimed -- the guard sits between two class definitions instead of at module end. The stated impact (maintainer confusion; a block that reads as the module's conclusion is followed by 46 more lines of test class) is fair, and it is measurably an outlier in this codebase: a grep for __main__ across tests/ returns 18 modules, and in the other 17 the guard is at the file's final lines (e.g. tests/test_orchestrator.py:435, tests/tools/test_npm_audit.py:221, tests/tools/test_eslint_security.py:183). The remediation -- move the block after line 89 -- is correct and matches the repo's own convention. The claim is under-stated rather than over-stated: it frames the issue as purely cosmetic ('may be confused'), but placement here also has a behavioral consequence under direct script execution, which I verified separately. Nothing contradicts the claim. findings.title: Main block misplaced in middle of file
findings.description: The `if __name__ == "__main__": unittest.main()` block at lines 40-41 appears before the TestRunTool class definition (lines 44-89). Conventional Python style places the main block at the end of the file after all class definitions.
findings.impact: Violates standard Python file structure conventions and may confuse readers about the module structure
findings.remediation: Move the `if __name__ == "__main__"` block to the end of the file, after all class definitions

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Verified verbatim by reading the file. tests/tools/test_base.py:40-41 contains `if __name__ == "__main__":` / `unittest.main()`, and `class TestRunTool(unittest.TestCase)` is defined afterwards at lines 44-89. Every factual element of the claim (line numbers, ordering, class span) matches the source. The convention assertion also holds inside this repository: every sibling test module places the guard as the final statement — e.g. tests/tools/test_eslint_security.py:183-184 is the last content in that file, and the same terminal placement recurs across tests/test_schema.py:183, tests/test_orchestrator.py:436, tests/test_verify_queue.py:123 and others. test_base.py is the sole deviation. The claim is not purely cosmetic either: because unittest.main() defaults to exit=True, running the file directly would sys.exit() before lines 44-89 are ever executed, so the misplacement has a latent functional edge in addition to the readability cost — which supports the MEDIUM rating even though no repo-documented workflow executes the file directly (CI, README.md:92 and CONTRIBUTING.md:13 all use `python -m pytest tests/ -q`, under which both classes are collected). One weakness worth passing to the auditor: the supplied reference (pep8.org anchor for 'block comments') has nothing to do with main-guard placement and does not support the claim; the finding stands on the code itself, not that citation.

findings.title: Test class defined after __main__ block
findings.description: TestRunTool class (line 44) is defined after the if __name__ == '__main__' block (line 40). This violates standard test organization conventions and can interfere with test discovery mechanisms.
findings.impact: Test discovery tools may not properly locate or execute the TestRunTool test class, reducing test coverage visibility.
findings.remediation: Move all test class definitions before the if __name__ == '__main__' block. The block should be at the end of the file after all test classes.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The structural fact is verified directly: tests/tools/test_base.py:40-41 holds the `if __name__ == "__main__": unittest.main()` guard and TestRunTool is declared afterwards at lines 44-89. The organizational-convention half of the claim is verified against the repo's own corpus — sibling suites such as tests/tools/test_eslint_security.py:183-184 and tests/test_schema.py:183 terminate with the guard, making test_base.py the outlier. The execution half is stated in hedged terms ('can interfere', 'may not properly locate or execute'), and one concrete path satisfies it: invoking `python tests/tools/test_base.py` calls unittest.main() at line 41, whose loader enumerates the module namespace at that moment — TestRunTool is not yet bound, and unittest.main() then sys.exit()s (exit=True default), so lines 44-89 never execute. The five TestRunTool cases, which are the regression tests for the F-CAL-1 stderr-excerpt behaviour in skill/scripts/tools/base.py:64-78 (run_tool), are silently omitted with no failure signal. I am scoping the confirmation deliberately: under the runner this project actually uses the impact does NOT materialise. .github/workflows/ci.yml:41, README.md:92 and CONTRIBUTING.md:13 all run `python -m pytest tests/ -q`; pyproject.toml sets no pytest options; there is no tests/__init__.py or tests/tools/__init__.py and no conftest.py. pytest imports the module (so `__name__` != '__main__', the guard is skipped, execution reaches line 44) and collects both unittest.TestCase subclasses. So there is no present coverage loss in CI — the exposure is that the guard is dead-but-misleading and that anyone running the file directly gets a silently truncated suite. MEDIUM is defensible on that latent basis; an auditor should not read this as current missing coverage.

findings.title: Inconsistent mock import style
findings.description: Line 6 uses `from unittest.mock import patch` while all other test files in the directory use `from unittest import mock`. This creates inconsistency across the test suite.
findings.impact: Code consistency issue; maintainers must adapt to different import patterns in similar test modules
findings.remediation: Change to `from unittest import mock` to match the pattern used in all other test files (test_base.py, test_brakeman.py, test_bundler_audit.py, test_cargo_audit.py, test_eslint_security.py, test_npm_audit.py, test_osv_scanner.py, test_pip_audit.py, test_spotbugs.py)

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Verified exactly as stated, and the claim does not overreach. /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/tests/tools/test_legacy_sarif.py:6 reads `from unittest.mock import patch`. A grep of import lines across tests/tools/ shows every other module in that directory that imports mock uses `from unittest import mock`: test_base.py:5, test_brakeman.py:5, test_bundler_audit.py:4, test_cargo_audit.py:5, test_eslint_security.py:6, test_npm_audit.py:5, test_osv_scanner.py:6, test_pip_audit.py:5, test_spotbugs.py:4 — i.e. all nine files the remediation enumerates, matched exactly. The remaining files in the directory (test_dependency_check.py, test_roslyn_secguard.py, and the *_integration.py modules) import mock not at all, so they neither support nor contradict the claim; test_legacy_sarif.py is the sole dissenter among mock-using modules there. Two qualifications that bound, but do not defeat, the finding: (1) repo-wide the pattern is not unique — tests/test_model_resolver.py:7 also uses `from unittest.mock import patch` — but the claim explicitly scopes itself to 'the directory', which is accurate; (2) the inconsistency is purely cosmetic, since `patch.object(subprocess, "run")` and `mock.patch("scripts.tools.base.subprocess.run")` patch the same attribute on the same singleton subprocess module and thus behave identically. The claim's stated impact is confined to consistency and maintainer cognitive load, which is what the evidence supports, and LOW severity is the right weight.

findings.title: Vacuous/tautological test provides no real verification of cargo-audit skip behavior
findings.description: `test_cargo_audit_skips_without_rust` only asserts `adapter is not None` and, when `cargo` is unavailable on the host, falls through to a bare `self.assertTrue(True)`. It never calls `adapter.is_applicable()` on a directory without `Cargo.toml`, never calls `adapter.invoke()` with a missing `cargo` binary, and never asserts anything about the actual 'skip without rust' behavior the test name promises. The file is also misleadingly named `test_rust_cs_integration.py` ('Rust + C#') yet contains zero C# coverage — that lives entirely in `test_csharp_integration.py`. Because the final assertion is `assertTrue(True)`, this test will pass unconditionally regardless of whether the underlying skip/applicability logic is correct or broken.
findings.impact: The test suite reports coverage for cargo-audit's non-Rust-environment behavior that does not actually exist. A regression in `CargoAuditAdapter.is_applicable()` or in how `run_tools.py` handles a missing `cargo` binary would go completely undetected, giving false confidence during review and CI.
findings.remediation: Replace the no-op branch with a real assertion, e.g. mock `shutil.which` to simulate a missing `cargo` binary and assert `adapter.is_applicable(tmp_without_cargo_toml)` is False, or assert that `invoke()` fails gracefully (non-crashing, propagated non-zero rc) when the binary is absent. Rename the file/class to reflect only the tool(s) it actually exercises, or add the promised C#-specific coverage.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Every specific factual sub-claim checks out against tests/tools/test_rust_cs_integration.py lines 11-16. The method body is: fetch ADAPTERS['cargo-audit'], assertIsNotNone, SkipTest if `shutil.which('cargo')`, else `self.assertTrue(True)`. It never calls `adapter.is_applicable()`, never calls `adapter.invoke()`, and asserts nothing about the 'skips without rust' behavior its name promises. The naming complaint is also verified: the file/class say 'rust_cs' / TestRustCsIntegration but there is zero C#/roslyn-secguard coverage in it; the only roslyn-secguard integration test lives in tests/tools/test_csharp_integration.py (test_roslyn_secguard_finds_aspnet_issues). Provenance corroborates intent: docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-01-scanner-ecosystem-expansion.md lines 1128-1150 label this file an 'integration placeholder' and contain the identical `self.assertTrue(True)` body, so the vacuity is inherited verbatim from the plan rather than an accident. One correction to the impact paragraph, which overstates: a regression in CargoAuditAdapter.is_applicable() would NOT go 'completely undetected' — tests/tools/test_cargo_audit.py:36-38 asserts is_applicable is True when Cargo.toml exists, and :46-54 pins the exact invoke argv ['cargo','audit','--format','json'] with cwd/timeout. The genuinely uncovered gaps are (i) the negative is_applicable path (no Cargo.toml) and (ii) missing-binary handling. On (ii), note the production path does not depend on host cargo at all: skill/scripts/run_tools.py:152-176 dispatches adapters inside the panopticon-tools Docker image via _run_adapter.py, so the host `shutil.which('cargo')` gate in this test does not model the real execution environment — which makes the test even less meaningful than the claim states. Severity MEDIUM is reasonable for a test-quality/dead-code finding; CWE-561 is an apt mapping.

findings.title: cargo-audit's hand-rolled CVSS v3.1 score approximation (_cvss_v3_score) has zero test coverage
findings.description: `scripts/tools/cargo_audit.py` defines `_cvss_v3_score()`, a fairly complex manual re-implementation of the CVSS v3.1 base-score formula (metric lookup tables, impact/exploitability sub-scores, scope-changed branch, `min(..., 10.0)` clamping) that determines whether a RUSTSEC advisory is bucketed CRITICAL/HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW. No test in `test_cargo_audit.py` (or anywhere else in the repo — confirmed by repo-wide search) exercises this function directly or indirectly. `CARGO_AUDIT_SAMPLE` explicitly sets `"cvss": None`, sidestepping the scoring path entirely, and `test_parse_produces_finding` never asserts on the resulting `severity` field at all, nor is the dict-form `cvss.get('score', 0)` branch tested.
findings.impact: A defect in the CVSS approximation (e.g. a wrong metric-table constant, an off-by-something in the impact/exploitability formula, or a scope-changed miscalculation) could silently misclassify a CRITICAL Rust dependency vulnerability as MEDIUM or LOW, causing it to be deprioritized or filtered out of downstream triage — with no test able to catch the regression.
findings.remediation: Add unit tests that pass known CVSS v3.1 vector strings with published reference base scores (both scope-unchanged and scope-changed) and assert `_cvss_v3_score()`/the resulting `severity` matches the expected NVD bucket, plus a case using the dict-form `cvss: {"score": N}` path.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning:
Verified independently. `_cvss_v3_score()` exists at /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/tools/cargo_audit.py:8-40 and is a hand-rolled CVSS v3.1 base-score implementation: ISS product formula with the {N:0, L:0.22, H:0.56} impact table, the scope-changed branch `7.52*(iss-0.029) - 3.25*(iss-0.02)**15`, exploitability `8.22*av*ac*pr*ui`, the nested PR table keyed on scope, and `min(..., 10.0)` clamping (note it omits the spec's Roundup step, so scores sit slightly below the NVD value near bucket edges). Its sole call site is cargo_audit.py:68, inside `parse()`, and its output drives the CRITICAL/HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW bucketing at lines 66/70.

A repo-wide grep for `_cvss_v3_score` returns exactly two hits, both in cargo_audit.py — no test references it. The claim's specific assertions about the test file all check out against tests/tools/test_cargo_audit.py: line 17 sets `"cvss": None`, which makes `parse()` skip both the dict branch (line 64) and the string branch (line 67) and fall through to the hardcoded `severity = "HIGH"` default; `test_parse_produces_finding` (lines 29-34) asserts only `source` and `tool_evidence.package_name`, never `severity`; and no test anywhere supplies the dict form `cvss: {"score": N}` for this adapter (grep for `cvss` across tests/ shows dict-form cvss only in test_synthesize.py/test_citations.py, which exercise synthesize/citation code, and CVSS vector strings only in test_osv_scanner.py/test_phase1_integration.py/test_schemas.py, which feed the separate OSV adapter whose `_cvss_bucket` IS tested at tests/tools/test_osv_scanner.py:84-89).

One nuance the claim overstates: tests/tools/test_rust_integration.py:15-34 can reach `parse()` with real cargo-audit output, which would indirectly call `_cvss_v3_score` if an advisory carries a string cvss — so 'indirectly' is not strictly true in a cargo-audit-equipped environment. But that test skips unless `cargo` is on PATH and the vulnerable-rust fixture is present, and CI (.github/workflows/ci.yml) installs no Rust tooling and never installs cargo-audit, so it will skip there; more importantly it asserts only that findings exist and carry RUSTSEC citations, never the severity. So no assertion anywhere validates the scoring output, and the substance of the claim — the severity-determining CVSS math is unguarded by any regression test — holds.

findings.short_title: cargo-audit's hand-rolled CVSS v3.1 score approximation (_cvss_v3_score) has zero test coverage

evidence.reasoning:
Verified independently. `_cvss_v3_score()` exists at /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/tools/cargo_audit.py:8-40 and is a hand-rolled CVSS v3.1 base-score implementation: ISS product formula with the {N:0, L:0.22, H:0.56} impact table, the scope-changed branch `7.52*(iss-0.029) - 3.25*(iss-0.02)**15`, exploitability `8.22*av*ac*pr*ui`, the nested PR table keyed on scope, and `min(..., 10.0)` clamping (note it omits the spec's Roundup step, so scores sit slightly below the NVD value near bucket edges). Its sole call site is cargo_audit.py:68, inside `parse()`, and its output drives the CRITICAL/HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW bucketing at lines 66/70.

A repo-wide grep for `_cvss_v3_score` returns exactly two hits, both in cargo_audit.py — no test references it. The claim's specific assertions about the test file all check out against tests/tools/test_cargo_audit.py: line 17 sets `"cvss": None`, which makes `parse()` skip both the dict branch (line 64) and the string branch (line 67) and fall through to the hardcoded `severity = "HIGH"` default; `test_parse_produces_finding` (lines 29-34) asserts only `source` and `tool_evidence.package_name`, never `severity`; and no test anywhere supplies the dict form `cvss: {"score": N}` for this adapter (grep for `cvss` across tests/ shows dict-form cvss only in test_synthesize.py/test_citations.py, which exercise synthesize/citation code, and CVSS vector strings only in test_osv_scanner.py/test_phase1_integration.py/test_schemas.py, which feed the separate OSV adapter whose `_cvss_bucket` IS tested at tests/tools/test_osv_scanner.py:84-89).

One nuance the claim overstates: tests/tools/test_rust_integration.py:15-34 can reach `parse()` with real cargo-audit output, which would indirectly call `_cvss_v3_score` if an advisory carries a string cvss — so 'indirectly' is not strictly true in a cargo-audit-equipped environment. But that test skips unless `cargo` is on PATH and the vulnerable-rust fixture is present, and CI (.github/workflows/ci.yml) installs no Rust tooling and never installs cargo-audit, so it will skip there; more importantly it asserts only that findings exist and carry RUSTSEC citations, never the severity. So no assertion anywhere validates the scoring output, and the substance of the claim — the severity-determining CVSS math is unguarded by any regression test — holds.

findings.title: No test covers malformed/incomplete pip-audit dependency entries, masking an unguarded-indexing crash risk
findings.description: `scripts/tools/pip_audit.py`'s `parse()` accesses `dep['name']` and `dep['version']` via direct dict indexing (not `.get()`), unlike every sibling adapter in this batch (npm_audit, dependency_check, brakeman, cargo_audit) which use `.get()` defensively. None of the tests in `test_pip_audit.py` supply a dependency entry missing `name` or `version`. `scripts/ingest_tools.py:ingest_dir()` wraps `adapter.parse()` in a broad `except Exception` per-file, so a single malformed dependency entry anywhere in a real pip-audit JSON report raises `KeyError` and silently drops every finding parsed from that file, not just the offending entry.
findings.impact: A partially malformed pip-audit report (e.g. an entry omitting `version` due to an editable/VCS install) would cause total, silent loss of all Python dependency-vulnerability findings for that scan, with only a terse stderr diagnostic and no test guarding against the regression.
findings.remediation: Add a test asserting behavior for a dependency dict missing `name`/`version` (either graceful `.get()`-based degradation in `pip_audit.py`, or an explicit per-entry try/except in `parse()` so one bad entry doesn't drop the whole file), matching the resilience pattern already established in `test_osv_scanner.py::test_parse_tolerates_malformed_entries`.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Every factual assertion in the claim checks out, and I found an additional unguarded index in the same block that makes the crash risk more likely than the claim's own example. (1) Direct indexing: skill/scripts/tools/pip_audit.py uses `dep['name']` / `dep['version']` at lines 58, 66, 71, 72 (e.g. line 58: `"title": f"{dep['name']} {dep['version']}: {vuln.get('id', 'vulnerability')}"`). (2) Sibling adapters are defensive: a repo-wide grep for bracket-literal dict access under skill/scripts/tools/ returns unguarded subscripts only in pip_audit.py; the hits in cargo_audit.py:89 (`advisory["url"]` guarded by `if advisory.get("url")`) and brakeman.py:85 are guarded, and npm_audit.py/osv_scanner.py/dependency_check.py use `.get()` throughout. (3) No test covers the gap: all four dep fixtures in tests/tools/test_pip_audit.py (lines 10-25 and 52-65) supply both `name` and `version`; nothing supplies a partial dep. (4) Blast radius is as described: skill/scripts/ingest_tools.py:78-82 wraps `adapter.parse(raw, group)` in `except Exception` at the whole-file level and `continue`s, so any KeyError discards every finding from that report with only a stderr line, while osv_scanner.py:54-55/65-67 shows the tolerant per-entry pattern the claim points to and tests/tools/test_osv_scanner.py:133-143 shows the corresponding test. Two caveats on severity. Downward: the claim's stated trigger (an entry omitting `version` for an editable/VCS install) is unlikely to fire in practice, because pip-audit renders such entries as skipped dependencies with no `vulns` key, so `dep.get('vulns', [])` yields [] and the inner loop never reaches the subscripts. Upward, and stronger: skill/scripts/tools/pip_audit.py:73 `"fixed_version": vuln.get("fix_versions", [None])[0]` raises IndexError when `fix_versions` is present but empty — a shape pip-audit emits routinely for a vulnerability with no known fix — and grep shows `fix_versions` appears in tests only as `["2.31.0"]` (tests/tools/test_pip_audit.py:18, tests/test_schemas.py:109) or absent entirely (test_parse_omits_none_tool_evidence_fields, which hits the `[None]` default, not the empty-list case). So the claim's thesis (unguarded indexing in pip_audit.parse, untested, amplified into whole-file finding loss by ingest_dir's broad except) is correct; only its illustrative trigger is off. I would file this at LOW-to-MEDIUM rather than MEDIUM as a test-coverage item, but the underlying line 73 defect is worth fixing on its own.

findings.title: roslyn-secguard hardcodes severity to HIGH for every finding; the only test carrying a SARIF 'level' field never asserts on severity
findings.description: `RoslynSecGuardAdapter.parse()` in `scripts/tools/roslyn_secguard.py` sets `"severity": normalize_severity("HIGH")` unconditionally for every result, ignoring the SARIF `level` field entirely (unlike `legacy_sarif.py`'s `sarif_to_findings`, which properly maps `level` -> severity via `LEVEL_TO_SEV`). `ROSLYN_SAMPLE_V1` in the test file even includes a `"level": "warning"` field, suggesting the fixture was adapted from a level-aware source, but `test_parse_v1_result_file` never asserts on the `severity` key, so the fixture field is dead weight and the hardcoded-HIGH behavior is neither documented nor pinned by any test.
findings.impact: Every SecurityCodeScan/roslyn-secguard finding is reported as HIGH regardless of the underlying rule's actual severity, which can over-alert on low-severity C# findings and erode signal quality; because no test exercises this, a future attempt to wire up real severity mapping (or an accidental further divergence) would be invisible to the suite.
findings.remediation: Either add a test that asserts severity is intentionally constant (documenting the design choice) or implement level/rule-based severity mapping analogous to `sarif_utils.LEVEL_TO_SEV` and add a test with a non-'warning'/non-default level to prove it varies.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning:
Every factual assertion in this claim is verifiable in the tree. (1) skill/scripts/tools/roslyn_secguard.py:123 is literally `"severity": normalize_severity("HIGH"),` inside the per-result loop of parse() -- a constant string argument, with no reference to `result.get("level")` anywhere in the file. (2) The fixture ROSLYN_SAMPLE_V1 at tests/tools/test_roslyn_secguard.py:25-41 does carry `"level": "warning"` on line 31, and test_parse_v1_result_file at lines 69-74 asserts only on len, location.file, location.line_start, and citations.cwe -- never on severity. I grepped the rest of the suite: no test anywhere asserts a severity value for this adapter (tests/tools/test_csharp_integration.py only asserts findings is truthy; tests/test_run_tools.py mentions roslyn-secguard only in a tool-name loop). (3) The contrast with level-aware SARIF handling is real: skill/scripts/tools/sarif_utils.py:15 defines LEVEL_TO_SEV = {"error": "HIGH", "warning": "MEDIUM", "note": "LOW", "none": "INFO"} and lines 73-74 apply it per result; legacy_sarif.py:52-54 delegates to that function.

I went further and found stronger corroboration than the claim itself offers: roslyn_secguard is the ONLY adapter in skill/scripts/tools/ that hardcodes a severity. npm_audit.py:31,66, dependency_check.py:78, bundler_audit.py:40, pip_audit.py:59 and brakeman.py:73 all pass tool-derived values to normalize_severity; cargo_audit.py:63-71 and osv_scanner.py:60-81 bucket CVSS scores; spotbugs.py:51 maps priority 1/2/3 to HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW; eslint_security.py:65 maps eslint's severity int. So the divergence is adapter-specific, not a house style. The concrete over-alert is demonstrable on the test's own fixture: SCS0001 arrives as level 'warning', which the repo's own LEVEL_TO_SEV would score MEDIUM, but parse() emits HIGH. Note one minor attribution slip that does not affect the substance -- sarif_to_findings lives in sarif_utils.py, not legacy_sarif.py, which merely calls it. LOW severity is appropriately conservative for what is really a signal-quality plus untested-invariant issue rather than a functional break. CWE-710 (Improper Adherence to Coding Standards) is a loose but not unreasonable fit given the adapter-wide convention it breaks; I have not asserted it as verified.

findings.title: Test asserts a retired, permanently-broken 'eslint' adapter is registered without exercising its failure path
findings.description: `test_registry_contains_legacy_adapters` loops over `("semgrep", "bandit", "trivy", "gitleaks", "gosec", "eslint")` and only checks each is present in `ADAPTERS` and correctly named. `legacy_sarif.py`'s own comment states eslint was 'retired (F-CAL-5)' and it has been removed from `LEGACY_SARIF_TOOLS`/`TOOL_CMD`, yet `scripts/tools/__init__.py` still registers `"eslint": LegacySarifAdapter("eslint")`. Because `LegacySarifAdapter.is_applicable()` unconditionally returns True and `invoke()` raises `NotImplementedError` for any name absent from `TOOL_CMD`, this registry entry is dead/broken by construction, and `test_invoke_raises_not_implemented_for_unknown_tool` only covers a `LegacySarifAdapter("unknown")` instance rather than the real `eslint` entry sitting in `ADAPTERS`.
findings.impact: A dead adapter remains discoverable/selectable (e.g. via `run_tools.py --tools eslint`) and will always fail at invoke time; the test suite currently certifies its presence without ever certifying (or warning about) this broken behavior, so the registry can silently accumulate more retired-but-still-listed adapters without any test surfacing the inconsistency.
findings.remediation: Either remove the 'eslint' key from `ADAPTERS` entirely (cleanup) or add an explicit test asserting `ADAPTERS["eslint"].invoke(...)` raises `NotImplementedError`, so the retired/broken state is a documented, intentional contract rather than an untested landmine.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Every factual assertion checks out, and I traced the reachability chain the claim only sketches. (a) tests/tools/test_legacy_sarif.py:84-88 loops `for name in ("semgrep", "bandit", "trivy", "gitleaks", "gosec", "eslint")` and asserts only membership in ADAPTERS, isinstance, and .name. (b) skill/scripts/tools/legacy_sarif.py:10-13 carries the retirement comment ('"eslint" retired (F-CAL-5)') and LEGACY_SARIF_TOOLS is `{"semgrep", "bandit", "trivy", "gitleaks", "gosec"}`; TOOL_CMD (lines 17-24) likewise has no eslint key. (c) skill/scripts/tools/__init__.py:24 still contains `"eslint": LegacySarifAdapter("eslint"),`. (d) is_applicable returns True unconditionally (legacy_sarif.py:38-39) and invoke raises `NotImplementedError(f"no command defined for tool {self.name}")` for any name absent from TOOL_CMD (lines 43-44). (e) test_invoke_raises_not_implemented_for_unknown_tool (line 75-78) instantiates LegacySarifAdapter("unknown"), never the registered eslint entry. The reachability is real and slightly worse than described: in skill/scripts/run_tools.py, `--tools eslint` hits `cmd = TOOL_CMD.get(tool)` (line 127) which is now None, falls through to the adapter path at line 152 where `ADAPTERS.get("eslint")` is truthy, and dispatches `_run_adapter.py eslint` in Docker; skill/scripts/_run_adapter.py:23-28 catches the NotImplementedError, prints 'adapter eslint crashed: ...; skipping' and returns 0, so run_tools sees rc 0 (inside the (0,1) success band) and writes an EMPTY .panopticon/tools/eslint.json (line 154-155 picks ext 'json' since eslint is no longer in LEGACY_SARIF_TOOLS). skill/scripts/ingest_tools.py:58 then resolves that stem back to the same dead adapter and json.loads of b'' fails into 'ingest error'. `select_adapters()` also returns eslint (is_applicable True), so `run_adapters()` would hit the same NotImplementedError. Two mitigations that justify the LOW severity rather than higher: the default CLI path filters selection through PHASE1_ADAPTERS/PHASE2_ADAPTERS (run_tools.py:200-201), neither of which contains 'eslint', and LANG_TOOL (line 19) no longer maps js/ts to it — so only an explicit --tools eslint reaches the dead path, and every failure is caught rather than crashing the run. docs/superpowers/2026-08-03-calibration-fixmes.md:62 records F-CAL-5 as resolved 'by deleting the legacy eslint entries', which the code shows was done for TOOL_CMD and LEGACY_SARIF_TOOLS but not for the ADAPTERS registry — the test at line 85 is what keeps that leftover pinned in place. CWE-561 (Dead Code) is an apt citation.

findings.title: Fixture-gated integration tests always skip in this checkout, giving false confidence of adapter coverage
findings.description: `test_java_integration.py`, `test_csharp_integration.py`, and `test_ruby_integration.py` each gate their sole test(s) on vendored external fixtures ('WebGoat', 'AspGoat', 'railsgoat') under `tests/fixtures/`. A repository-wide search confirms none of these directories are vendored in this checkout (only `insecure-js/`, `manifest.json`, `semgrep.sarif`, `vulnerable-node/`, `vulnerable-python/`, `vulnerable-rust/` exist). Every test in these three files therefore calls `self.skipTest(...)` and reports as skipped, not passed or failed, on any standard run of this suite.
findings.impact: CI/local runs report these files as 'passing' (skipped tests don't fail a run) while providing zero actual verification that spotbugs, dependency-check, brakeman, bundler-audit, or roslyn-secguard correctly find real vulnerabilities end-to-end. A regression in any of these adapters' `invoke()`/`parse()` real-world behavior would not be caught unless a developer happens to have the large vendored fixture repos checked out locally, which most contributors and CI will not.
findings.remediation: Either vendor the fixtures (as submodules or a documented setup step) and fail loudly (not skip) when a CI job that's supposed to run integration tests can't find them, or replace these with smaller committed synthetic fixtures that don't depend on external vendored apps, so the adapters get real coverage on every run.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Every mechanical assertion checks out. tests/tools/test_java_integration.py:17-45 gates both tests on os.path.isdir(FIXTURE_ROOT/'WebGoat') -> self.skipTest('WebGoat fixture not vendored'); test_ruby_integration.py:17-41 does the same for 'railsgoat'; test_csharp_integration.py:14-27 for 'AspGoat'. FIXTURE_ROOT defaults to tests/fixtures (line 8-10 of each file). A recursive glob of tests/fixtures/** returns only insecure-js/app.js, manifest.json, semgrep.sarif, vulnerable-node/{package.json,package-lock.json}, vulnerable-python/requirements.txt, vulnerable-rust/{Cargo.toml,Cargo.lock,.gitignore,src/main.rs} — no WebGoat, railsgoat, or AspGoat directory exists in the checkout, and .gitignore has no entry for them (they are simply not vendored). .github/workflows/ci.yml:41 runs `python -m pytest tests/ -q` with no FIXTURE_ROOT env and no Docker fixture image, so on CI all five tests in those three files skip; skips do not fail a pytest run. Adapter parse() does have synthetic unit coverage (e.g. tests/tools/test_spotbugs.py feeds a hand-written BugCollection XML), but invoke() and real-tool end-to-end behavior for spotbugs, dependency-check, brakeman, bundler-audit, and roslyn-secguard are exercised only by these gated tests, matching the claim's impact statement. Two mitigating facts the claim omits, which bear on severity but not on correctness: the repo ships a deliberate out-of-band harness — Dockerfile.fixtures clones railsgoat/WebGoat/AspGoat into /opt/panopticon-fixtures and sets ENV FIXTURE_ROOT=/opt/panopticon-fixtures (lines 26-32, 51), driven by skill/scripts/run_fixture_tests.py and documented in DEVELOPMENT.md:74-83 — and docs/superpowers/2026-08-03-calibration-fixmes.md:9-11 records a run where all four fixtures were present and green. So this is an intentional opt-in design, not an oversight; contributors do not need to 'happen to' have the repos, they run one documented command. That said, the claim's remediation point about failing loudly is independently supported: run_fixture_tests.py:125-138 prints '[MISSING] <name>' but still returns only pytest's exit code, and since missing fixtures produce skips (not failures), the dedicated fixture runner also exits 0 with zero adapters actually exercised. Verdict CONFIRMED on the verified facts; LOW severity is appropriate and arguably generous given the documented harness.
