So this is an intentional opt-in design, not an oversight; contributors do not need to 'happen to' have the repos, they run one documented command. That said, the claim's remediation point about failing loudly is independently supported: run_fixture_tests.py:125-138 prints '[MISSING] <name>' but still returns only pytest's exit code, and since missing fixtures produce skips (not failures), the dedicated fixture runner also exits 0 with zero adapters actually exercised. Verdict CONFIRMED on the verified facts; LOW severity is appropriate and arguably generous given the documented harness.

findings.title: base.ID_RE finding-ID format regex is untested and diverges from the canonical validator in synthesize.py
findings.description: `scripts/tools/base.py` defines `ID_RE = re.compile(r"^[A-Z]{2,4}-\d{3,}$")` but `test_base.py` never references or asserts against it. The canonical/actually-enforced finding-ID validator lives in `scripts/synthesize.py` (`ID_RE = re.compile(r"^[A-Z]{2,8}-\d{3,}$")`, explicitly commented '{2,8}: real agents emit e.g. STRUCT-001'), which allows longer prefixes than base.py's copy. base.ID_RE currently has no callers anywhere in `scripts/` (grep confirms), making it dead code with a narrower, silently-inconsistent contract relative to the format actually enforced by the pipeline.
findings.impact: Low direct risk today since it's unused, but it's a latent trap: if a future adapter or refactor starts validating IDs with `base.ID_RE` instead of `synthesize.ID_RE`, any prefix longer than 4 characters (e.g. a hypothetical 'ESLINT' or other 5-8 char prefix that `synthesize.py`'s own docstring anticipates) would be silently rejected by one validator and accepted by the other, and no test exists to catch that divergence.
findings.remediation: Remove the unused `ID_RE` from `base.py` (import the shared one from `synthesize.py` or a common module if still needed), or if it must remain, add a test in `test_base.py` pinning its contract and asserting it matches `synthesize.ID_RE`'s bounds.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Every factual assertion in the claim checks out. (1) `skill/scripts/tools/base.py:38` defines `ID_RE = re.compile(r"^[A-Z]{2,4}-\d{3,}$")` verbatim. (2) `skill/scripts/synthesize.py:454` defines `ID_RE = re.compile(r"^[A-Z]{2,8}-\d{3,}$")  # {2,8}: real agents emit e.g. STRUCT-001`, and it is the enforced one — it is the only ID validator actually invoked, at synthesize.py:723 (`if not ID_RE.match(f.get("id", "")):`). So the two copies genuinely disagree on prefix length (4 vs 8). (3) I read all 90 lines of tests/tools/test_base.py: it covers normalize_severity, new_finding_id, omit_none, attach_tool_provenance and run_tool, and never mentions ID_RE. A repo-wide grep for `ID_RE` returns only base.py:38, synthesize.py:454/723, tests/test_synthesize.py:1437-1439/1537 (which test `syn.ID_RE`, i.e. the synthesize copy), and two docs files — no test touches base.ID_RE. (4) The dead-code assertion holds: no module imports ID_RE from base. Grepping every `from .base import` / `from scripts.tools.base import` across skill/scripts/tools/ (brakeman, bundler_audit, cargo_audit, npm_audit, pip_audit, osv_scanner, eslint_security, spotbugs, dependency_check, roslyn_secguard, legacy_sarif) shows the imported names are only attach_tool_provenance, normalize_severity, new_finding_id, omit_none, run_tool; there are no `import *` statements anywhere under skill/. Corroborating history: docs/superpowers/2026-08-03-calibration-fixmes.md:61 and :88 record F-CAL-4 ('ID_RE rejects real agent ids ... Widen to {2,8}') as resolved 'by widening ID_RE to {2,8}' — the fix was applied to synthesize.py only and base.py's copy was left behind at {2,4}, which is exactly the stale-duplicate divergence described. Severity LOW and category test-coverage are appropriate: the regex is currently unreachable, so the impact is latent, not active. The claim's references use paths without the `skill/` prefix in one field but the `references` array cites the correct `skill/scripts/...` paths and both line numbers are exact.

findings.title: Misleadingly named test verifies a static dict lookup, not a CWE-uppercasing transformation
findings.description: `test_parse_uppercases_cwe` asserts `findings[0]["citations"]["cwe"] == ["CWE-95"]`, but `eslint_security.py`'s `parse()` never uppercases anything — it does a direct `RULE_CWE.get(rule)` lookup into a dict whose values are already the literal string `"CWE-95"`. There is no `.upper()` call or case-normalization logic anywhere in the CWE path of this adapter. This is unlike the correctly-named `test_parse_uppercases_cve` tests in `test_npm_audit.py`/`test_osv_scanner.py`, which genuinely exercise `.upper()` calls (`c.upper()` / `a.upper()`) on tool-supplied CVE strings.
findings.impact: The test name misleads future maintainers into believing CWE case-normalization is implemented and tested for eslint-security, when in fact any future change accepting externally-supplied CWE strings (e.g. from a rule config) with inconsistent casing would have no real test coverage for normalization.
findings.remediation: Rename the test to reflect what it actually checks (e.g. `test_parse_maps_rule_to_cwe`), and if CWE case-normalization is a desired guarantee for this adapter, add a fixture that would fail if the lookup weren't case-safe.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Verified on both sides. In skill/scripts/tools/eslint_security.py the CWE path is a plain dict lookup: line 66 `cwe = RULE_CWE.get(rule)` against the module-level `RULE_CWE` (lines 10-22) whose values are already the literal strings `"CWE-95"`, `"CWE-114"`, etc.; lines 83-84 then set `finding["citations"] = {"cwe": [cwe]}`. A repo-wide grep for `upper()` in skill/scripts/tools/ returns hits only in cargo_audit.py:73, npm_audit.py:27/60, sarif_utils.py:88-89, osv_scanner.py:69-70, bundler_audit.py:50 and pip_audit.py:55 — none in eslint_security.py. So there is no case-normalization anywhere in this adapter's CWE path, and `test_parse_uppercases_cwe` (tests/tools/test_eslint_security.py:48-63) feeds an already-correctly-cased `ruleId` and asserts the dict's own literal value comes back; the name promises a transformation the test cannot exercise. The claim's contrast is also accurate: tests/tools/test_npm_audit.py:38-54 feeds lowercase `"cves": ["cve-2021-23337"]` and expects `"CVE-2021-23337"`, genuinely exercising npm_audit.py:27's `c.upper()`; tests/tools/test_osv_scanner.py:91-95 likewise uses the lowercase alias `"cve-2024-47081"` (line 30) and expects `"CVE-2024-47081"`, exercising osv_scanner.py:69-70. Scope caveats that keep this at LOW: the test is not worthless — line 63 is the only assertion in the file covering the `RULE_CWE` -> `citations.cwe` mapping at all, so it has real value under a corrected name; and the claimed impact is somewhat speculative since `RULE_CWE` values are hardcoded constants, not externally supplied. The defect is genuine but is a test-naming/accuracy issue, not a coverage hole. Cited CWE-710 is a generic 'coding standards' bucket and is at best a loose fit; I did not treat it as verified.

findings.title: test_parse_produces_finding never asserts the severity field despite the fixture defining severity: HIGH
findings.description: `DC_SAMPLE` sets `"severity": "HIGH"` for its vulnerability entry, and `dependency_check.py`'s `parse()` computes `"severity": normalize_severity(vuln.get("severity"))`, but `test_parse_produces_finding` checks `source`, `citations["cve"]`, `citations["cwe"]`, and `tool_evidence["package_name"]` — never `f["severity"]`. This is the only adapter test file in the batch whose primary happy-path test omits a severity assertion despite the fixture explicitly carrying a severity value.
findings.impact: A regression that broke severity normalization for dependency-check specifically (e.g. a typo passing the wrong field name into `normalize_severity`) would not be caught by this file's tests.
findings.remediation: Add `self.assertEqual(f["severity"], "HIGH")` to `test_parse_produces_finding` for parity with the other adapter test files' happy-path coverage.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The load-bearing facts check out. DC_SAMPLE at tests/tools/test_dependency_check.py:16 sets "severity": "HIGH"; skill/scripts/tools/dependency_check.py:78 computes `"severity": normalize_severity(vuln.get("severity"))`; and test_parse_produces_finding (lines 27-34) asserts only len(findings), f["source"], f["citations"]["cve"], f["citations"]["cwe"] and f["tool_evidence"]["package_name"] — never f["severity"]. No other test in the file or elsewhere in tests/ asserts a dependency-check severity value. The proposed remediation is correct: normalize_severity in skill/scripts/tools/base.py:41-44 maps "high" -> "HIGH" via SEV_MAP, so `self.assertEqual(f["severity"], "HIGH")` would pass today and would catch a regression that passed the wrong field name (which would silently fall through to the "INFO" default, since normalize_severity returns "INFO" for both non-str and unmapped input — a genuinely silent failure mode). One qualifier in the description is false and should be struck: this is NOT the only adapter test file whose happy path omits a severity assertion despite a severity-carrying fixture. tests/tools/test_bundler_audit.py's BUNDLE_AUDIT_SAMPLE carries "Criticality: High" and "Criticality: Medium" (lines 14, 23) yet test_parse_produces_findings (lines 31-35) asserts only package_name and citations.cve. By contrast, test_cargo_audit.py's fixture has "cvss": None and test_roslyn_secguard.py's ROSLYN_SAMPLE carries no level field, so those two are legitimately excluded. The correction broadens rather than undermines the finding.

findings.title: Missing tests for dependency_check invoke and is_applicable methods
findings.description: DependencyCheckAdapter has invoke() (lines 18-40) and is_applicable() (lines 14-16) methods that are not tested at all. Only parse() is tested. invoke() has complex logic with temp directory, NVD_API_KEY env var handling, and file I/O.
findings.impact: Critical adapter methods are completely untested; invoke logic including env var handling, temp dir cleanup, and JSON file reading are not validated.
findings.remediation: Add comprehensive test coverage for invoke() including temp directory creation, NVD API key handling, and file operations. Add test for is_applicable() with pom.xml, build.gradle, and build.gradle.kts.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning:
The core factual assertion holds. The adapter lives at skill/scripts/tools/dependency_check.py (NOT scripts/tools/dependency_check.py as cited — that path does not exist at repo root; the test file makes it importable as scripts.tools.dependency_check via `sys.path.insert(0, .../skill)`). In that file DependencyCheckAdapter.is_applicable is lines 14-16 and invoke is lines 18-42 (the claim says 18-40, slightly short: the try/finally shutil.rmtree cleanup runs to line 42). tests/tools/test_dependency_check.py contains exactly four tests, all covering parse() and the static _normalize_cwe() helper; grep across tests/ for `is_applicable|\.invoke\(` confirms no unit test constructs DependencyCheckAdapter and calls either method.

I chased the one cross-file reference that could refute this: tests/tools/test_java_integration.py:30-45 (`test_dependency_check_finds_webgoat_vulns`) does call `adapter.is_applicable(target)` and `adapter.invoke(target)` via ADAPTERS['dependency-check']. However it is gated by `if not os.path.isdir(target): self.skipTest('WebGoat fixture not vendored')`, and the WebGoat fixture is not in the repo — tests/fixtures/ contains only insecure-js, manifest.json, semgrep.sarif, vulnerable-node, vulnerable-python, vulnerable-rust. WebGoat is cloned only inside the Docker fixtures image (Dockerfile.fixtures:29 git clone WebGoat, Dockerfile.fixtures:51 ENV FIXTURE_ROOT=/opt/panopticon-fixtures). So on a normal `python -m unittest` run the invoke/is_applicable path never executes; and even inside the fixtures container the test skips again on a non-zero/non-one rc. It is also an end-to-end test that would not isolate the NVD_API_KEY branch (line 25/33-34), the DEPENDENCY_CHECK_HOME default (line 21), the missing-report `return b'{}'` fallback (line 40), or the tempdir cleanup. So 'not tested at all' is a mild overstatement but the substance — no effective unit coverage — is correct.

The gap is also anomalous against a clear repo convention: peer adapters have mock-based unit tests for both methods (tests/tools/test_npm_audit.py:74-96, test_pip_audit.py:72-126, test_brakeman.py:37-56, test_bundler_audit.py:37-50, test_cargo_audit.py:36-49, test_osv_scanner.py:103-124, test_eslint_security.py:110-155). dependency_check and spotbugs are the outliers (test_spotbugs.py:31 covers is_applicable but not invoke), so the same gap arguably applies to spotbugs' invoke too.

Two qualifications on the claim's metadata rather than its facts: (a) HIGH severity is inflated — this is a missing-unit-test gap on a subprocess wrapper with no security-relevant decision logic (the NVD_API_KEY branch only toggles a --noupdate flag), and MEDIUM/LOW would be the honest grade; (b) the CWE-1164 ('Irrelevant Code') citation is a poor mapping for missing test coverage and is already marked verified:false — I could not substantiate it and do not carry it forward.

findings.title: Duplicate FIXTURE_ROOT initialization across integration tests
findings.description: FIXTURE_ROOT constant (lines 8-10) is identically defined in test_java_integration.py, test_ruby_integration.py, test_csharp_integration.py, and test_rust_integration.py. This repetition violates DRY and increases maintenance burden.
findings.impact: Same initialization logic must be maintained across multiple files. Environment variable handling is inconsistent if updated in one file.
findings.remediation: Define FIXTURE_ROOT once in a shared location (conftest.py or base test module) and import it in all integration test files.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Verified verbatim. The three-line block `FIXTURE_ROOT = os.environ.get("FIXTURE_ROOT", os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), "..", "fixtures"))` appears character-identically in tests/tools/test_java_integration.py:8-10, tests/tools/test_ruby_integration.py:8-10, tests/tools/test_csharp_integration.py:8-10, and tests/tools/test_rust_integration.py:9-11 (offset by one only because that file also imports shutil). A grep for FIXTURE_ROOT across tests/ returns exactly these four definitions and no other. The remediation is also actionable as written: a Glob for **/conftest.py returns no files anywhere in the repo, so there is currently no shared test-support module, and each of the four files additionally repeats the same `sys.path.insert(0, ..."skill")` bootstrap line. Note the duplication extends slightly further than the claim states — test_java_integration.py and test_ruby_integration.py wrap FIXTURE_ROOT in a _target() helper while test_csharp_integration.py:15 and test_rust_integration.py:18 inline os.path.join(FIXTURE_ROOT, ...), so the four copies are already used inconsistently, which reinforces rather than undercuts the claim. This is an accurate but genuinely trivial DRY observation (three duplicated lines, no behavioral defect); LOW severity is correct and no functional risk was found.

findings.title: roslyn-secguard runs `dotnet build` on scanned code, executing arbitrary MSBuild targets/NuGet package content
findings.description: RoslynSecGuardAdapter.invoke() (exercised by tests/tools/test_roslyn_secguard.py::test_invoke_builds_in_temp_copy and tests/tools/test_csharp_integration.py::test_roslyn_secguard_finds_aspnet_issues) copies the scanned target into a temp dir and runs `dotnet build` against it to obtain SecurityCodeScan SARIF output. Unlike every other adapter in this panel (brakeman, spotbugs, eslint-security, bandit/semgrep via legacy_sarif), which are pure static analyzers that never execute the scanned code, `dotnet build` performs a full MSBuild run: it restores NuGet packages (potentially from feeds configured in the scanned repo's own nuget.config) and executes any MSBuild `.targets`/`.props`/custom Tasks the project references. MSBuild targets and NuGet packages are well-known vectors for build-time code execution (PowerShell/exe payloads shipped as package content, `Target BeforeTargets="Build"` blocks, custom `UsingTask` assemblies). No `--no-restore`, source allow-list, or sandboxing flag is used to constrain this.
findings.impact: Any repository (or malicious PR/fork) scanned by this pipeline can achieve arbitrary code execution inside the security-scanning environment simply by shipping a `.csproj`/`.sln` with a malicious MSBuild target or a NuGet package with build-time scripts — before any actual security analysis takes place. This can be used to exfiltrate secrets available to the scanning process (e.g., NVD_API_KEY used by the sibling dependency-check adapter, git credentials, CI tokens), tamper with in-flight findings, or pivot to other scan targets/hosts.
findings.remediation: Do not build untrusted code as part of static analysis. findings.title: RoslynSecGuardAdapter executes untrusted repository code via a live `dotnet build` (arbitrary MSBuild task execution)
findings.description: invoke() runs `dotnet build tmp_target -p:TreatWarningsAsErrors=false -p:ErrorLog=...` directly against the scanned target repository — precisely the (potentially adversarial) input under review. Unlike every other adapter in this package (brakeman, bundler-audit, cargo-audit, spotbugs, npm-audit, pip-audit-with-lockfile, osv-scanner), which only parse manifests/bytecode/AST, `dotnet build` fully evaluates and executes the project's `.csproj`/`.sln`/`.props`/`.targets` files. MSBuild natively supports inline `<Target><Exec Command="..."/></Target>` elements and custom `UsingTask` task assemblies that run arbitrary OS commands as part of a normal build, and NuGet package restore can pull in packages whose own `.targets` do the same. None of this requires anything beyond a `.csproj`/`.sln` file existing in the scanned repo (which is exactly what `is_applicable()` looks for).
findings.impact: A malicious or compromised C# repository submitted for automated review (e.g. a hostile fork PR) achieves arbitrary code execution inside the panopticon-tools scanning container before any finding is ever produced. This can be used to exfiltrate anything reachable from the container (other tool adapters' secrets such as NVD_API_KEY, the read-only mounted scripts directory, network-reachable services), tamper with or suppress the resulting SARIF/finding output to hide real vulnerabilities, or pivot further if the container has any elevated access.
findings.remediation: Do not build untrusted source directly in the shared scanning environment. Either (a) run this adapter in a fully isolated, network-disabled, secrets-free, single-use container with a hard wall-clock/resource limit and no access to other adapters' mounts, or (b) replace the build-based approach with a compile-free static analysis path (e.g. Roslyn syntax/semantic analysis via `Microsoft.CodeAnalysis` against source only, without invoking MSBuild targets or NuGet restore).

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Independently verified against the code. /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/tools/roslyn_secguard.py:61-66 builds the command `dotnet build <tmp copy of scanned repo> -p:TreatWarningsAsErrors=false -p:ErrorLog=<tmp>/out.sarif,version=2.1` and executes it through `run_tool` -> `subprocess.run` (skill/scripts/tools/base.py:64-78). `dotnet build` evaluates and executes the scanned repo's MSBuild project files, and with no `--no-restore` it also restores NuGet packages, so attacker-authored `<Target><Exec/></Target>`, `UsingTask` assemblies, or package build targets execute before any analysis output exists. The claim's trigger condition is accurate: `is_applicable()` (lines 26-31) only requires a top-level `.csproj`/`.sln`, `select_adapters()` filters on exactly that (run_tools.py:88-91), roslyn-secguard is listed in PHASE2_ADAPTERS (run_tools.py:26-29), and run_tools.py:151-181 dispatches it into the panopticon-tools container, whose Dockerfile:85-101 installs the .NET SDK and a repo-wide `/Directory.Build.props`. Note `_build_target()` (lines 33-47) picks the first sorted `.sln` else `.csproj` found recursively, so a solution build pulls in every referenced project. I confirmed the comparator claim for the two adapters I read (spotbugs.py analyzes existing class files; cargo_audit.py only runs `cargo audit --format json`); neither compiles the target. The project's own documented invariant (DEVELOPMENT.md:55-56, 'SAST/SCA only parse code, never execute it') is the stated justification for dropping `--network none`, and this adapter breaks it. Scope change (S:C) would require a container escape, which I found no evidence for. The core defect — executing untrusted repository build logic inside the scanning environment with network access and no sandboxing flags — is confirmed. This is the same underlying defect as claim 008-SEC-101; the two are duplicates.

findings.title: eslint-security's own code comment confirms plugin resolution is project-root-relative, creating a plugin-hijack RCE vector
findings.description: invoke() (covered by tests/tools/test_eslint_security.py::test_invoke_runs_eslint_security / test_invoke_enables_all_rule_cwe_rules) always passes `--plugin security` and only appends global node_modules directories to NODE_PATH as a fallback. The adapter's own inline comment states: 'eslint v10 resolves plugins relative to the project root' — i.e., the scanned target's own `node_modules/eslint-plugin-security`, not the globally installed trusted copy, is what ESLint's module resolution will find first if present. ESLint plugins are ordinary Node modules: their top-level code executes immediately on `require()`, before any lint rule runs. No `cwd` isolation, `--resolve-plugins-relative-to`, or integrity check pins resolution to the trusted global plugin.
findings.impact: Any scanned JavaScript/TypeScript repository that ships its own `node_modules/eslint-plugin-security` (via a compromised/typosquatted transitive dependency, dependency confusion, or a deliberately malicious fixture) has that code loaded and executed inside the scanning process at lint time, before the scan produces any output — full RCE in the scanner's context, including access to other adapters' credentials (e.g., NVD_API_KEY, git tokens) available in the same environment.
findings.remediation: Force plugin resolution to a fixed, trusted location: use `--resolve-plugins-relative-to <trusted-dir>` (or ESLint's flat-config `plugins` object with an explicitly `require()`d module from a pinned path) instead of relying on ambient/NODE_PATH resolution order. Consider running the scanned target's own dependencies with `--ignore-pattern node_modules` excluded from resolution, or vendoring the security plugin so the trusted copy always wins regardless of the target's node_modules contents.
findings.exploit_scenario: A scanned JS repository (or a dependency pulled in via `npm install` before scanning) includes `node_modules/eslint-plugin-security/index.js` containing attacker JS that exfiltrates environment variables on load. When eslint-security's invoke() runs `eslint --plugin security ... <target>`, Node resolves `eslint-plugin-security` from the target's own node_modules ahead of the NODE_PATH fallback, executing the attacker's code inside the scanning container with the scanner's environment (including any credentials other adapters rely on, such as NVD_API_KEY).

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The mechanism the claim describes is present in the code and I could trace the whole path. `/Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/tools/eslint_security.py:36-52` builds `['eslint', '--no-config-lookup', '--parser-options', 'ecmaVersion:latest', '--plugin', 'security', ...]` and passes only `env` to `run_tool`; there is no `--resolve-plugins-relative-to`, no `cwd=` argument, and no integrity check. `run_tool` in `skill/scripts/tools/base.py:64-78` calls `subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, timeout=..., **kwargs)`, so with no `cwd` kwarg the eslint child inherits the parent's cwd. In the documented execution path (README `python skill/scripts/run_tools.py --target . --deps` -> `run_tools.run_tools` lines 151-167) the adapter is dispatched as `docker run --rm -v <target>:/src:ro -v <scripts>:/opt/panopticon/scripts:ro panopticon-tools python3 /opt/panopticon/scripts/_run_adapter.py eslint-security`, and `Dockerfile:111` sets `WORKDIR /src`. So eslint runs with cwd == the scanned target root, and `_run_adapter.py:17` passes target `/src`. Node's CJS resolver (`Module._resolveLookupPaths`) concatenates the parent's node_modules walk BEFORE `modulePaths` (the NODE_PATH/global folders), so `/src/node_modules/eslint-plugin-security` is found ahead of the `/usr/local/lib/node_modules` entry the adapter appends at lines 47-51 — NODE_PATH is a fallback, exactly as the adapter's own comment implies. ESLint's flat-config `--plugin` handling resolves plugin names through a module importer rooted at the cwd, and requiring a plugin executes its top-level module code before any rule runs. Supporting evidence that this breaks a stated design assumption: `skill/scripts/run_tools.py:1-5` docstring says 'Network is allowed (tools only parse source, never execute it)' — the container is not run with `--network none`, so exfiltration from a hijacked plugin is unimpeded. The NVD_API_KEY part of the impact is also real for this adapter: `run_tools.py:157-158` forwards `-e NVD_API_KEY` on the same Phase-1 adapter dispatch path that runs eslint-security. Caveats the auditor should apply when triaging severity, none of which contradict the mechanism: (1) execution is confined to the panopticon-tools container running as uid 1000 `scanner` with the target mounted `:ro`, so CVSS 9.1 AV:N is inflated — AV:L / scope-limited is the honest rating; (2) the claim's 'git tokens' is unsupported — NVD_API_KEY is the only credential I found forwarded; (3) the image already executes target-controlled build logic by design (`skill/scripts/tools/roslyn_secguard.py:61-66` runs `dotnet build` on the copied target, which runs the target's MSBuild targets), so the trust boundary is already porous, which weakens 'HIGH/new RCE vector' but arguably strengthens the case for hardening; (4) the proposed remediation `--resolve-plugins-relative-to` was removed for flat config in ESLint v9+, and this adapter uses `--no-config-lookup` (flat-config mode), so the actionable fix is to pin the child's cwd to a trusted directory (e.g. `run_tool(cmd, cwd='/opt/panopticon')`) or supply an explicit flat config that requires the plugin by absolute path. Also note `--no-config-lookup` already blocks the larger eslint.config.js RCE vector, so the authors were partially aware of this class. Verdict is CONFIRMED on the code weakness; exploitation additionally requires the scanned target to contain a hostile `node_modules/eslint-plugin-security`, which no repository evidence can settle (inherent to a supply-chain trust-boundary claim).

findings.title: shutil.copytree dereferences symlinks in the scanned target before building it
findings.description: `shutil.copytree(target, tmp, dirs_exist_ok=True)` is called with the default `symlinks=False`, so any symlink present in the scanned repository (git tracks symlinks) is followed and the *contents* of its link target are copied into the temp build directory under the repo's filename. tests/tools/test_roslyn_secguard.py's `test_invoke_builds_in_temp_copy` mocks `copytree` entirely and never exercises real symlink handling, so this behavior is untested.
findings.impact: A malicious or compromised repository containing a symlink pointing to a sensitive absolute path readable inside the scanning container (e.g. a mounted credentials file, `~/.aws/credentials`, a Kubernetes service-account token, or another scan target's checkout) would have that file's contents copied into the roslyn temp build directory, where it becomes part of what `dotnet build`/MSBuild processes and, depending on build output handling, could be echoed into logs or scan artifacts.
findings.remediation: Call `shutil.copytree(target, tmp, dirs_exist_ok=True, symlinks=True)` so symlinks are recreated as symlinks rather than dereferenced, and/or reject/skip symlinks that point outside the scanned target root before copying.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Verified the code fact exactly as claimed. /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/tools/roslyn_secguard.py:58 is `shutil.copytree(target, tmp, dirs_exist_ok=True)` with no `symlinks=` argument. shutil.copytree's signature defaults to symlinks=False, which dereferences symlinks and copies the linked file's *contents* into the destination under the repo-controlled filename (and, for symlinked directories, recursively copies the linked tree; a dangling symlink additionally raises shutil.Error since ignore_dangling_symlinks also defaults to False). This is the only copytree call in skill/ (grep over the whole skill tree returned exactly one hit). The test claim is also accurate: tests/tools/test_roslyn_secguard.py:114 replaces rs.shutil.copytree with `def fake_copytree(src, dst, dirs_exist_ok=False)` that just touches x.csproj, so no real copy semantics -- symlink or otherwise -- are exercised; that stub would even TypeError if the fix (symlinks=True) were applied, so the test actively pins the vulnerable call shape. Caveat on the impact narrative, which I could not fully substantiate and which the claim itself hedges: in the intended execution path (skill/scripts/run_tools.py:156-167) the adapter runs inside the panopticon-tools container whose only bind mounts are the target at /src:ro and the checkout's scripts dir at /opt/panopticon/scripts:ro, so a symlink escaping the repo lands in a mostly empty container filesystem, and invoke() returns only tmp/out.sarif (not build stdout) with the tmp tree removed in the finally block -- so a concrete exfiltration channel is not demonstrated by this repo. The defect (unbounded symlink dereference of attacker-controlled repo content into a build sandbox, plus hard failure on dangling symlinks, which run_adapters at run_tools.py:110-111 swallows as 'adapter failed; skipping') is real and untested; the MEDIUM severity rests on the speculative leak path rather than a proven one.

findings.title: shutil.copytree() dereferences symlinks in the scanned repo, enabling file exfiltration or a symlink-loop DoS
findings.description: `shutil.copytree(target, tmp, dirs_exist_ok=True)` uses the default `symlinks=False`, meaning any symbolic link inside the scanned repository is followed and the *contents* of its target are copied into the temporary build tree rather than the link itself. A repository under scan can therefore include a symlink (e.g. `x.cs -> /etc/passwd`, or pointing at any other container-readable path) whose referenced file content is silently pulled into the build tree that `dotnet build`/the Roslyn analyzer subsequently processes. A symlinked directory that loops back on an ancestor also makes the recursive copy run unbounded.
findings.impact: Potential disclosure of files outside the intended scan target if any compiler/analyzer diagnostic reflects part of the copied content into the SARIF report (and hence into panopticon's findings output), plus a resource-exhaustion denial-of-service via a symlink loop.
findings.remediation: Call `shutil.copytree(target, tmp, dirs_exist_ok=True, symlinks=True)` so links are preserved as links instead of dereferenced, or pre-walk the tree and reject/skip any symlink whose resolved target escapes `target` before copying.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The code fact is certain: /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/tools/roslyn_secguard.py:58 is `shutil.copytree(target, tmp, dirs_exist_ok=True)` with no `symlinks=` argument, so CPython's default `symlinks=False` applies — file symlinks are dereferenced and their target's *contents* are copied into the writable temp build tree, and symlinked directories are recursed into. A repo-wide grep found `copytree` used only at this one call site (the only other hits are the monkeypatched `fake_copytree` in /tests/tools/test_roslyn_secguard.py:112-133, which itself takes no `symlinks` parameter and would break if one were added). Git stores symlinks (mode 120000), so a PR can introduce `leak.cs -> /etc/passwd` or `-> /opt/panopticon/scripts/...` (that path is mounted into the container at run_tools.py:166). The exfiltration channel is more concrete than the claim states: `-p:ErrorLog=` (line 64) makes csc emit ALL diagnostics, including plain compile errors, into the SARIF; MSBuild returning 1 on build failure is inside `ok_codes=(0,1)` in base.py:64-78 and inside the `rc in (0,1)` gate in run_tools.py:104 / _run_adapter.py, so the SARIF is still ingested, and parse() (lines 109-142) copies each result's message text straight into a finding's `title` and `description` — and csc syntax-error messages quote offending tokens from the source. findings.title: Unguarded `shutil.copytree(target, tmp, dirs_exist_ok=True)` dereferences attacker-controlled symlinks, enabling arbitrary file read outside the scanned tree
findings.description: `RoslynSecGuardAdapter.invoke()` calls `shutil.copytree(target, tmp, dirs_exist_ok=True)` without `symlinks=True`. Python's `shutil.copytree` defaults to `symlinks=False`, meaning any symbolic link inside the scanned repository is *dereferenced* and the **contents** of its target are copied into the staging directory, rather than the link itself. A repository under scan is fully attacker-controlled content (this is exactly the trust boundary panopticon exists to police), so a crafted symlink such as `secret.cs -> /etc/passwd` or `secret.cs -> /proc/1/environ` (or any other file readable by the scanning process/container, including files brought in by other volume mounts such as the scripts directory mounted in `run_tools.py`) causes that file's contents to be copied into the roslyn-secguard build workspace. Because this happens before/independently of the `dotnet build` step covered in SECPR-001, it is a standalone primitive: even if the build-execution issue were mitigated, the plain copy step still discloses out-of-tree file contents into the scan workspace, from where they can surface in build diagnostics/SARIF `message` text that flows into the reported finding (visible to whoever can read the scan output, e.g. the PR author).
findings.impact: Arbitrary local file disclosure limited to files readable by the scanning process/container filesystem, independent of whether `dotnet build` code execution is otherwise mitigated. Combined with SECPR-001, this provides a second, lower-effort route (no working C# required, just a crafted symlink) to leak container secrets, other mounted paths, or host files into build output that later becomes part of the emitted finding text.
findings.remediation: Pass `symlinks=True` to `shutil.copytree` (or use `ignore_dangling_symlinks`/manually re-create symlinks pointing only within the copied tree) so links are preserved rather than dereferenced, and additionally validate/reject symlinks whose resolved target escapes the source directory before compiling. If build isolation per SECPR-001 is implemented (network/off, restricted mounts), this closes the remaining pre-build file-read primitive.
findings.exploit_scenario: A malicious PR adds `payload.cs` as a symlink pointing to a sensitive file readable inside the scanning container (e.g. a mounted credentials file or `/proc/self/environ`). `RoslynSecGuardAdapter.invoke()` copies the repository with `shutil.copytree`, which silently dereferences the symlink and materializes the sensitive file's contents inside the roslyn build workspace as `payload.cs`. If that content is not valid C#, the resulting compiler diagnostic (file path plus a source excerpt) is captured into `out.sarif` and surfaces verbatim in the finding reported back to the PR author, leaking the secret's contents through the security report itself.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning:
The cited code is exactly as claimed. /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/tools/roslyn_secguard.py:58 reads `shutil.copytree(target, tmp, dirs_exist_ok=True)` inside `RoslynSecGuardAdapter.invoke()`, with no `symlinks=` argument. Python's documented default is `symlinks=False`, i.e. symlinks in the source tree are dereferenced and their target's CONTENTS are copied. A repo-wide grep for `copytree|islink|symlink|realpath|lstat` across all .py files returns exactly one production copytree (this one) and no symlink guard anywhere in `skill/scripts/`; the only other realpath use is an unrelated containment check in orchestrator.py:308 `_within()`. So the missing-guard core of the claim is verified.

Reachability with attacker-controlled content is verified end to end: `RoslynSecGuardAdapter` is registered in skill/scripts/tools/__init__.py as `roslyn-secguard`; run_tools.py lists it in `PHASE2_ADAPTERS` and selects it via `select_adapters()` -> `is_applicable()` (any *.csproj/*.sln at the target root, which a PR author can add); run_tools.py:156-167 then dispatches it inside the container as `docker run -v <target>:/src:ro -v <skill/scripts>:/opt/panopticon/scripts:ro panopticon-tools python3 /opt/panopticon/scripts/_run_adapter.py roslyn-secguard`, and _run_adapter.py:17 defaults `target="/src"`. .github/workflows/security.yml:6,20,51 runs this on `pull_request` against a plain `actions/checkout@v4`, so untrusted PR content is scanned; the tool is also, by design, pointed at arbitrary third-party repos. `run_tool()` in tools/base.py accepts rc 0/1, so a FAILING build still returns out.sarif, and `parse()` copies SARIF `message` text verbatim into the finding `title`/`description` (roslyn_secguard.py:119,129) with no sanitization in ingest_tools.ingest_dir, so compiler-diagnostic text does reach the emitted report (the CI job even prints titles). Roslyn is wired in image-wide via `/Directory.Build.props` (Dockerfile:91-101) and `-p:ErrorLog=` (roslyn_secguard.py:64), so compiler CS#### diagnostics land in the SARIF too.

Caveats that qualify the claim's impact framing (I confirm the defect, not the full severity): (1) In the primary Docker path the copy runs inside the container as uid 1000 `scanner` (Dockerfile:103-111), so symlinks resolve in the CONTAINER namespace — only container files, the two ro mounts, and /proc/self/environ (which carries NVD_API_KEY when run_tools.py:157-158 forwards it) are reachable, NOT arbitrary host files. Host-file reach exists only in the non-Docker paths (`run_adapters()`, direct `_run_adapter.py`, tests/tools/test_csharp_integration.py:23), which are not the shipped CLI flow. (2) The copy alone is not an exfiltration channel: tmp is removed in the `finally` (line 72), so disclosure still depends on content escaping through compiler diagnostics, which typically leak identifier tokens/excerpts rather than whole files — plausible and unsanitized, but I could not verify full-content leakage from the repo alone. (3) The claim's primary remediation (`symlinks=True`) would NOT close the read: with the link preserved, `dotnet build` dereferences it at compile time anyway; only the claim's secondary advice (reject symlinks whose resolved target escapes the source tree) actually fixes it. (4) The 'standalone, independent of SECPR-001' framing is weak, since the attacker also controls the .csproj/MSBuild files being built and MSBuild tasks can read arbitrary files directly — this symlink path is a lower-effort variant, not an orthogonal primitive. An unclaimed but real side effect of the same defect: `symlinks=False` also recurses THROUGH symlinked directories, so a link to `/` or a symlink loop turns the copy into a filesystem-exhaustion/timeout DoS.

Net: the code supports the claim's technical assertion and reachability. I would keep it CONFIRMED but suggest downgrading severity from HIGH/7.5 (the CVSS C:H 'arbitrary file read' overstates the container-scoped, diagnostic-mediated leak) and correcting the remediation to require escaping-symlink rejection rather than `symlinks=True` alone.

findings.title: Brakeman's `confidence` field is reused as panopticon `severity`, silently downgrading low-confidence critical vulnerabilities to INFO
findings.description: `"severity": normalize_severity(w.get("confidence", "medium"))` and `"confidence": _normalize_confidence(w.get("confidence", "medium"))` both derive from the same Brakeman `confidence` value, so severity is never based on the actual vulnerability class (SQL Injection, Command Injection, Mass Assignment, etc. — see `_BRAKEMAN_CWE`). Real Brakeman output uses confidence levels `High`/`Medium`/`Weak` (not `Low`); `base.SEV_MAP` (skill/scripts/tools/base.py:25-36) has no `weak` key, so `normalize_severity("Weak")` falls through to its default and returns `INFO`. tests/tools/test_brakeman.py only exercises `confidence: "High"`, so this collapse is untested.
findings.impact: Any Brakeman warning Brakeman itself rates 'Weak' confidence — including SQL Injection, Command Injection, or Dangerous Eval, which are CRITICAL/HIGH-impact vulnerability classes when real — is reported to panopticon as severity INFO regardless of the underlying vulnerability's actual severity. Downstream triage/gating that filters or deprioritizes on severity will silently drop these findings, producing false negatives for exactly the class of finding a security panel exists to catch.
findings.remediation: Derive `severity` from the Brakeman `warning_type` (already mapped in `_BRAKEMAN_CWE`) via a severity-per-warning-type table, and use `confidence` only to populate the finding's `confidence` field. Add `SEV_MAP["weak"]` as a defensive fallback regardless, and add a test asserting `confidence: "Weak"` for a high-impact `warning_type` (e.g. SQL Injection) still yields at least MEDIUM/HIGH severity.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Verified in code. skill/scripts/tools/brakeman.py:73-74 sets `"severity": normalize_severity(w.get("confidence", "medium"))` and `"confidence": _normalize_confidence(w.get("confidence", "medium"))` — both fields derive from the single Brakeman `confidence` value. `warning_type` (line 67) is used only for the title, the CWE lookup (_BRAKEMAN_CWE, lines 21-34), and tool_evidence.rule_id; it never influences severity. skill/scripts/tools/base.py:25-36 confirms SEV_MAP has keys critical/high/severe/important/moderate/medium/low/info/informational/none and no `weak`, and normalize_severity (base.py:41-44) returns "INFO" for any unmapped string AND for any non-string input. So any Brakeman confidence token outside that map collapses to INFO regardless of the vulnerability class. The downstream impact is real and not theoretical: skill/scripts/ingest_tools.py passes adapter output through without re-deriving severity, and skill/scripts/synthesize.py filters and gates on it — `--severity` threshold filter at lines 944-946, gate_verdict at 430-441, grade/risk_level at 409-427, and top-findings selection restricted to CRITICAL/HIGH at line 670. An INFO-rated SQL Injection would be dropped by `--severity medium` and would never fail a CI gate. Test coverage matches the claim: tests/tools/test_brakeman.py:18 uses only `"confidence": "High"` and asserts severity HIGH; no test exercises Medium/Weak/absent/non-string confidence. The repo's own design doc corroborates that the intended mapping was different from what shipped — docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-01-scanner-ecosystem-expansion-design.md:57 says 'Map Brakeman confidence (High -> HIGH, Medium -> MEDIUM, Low -> LOW) AND WARNING TYPE to severity', and docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-01-scanner-ecosystem-expansion.md:152-153 shows the implemented shortcut (both fields from confidence). Note the spec assumed a `Low` confidence level; the one part of the claim I cannot verify from the repository is Brakeman's actual emitted token set — there is no vendored Brakeman fixture anywhere (Glob **/brakeman* returns only the adapter and its .pyc). Per Brakeman's published documentation the confidence levels are High/Medium/Weak, which is exactly the value the spec got wrong and which SEV_MAP lacks; on that external fact rests the specific 'Weak -> INFO' consequence. The structural defect (severity == confidence, no warning-type severity table, unknown token -> INFO, untested) is fully verified in-repo independent of that fact, so I confirm at LIKELY rather than CERTAIN. Also worth noting for the auditor: even the best case is a downgrade — a High-confidence SQL Injection can never exceed HIGH and can never be CRITICAL.

findings.title: run_tool's F-CAL-1 stderr diagnostic prints raw subprocess stderr with no secret redaction
findings.description: On any exit code outside `ok_codes`, `run_tool()` prints up to the last 1000 bytes of the subprocess's raw stderr to panopticon's own stderr (tests/tools/test_base.py::TestRunTool::test_error_exit_logs_stderr_excerpt / test_stderr_excerpt_is_capped confirm and exercise this). No adapter or `run_tool` itself redacts credentials that a scanner might echo on failure — e.g. dependency-check reads `NVD_API_KEY` from the environment (skill/scripts/tools/dependency_check.py:25) and could include it in an authentication-failure message; gitleaks/semgrep can be configured with tokens.
findings.impact: If any wrapped scanner ever includes a secret (API key, token) in an error message on a non-clean exit, that secret is copied verbatim into panopticon's own stderr/CI logs, which are typically retained and more broadly readable than the original process environment — turning a tool failure into a credential leak.
findings.remediation: Apply a redaction pass to the captured stderr excerpt (e.g. strip/replace values matching known secret env vars such as `NVD_API_KEY`, or generic high-entropy token patterns) before printing it in `run_tool`.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The code behavior the claim describes is exactly what /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/tools/base.py does. Lines 72-78: `res = subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, timeout=timeout, **kwargs)` then, when `rc not in ok_codes`, `excerpt = (res.stderr or b'')[-1000:].decode('utf-8', errors='replace').strip()` and `print('tool %s exited %d%s' % (cmd[0], rc, (': %s' % excerpt) if excerpt else ''), file=sys.stderr)`. There is no redaction, filtering, or allow-listing of the excerpt anywhere. I grepped the whole skill/ tree for redact|scrub|sanitize|REDACT and the only hit is an unrelated queue-id sanitizer in skill/scripts/evidence.py:104 — no secret-redaction helper exists in this repo. The tests the claim names do exist and pin the behavior verbatim (tests/tools/test_base.py:54-63 asserts the raw stderr string 'boom: bad flag' appears in stderr; :65-72 asserts the cap). The secret-in-environment precondition is also real: skill/scripts/run_tools.py:156-158 forwards `NVD_API_KEY` via `docker run -e NVD_API_KEY` for EVERY adapter in the ADAPTERS dispatch branch (not just dependency-check), and skill/scripts/tools/dependency_check.py:25 reads it. findings.title: Missing blank line before module-level function definition
findings.description: Function `run_tool` at line 64 has only 1 blank line before it (line 63). PEP 8 requires 2 blank lines between top-level function definitions.
findings.impact: Inconsistent spacing reduces code readability and violates PEP 8 style guidelines.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Verified directly in the source. In /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/tools/base.py, line 62 is the last body line of the `ToolAdapter` Protocol class (`        ...`), line 63 is a single blank line, and line 64 is `def run_tool(cmd, timeout, ok_codes=(0, 1), **kwargs):`. findings.title: Shared `run_tool()` subprocess helper inherits the full parent environment for every scanner invocation
findings.description: `run_tool()` calls `subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, timeout=timeout, **kwargs)` and none of the fourteen adapters that use it pass an explicit, minimized `env=`. Only `eslint_security.py` touches `env` at all, and it does so via `os.environ.copy()` (still the full inherited environment, plus `NODE_PATH`). By default Python subprocesses inherit the entire parent environment, so every third-party scanner binary (brakeman, bundle-audit, cargo audit, dependency-check.sh, spotbugs, dotnet, npm, pip-audit, osv-scanner, eslint, semgrep, gitleaks, trivy, gosec, bandit) runs with visibility into whatever secrets happen to be present in the orchestrator/container environment (e.g. `NVD_API_KEY`, CI tokens, cloud credentials). This is a defense-in-depth gap on its own, and becomes directly exploitable in combination with SECPR-001: the roslyn-secguard adapter's `dotnet build` step (which executes attacker-influenced MSBuild/C# code) runs under this same unrestricted environment inheritance, giving a malicious build script direct access to any secret set in the process environment.
findings.impact: Increases the blast radius of any compromised or vulnerable third-party scanner binary, and specifically enables the RCE described in SECPR-001 to read and exfiltrate operator secrets (e.g. NVD_API_KEY, and — per `run_tools.py`'s unconditional propagation to every adapter container when set — any other credential an operator adds following that same pattern).
findings.remediation: Have `run_tool()` accept and default to a minimal, explicit environment (e.g. `PATH`, locale vars, and only the specific credentials a given adapter documents needing) rather than silently inheriting the full parent environment. Pass secrets like `NVD_API_KEY` only to the one adapter that needs them (dependency-check), never to code-execution-capable adapters such as roslyn-secguard.

cwe.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor
Insufficiently Protected Credentials

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Every factual code assertion in the claim checks out. skill/scripts/tools/base.py:72 is `res = subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, timeout=timeout, **kwargs)` with no `env=` default, so absent an explicit override the child inherits os.environ in full. I grepped `run_tool|env=|os.environ` across skill/scripts: the call sites are cargo_audit.py:52, brakeman.py:54, npm_audit.py:18, legacy_sarif.py:50 (which backs the semgrep/bandit/trivy/gitleaks/gosec adapter entries in tools/__init__.py:19-23), spotbugs.py:39, pip_audit.py:42, dependency_check.py:35, bundler_audit.py:29, osv_scanner.py:36, roslyn_secguard.py:66 — none passes env. The single exception is eslint_security.py:44-52, which is `env = os.environ.copy()` plus a NODE_PATH append, i.e. still the full inherited environment, exactly as the claim states. The NVD_API_KEY propagation detail is also verified and is the strongest part of the claim: skill/scripts/run_tools.py:156-158 places `-e NVD_API_KEY` on the docker command inside the GENERIC adapter-dispatch branch (`adapter = ADAPTERS.get(tool)`, line 152), so it is forwarded to whichever adapter is running — including roslyn-secguard, whose invoke() shells out to `dotnet build` on a copy of the target tree (roslyn_secguard.py:61-66). tests/test_run_tools.py:141-159 pins that forwarding. So a credential intended only for dependency-check is in fact visible to a code-execution-capable adapter, and skill/scripts/tools/dependency_check.py:25 never even passes the key on argv (it uses it only as a boolean to drop --noupdate), which makes the over-broad forwarding harder to justify. Two corrections the auditor should apply to the impact narrative before accepting MEDIUM: (1) 'CI tokens, cloud credentials' overstates it for the production path — the scanners run inside the panopticon-tools container launched by `docker run` with no --env-file and only the conditional `-e NVD_API_KEY`, and the Dockerfile bakes no secrets (only PYTHONPATH, CARGO_HOME, RUSTUP_HOME, PATH, DOTNET_ROOT, SPOTBUGS_HOME-style vars), so host CI/cloud credentials are not present in the child environment there. Full host-environment inheritance only bites on the in-process path (run_tools.run_adapters, unused outside tests, or a direct `_run_adapter.py` invocation on a developer host). (2) The 'directly exploitable in combination with SECPR-001' clause depends on a separate claim I did not evaluate and must not be counted as verified here. Judged on its own, this is a real, precisely-located defense-in-depth gap plus a concrete over-scoped-credential issue at run_tools.py:156-158.

findings.title: bandit noise suppression drops B101 project-wide and all findings under any path that merely looks like a test path
findings.description: `if tool_name == "bandit" and (rule_id in NOISE_RULES or _is_test_path(loc.get("file"))): continue` suppresses (a) every B101 (assert-used) finding regardless of whether it is in a test file or production code, and (b) every bandit finding of any rule under a path matching `tests/`, `test_*.py`, or `*_test.py`. Neither test_legacy_sarif.py nor any other file in this list exercises `_is_test_path`/`NOISE_RULES`, so this scope is unverified by tests.
findings.impact: B101 also fires on `assert` used as a security/authorization control in production code (CWE-703/CWE-617-adjacent: assertions are stripped when Python runs with `-O`), which is a real, high-value bandit finding when it occurs outside test files — but the current filter discards it unconditionally. Separately, blanket-excluding every finding under 'test' paths means genuinely dangerous patterns in test fixtures/helpers (e.g. hardcoded credentials — bandit B105/B106/B107, shell=True, weak crypto) that could be copy-pasted into production code or that reflect real leaked secrets are never surfaced.
findings.remediation: Scope the B101 suppression to test paths only (`rule_id in NOISE_RULES and _is_test_path(...)`), and consider a narrower test-path exclusion that still surfaces high-confidence rules like hardcoded-secret detectors (B105-B107) regardless of path. Add a regression test asserting a B101 finding in a non-test file is NOT suppressed.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The behavioral core of the claim is exactly what the code does. skill/scripts/tools/sarif_utils.py:82-84 reads `if tool_name == "bandit" and (rule_id in NOISE_RULES or _is_test_path(loc.get("file"))): continue`, with NOISE_RULES = {"B101"} (line 24) and _is_test_path matching `tests/` prefix, `test_*` basename, or `*_test.py` basename (lines 27-35). Because the two conditions are OR'd, (a) every B101 result is dropped regardless of location — there is no path-scoping on the NOISE_RULES arm — and (b) every bandit result of any rule id (B105/B106/B107 hardcoded secrets, B602 shell=True, etc.) is dropped when its normalized path looks test-like. This filter is on the shared ingestion path used by LegacySarifAdapter.parse (skill/scripts/tools/legacy_sarif.py:52-54) and re-exported by skill/scripts/ingest_tools.py:13-23, so it applies to every bandit scan of every target repo, not just self-scans. Two corrections to the claim's supporting evidence, neither of which changes the verdict on the code behavior: (1) the assertion that no file exercises _is_test_path/NOISE_RULES is FALSE — /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/tests/test_ingest_tools.py:115-135 contains two tests that cover both arms, and test_ingest_filters_nonnoise_bandit_under_test_path explicitly asserts a non-noise rule (B608) under `tests/test_x.py` is dropped, with a comment stating 'test-path suppression is bandit-wide, not just B101'; (2) the scope is a deliberate, documented tuning decision, not an oversight — sarif_utils.py:21-24 explains the rationale and DEVELOPMENT.md:202-203 records its origin ('bandit emitted 579 B101 "assert used" findings from tests/ on one run'). So the claim's remediation ('add a regression test asserting B101 in a non-test file is NOT suppressed') is a request to change intentional behavior, not to fix a bug the tests missed. The residual detection gap the claim identifies is real (assert-as-authorization-control in production code and secrets in test fixtures are never surfaced from bandit), but this is a scanner tuning tradeoff in panopticon's own ingest layer rather than an exploitable weakness in the product, so MEDIUM/security-panel framing overstates it; LOW/quality would be more accurate.

findings.title: Brakeman 'Dangerous Eval' maps to CWE-94 while the equivalent JS eval pattern maps to the more precise CWE-95
findings.description: `_BRAKEMAN_CWE["Dangerous Eval"] = "CWE-94"` (generic 'Code Injection'), whereas the same codebase's `eslint_security.py` maps the equivalent JS pattern `security/detect-eval-with-expression` to `"CWE-95"` (the precise 'Eval Injection' CWE — skill/scripts/tools/eslint_security.py:11). Both findings represent the identical vulnerability class (attacker-influenced input reaching a language `eval`).
findings.impact: Internally inconsistent CWE tagging for the same vulnerability class reduces the accuracy of any CWE-based aggregation, OWASP Top-10 mapping, or trend reporting built on top of panopticon's citations, and could cause the same underlying issue to be bucketed differently depending on which language's scanner found it.
findings.remediation: Change `_BRAKEMAN_CWE["Dangerous Eval"]` to `"CWE-95"` to align with the eslint-security mapping for the equivalent pattern.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Both halves of the factual assertion verified by direct read. `skill/scripts/tools/brakeman.py:31` contains `"Dangerous Eval": "CWE-94"`, and `skill/scripts/tools/eslint_security.py:11` contains `"security/detect-eval-with-expression": "CWE-95"`, asserted by `tests/tools/test_eslint_security.py:63`. Both warning types describe attacker-influenced input reaching a language-level eval, so the two scanners tag the same vulnerability class with different CWEs. CWE-95 is available and supported in this codebase: `skill/reference/cwe-catalog.json:8` defines it and `tests/test_citations.py:73-74` asserts its presence in the catalog and its OWASP mapping, so the proposed remediation would not break citation validation. Two caveats that bound the severity: (1) CWE-95 is a child of CWE-94 in MITRE's hierarchy, so the current tag is imprecise rather than wrong — this is a consistency/precision nit, correctly filed as LOW; (2) the claimed OWASP-aggregation impact does not materialize, because `skill/reference/cwe-catalog.json:43-44` maps BOTH CWE-94 and CWE-95 to A03:2021-Injection, so OWASP-level rollups are identical either way. Only raw-CWE bucketing is affected. Note also that `eslint_security.py:19` uses CWE-94 for `security/detect-object-injection`, so CWE-94 is in active use for a different pattern in the same file.

findings.title: dependency-check silently falls back to a stale, unrefreshed vulnerability DB when NVD_API_KEY is unset, with no signal surfaced in findings
findings.description: When `NVD_API_KEY` is unset, `invoke()` appends `--noupdate`, relying entirely on 'a pre-seeded DB inside the image or on the host' (per the adapter's own comment). Neither `invoke()` nor `parse()` records the DB's staleness/last-update time anywhere in the emitted findings or in the adapter's absence-of-findings case, and no test (test_dependency_check.py has no invoke()/is_applicable() test at all — see SEC-108) verifies this fallback path.
findings.impact: A scan can silently run against an out-of-date NVD snapshot and report 'no dependency vulnerabilities' when in fact the database is simply stale, producing false negatives for recently disclosed CVEs in Java dependencies with no indication in the report that this happened.
findings.remediation: Surface DB staleness as metadata on the tool run (e.g. an INFO finding or a `meta` field noting `--noupdate` was used and since when), and/or fail loudly rather than silently when the local DB is older than a configurable threshold.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Every code-level assertion in the claim checks out. /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/tools/dependency_check.py:25 computes `has_nvd_key = bool(os.environ.get('NVD_API_KEY'))` and lines 33-34 append '--noupdate' when it is falsey; the adapter's own comment at lines 22-24 states findings 'then depend on a pre-seeded DB inside the image or on the host.' Neither invoke() nor parse() (lines 56-103) emits any record of which mode was used or how old the DB is: parse() builds findings purely from data['dependencies'][*]['vulnerabilities'][*] and returns [] for an empty report, and the emitted finding dict has no meta/staleness field. Nothing downstream compensates — I grepped skill/ for tools_run/tool_runs/metadata/scan_info and read the report schema at skill/reference/report-schema.json; report meta carries target/tool_policy_mode/models_used and per-finding tool_evidence, but there is no place where a tool records DB freshness or a degraded-mode flag, and run_adapters/run_tools (skill/scripts/run_tools.py:94-181) only print 'adapter X exited N; skipping' to stderr, which never reaches the report. The 'no test verifies this fallback path' sub-claim is also true: tests/tools/test_dependency_check.py covers only parse()/_normalize_cwe(), and tests/test_run_tools.py:141 tests only the docker `-e NVD_API_KEY` argv propagation with a stubbed runner, never the adapter branch. One point strengthens rather than weakens the claim: the Dockerfile (lines 71-76) only unzips the dependency-check 10.0.3 release and never runs an --updateonly seeding step, so in the shipped image there is no pre-seeded NVD DB at all — the 'stale DB' assumption the comment relies on is not established anywhere in this repo. I mark LIKELY rather than CERTAIN because the exact runtime consequence (empty report vs. hard failure with a non-(0,1) exit that run_adapters silently skips) depends on the host/image DB state, which the repository alone cannot settle; but in both outcomes the report shows no dependency-vulnerability findings with no signal that the SCA layer ran degraded, which is precisely what the claim asserts. Severity LOW and the design-level remediation are proportionate.

findings.impact: Regressions in the NVD_API_KEY-gated --noupdate flag, the report-file-missing fallback, or the tempdir cleanup path would not be caught by the test suite; a broken invoke() would only surface in production (or the skipped fixture-based integration test) rather than in unit tests.
findings.remediation: Add is_applicable() true/false tests for the three markers, and invoke() tests that mock subprocess.run (or run_tool) plus the filesystem to verify the --noupdate flag toggling and the report-file read/fallback behavior.

findings.title: test_roslyn_secguard.py has no is_applicable() test, leaving the trigger for the dotnet-build RCE surface (SEC-101) unguarded
findings.description: Unlike test_brakeman.py, test_bundler_audit.py, test_cargo_audit.py, test_eslint_security.py, test_npm_audit.py, test_osv_scanner.py, and test_pip_audit.py, this file never tests `RoslynSecGuardAdapter.is_applicable()`, which decides whether the `dotnet build`-based invoke() path (SEC-101) runs at all for a given target.
findings.impact: A regression in `is_applicable()` that broadens its matching (e.g. matching on a stray `.csproj`-named file that isn't a real C# project) would not be caught by this test suite, silently expanding the surface exposed to the arbitrary-code-execution risk documented in SEC-101.
findings.remediation: Add `is_applicable()` tests mirroring the pattern in the sibling adapter test files (true when a `.csproj`/`.sln` is present at the target root, false otherwise).

provenance.confirmation_reasoning:
The coverage gap is real and verified. I read tests/tools/test_roslyn_secguard.py in full (140 lines): it contains test_parse_produces_finding, test_parse_v1_result_file, test_parse_string_message, test_parse_includes_provenance, test_build_target_prefers_solution and test_invoke_builds_in_temp_copy — and no test of `RoslynSecGuardAdapter.is_applicable()`. A grep for `is_applicable` across tests/ confirms the file does not appear in the results at all, while every sibling the claim names does: test_brakeman.py:37,41; test_bundler_audit.py:37; test_cargo_audit.py:36; test_eslint_security.py:110-133; test_npm_audit.py:74,78,82; test_osv_scanner.py:103,110; test_pip_audit.py:72-99. The only other reference to roslyn's is_applicable in the suite is tests/tools/test_csharp_integration.py:21, where it is used as a `skipTest` gate against an AspGoat fixture that is skipped outright if not vendored (lines 19-20) — it asserts nothing about is_applicable and cannot catch a broadening regression.

I also confirmed the causal link the claim asserts: `select_adapters()` at skill/scripts/run_tools.py:91 filters adapters purely by `adapter.is_applicable(target)`, and `run_adapters()` calls `adapter.invoke(target)` at line 103 for exactly that surviving set. RoslynSecGuardAdapter is registered in skill/scripts/tools/__init__.py:30, so its is_applicable genuinely is the sole gate on the `dotnet build` invoke path (skill/scripts/tools/roslyn_secguard.py:49-72). The implementation at roslyn_secguard.py:26-31 matches any root-level regular file whose name ends in `.csproj` or `.sln`, with no content validation — so the claim's example regression scenario (a stray `.csproj`-named file) is plausible in kind.

Two qualifications, neither of which defeats the claim. First, the impact framing is speculative: the finding does not identify any actual defect in is_applicable, only that a hypothetical future regression would go uncaught; LOW severity is appropriate and the SEC-101 RCE linkage is inherited context I did not independently verify. Second, the cited CWE-829 (Inclusion of Functionality from Untrusted Control Sphere) describes SEC-101's alleged build-execution risk, not this missing test; I could not substantiate it as the citation for a coverage gap and did not adopt it. Verdict rests solely on the verified absence of the test and the verified is_applicable -> invoke gating.

findings.title: Missing test for brakeman invoke with rc=2 and rc=3
findings.description: BrakemanAdapter.invoke() handles special exit codes 2 and 3 (lines 54-59 in brakeman.py: converts them to rc=0) but test_invoke_runs_brakeman_json only tests rc=0. No coverage for the normalization logic.
findings.impact: Uncovered code path for handling Brakeman's non-standard exit codes could cause regressions when findings are present.
findings.remediation: Add test cases for invoke() with mocked subprocess returning rc=2 and rc=3, verifying both are normalized to 0.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The uncovered branch exists and is genuinely untested. skill/scripts/tools/brakeman.py:52-60 is `def invoke(...)`: it calls `run_tool(cmd, timeout=300, ok_codes=(0, 1, 2, 3))` (line 54) and then at lines 58-59 does `if rc in (2, 3): rc = 0` before returning. tests/tools/test_brakeman.py has exactly one invoke test, test_invoke_runs_brakeman_json (lines 52-61), whose mock returns `returncode=0`, so the `rc in (2, 3)` branch never executes; it also asserts the argv/timeout only. I checked for coverage elsewhere: a repo-wide grep for brakeman in tests/ surfaces only test_brakeman.py, tests/tools/test_ruby_integration.py, test_run_tools.py:33 (asserts brakeman is NOT selected for python/go), test_provenance.py, test_dockerfile.py and test_html_report.py — none of which exercise the normalization. test_ruby_integration.py:17-28 would call the real adapter.invoke, but it self-skips when the railsgoat fixture is absent, and tests/fixtures/ contains only insecure-js, vulnerable-node, vulnerable-python, vulnerable-rust, semgrep.sarif and manifest.json (no railsgoat), so it always skips; it also treats rc not in (0,1) as a skip rather than an assertion. Note the nearest neighbouring coverage is generic, not brakeman-specific: tests/tools/test_base.py:54-72 exercises run_tool with returncodes 2 and 3, but that only pins the stderr-excerpt logging in base.run_tool and asserts rc stays 2 — it says nothing about brakeman's normalization to 0. Minor inaccuracies that do not change the verdict: the conversion is at lines 58-59 (line 54 is the ok_codes pass-through), and the reference path is `scripts/tools/brakeman.py` where the repo path is `skill/scripts/tools/brakeman.py`. The claimed MEDIUM severity is arguably generous for a single-branch unit-test gap in a two-line normalization, but the factual coverage gap is real. The cited CWE-1164 (Irrelevant Code) is a poor fit for a missing-test finding; I do not endorse it.

findings.title: Missing test for brakeman is_applicable with app directory and .gemspec files
findings.description: BrakemanAdapter.is_applicable() checks for app/ directory (lines 45-47) and .gemspec files (line 50) but test_is_applicable_* only tests Gemfile marker. No coverage for app directory detection or .gemspec file detection.
findings.impact: Two fallback detection mechanisms in is_applicable are untested and could silently fail to detect Rails projects.
findings.remediation: Add test cases for is_applicable() checking for presence of app/ directory and .gemspec files.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Verified by tracing both is_applicable tests against the implementation. skill/scripts/tools/brakeman.py:41-50 has three detection tiers: markers Gemfile/config/routes.rb (lines 42-44), an `app/` directory check (lines 45-47), and a `.gemspec` scan via os.listdir (line 50, guarded by the `not os.path.isdir(target)` early return at 48-49). tests/tools/test_brakeman.py has only two is_applicable tests. test_is_applicable_when_rails_files_present (lines 37-39) patches os.path.exists with `side_effect=lambda p: p.endswith("Gemfile")`, so it returns True at line 44 and never reaches lines 45-50. test_is_applicable_false_without_rails_files (lines 41-44) patches os.path.exists to False and os.path.isdir to False, so line 46 is False and line 48's `not os.path.isdir(target)` is True, returning False at line 49 — the `return True` at line 47 and the entire listdir/.gemspec expression at line 50 are never executed. Neither the app/-directory positive nor the .gemspec positive/negative path is covered anywhere else: a repo-wide grep for brakeman in tests/ shows the only other caller of is_applicable is tests/tools/test_ruby_integration.py:22, which self-skips because the railsgoat fixture is not vendored (tests/fixtures/ contains only insecure-js, vulnerable-node, vulnerable-python, vulnerable-rust, semgrep.sarif, manifest.json) — and even if vendored, railsgoat has a Gemfile so it would short-circuit at line 44 anyway. The claim's cited implementation lines (45-47 and 50) are exact. As with COV-001 the MEDIUM severity is generous for a unit-test gap in a heuristic-applicability helper, and the CWE-1164 citation is a poor fit for a missing-test finding; the coverage gap itself is unambiguous.

findings.title: test_spotbugs.py has no invoke() test, breaking parallel structure with every sibling adapter test module
findings.description: Every other tool-adapter unit-test module in tests/tools/ that pairs with an adapter exposing an invoke() method includes a dedicated `test_invoke_*` test that patches `scripts.tools.base.subprocess.run` and asserts on the exact command/kwargs built (test_cargo_audit.py:46 test_invoke_runs_cargo_audit, test_brakeman.py:52 test_invoke_runs_brakeman_json, test_pip_audit.py:107/121, test_npm_audit.py:92, test_osv_scanner.py:120, test_eslint_security.py:135/151, test_bundler_audit.py:47, test_roslyn_secguard.py:99, test_legacy_sarif.py:49/64/75). tests/tools/test_spotbugs.py (TestSpotBugsAdapter, lines 20-43) is the only such module missing this coverage. skill/scripts/tools/spotbugs.py:26-39 `invoke()` builds a nontrivial command: it resolves a `classes` directory via a 3-way fallback (target/target/classes -> target/build/classes -> target itself), reads `SPOTBUGS_HOME` from the environment (default `/opt/spotbugs`), and joins it into both the spotbugs binary path and the FindSecBugs plugin-jar path before assembling the `-textui -xml -pluginList <jar> <classes>` argument list. None of that logic is exercised by any unit test; the only place it is exercised at all is the WebGoat-fixture integration test in tests/tools/test_java_integration.py (test_spotbugs_finds_webgoat_issues), which self-skips whenever the WebGoat fixture isn't vendored or a real `spotbugs`/`findsecbugs-plugin.jar` install isn't present at SPOTBUGS_HOME -- conditions that are almost certainly true in ordinary CI.

findings.remediation: Add a `test_invoke_runs_spotbugs` (mirroring test_cargo_audit.py:46-54) that mocks `scripts.tools.base.subprocess.run`, calls `SpotBugsAdapter().invoke(target)`, and asserts the constructed argv (spotbugs binary path, `-textui`, `-xml`, `-pluginList`, plugin jar path, classes dir) and `timeout=600`. Add companion cases (or parametrize) covering the three `classes` fallback branches (target/classes present, build/classes present, neither present) and an `SPOTBUGS_HOME` override via `mock.patch.dict(os.environ, ...)`.

findings.title: SpotBugs adapter test suite has no coverage for malformed/adversarial XML (entity-expansion DoS, CWE-776)
findings.description: test_spotbugs.py exercises SpotBugsAdapter.parse() with a single well-formed, benign XML fixture (SPOTBUGS_SAMPLE, lines 9-17) and an empty-bytes case. There is no test for malformed XML, an entity-expansion ('billion laughs'/quadratic-blowup) payload, or an oversized BugInstance list. The adapter under test (skill/scripts/tools/spotbugs.py:45) calls `xml.etree.ElementTree.fromstring(text)` directly on raw bytes with no size cap, no defusedxml hardening, and no exception handling around the parse call itself. Per CPython's documented XML vulnerability matrix, xml.etree.ElementTree remains vulnerable to billion-laughs and quadratic-blowup entity-expansion attacks (only external-entity/DTD-retrieval is mitigated by default). Because skill/scripts/ingest_tools.py:ingest_dir() routes any `*.json`/`*.sarif` file in a tools-output directory to the matching adapter's parse() purely by filename convention (tool = basename of the file), any actor able to place or influence a file named e.g. `spotbugs.json` supplies fully attacker-controlled bytes to this code path. The broad `except Exception` in ingest_dir() catches a parse *error* but does not bound parse *time/memory*, so a crafted entity-expansion payload can still hang or exhaust memory before any exception is raised.
findings.impact: A corrupted or attacker-supplied SpotBugs report artifact can cause the ingestion step to hang or exhaust memory, denying service to the review pipeline itself; the test suite provides zero evidence this is actually guarded against.
findings.remediation: Add negative tests to test_spotbugs.py covering malformed XML, an entity-expansion payload, and a very large BugInstance list, asserting bounded time/memory and graceful (non-crashing, non-hanging) behavior. Harden SpotBugsAdapter.parse() to use a safer parser (e.g. defusedxml.ElementTree, or explicit expat entity/size limits) and enforce a parse-time budget independent of the outer try/except in ingest_dir().

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Every repository-checkable assertion holds; the residual uncertainty is only in the DoS impact, which cannot be settled without executing code. Verified: (1) tests/tools/test_spotbugs.py exercises parse() with exactly one benign fixture (SPOTBUGS_SAMPLE, lines 9-17) plus b'' (line 41-43) — no malformed XML, no entity expansion, no oversized input. (2) skill/scripts/tools/spotbugs.py:45 is a bare `root = ET.fromstring(text)` on decoded raw bytes with no size cap, no defusedxml, and no local try/except; a repo-wide grep for 'fromstring|ElementTree|defusedxml|XMLParser' across all .py files returns only spotbugs.py:4 and :45, so no hardening exists anywhere. (3) The reachability chain is real and stronger than the claim states: skill/scripts/run_tools.py:100-101 and :154-155 write the spotbugs artifact as `<out_dir>/spotbugs.json` (ext defaults to 'json' because spotbugs is not in LEGACY_SARIF_TOOLS) even though the payload is XML, and skill/scripts/ingest_tools.py:55-58 globs *.json and routes purely on basename, so `spotbugs.json` is the ordinary, expected filename. (4) The `except Exception` at ingest_tools.py:80 catches a raised error but does not bound parse time or memory, exactly as claimed. (5) The threat model is plausible: .github/workflows/security.yml checks out the PR head and then ingests $TOOLS_OUT=.panopticon/tools; a PR that commits .panopticon/tools/spotbugs.json survives the run_tools step whenever the spotbugs adapter does not run (this repo has no pom.xml, so is_applicable is False and nothing overwrites the file), and is then fed to SpotBugsAdapter.parse. (6) The codebase already treats this class of hardening test as in-scope — tests/test_ingest_tools.py:108-113 is a deeply-nested-JSON resource-exhaustion test — so the missing XML analogue is a genuine asymmetry, not a novel demand. WHY LIKELY AND NOT CERTAIN: the CWE-776 impact is unproven. The Python docs matrix cited does list xml.etree.ElementTree as vulnerable to billion-laughs/quadratic-blowup, but libexpat >= 2.4.0 enables billion-laughs amplification protection by default (max amplification 100.0, 8 MiB activation threshold), so on a modern CPython the practical hang/OOM may not materialize; the linked libexpat version is not determinable from this repository and the claim itself states it was never executed against a payload. I would also downgrade the framing: category 'known_vulns' is wrong (no CVE is involved) — this is a hardening plus test-coverage gap, and the realistic worst case is a self-DoS of a CI job holding only `contents: read`. INCIDENTAL BUG FOUND ON THIS PATH (not part of any claim, but the parent should know): skill/scripts/ingest_tools.py:72-77 strips everything before the first `{` or `[` in the raw bytes. Real SpotBugs XML contains `[` inside JVM method signatures (e.g. signature="([Ljava/lang/String;)V"), so this prefix-strip will truncate the XML declaration and root element, ET.fromstring will raise ParseError, and the entire spotbugs.json will be silently discarded at line 80-82 with only a stderr note — i.e. the SpotBugs ingest path is likely broken for real output today, which no test would catch.
