findings.title: Missing test for run_tool subprocess timeout exception
findings.description: run_tool() is called with timeout parameter but no test verifies timeout exception handling. subprocess.TimeoutExpired is not caught and tested, though it could occur during real execution.
findings.impact: Timeout exception propagation is untested; tool execution could crash ungracefully if timeout is exceeded.
findings.remediation: Add test case that mocks subprocess.run to raise subprocess.TimeoutExpired and verifies proper error handling.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The factual core is verified. skill/scripts/tools/base.py:64-78 defines `run_tool(cmd, timeout, ok_codes=(0,1), **kwargs)` which calls `subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, timeout=timeout, **kwargs)` with no try/except; `subprocess.TimeoutExpired` therefore propagates to the caller. Reading all five TestRunTool cases (tests/tools/test_base.py:48-89), every one patches `scripts.tools.base.subprocess.run` with a `return_value` Mock; none uses `side_effect=subprocess.TimeoutExpired`. The line-84 test only asserts the timeout value is forwarded (`rec.assert_called_once_with(["t"], capture_output=True, timeout=7, cwd="/x", env={"A": "1"})`), i.e. the parameter plumbing is covered but the exception path is not. A repo-wide grep for TimeoutExpired shows the only test exercising a timeout is tests/test_run_tools.py:35-44, which covers `run_tools()`'s own timeout handling (skill/scripts/run_tools.py:145-146 and 177-178), a different function on the Docker path — not base.run_tool, which is what all ten adapters use (cargo_audit.py:52, brakeman.py:54, npm_audit.py:18, legacy_sarif.py:50, spotbugs.py:39, eslint_security.py:52, roslyn_secguard.py:66, dependency_check.py:35, osv_scanner.py:36, bundler_audit.py:29, pip_audit.py:42). Two caveats that should downgrade this below MEDIUM. First, the stated impact ('tool execution could crash ungracefully') is contradicted by the code: both call sites wrap `adapter.invoke()` in a broad handler — skill/scripts/run_tools.py:110 `except Exception as e: print(f"adapter {name} failed: {e}; skipping")` and skill/scripts/_run_adapter.py:25-28 `except Exception as exc: ... return 0` — and TimeoutExpired subclasses SubprocessError subclasses Exception, so a timeout degrades to a skipped adapter, not a crash. Second, run_tool contains no timeout-handling code, so this is not an uncovered branch; a test would only pin the implicit propagate-to-caller contract. The reference path 'scripts/tools/base.py:64-78' is also slightly wrong (actual: skill/scripts/tools/base.py), though the line range is exact. Confirmed as a genuine, low-value test-design gap; the severity and impact as written are overstated.

findings.title: Missing test for cargo_audit._cvss_v3_score helper function
findings.description: _cvss_v3_score() (lines 8-40 in cargo_audit.py) is a 33-line helper function that parses and calculates CVSS v3.1 scores but is never directly tested. It is only used indirectly via parse().
findings.impact: Complex CVSS scoring logic is untested and could produce incorrect severity mappings without detection.
findings.remediation: Add direct unit tests for _cvss_v3_score() with various CVSS vector inputs and edge cases.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning:
Verified against the source. `_cvss_v3_score` occupies skill/scripts/tools/cargo_audit.py:8-40 — exactly the 33-line span the claim cites — and parses a CVSS v3.1 vector string into a base score. A repo-wide grep for `_cvss_v3_score` yields only its definition (line 8) and its single call site (line 68, inside `CargoAuditAdapter.parse`), which confirms the claim's 'only used indirectly via parse()' and that no test invokes it directly.

The indirect path is also effectively dead in the unit suite: tests/tools/test_cargo_audit.py:17 sets `"cvss": None`, so `parse()` takes neither the `isinstance(cvss, dict)` branch at line 64 nor the `isinstance(cvss, str)` branch at line 67, and severity stays at the hardcoded "HIGH" default. No test in the repo feeds a string cvss to this adapter (grep for CVSS vector strings across tests/ shows them only in test_osv_scanner.py, test_phase1_integration.py and test_schemas.py, all of which route to the OSV adapter, whose own `_cvss_bucket` is tested at tests/tools/test_osv_scanner.py:84-89 — a useful contrast showing the pattern exists elsewhere but was skipped here). tests/tools/test_rust_integration.py could reach the function with live cargo-audit output, but it skips absent `cargo` on PATH (CI at .github/workflows/ci.yml installs no Rust tooling and never installs cargo-audit) and asserts nothing about severity, so it provides no regression signal for the scoring math.

On impact: the formula tracks the FIRST v3.1 spec closely (ISS, 6.42*ISS unchanged / 7.52*(ISS-0.029)-3.25*(ISS-0.02)^15 changed, 8.22*AV*AC*PR*UI, 1.08x for scope-changed), and the conditional-expression precedence at line 25 parses correctly. It does omit the spec's Roundup-to-one-decimal step, which can leave a score marginally under a bucket boundary (e.g. 8.97 staying HIGH instead of rounding to 9.0/CRITICAL) — a concrete example of the untested-misclassification risk the claim describes, though I did not execute anything to demonstrate a specific vector. Note this claim substantially duplicates CDPR-002 in this batch; I judged it solely on the evidence above.

findings.title: Missing direct test for pip_audit._find_requirement helper method
findings.description: PipAuditAdapter._find_requirement() (lines 44-47) is a helper method that searches for requirements files but is never directly tested. It is only used indirectly via invoke().
findings.impact: Helper method logic is untested; glob matching and file discovery could fail without detection.
findings.remediation: Add direct unit test for _find_requirement() with various requirement file configurations.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning:
Verified factually. `PipAuditAdapter._find_requirement()` is defined at /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/tools/pip_audit.py:44-47 exactly as cited. A repo-wide grep for `_find_requirement` returns only two live references: the definition (pip_audit.py:44) and its single call site inside `invoke()` (pip_audit.py:32); the only other hit is a design doc (docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-01-static-analysis-phase1.md:300,308). tests/tools/test_pip_audit.py contains no test that names or calls `_find_requirement`, so the claim that it is never directly tested is correct.

Caveat that tempers (but does not contradict) the claim: both branches of `_find_requirement` ARE exercised indirectly. test_invoke_uses_requirements_txt_when_present (lines 107-119) patches `scripts.tools.pip_audit.glob.glob` to return ['/tmp/fake/requirements.txt'] and asserts the resulting argv contains `--requirement /tmp/fake/requirements.txt`; test_invoke_falls_back_to_pyproject_toml (lines 121-133) patches glob to return [] and asserts the positional-path form. findings.title: Missing test for roslyn_secguard._build_target edge cases
findings.description: _build_target() (lines 33-47) has conditional logic for multiple .sln files and .csproj files with sorting, but test_build_target_prefers_solution only tests basic preference. No test for multiple .sln files or edge cases.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning:
Both halves of the claim check out. skill/scripts/tools/roslyn_secguard.py:33-47 is exactly `_build_target`, and it contains three distinct outcomes: `sorted(sln_files)[0]` when any .sln exists, `sorted(csproj_files)[0]` as fallback, and `return target` when neither exists -- all reached via a recursive `os.walk(target)`. The only test is test_build_target_prefers_solution at tests/tools/test_roslyn_secguard.py:90-97, which creates exactly one a.csproj and one b.sln in a single flat temp directory and asserts the .sln wins. I grepped the whole repository for `_build_target` and found no other caller or test; the only other roslyn tests are the parse tests in the same file, tests/tools/test_csharp_integration.py (which only asserts `findings` is truthy and skips unless a vendored AspGoat fixture and a working dotnet toolchain are present), and a tool-name loop at tests/test_run_tools.py:133. So the sorting tie-break with multiple .sln files, the csproj-only fallback path, the no-build-file `return target` path, and the recursive-subdirectory discovery are all unexercised.

The gap is not purely cosmetic, which supports keeping it above trivial: `_build_target`'s recursive walk diverges from `is_applicable` (roslyn_secguard.py:26-31), which only inspects top-level files via os.listdir. And `invoke` at roslyn_secguard.py:56-57 feeds the result into `os.path.relpath(build_target, target)`; on the untested `return target` branch that yields ".", making tmp_target `<tmp>/.` -- a real behavioural corner no test pins. findings.title: Test uses direct module state patching instead of context managers
findings.description: Lines 111-112 save original module references, then lines 123-124 directly patch module attributes. This manual patching using try/finally without proper context managers reduces test isolation and is not thread-safe for parallel test execution. Should use mock.patch() context managers instead.
findings.impact: Tests may interfere with each other when run in parallel, and the manual restoration logic is fragile and error-prone.
findings.remediation: Replace direct attribute patching with mock.patch() context managers: use 'with mock.patch("scripts.tools.base.subprocess.run", side_effect=fake_run)' and 'with mock.patch("scripts.tools.roslyn_secguard.shutil.copytree", side_effect=fake_copytree)'.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning:
The descriptive core of the claim is exactly right and the line numbers are precise. In /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/tests/tools/test_roslyn_secguard.py, test_invoke_builds_in_temp_copy saves originals at lines 111-112 (`old_run = tools_base.subprocess.run`, `old_copytree = rs.shutil.copytree`), assigns fakes at lines 123-124, and restores in a finally at lines 132-133. No mock.patch is used. This is a genuine outlier in this repo: every other adapter test uses context managers -- tests/tools/test_base.py:49,56,67,76,86; tests/tools/test_eslint_security.py:138,154; tests/tools/test_osv_scanner.py:123; tests/tools/test_pip_audit.py:110,124; tests/tools/test_brakeman.py:55; tests/tools/test_cargo_audit.py:48; tests/tools/test_bundler_audit.py:49 all use `mock.patch("scripts.tools.base.subprocess.run", ...)`. I also confirmed the patch targets are process-global stdlib module objects, not module-local aliases: skill/scripts/tools/base.py:6 does `import subprocess` and skill/scripts/tools/roslyn_secguard.py:5 does `import shutil`, so `tools_base.subprocess` IS the stdlib subprocess module and `rs.shutil` IS the stdlib shutil module. Assigning to their attributes mutates them for the whole interpreter, which is a real isolation concern.

Two qualifications that argue the claim is over-stated and its remediation partly misinformed. (1) The recommended fix does not address the stated thread-safety impact: unittest.mock.patch performs the identical global setattr/delattr on the same module objects, so switching to mock.patch gives automatic restoration, not thread safety. (2) 'the manual restoration logic is fragile and error-prone' is not demonstrated here -- the try/finally at lines 113/131-133 is correctly placed (the saves happen before the try, the assignments inside it) and restores on the exception path too, so behaviour is equivalent to mock.patch. Additionally, CI runs the suite serially (`python -m pytest tests/ -q` in .github/workflows/ci.yml:41) with no pytest-xdist configured and no pytest config section in pyproject.toml, so the 'tests may interfere when run in parallel' impact is hypothetical today. Net: the factual claim is CONFIRMED, but this is a style/consistency defect worth LOW, not HIGH -- there is no correctness or leakage bug in the current code.

findings.title: Incomplete verification of command structure in mock assertion
findings.description: Lines 158-160 loop through rules and check for presence of '--rule' and rule strings, but don't verify the proper pairing or order expected in the actual command list. The test should verify that for each rule, the --rule flag precedes the rule:error string.
findings.impact: Test may pass even if the command is malformed or rules are in wrong positions, failing to catch integration issues.
findings.remediation: Enhance verification to check proper pairing: verify that '--rule' appears before each 'rule: error' string, or use positional assertions to verify exact command structure.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The factual description is accurate. At tests/tools/test_eslint_security.py:156-160 the test extracts `cmd = args[0]` (the argv list handed to `subprocess.run`) and, per rule, asserts only that the token `'--rule'` is somewhere in the list and that the token `'{rule}: error'` is somewhere in the list. It never asserts adjacency, ordering, or that the number of `'--rule'` occurrences matches the number of rules. Because `assertIn` on a list is unordered element membership, a regression in skill/scripts/tools/eslint_security.py:41-42 such as changing `cmd.extend(["--rule", f"{rule}: error"])` to emit a single leading `'--rule'` followed by N bare rule tokens would still pass this test while producing an argv that eslint would reject. I checked whether this is caught elsewhere: tests/test_phase1_integration.py:80-93 (`test_eslint_security_finds_eval`) does really invoke the adapter against tests/fixtures/insecure-js, but it self-skips on `FileNotFoundError` and on `if rc not in (0, 1)` — which is exactly the exit status a malformed eslint invocation would produce — so the malformed-argv case is silently skipped rather than failed. No other file exercises this command construction. Confidence is LIKELY rather than CERTAIN only because the residual risk is narrow: the per-rule token assertion at line 160 already pins each rule's presence, so the uncovered surface is limited to flag/value pairing, which is why LOW severity is the right weight. The remediation (assert `cmd[cmd.index(f'{rule}: error') - 1] == '--rule'`, or compare `cmd.count('--rule')` to `len(RULE_CWE)`) is sound and, unlike the remediation attached to the sibling claim TQ-008 in this batch, would pass against the current correct implementation.

findings.title: test_base.py places `if __name__ == "__main__": unittest.main()` mid-file, silently dropping TestRunTool when run as a script
findings.description: tests/tools/test_base.py defines `class TestBase` (line 10), then at lines 39-40 has `if __name__ == "__main__": unittest.main()`, and only after that (line 43) defines `class TestRunTool` — the suite covering F-CAL-1 (run_tool's capped stderr-excerpt logging on non-(0,1) exit codes). Every other file in this group (test_brakeman.py, test_bundler_audit.py, test_cargo_audit.py, test_eslint_security.py, test_npm_audit.py, test_osv_scanner.py, test_pip_audit.py, test_ruby_integration.py, test_java_integration.py, test_csharp_integration.py, test_legacy_sarif.py) places this guard at the very end of the file, after all TestCase classes are defined. Under pytest (the only invocation path used by CI per .github/workflows/ci.yml and CONTRIBUTING.md — `python -m pytest tests/ -q`), `__name__` is the dotted module path, not `"__main__"`, so the guard is a no-op and both classes are collected normally; this is why the bug is currently latent.
findings.impact: If this file is ever executed directly (`python tests/tools/test_base.py`), Python evaluates the module top-to-bottom: it defines TestBase, then reaches the `if __name__ == "__main__":` block (true in that mode) and calls `unittest.main()`, which discovers tests only from what has been defined in the module *so far* (TestBase) and then calls `sys.exit()` — terminating the interpreter before `class TestRunTool` on line 43 is ever executed. All four TestRunTool cases (including the F-CAL-1 stderr-excerpt regression tests) silently never run in that mode, with no error or skip message indicating anything was omitted.
findings.remediation: Move the `if __name__ == "__main__": unittest.main()` block to the end of the file, after both TestBase and TestRunTool are defined, matching every sibling test file in this group.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Verified directly in tests/tools/test_base.py: `class TestBase(unittest.TestCase)` at line 10, then lines 40-41 contain `if __name__ == "__main__":` / `unittest.main()`, and `class TestRunTool(unittest.TestCase)` is only defined at line 44, running through line 89 (file is 90 lines). The claim's line citations are off by one (it says 39-40 and 43) but the structural fact is exactly as described. The mechanism holds: under `python tests/tools/test_base.py`, Python executes top-to-bottom, the guard is true, `unittest.main()` runs with the default `exit=True` and calls `sys.exit()` after discovering only the classes bound in the module namespace at that point (TestBase alone), so the interpreter terminates before line 44 is ever executed. The four TestRunTool cases — including the F-CAL-1 regression tests at lines 54-72 that assert run_tool emits a capped stderr excerpt for exit codes outside (0,1), guarding skill/scripts/tools/base.py:74-77 — would silently never run, with no error or skip indication. I confirmed the sibling-file comparison: tests/tools/test_java_integration.py has the guard at lines 48-49 of a 49-line file (EOF), and grep shows the same EOF placement in test_eslint_security.py:183, test_npm_audit.py:221, test_osv_scanner.py:150, test_pip_audit.py:136, test_legacy_sarif.py:91, test_ruby_integration.py:44, test_csharp_integration.py:30, test_rust_integration.py:37; test_base.py:40 is the only mid-file occurrence. I also confirmed the latency claim: every documented invocation path uses pytest (.github/workflows/ci.yml:41 `python -m pytest tests/ -q`, CONTRIBUTING.md:13, README.md:92, DEVELOPMENT.md:72, skill/scripts/run_fixture_tests.py:75-78), and no Makefile/script invokes a test module directly, so under pytest `__name__` is the dotted module path and both classes are collected. Severity is therefore correctly bounded as latent/maintainability, not an active CI coverage hole — MEDIUM is arguably generous, but the defect and the fix (move the guard to EOF) are real and unambiguous.

findings.title: test_cargo_audit.py never exercises the custom CVSS v3.1 scoring math that determines cargo-audit finding severity
findings.description: cargo_audit.py's `_cvss_v3_score` (lines 8-40) hand-implements the CVSS v3.1 base-score formula (ISS/Impact/Exploitability from a vector string) to bucket severity, and the adjacent `isinstance(cvss, dict)` branch (lines 64-66) buckets from a numeric score directly. tests/tools/test_cargo_audit.py's only fixture, CARGO_AUDIT_SAMPLE, hardcodes `"cvss": None` (line 17), so every assertion in the file exercises solely the `severity = "HIGH"` fallback default (cargo_audit.py line 63) — neither the vector-parsing arithmetic nor the dict-score branch nor the CRITICAL/HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW bucket boundaries are ever run. Contrast with osv_scanner.py's `_cvss_bucket`, which test_osv_scanner.py directly unit-tests at its boundaries (`test_cvss_bucket_boundaries`, values 9.0/7.0/6.9/4.0/3.9) — cargo_audit.py's parallel scoring path has no analogous test. Notably, unlike the official CVSS spec's `Roundup()` step, `_cvss_v3_score` returns the raw (non-rounded) float, so a value that should officially round up to a bucket boundary (e.g., raw 6.951 vs. spec-rounded 7.0) can land in the wrong bucket — exactly the class of bug a boundary-value unit test would catch.
findings.impact: A defect in the vector-parsing (mistyped metric-weight table, wrong exponent, wrong Scope-Changed branch selection) or in the missing-roundup boundary behavior could silently misclassify a CRITICAL Rust CVE as MEDIUM or LOW, changing triage priority for real vulnerable-dependency findings with no test failure to reveal it.
findings.remediation: Add fixtures that route CARGO_AUDIT_SAMPLE (or new samples) through both the CVSS-vector-string branch and the CVSS-dict-score branch, including boundary vectors that land just above/below each of the 9.0/7.0/4.0 thresholds, mirroring test_osv_scanner.py's `test_cvss_bucket_boundaries`.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Every factual assertion checks out against the source. (1) `_cvss_v3_score` occupies lines 8-40 of /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/tools/cargo_audit.py and hand-rolls the CVSS v3.1 ISS/Impact/Exploitability formula from a vector string. (2) The numeric-score branch is exactly at lines 64-66 (`isinstance(cvss, dict)` -> bucket from `cvss.get("score", 0)`), and the string branch at lines 67-70. (3) /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/tests/tools/test_cargo_audit.py's only fixture sets `"cvss": None` at line 17, so both branches are skipped and parse falls through to the line-63 `severity = "HIGH"` default in all four tests; a repo-wide grep for `_cvss_v3_score` finds no reference outside cargo_audit.py, confirming no direct unit test either. (4) The osv_scanner contrast is real: tests/tools/test_osv_scanner.py lines 84-89 `test_cvss_bucket_boundaries` asserts `osv._cvss_bucket` at 9.0/7.0/6.9/4.0/3.9 exactly as described, and cargo_audit has no analogue. (5) The rounding observation is correct: line 38 is `return score` with no CVSS `Roundup()` step, and the buckets at lines 66/70 compare the raw float, so a raw 6.951 (spec Roundup -> 7.0 -> HIGH) buckets as MEDIUM here — a genuine, boundary-test-detectable divergence from the spec. Minor imprecision that does not change the verdict: the test file makes no severity assertion at all, so it is more accurate to say the tests only ever traverse the fallback path than that they assert on it. The one path that could execute the vector math, tests/tools/test_rust_integration.py, is skip-gated on cargo/fixture/return code and asserts nothing about severity, and CI (.github/workflows/ci.yml) installs no Rust toolchain, so it does not close the gap. This is an accurate coverage gap; I found no actual arithmetic defect, so MEDIUM severity is apt.

findings.title: Untested CVSS v3.1 scoring function in cargo_audit adapter
findings.description: The _cvss_v3_score function (lines 8-40) implements complex CVSS v3.1 base score calculation but lacks any direct unit tests. The function is only called when cvss is a string, but the test suite uses cvss=None to avoid testing this code path.
findings.impact: Mathematical errors in CVSS score calculation cannot be detected. The function's correctness is unverified, potentially leading to incorrect severity classifications for Rust vulnerabilities.
findings.remediation: Add comprehensive unit tests for _cvss_v3_score function covering: (1) valid CVSS v3.1 vector strings, (2) edge cases with missing metrics, (3) malformed vector strings, (4) boundary condition scores (9.0, 7.0, 4.0, 3.9).

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Verified directly. `_cvss_v3_score` occupies exactly lines 8-40 of /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/tools/cargo_audit.py and is called from exactly one place, line 68, inside the `elif isinstance(cvss, str)` branch of `parse`. A repo-wide grep for `_cvss_v3_score` returns only its definition (line 8) and that single call site (line 68) — no test file references it. The only unit-test fixture, CARGO_AUDIT_SAMPLE in /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/tests/tools/test_cargo_audit.py line 17, sets `"cvss": None`, so the string branch is never entered; a grep for `cvss` across tests/ shows no cargo-audit fixture with a vector string. The only other path that could reach the function is tests/tools/test_rust_integration.py, which requires a real `cargo` binary plus a working `cargo audit` subcommand (it self-skips at lines 16-17 and 27-28) and is not installed by .github/workflows/ci.yml (ubuntu-latest, pip installs only pytest/ruff/pyyaml/jsonschema) — and even when it runs it asserts only that some finding's citations contain "RUSTSEC-", never a severity or score. So no assertion anywhere constrains this function's arithmetic. The impact statement is not hypothetical: the implementation returns the raw float at line 38 with no CVSS v3.1 roundup (spec requires rounding up to one decimal), so a vector scoring 8.95 raw yields "HIGH" where the published score 9.0 is "CRITICAL" — precisely the class of silent misclassification a unit test would catch. Note also that the sibling adapter already has the tested equivalent for the bucketing half (`_cvss_bucket` in skill/scripts/tools/osv_scanner.py lines 9-17, with boundary tests at tests/tools/test_osv_scanner.py lines 84-89), which shows the project's own standard for this code and that cargo_audit was left below it. The claim's CWE-1104 citation is a poor fit (unmaintained third-party components) and should not be relied on.

findings.title: test_roslyn_secguard.py never tests is_applicable(), which lacks the missing-directory guard its sibling adapters have
findings.description: tests/tools/test_roslyn_secguard.py covers parse(), _build_target(), and invoke(), but has no test for is_applicable() at all. That method (roslyn_secguard.py lines 26-31) calls `os.listdir(target)` unconditionally with no existence/`isdir` check first — unlike BrakemanAdapter.is_applicable() (brakeman.py), which explicitly does `if not os.path.isdir(target): return False` before any os.listdir()-equivalent call. Because select_adapters() in run_tools.py calls `adapter.is_applicable(target)` for every registered adapter against the same target path, a target that doesn't exist (or a race where it's removed between checks) would raise an unhandled FileNotFoundError/NotADirectoryError from RoslynSecGuardAdapter specifically, and there is no test — positive or negative — that would surface this.
findings.impact: An untested crash path in adapter selection: is_applicable() being called on a nonexistent/inaccessible target directory raises instead of returning False, unlike the equivalent case in BrakemanAdapter, and this asymmetry is invisible without a dedicated test.
findings.remediation: Add is_applicable() tests (true with a .csproj/.sln present, false with neither present) and a test for a missing target directory verifying it returns False rather than raising, adding the same os.path.isdir guard as BrakemanAdapter if the raise is unintended.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Every factual element checks out. (1) roslyn_secguard.py:26-31 is_applicable() calls `os.listdir(target)` with no prior os.path.exists/isdir guard. (2) BrakemanAdapter.is_applicable (skill/scripts/tools/brakeman.py:48-50) does exactly `if not os.path.isdir(target): return False` immediately before its os.listdir call, so the asymmetry is real. (3) select_adapters (skill/scripts/run_tools.py:88-91) evaluates `adapter.is_applicable(target)` for every entry in ADAPTERS against the same target, and the CLI call site at run_tools.py:199 is not wrapped in try/except -- so a nonexistent/non-directory --target propagates FileNotFoundError/NotADirectoryError out of main. (4) I checked the other ten adapters' is_applicable implementations (pip_audit, npm_audit, osv_scanner, cargo_audit, spotbugs, dependency_check, bundler_audit use os.path.exists/isfile; eslint_security uses glob.glob; legacy_sarif returns True; brakeman is guarded) -- RoslynSecGuardAdapter is the only one that raises, so the claim's 'from RoslynSecGuardAdapter specifically' is accurate. (5) tests/tools/test_roslyn_secguard.py contains only parse (x4), _build_target, and invoke tests -- no is_applicable test, positive or negative; a repo-wide grep for 'roslyn' under tests/ finds no other assertion on it. tests/tools/test_csharp_integration.py:19-21 does call is_applicable but only after `if not os.path.isdir(target): self.skipTest(...)`, and the AspGoat fixture is not vendored (tests/fixtures/ holds only manifest.json and semgrep.sarif), so that test always skips. The only incidental execution is tests/test_run_tools.py:82-87 (select_adapters on an existing temp dir), which asserts nothing about roslyn and passes an existing directory, so it cannot surface the missing-dir raise -- exactly as the claim states.

findings.title: `RoslynSecGuardAdapter.is_applicable()` raises an unhandled exception on a missing/inaccessible target directory
findings.description: Unlike `brakeman.py` (`if not os.path.isdir(target): return False`), `bundler_audit.py` (`os.path.exists`), and the other adapters that guard with `os.path.exists`/`os.path.isfile`/`glob`, `RoslynSecGuardAdapter.is_applicable()` calls `os.listdir(target)` directly with no existence/type check. If `target` does not exist or is not a directory (e.g. a transient checkout race, a misconfigured path, or a permissions issue), this raises `FileNotFoundError`/`NotADirectoryError`/`PermissionError`, which is not caught by `select_adapters()` in `run_tools.py` and would abort the whole adapter-selection pass rather than just skipping this one adapter.
findings.impact: A single bad/missing target path can crash the tool-selection stage for the entire scan (all adapters), rather than degrading gracefully to "roslyn-secguard not applicable," reducing the availability/robustness of the overall scanning pipeline.
findings.remediation: Guard with an `os.path.isdir(target)` check (and wrap the `os.listdir` call) mirroring the pattern already used in `brakeman.py`, returning `False` on any access error instead of propagating the exception.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Every factual element of the claim checks out. RoslynSecGuardAdapter.is_applicable (/Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/tools/roslyn_secguard.py:26-31) calls os.listdir(target) with no prior existence or type check, so a missing path raises FileNotFoundError, a file path raises NotADirectoryError, and an unreadable directory raises PermissionError. The comparison adapters are as described: brakeman.py:48-49 has `if not os.path.isdir(target): return False` immediately before its own os.listdir; bundler_audit.py:25 uses os.path.exists; cargo_audit.py:48 os.path.exists; npm_audit.py:13-14 os.path.isfile; osv_scanner.py:32 os.path.isfile; spotbugs.py:24 and dependency_check.py:16 os.path.exists; pip_audit.py:17-25 glob/os.path.exists; eslint_security.py:30-34 glob/os.path.isfile; legacy_sarif.py:39 returns True. Roslyn is the only adapter whose applicability probe can raise. The propagation path is real: select_adapters at /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/run_tools.py:88-91 is a bare dict comprehension `{name: adapter for name, adapter in adapters.items() if adapter.is_applicable(target)}` with no try/except, and its only production caller (run_tools.py:199, inside __main__, using the user-supplied --target which defaults to '.') is likewise unguarded, so one raise aborts the entire selection pass rather than skipping one adapter. Note the contrast the claim implies is genuine: the sibling function run_adapters (run_tools.py:102-111) DOES wrap adapter.invoke in `except Exception as e: print(f"adapter {name} failed: {e}; skipping")`, so the defensive pattern exists elsewhere in the same module and is simply absent from selection. Because ADAPTERS iteration order (skill/scripts/tools/__init__.py:14-31) reaches roslyn-secguard last and every preceding probe is exception-safe, a bad target reliably reaches the raising call. No test covers this: the only select_adapters tests (tests/test_run_tools.py:82-87, 161-169) use existing tempfile directories. LOW severity is appropriate -- the consequence is a traceback on a misconfigured/racing path rather than graceful degradation, not a security-boundary failure. CWE-248 (Uncaught Exception) is an apt mapping.

findings.remediation: Add `test_is_applicable_false_when_no_cargo_toml` and `test_is_applicable_false_when_no_gemfile_lock` tests mirroring the pattern already used by the other five adapter test files in this group.

findings.title: test_bundler_audit.py's fixture never exercises an advisory block missing a CVE line, even though _BLOCK_RE requires one
findings.impact: If bundle-audit ever emits an advisory block without a CVE line, `_BLOCK_RE.finditer()` will not match that block at all (regex requires the literal `CVE:` line to be present for the whole block to match), so the entire advisory — including its package name, version, and remediation — is silently dropped from findings with no error, log line, or test to catch the loss of a real vulnerability.
findings.remediation: Make the CVE field capture optional (mirroring the GHSA field) and add a fixture block with GHSA present but no CVE line, asserting the finding is still produced (with `citations` omitting `cve` when absent, as the existing `if not finding["citations"]:` handling already supports).

findings.title: bundler_audit.py: optional GHSA line and non-CVE Criticality/CVE branches untested
findings.description: BUNDLE_AUDIT_SAMPLE in test_bundler_audit.py always includes a GHSA: line and a well-formed CVE-YYYY-NNNN value in every block. The `(?:GHSA:\s*...)?` optional regex group (line 11) and the `if cve.upper().startswith("CVE-")` false branch that pops citations entirely (lines 50, 59-60) are never exercised.
findings.impact: A block missing the optional GHSA line, or one whose CVE field is blank/non-CVE (both of which real bundler-audit output can produce), could silently fail to match the block regex or silently drop citations without a test noticing.
findings.remediation: Add a fixture block without a GHSA: line, and one whose CVE: field is empty, asserting the parser still matches and that citations is correctly omitted when there is no CVE.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Both named branches are demonstrably unexercised. (1) The optional GHSA group at /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/tools/bundler_audit.py line 11 `(?:GHSA:\s*(?P<ghsa>[^\n]+)\n)?`: both fixture blocks in /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/tests/tools/test_bundler_audit.py include a `GHSA:` line (lines 13 and 22), so the group-absent path never runs. (2) The false branch of `"citations": {"cve": [cve]} if cve.upper().startswith("CVE-") else {}` (line 50) and the follow-on `if not finding["citations"]: finding.pop("citations", None)` (lines 59-60): both fixture CVE values are `CVE-2020-8164` and `CVE-2020-7595`, so citations are always populated and the pop never executes. A grep of the entire tests tree for bundler/GHSA/Criticality shows BUNDLE_AUDIT_SAMPLE is the only unit fixture; the sole other consumer, tests/tools/test_ruby_integration.py, is skip-gated on a vendored railsgoat fixture plus an installed bundle-audit and asserts only that findings is non-empty, so it pins neither branch. One correction to the claim's impact wording, which does not change the verdict: a block missing only the GHSA line matches the regex perfectly well (the group is optional and the surrounding lines are unambiguous), so it will not 'silently fail to match'. The genuinely fragile case is the blank/non-CVE field — with `CVE:` followed by nothing, greedy `\s*` consumes the newline and the cve group captures the next line's text (e.g. `GHSA: GHSA-xxxx`), which then fails the `startswith("CVE-")` test, drops citations, and leaves that garbage string as `tool_evidence.rule_id` (line 52) and as the provenance reasoning (line 61). That makes the untested branch worse than the claim states, not better. Severity LOW is appropriate. CWE-755 is a stretch for a coverage gap and is marked unverified in the claim; I did not verify it.

findings.title: Only the happy-path branch of each conditional is tested; several severity/marker branches are unverified
findings.description: test_is_applicable_when_pom_present (lines 31-33) only exercises the True branch of `SpotBugsAdapter.is_applicable()` (skill/scripts/tools/spotbugs.py:22-24); there is no negative test proving `is_applicable()` returns False when none of pom.xml/build.gradle/build.gradle.kts exist, unlike the paired positive+negative tests in tests/tools/test_brakeman.py (`test_is_applicable_when_rails_files_present` at line 37 and `test_is_applicable_false_without_rails_files` at line 41 for the same style of marker-file check). Likewise, test_parse_produces_finding (lines 21-29) only supplies `priority="1"` in SPOTBUGS_SAMPLE, so the parser's severity map `{"1": "HIGH", "2": "MEDIUM", "3": "LOW"}.get(priority, "MEDIUM")` (spotbugs.py:51) is verified only for the HIGH case -- the MEDIUM, LOW, and unknown-priority-defaults-to-MEDIUM branches, the missing-SourceLine fallback (`file_path=""`, `line=1`), and the unknown-bug-type path where `citations` is popped entirely (spotbugs.py:69-74, since `btype` not in `_SPOTBUGS_CWE`) are never exercised by any test in this file.
findings.impact: Regressions in the severity-priority mapping, the no-SourceLine fallback, the unknown-bug-type/no-CWE code path, or the is_applicable() False branch could ship without a failing test, since only a single representative input shape is checked.
findings.remediation: Add is_applicable-false coverage (mirroring test_brakeman.py:41-44) and parametrize/duplicate test_parse_produces_finding with priority="2", priority="3", an unmapped priority value, a BugInstance with no <SourceLine>, and a btype absent from _SPOTBUGS_CWE, asserting the resulting severity, location fallback, and citations-key-omission behavior respectively.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Every specific assertion and line reference is accurate. (1) tests/tools/test_spotbugs.py:31-33 is the only is_applicable test and asserts only assertTrue with os.path.exists mocked to match pom.xml; there is no False-branch test for skill/scripts/tools/spotbugs.py:22-24. The paired negative test the claim cites does exist at tests/tools/test_brakeman.py:41-44, and the same positive+negative pairing exists in test_npm_audit.py:82, test_osv_scanner.py:110, test_eslint_security.py:131, and test_pip_audit.py:86/91/96 — so spotbugs is a genuine outlier, not a house style. (2) SPOTBUGS_SAMPLE (test_spotbugs.py:9-17) contains a single BugInstance with priority="1", so the severity map at spotbugs.py:51 is exercised only for the "1"->HIGH entry; "2"->MEDIUM, "3"->LOW, and the .get(priority, "MEDIUM") default for an unmapped value are all unreached. Note the default is genuinely reachable in the branch sense but also masked: bug.get("priority", "3") at line 50 only defaults to "3" when the attribute is absent, so an out-of-range value like "4" is what hits the MEDIUM default — worth a test precisely because that interaction is non-obvious. findings.title: Duplicated parse() calls across tests and no assertion of full finding-schema conformance
findings.description: `test_parse_produces_finding` (lines 21-29) and `test_parse_includes_provenance` (lines 35-39) each independently call `sb.SpotBugsAdapter().parse(SPOTBUGS_SAMPLE, "g1")` against the identical fixture rather than sharing a `setUp()`-computed result, which is a minor duplication/maintainability issue as the fixture grows (see TEST-005). findings.impact: Regressions in unexercised fields (e.g. `_group` not being threaded through, or `id` format drifting from the `PREFIX-NNN` convention other tooling depends on for deduplication/fingerprinting) would not be caught by this test file.
findings.remediation: Compute `findings` once in `setUp()` and reuse it across test methods; add assertions for `id`, `confidence`, `category`, `panel`, and `_group` to close the schema-conformance gap.

findings.title: Fixture implies category-based filtering that the adapter (and tests) never actually verify
findings.description: SPOTBUGS_SAMPLE (tests/tools/test_spotbugs.py:9-17) tags its single `<BugInstance>` with `category="SECURITY"`, and the surrounding test suite treats every parsed finding as belonging to the 'security' panel (spotbugs.py:61 hardcodes `"panel": "security"`). However, `SpotBugsAdapter.parse()` (skill/scripts/tools/spotbugs.py:48, `for bug in root.findall("BugInstance")`) never reads or filters on `bug.get("category")` -- it converts *every* `<BugInstance>` element in the report into a `panel: security` finding, regardless of category. Because the test fixture only ever contains one SECURITY-category instance, no test in this file (or elsewhere) proves what happens when a real spotbugs+findsecbugs XML report -- which mixes core-SpotBugs categories such as STYLE, PERFORMANCE, CORRECTNESS, BAD_PRACTICE alongside FindSecBugs's SECURITY category -- is parsed.
findings.impact: As currently tested/implemented, running real SpotBugs (which the invoke() command in spotbugs.py:34-38 does not restrict to security-only output, e.g. no `-effort` or category filter is passed) against a target with core-SpotBugs warnings would surface ordinary code-quality bugs as 'security' panel findings, diluting the security signal in synthesized reports. The test suite gives no evidence either way because it never includes a non-SECURITY BugInstance in its fixture.
findings.remediation: Either add explicit category filtering to SpotBugsAdapter.parse() (skip BugInstance elements whose category != 'SECURITY') and add a test asserting a non-SECURITY BugInstance is excluded, or, if all-categories inclusion is intentional, add a test proving a non-SECURITY BugInstance is still correctly parsed/categorized so the current behavior is a documented, verified contract rather than an untested assumption.
references: skill/scripts/tools/spotbugs.py:34-38 (invoke passes -pluginList only; no -include/-onlyAnalyze category restriction)
docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-01-scanner-ecosystem-expansion-design.md:83 (spec says to parse 'category'; implementation drops it)
tests/tools/test_java_integration.py:17-28 (only other parse consumer; skips because WebGoat fixture is not vendored)

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Every factual assertion in the claim checks out against the code. (1) The fixture at /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/tests/tools/test_spotbugs.py:11 does carry category="SECURITY" on its single BugInstance. (2) /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/tools/spotbugs.py:61 hardcodes "panel": "security" and :62 hardcodes "category": "jvm_security". (3) I read parse() in full (spotbugs.py:41-78): it reads only bug.get("type") and bug.get("priority") plus the nested SourceLine. There is no reference to bug.get("category") anywhere in the file — I grepped the whole skill/scripts tree for the string SECURITY and the only hit is the unrelated "jvm_security" literal, so no category gating exists in the adapter or downstream. (4) invoke() (spotbugs.py:26-39) builds [<spotbugs_home>/bin/spotbugs, -textui, -xml, -pluginList, <findsecbugs-plugin.jar>, classes] — -pluginList only *adds* the FindSecBugs detectors; there is no -include filter file, no -onlyAnalyze, and no visitor restriction, so core SpotBugs detectors (STYLE/PERFORMANCE/CORRECTNESS/BAD_PRACTICE/etc.) still run and emit BugInstances that parse() will convert into panel:security findings. (5) No test anywhere covers a non-SECURITY BugInstance: the only spotbugs XML fixture in the repo is SPOTBUGS_SAMPLE, and the only other consumer, tests/tools/test_java_integration.py:17-28, self-skips because the WebGoat fixture is not vendored (tests/fixtures/ contains only manifest.json and semgrep.sarif). (6) Downstream does not compensate: skill/scripts/synthesize.py only validates panel against VALID_PANELS and buckets by it (synthesize.py:57-58, :652, :733-746); ingest_tools.py performs no panel/category filtering. Additional supporting evidence the claim did not cite: the design spec at docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-01-scanner-ecosystem-expansion-design.md:83 explicitly says the adapter should parse `type`, `category`, `priority`, `Class/SourceLine` — the implementation silently drops `category`, so this is a documented-intent-vs-code gap, not merely a stylistic quibble. Confidence is LIKELY rather than CERTAIN only because the predicted real-world impact (mixed-category output from a live spotbugs+findsecbugs run) cannot be observed from the repository alone — there is no recorded real SpotBugs XML artifact checked in; the claim's own remediation (add a non-SECURITY BugInstance test) is precisely what would settle it. Minor imprecision in the claim that does not change the verdict: `-effort` is a analysis-depth flag, not a category filter, so citing its absence is not evidence either way; the load-bearing evidence is the absence of any -include/-onlyAnalyze and of any category read in parse().

findings.title: Test fixture hardcodes category="SECURITY" but the adapter never filters on it, masking a mislabeling risk
findings.description: SPOTBUGS_SAMPLE's only <BugInstance> is tagged category="SECURITY", and test_parse_produces_finding only validates parsing of that security-tagged bug. The adapter under test (skill/scripts/tools/spotbugs.py:48, `for bug in root.findall("BugInstance"):`) never reads or filters on the `category` attribute at all. A real SpotBugs run also emits CORRECTNESS/STYLE/PERFORMANCE/MT_CORRECTNESS/etc.-categorized bugs, all of which would be unconditionally stamped `panel: security` and `category: jvm_security` by this adapter. No test in the suite proves or disproves this behavior, so the misclassification risk is invisible to CI.
findings.impact: Non-security static-analysis noise would be injected into the security panel at full priority mixed with genuine security findings, degrading signal-to-noise and creating a plausible path for real vulnerabilities to be overlooked amid mislabeled noise.
findings.remediation: Add a test case with a non-SECURITY-category BugInstance and assert the adapter's intended behavior (exclude it, or explicitly relabel panel/category); update SpotBugsAdapter.parse() to branch on the `category` attribute accordingly.
references: skill/scripts/tools/spotbugs.py:48-62 (BugInstance loop ignores the category attribute; panel/category hardcoded)
skill/scripts/ingest_tools.py:72-77 (JSON-prefix trim applied to XML written as spotbugs.json — caveat on downstream impact)

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The code-level assertions are all verified. tests/tools/test_spotbugs.py:11 is the sole BugInstance in the suite and is tagged category="SECURITY" (a repo-wide grep for `BugInstance` outside .panopticon.prev-* returns only this fixture, skill/scripts/tools/spotbugs.py:48, and the two design/plan docs). skill/scripts/tools/spotbugs.py:41-78 reads only `type`, `priority`, and the nested SourceLine; it never calls bug.get("category") and unconditionally stamps `"panel": "security"` (line 61) and `"category": "jvm_security"` (line 62) on every BugInstance. The invocation is not narrowed either: skill/scripts/tools/spotbugs.py:34-38 builds `[spotbugs, -textui, -xml, -pluginList, findsecbugs-plugin.jar, classes]` with no `-bugCategories`/`-include` filter, and a grep of the Dockerfile (lines 61-69) shows only SpotBugs + the FindSecBugs plugin installed, no filter file — so the core SpotBugs detectors (CORRECTNESS/STYLE/PERFORMANCE/MT_CORRECTNESS) still run and their output would flow through parse() labeled security, with priority=1 mapping to HIGH (line 51). Two pieces of extra corroboration the claim did not cite: the design doc at docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-01-scanner-ecosystem-expansion-design.md:83 explicitly specifies parsing `category` from BugInstance, so the implementation diverges from documented intent; and no schema/behavioral test compensates (tests/test_schemas.py has no spotbugs case, tests/tools/test_java_integration.py:17-28 is skip-gated and only asserts truthiness). Caveat on the claimed impact rather than the mechanism, which is why I withhold CERTAIN: I could not confirm the mislabeled findings actually reach a report. spotbugs is absent from LEGACY_SARIF_TOOLS (skill/scripts/tools/legacy_sarif.py:13), so run_tools.py:154-155 writes its XML to `spotbugs.json`, and ingest_dir (skill/scripts/ingest_tools.py:72-77) then trims the payload to the first `{` or `[` byte. Real SpotBugs XML begins with `<?xml` but typically contains `[` inside method signatures, which would truncate the document and make ET.fromstring raise, causing all spotbugs findings to be dropped at ingest. Confirming or refuting that requires real SpotBugs output (a separate defect either way). The parse()-level misclassification and the fixture blind spot are real regardless; severity LOW is appropriate, and the finding is better characterized as a classification/test-coverage gap than a security vulnerability (citation_quality: none is accurate).

findings.title: parse() branch coverage gaps: priority mapping, missing SourceLine, unmapped bug type, and multi-instance handling are all untested
findings.description: `SPOTBUGS_SAMPLE` and its consuming test exercise exactly one `BugInstance`, with `priority="1"` (HIGH) and a bug `type` present in `_SPOTBUGS_CWE`. Several distinct branches in `SpotBugsAdapter.parse()` (skill/scripts/tools/spotbugs.py:41-78) are never exercised: (1) priority `"2"`/`"3"`/any other value going through `severity = {"1":"HIGH","2":"MEDIUM","3":"LOW"}.get(priority, "MEDIUM")`; (2) a `BugInstance` with no nested `<SourceLine>` element, where `source is None` and the code falls back to `file_path=""`, `line=1`; (3) a bug `type` absent from `_SPOTBUGS_CWE`, which takes the `finding.pop("citations", None)` path (every type in the current sample has a mapped CWE, so this branch — which produces a finding with no citations at all — is never exercised); (4) multiple `BugInstance` elements in one report, which would exercise the `id`-increment logic (`SB-001`, `SB-002`, ...).
findings.impact: Real-world SpotBugs/FindSecBugs XML routinely contains bug types outside the small `_SPOTBUGS_CWE` map, missing SourceLine elements (e.g. synthetic/generated code), and multiple findings per run; none of these realistic shapes are covered, so a regression in any of these branches (e.g. an exception on `source is None`, or an incorrect fallback `line`/`file` value reaching a report) would not be caught.
findings.remediation: Extend SPOTBUGS_SAMPLE (or add parametrized fixtures) covering: priority 2 and 3, a BugInstance without SourceLine, a bug type not in _SPOTBUGS_CWE (asserting `"citations" not in finding`), and multiple BugInstance entries (asserting sequential ids).
references: skill/scripts/tools/spotbugs.py:41-78 (parse; priority map, SourceLine fallback, citations pop, id increment)
skill/scripts/tools/spotbugs.py:69,73-74 (citations None -> pop path never exercised)
skill/scripts/tools/spotbugs.py:47,57,77 + skill/scripts/tools/base.py:47-48 (id increment never exercised beyond SB-001)

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: All four claimed untested branches are real branches in parse() and none is exercised by any test in the repository. Reading skill/scripts/tools/spotbugs.py:41-78: (1) line 51 is `severity = { "1": "HIGH", "2": "MEDIUM", "3": "LOW" }.get(priority, "MEDIUM")`; the only fixture uses priority="1" (test_spotbugs.py:11) and the only severity assertion is `assertEqual(f["severity"], "HIGH")` (test_spotbugs.py:26), so the "2"/"3"/default-"MEDIUM" arms are dead in test. (2) lines 52-54 are `source = bug.find(".//SourceLine")` then two `if source is not None else` fallbacks yielding file_path="" and line=1; the fixture always nests a SourceLine (test_spotbugs.py:13), so the None arm is never taken. Note the fallback is benign — `line` becomes the int 1 and line 64's `int(line) if line else 1` handles it without raising — so this is a coverage gap, not a latent crash. (3) lines 55/69/73-74: when btype is absent from _SPOTBUGS_CWE (spotbugs.py:7-15) the finding's "citations" is set to None and then popped; the sole fixture type SQL_NONCONSTANT_STRING_PASSED_TO_EXECUTE is mapped, and test_spotbugs.py:29 asserts CWE-89 is present, so the pop path is never executed. (4) lines 47/57/77: `n` starts at 1 and increments per BugInstance feeding new_finding_id (base.py:47-48, f"{prefix}-{n:03d}"); the fixture has exactly one BugInstance and test_spotbugs.py:23 asserts len(findings)==1, so SB-002 and beyond are never produced. I confirmed no other test covers these: grepping the repo for spotbugs found only tests/tools/test_spotbugs.py, tests/tools/test_java_integration.py, and tests/test_run_tools.py; the java integration test (test_java_integration.py:17-28) self-skips because tests/fixtures/ contains only manifest.json and semgrep.sarif (no WebGoat), and it asserts nothing beyond `assertTrue(findings)`; tests/test_run_tools.py:133 only checks docker mount strings. The claim's attached citations (CWE-89 / A03:2021-Injection) are spurious — they describe the bug type inside the sample fixture, not the coverage gap being reported — so I have not carried them forward, but that mislabeling does not affect the substance of the finding.

findings.title: Overlapping/near-duplicate coverage with the confusingly named tests/tools/test_rust_cs_integration.py
findings.description: tests/tools/test_rust_integration.py's single test already guards its cargo-audit fixture run with `if not shutil.which("cargo"): self.skipTest(...)` (line 16-17), so the 'cargo toolchain absent' path is already implicitly covered by that skip. A sibling file, tests/tools/test_rust_cs_integration.py, exists solely to re-assert the inverse of that same condition: `TestRustCsIntegration.test_cargo_audit_skips_without_rust` checks `ADAPTERS["cargo-audit"]` is registered and, only when `shutil.which("cargo")` is falsy, ends with a no-op `self.assertTrue(True)` (a tautological assertion that can never fail and verifies nothing beyond adapter registration, which test_rust_integration.py already implicitly requires via `ADAPTERS["cargo-audit"]`). The file's name ('rust_cs') and its `raise unittest.SkipTest(...)` when cargo IS available suggest it may be a leftover/orphaned artifact from a prior refactor (e.g. an abandoned combined Rust+C# integration module), since it contains no C#-related content and its only meaningful assertion is a tautology.
findings.impact: Confusing test-suite organization: a reader looking for Rust integration coverage must reconcile two similarly-scoped files with different names and no clear division of responsibility, and the tautological `assertTrue(True)` gives false confidence of coverage for the 'cargo unavailable' scenario without actually verifying any adapter behavior in that state.
findings.remediation: Either delete tests/tools/test_rust_cs_integration.py (its registration check is already covered by test_rust_integration.py and the module-level `ADAPTERS` dict is unconditionally populated in skill/scripts/tools/__init__.py) or repurpose/rename it to assert something meaningful when cargo is absent, e.g. that `adapter.is_applicable(target)` still correctly reports True/False based on Cargo.toml presence independent of the cargo binary's availability.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning:
The factual description of `/Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/tests/tools/test_rust_cs_integration.py` is exact. The whole file is 16 lines: `adapter = ADAPTERS["cargo-audit"]`, `assertIsNotNone(adapter)`, `if shutil.which("cargo"): raise unittest.SkipTest("cargo is available; run full fixture test instead")`, then `self.assertTrue(True)`. So when cargo IS present the test skips, and when cargo is ABSENT the only thing it verifies is a tautology. `assertIsNotNone(adapter)` is effectively tautological too, since `skill/scripts/tools/__init__.py:14-31` populates `ADAPTERS` unconditionally with instances. The file contains zero C#-related content despite the `rust_cs` name; C# coverage lives in a separate `tests/tools/test_csharp_integration.py`.

The 'orphaned artifact' hypothesis is confirmed by the repo's own plan documents. `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-01-scanner-ecosystem-expansion.md:1098-1150` (Task 9, 'Register Rust/C# adapters and add integration test') creates this file verbatim and labels it 'Step 2: Add integration placeholder', with expected outcome 'PASS or SKIP'. The later plan `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-02-local-scanner-fixture-suite.md:34,555-604` then adds the real fixture-backed `test_rust_integration.py` (and `test_csharp_integration.py` per the design doc at `specs/2026-08-02-local-scanner-fixture-suite-design.md:219`). So it is a superseded placeholder from the earlier phase, left in place — which is the claim's core structural point, correctly hedged in the original text.

One caveat that does not overturn the claim but does undercut its remediation: the assertion that the registration check 'is already covered by test_rust_integration.py' is not accurate. `test_rust_integration.py:19-20` uses `if "cargo-audit" not in ADAPTERS: self.skipTest(...)` — a skip, not a failure — and it is preceded by the `shutil.which("cargo")` skip at 16-17, so on a cargo-less machine it never reaches that line. Grepping all uses of `ADAPTERS` in `tests/` shows registry assertions only for eslint-security (`test_eslint_security.py:174-175`) and the legacy SARIF family (`test_legacy_sarif.py:86-88`); `test_cargo_audit.py` imports the class directly and never touches the registry. So `test_rust_cs_integration.py:12` is currently the only unconditional check that would fail (KeyError) if `cargo-audit` were dropped from the registry. Deleting the file as the remediation suggests would silently remove that one signal; the remediation's alternative (repurpose it to assert something meaningful) is the safe branch. Confidence LIKELY rather than CERTAIN because the 'overlapping/near-duplicate coverage' framing is a judgment call and the remediation rationale is partly wrong, while the underlying facts — tautological assertion, misleading name, superseded placeholder — are all verified.

findings.title: sys.path.insert boilerplate duplicated identically in both reviewed files (and every other test module); no conftest.py
findings.description: tests/tools/test_rust_integration.py:6 and tests/tools/test_spotbugs.py:6 both execute the identical `sys.path.insert(0, os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), os.pardir, os.pardir, "skill"))` before importing `scripts.tools.*`. This same line, byte-for-byte equivalent modulo the relative pardir count, is repeated across all 27 files under tests/ and tests/tools/ (confirmed: no tests/conftest.py exists anywhere in the repository, and no `[tool.pytest.ini_options] pythonpath` is set in pyproject.toml).
findings.impact: Purely cosmetic/maintainability nit -- currently consistent, but any future rename or restructuring of the `skill/` layout requires editing this line in every test file individually rather than in one place; it also makes each file's import section noisier than a package-relative import would be.
findings.remediation: Introduce a tests/conftest.py that performs the sys.path.insert once, or add `[tool.pytest.ini_options] pythonpath = ["skill"]` to pyproject.toml, and drop the per-file duplication from test_rust_integration.py and test_spotbugs.py (and the rest of the suite).

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: All three verifiable sub-claims hold. (1) tests/tools/test_rust_integration.py:6 and tests/tools/test_spotbugs.py:6 contain the byte-identical line `sys.path.insert(0, os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), os.pardir, os.pardir, "skill"))`. (2) A repo-wide Glob for **/conftest.py returns no files — there is no conftest.py anywhere. (3) pyproject.toml contains only [project], [project.urls] and [tool.ruff] sections; there is no [tool.pytest.ini_options] and a repo-wide grep for 'pythonpath' / 'pytest.ini_options' returns zero hits, and no pytest.ini, setup.cfg, tox.ini or setup.py exists. So the duplication is real and there is genuinely no single place to change it. One factual correction for the auditor: the claimed count of 27 files is wrong — grep for sys.path.insert across tests/ returns 35 occurrences in 35 files, and the word 'all' is also inaccurate since 4 of the 39 test modules (e.g. tests/test_assets.py) do not contain the line at all. The miscount does not affect the substance. This is correctly filed as INFO/style; the impact statement ('purely cosmetic/maintainability nit') is honest, and the remediation is the standard pytest fix. Note the same pattern is not confined to tests: skill/scripts/tools/base.py:9 does its own sys.path.insert, so a conftest-only fix would not remove all such boilerplate from the repo.

findings.title: Sole RUSTSEC/known-vulnerability regression test skips (rather than fails) whenever tooling or network access is unavailable
findings.description: This is the only test validating that panopticon's cargo-audit adapter correctly surfaces known RUSTSEC/CVE advisories for a vulnerable dependency. It contains five separate `self.skipTest(...)` escape hatches: `cargo` not installed (line 17), `cargo-audit` adapter unregistered (line 20), fixture directory absent (line 23), adapter not applicable (line 25), and any `cargo audit` exit code outside (0, 1) (line 28) — the last of which also covers cargo-audit failing to reach the RustSec advisory database over the network (e.g. an offline/sandboxed CI runner). Most CI reporting treats a skipped test the same as a passing one, so any environment lacking the Rust toolchain, the registered adapter, or outbound network access will silently report this security-detection test as non-failing.
findings.impact: A real regression in the RUSTSEC/CVE citation or severity-scoring logic in skill/scripts/tools/cargo_audit.py can ship undetected in any CI lane that lacks cargo, cargo-audit, or network access to the advisory database, since the only guardrail against that regression skips instead of failing.
findings.remediation: Ensure at least one CI lane has the Rust toolchain, cargo-audit, and network access (or a vendored/offline RustSec advisory snapshot) so this test executes and can fail; convert the adapter-registration and fixture-presence checks to hard failures rather than skips, reserving skipTest only for genuinely optional/local-dev conditions.
references: tests/tools/test_rust_integration.py:16-28 (five skipTest branches gating the only assertions)
.github/workflows/ci.yml:36-41 (test lane installs pytest/ruff/pyyaml/jsonschema only; no cargo-audit)
Dockerfile.fixtures:20,54-55 (only place cargo-audit is installed; explicitly local-use-only)
skill/scripts/tools/base.py:64-78 (run_tool returns raw returncode; any cargo-audit failure yields rc outside (0,1))

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Verified line-by-line. tests/tools/test_rust_integration.py contains exactly the five skipTest escape hatches at the cited lines: cargo missing (L16-17), adapter unregistered (L19-20), fixture directory absent (L22-23), adapter not applicable (L24-25), and rc not in (0,1) (L27-28). Only after all five pass do the two real assertions run (L30-34). The claim's central assertion — that no CI lane actually executes those assertions — is confirmed from the repo: .github/workflows/ci.yml is the only workflow that runs the suite (`python -m pytest tests/ -q` on ubuntu-latest) and installs only `pytest ruff pyyaml jsonschema`; cargo-audit is never installed there. findings.title: Five cascading skip conditions plus an implicit network dependency reduce this test to a near-permanent skip that masks real failures
findings.description: The single test method in this file gates its assertions behind five sequential `skipTest` conditions: `cargo` binary present, `cargo-audit` adapter registered, `vulnerable-rust` fixture present, `adapter.is_applicable(target)` true, and `rc in (0, 1)`. `cargo audit` also needs network access on most runs to fetch/update the RustSec advisory database (`~/.cargo/advisory-db`), which is not accounted for at all — a network-restricted CI sandbox will typically produce a non-(0,1) exit code and hit the final skip. Because unittest reports skipped tests as neither pass nor fail, any of these conditions failing silently converts a real regression (e.g. a broken adapter, a broken fixture, or a broken `cargo audit` invocation) into 'skipped' rather than 'failed', with no counter or CI signal distinguishing 'skipped because environment lacks cargo/network' from 'skipped because the adapter itself is broken'. The same pattern repeats in test_java_integration.py, test_ruby_integration.py, and test_csharp_integration.py, but is reviewed here as it applies to this file.
findings.impact: In typical sandboxed/offline CI, this is effectively the only test exercising `CargoAuditAdapter.invoke()` against a real `cargo audit` process end-to-end, and it will silently skip rather than fail if the adapter regresses, giving false confidence that Rust dependency scanning is verified when it may not be running at all.
findings.remediation: Track and surface skip counts (e.g., fail the suite or emit a warning if this test has been skipped for more than N consecutive CI runs), or add a mocked-subprocess unit test (following the pattern in test_cargo_audit.py::test_invoke_runs_cargo_audit) that exercises the same invoke()->parse() path without requiring cargo/network, so the assertions run unconditionally in CI.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning:
Verified against the file itself. `/Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/tests/tools/test_rust_integration.py` contains exactly one test method, and the claimed five sequential skip gates are present verbatim: `shutil.which("cargo")` (16-17), `"cargo-audit" not in ADAPTERS` (19-20), `os.path.isdir(target)` (22-23), `adapter.is_applicable(target)` (24-25), and `rc not in (0, 1)` (27-28). Only after all five does any assertion run (30-34).

The 'near-permanent skip in CI' part checks out for the repo's actual CI. `.github/workflows/ci.yml` is the only workflow that runs the suite (`python -m pytest tests/ -q` on ubuntu-latest) and installs only `pytest ruff pyyaml jsonschema` — it never installs `cargo-audit`. `.github/workflows/security.yml` runs `run_tools.py`, not pytest. Grepping `.github/` for cargo/rust returns zero matches. So on a GitHub runner the adapter's `invoke()` (`skill/scripts/tools/cargo_audit.py:50-52`, `["cargo", "audit", "--format", "json"]`) cannot succeed and the test lands on the fifth skip (or the first, if `cargo` is absent). The fixture itself is present and valid (`tests/fixtures/vulnerable-rust/Cargo.toml`, `Cargo.lock`), so the fixture gate is not the blocker — the tool gate is.

The implicit-network point is supported by repo evidence, not just general knowledge: `Dockerfile.fixtures:20` installs `cargo install cargo-audit --version 0.22.2` but line 42 only runs `cargo build`, whereas the design spec it was built from (`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-02-local-scanner-fixture-suite-design.md:90`) specified `cargo build && cargo audit`. The advisory DB is therefore never warmed into the image, so `cargo audit` must fetch `~/.cargo/advisory-db` at test runtime, i.e. the test needs network in the container. Nothing in the test accounts for this; a fetch failure yields a non-(0,1) rc and hits the same silent skip.

On 'no counter or CI signal': I found no skip-count gate anywhere. `ci.yml` uses `-q` without `-rs`, so skip reasons are not even printed. The dedicated harness `skill/scripts/run_fixture_tests.py:87-88,132-138` returns pytest's exit code, which is 0 when every test skips, and its printed summary counts fixtures present/missing — never skips. Notably, `docs/superpowers/2026-08-03-calibration-fixmes.md:9-11` asserts the fixture integration tests are 'green', a statement that pytest's exit code cannot distinguish from 'all skipped' — exactly the failure mode the claim describes. The same cascading pattern is confirmed in `test_java_integration.py:20-26,33-39`, `test_ruby_integration.py:20-26,33-39`, `test_csharp_integration.py:16-25`.

One mild overstatement: `tests/tools/test_cargo_audit.py:46-54` does cover the `invoke()` argv with a mocked `subprocess.run`, so a broken command line would be caught; the claim itself acknowledges this in its remediation. The uncovered gap is the real-process invoke->parse path, which is what the claim's impact actually rests on. Confidence LIKELY rather than CERTAIN because the test does run for real in the Docker fixtures harness (the intended environment), so it is not literally dead — but that harness is manual (DEVELOPMENT.md:79-80, skill/SKILL.md:104-110), not CI-gated, and cannot distinguish skip from pass either. Note: the attached CWE-1104 on the sibling claim would be wrong here; CWE-392 is a defensible fit for a silently-swallowed error condition.

findings.title: Single test method verifies only 'some findings exist'; no assertions on severity, group propagation, id format, or tool_evidence
findings.description: This file contains exactly one test. Beyond `assertTrue(findings)` and the RUSTSEC-citation check, it never asserts on: the computed `severity` (exercising `_cvss_v3_score`/dict-vs-string CVSS handling in cargo_audit.py), `finding["_group"]` propagation of the `"g1"` argument, `finding["id"]` format (`CA-001`, ...), or `tool_evidence` contents (`package_name`, `vulnerable_versions`, `advisory_url`). Because this is the only test that runs the adapter against *real* `cargo audit` JSON output (the unit tests in test_cargo_audit.py use a synthetic, hand-written payload), a divergence between real cargo-audit's actual JSON shape and what the synthetic unit-test fixture assumes would not be caught by either suite.
findings.impact: Regressions in severity classification (e.g. the CVSS-string parsing math in `_cvss_v3_score`), group-tagging (needed for report aggregation), or tool_evidence fields would not be detected by any test in this file, and the unit tests elsewhere use synthetic data that may drift from real tool output undetected.
findings.remediation: Add assertions on severity, `_group`, `id` format, and `tool_evidence` fields to this integration test, mirroring the depth already present in `test_spotbugs.py::test_parse_produces_finding` for a sibling adapter.
references: tests/tools/test_cargo_audit.py:10-25 (synthetic fixture used for the unit-level tests)

There is no assertion on `severity`, `_group`, `id`, or `tool_evidence` — the claim's inventory is exact.

The cross-file part also holds, and is stronger than the claim states. `skill/scripts/tools/cargo_audit.py:62-71` has three severity branches (dict CVSS, string CVSS via `_cvss_v3_score`, and the `"HIGH"` default), and `_cvss_v3_score` (lines 8-40) implements ~30 lines of CVSS v3.1 base-score arithmetic. findings.title: Fragile stringified-dict substring assertion instead of structural check on citations
findings.description: The only assertion beyond 'findings exist' is `any("RUSTSEC-" in str(f.get("citations")) for f in findings)`. This stringifies the whole `citations` dict and does a substring search rather than checking the actual contract produced by `CargoAuditAdapter.parse()` (`citations["rustsec"]` is a list of strings). A regression that puts a RUSTSEC id in the wrong field, or a coincidental 'RUSTSEC-' substring appearing anywhere else in the stringified dict (e.g. inside a CVE alias list or a future field), would pass this test even though the real structural contract is broken; conversely a correct citations dict under a different key name than expected would also pass. `test_cargo_audit.py` (unit tests, same adapter) shows the more precise pattern is available (asserting concrete dict keys) but this integration test does not use it.
findings.impact: A structural regression in how cargo-audit findings attach RUSTSEC citations (used downstream for citation enrichment and issue identity/fingerprinting) could go undetected by this test even though it is the only test that exercises the adapter against real `cargo audit` output.
findings.remediation: Replace the stringified substring check with a direct structural assertion, e.g. `self.assertTrue(any(any(r.startswith("RUSTSEC-") for r in f.get("citations", {}).get("rustsec", [])) for f in findings))`.
references: tests/tools/test_cargo_audit.py:33-34 (precise dict-key assertion pattern used elsewhere for the same adapter)
skill/scripts/tools/cargo_audit.py:72-76 and :99-100 (citations dict construction and removal when empty)
tests/tools/test_dependency_check.py:32-33 (structural citations["cve"]/["cwe"] assertion pattern used by every other adapter test)

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The quoted assertion is verbatim at tests/tools/test_rust_integration.py:31-34: `any("RUSTSEC-" in str(f.get("citations")) for f in findings)`. The real contract in skill/scripts/tools/cargo_audit.py:74-76 is `citations = {"rustsec": [advisory_id]}` plus an optional `citations["cve"]`, and L99-100 pops the key entirely when empty (so `f.get("citations")` can be None and stringify to 'None'). Stringifying the whole dict means the test passes on any regression that keeps the id somewhere in the mapping under a wrong key — e.g. `{"advisory": ["RUSTSEC-2020-0071"]}` or `{"rustsec_ids": ...}` — which is exactly the fragility claimed. The corroborating evidence is stronger than the claim states: grepping tests/tools/ for 'citations' shows every other adapter test uses the precise structural form (test_dependency_check.py:32-33, test_pip_audit.py:36, test_npm_audit.py:35, test_bundler_audit.py:35, test_osv_scanner.py:94, test_spotbugs.py:29, test_brakeman.py:35, test_roslyn_secguard.py:67, test_legacy_sarif.py:37, test_eslint_security.py:63), and no test anywhere asserts `citations["rustsec"]` structurally — cargo-audit is the only adapter emitting that key and it has zero structural coverage (test_cargo_audit.py never touches citations). Only test_java_integration.py:43-44 shares the same loose stringified pattern. Two minor over-reaches keep this at LIKELY rather than CERTAIN: (a) the 'coincidental RUSTSEC- inside a CVE alias list' scenario is not currently reachable, because cargo_audit.py:73 filters aliases to entries starting with 'CVE-'; (b) the reference to test_cargo_audit.py:33-34 as the 'precise dict-key assertion pattern for the same adapter' is accurate as literal dict-key assertions but those lines assert `source` and `tool_evidence["package_name"]`, not citations. The core defect and the proposed remediation are sound; severity LOW is appropriate.

findings.title: is_applicable() branch coverage gap: build.gradle/build.gradle.kts and the False path are never tested
findings.description: `SpotBugsAdapter.is_applicable()` (skill/scripts/tools/spotbugs.py:22-24) returns True if any of three markers exists: `pom.xml`, `build.gradle`, or `build.gradle.kts`. The test file exercises only the `pom.xml` True branch via a mock that matches paths ending in `pom.xml`; it never verifies the Gradle/Kotlin-DSL branches, nor the False case (no markers present). Sibling adapter test suites in the same directory consistently test both the positive and negative branches (test_pip_audit.py: `test_is_applicable_false_for_setup_py`/`_false_when_no_manifest`; test_npm_audit.py: `test_is_applicable_false_when_no_lockfile`; test_osv_scanner.py: `test_is_applicable_detects_each_marker` iterating every marker plus `test_is_applicable_false_when_no_marker`; test_brakeman.py: `test_is_applicable_false_without_rails_files`), making this an inconsistency specific to test_spotbugs.py.
findings.impact: A regression that breaks the `build.gradle`/`build.gradle.kts` OR-branches (e.g. an accidental `and` instead of `any(...)`, or a typo in a marker string) would silently disable SpotBugs/FindSecBugs from ever running against Gradle-based Java/Kotlin projects, without any test detecting it — matching the class of 'silent false negative' risk this project's own self-scan (FIXME-10) flags as the most misleading failure mode for a security review.
findings.remediation: Add tests for build.gradle and build.gradle.kts presence (each independently, per the osv_scanner pattern) and a test_is_applicable_false_when_no_marker case asserting False when none of the three files exist.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The core factual claim is verified. skill/scripts/tools/spotbugs.py:22-24 is `markers = ["pom.xml", "build.gradle", "build.gradle.kts"]; return any(os.path.exists(os.path.join(target, m)) for m in markers)`. findings.title: SpotBugsAdapter.invoke() has zero test coverage, unlike the equivalent cargo-audit unit test
findings.description: test_spotbugs.py has no test for `SpotBugsAdapter.invoke()` (skill/scripts/tools/spotbugs.py:26-39). That method contains a three-way fallback for locating compiled classes (`target/classes` -> `build/classes` -> `target` itself) and builds the SpotBugs command line from `SPOTBUGS_HOME` (default `/opt/spotbugs`) plus the FindSecBugs plugin path — none of which is exercised. By contrast, the parallel adapter's unit test suite, test_cargo_audit.py::test_invoke_runs_cargo_audit, mocks `subprocess.run` and asserts the exact command/kwargs passed to `run_tool`, giving that adapter's invoke() real coverage.
findings.impact: A bug in the classes-directory fallback order (e.g. checking `build/classes` before `target/classes`, or an inverted `os.path.isdir` condition) could cause SpotBugs to silently analyze an empty or wrong directory. Because `SpotBugsAdapter.parse()` returns `[]` for empty output without erroring, this failure mode looks identical to 'no security bugs found' and would not be caught anywhere in the test suite — the same 'looks like a clean bill of health, actually didn't run' failure class this project's own self-scan doc (docs/superpowers/2026-08-04-run2-fixmes.md, FIXME-10) explicitly calls out as the most misleading way a security review can fail.
findings.remediation: Add a mocked-subprocess test for invoke() covering each of the three classes-directory branches (target/classes present, build/classes present, neither present) and asserting the constructed command includes the expected classes path and plugin jar, following the pattern in tests/tools/test_cargo_audit.py::test_invoke_runs_cargo_audit.

skill/scripts/tools/spotbugs.py:26-39 (invoke; classes-dir fallback, SPOTBUGS_HOME command construction)
tests/tools/test_cargo_audit.py:46-54 (test_invoke_runs_cargo_audit; the pattern this file lacks)
docs/superpowers/2026-08-04-run2-fixmes.md:125-146 (FIXME-10: silent 'no security findings' as the most misleading failure mode)
