findings.title: Undefined 'repo-scope' term in architecture panel scheduling
findings.description: scout.md line 47 states 'architecture' panel should be scheduled 'if any file is repo-scope', but 'repo-scope' is never defined. This creates ambiguity about which files trigger architecture reviews.
findings.impact: Scout agents cannot reliably determine whether to schedule the architecture panel, potentially missing architecture-layer issues or over-scheduling unnecessary reviews.
findings.remediation: Define 'repo-scope' files explicitly (e.g., '.github/workflows/*', 'Dockerfile*', 'docker-compose*.yml', 'k8s/**', '**/package*.json', '**/requirements*.txt', '.gitignore', 'CI config files'). Update scout.md section on surface detection to include specific file patterns.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The literal assertion holds: scout.md:47 reads '- `architecture` if any file is repo-scope' and the term 'repo-scope' is defined nowhere in scout.md. I grepped the whole repository for repo-scope/repo scope/repo_scope; the only occurrences are (a) scout.md:47 itself, (b) its pinned golden tests/goldens/scout.rendered.txt:39 and the eleven previously rendered scout prompts, (c) an orchestrator.py:87 docstring comment, and (d) the design docs, where the term IS defined — docs/superpowers/plans/2026-07-25-panopticon-kimi-port.md:223 says 'architecture if any file is repo-scope (root config, `.github/`, Dockerfile, k8s/helm, docker-compose)' and the design spec at 2026-07-25-panopticon-kimi-port-design.md:61 gives the same gloss. The defining parenthetical was dropped when the rule was copied into the operational prompt. This matters because the scout sees nothing but scout.md's body plus a bare assignment stanza at runtime: I verified this against the real rendered prompt .panopticon.prev-20260803/scout-prompts/._1.md, whose Assignment section supplies only group name, security_mode and a file list — no precomputed surfaces, and no access to orchestrator.py's mechanical ARCHITECTURE_PATTERNS (orchestrator.py:50-59), which is the de facto definition the rest of the system uses. Note also the structural inconsistency: every sibling rule in that list keys off either a named surface ('`database` if `db_sql` surface present') or a plain condition, while line 47 alone introduces an undefined term instead of saying 'if the `architecture` surface is present'. I found empirical support for the resulting ambiguity across one real run: .panopticon.prev-20260803/scout-._5.json lists 'architecture' in `surfaces` yet omits the architecture panel (panels: ['code','security']), while scout-._4.json and scout-._7.json both list the same surface and DO schedule the panel — inconsistent application of the same rule within a single run. Confidence is LIKELY rather than CERTAIN because the ambiguity is partially mitigated: scout.md:25 defines the `architecture` surface as 'repo layout, CI/CD, Docker/k8s, GitHub configs' just 22 lines earlier, which a competent scout can read as the intended synonym — so this is genuine under-specification rather than a total gap, and MEDIUM severity is fair or slightly generous.

findings.title: No documented behavior for output size limit overflow
findings.description: model-profiles.yml defines max_output_size constraints (e.g., 8192 for lens_sweep), but neither lens-sweep.md, panel-review.md, advisor.md, nor scout.md document what happens when an agent's output exceeds these limits. No truncation, retry, or fallback strategy is specified.
findings.impact: Findings may be silently truncated, incomplete, or cause agent failures. Pipeline behavior is undefined when findings exceed output size limits, creating unpredictability in review completeness.
findings.remediation: Document in agent skill files the handling strategy for output overflow: (1) truncation policy and warning mechanism, (2) retry with reduced scope, or (3) multi-batch output mode. Update model-profiles.yml with rationale for size constraints per role.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The documentation gap is real and verified. model-profiles.yml declares max_output_size at lines 6,10,14,18,32,36,40,44 (lens_sweep is indeed 8192 for the kimi host, line 10). A case-insensitive grep for 'truncat|overflow|output size|output_size|too large|cap|limit' across all of skill/**/*.md returns only unrelated hits (SKILL.md:38 '--max-verify N cap the verify queue', two security-checklist bullets). I read scout.md, lens-sweep.md and panel-review.md in full and grepped advisor.md: none of them mention output size, truncation, retry, batching, or any 'if your findings are too many' policy. So the literal claim -- no documented overflow behavior -- is correct. Two important corrections to the claim's framing, which the auditor should apply before acting on it. (1) The mechanism is mis-attributed: max_output_size/max_context_size are inert metadata in this repo. Grep shows they are read nowhere outside model_resolver.py's own fallback tables and tests/test_model_resolver.py:17. dispatch.py:261,286 embed the whole resolve_model() dict as plan entry 'model', and SKILL.md:49 and :79 instruct the host to use only `entry.model.model`. Nothing enforces or checks these caps, so they cannot themselves cause truncation; the real limit is whatever the host model imposes. (2) The consequence is nonetheless real and undocumented: panel-review.md:17 and lens-sweep.md:17 require each reviewer to return the ENTIRE findings JSON as its final message, and synthesize.py:96-118 loads that via evidence.py:155-167 load_json_tolerant, which does not repair truncated JSON -- a cut-off object raises and synthesize.py:106-111 drops the whole file with a single stderr 'PARSE ERROR' line, then grades and gates on the surviving findings. That is precisely the 'silently incomplete review' the claim's impact section describes, so the finding survives; MEDIUM severity is arguably inflated for what is a documentation-only defect, and the remediation should target the agent templates and the load path rather than the yml comments.

findings.title: Finding-ID regex diverges between agent prompts and the report schema
findings.description: The three fan-out agent prompts (`skill/agents/lens-sweep.md` line 28, `skill/agents/panel-review.md` line 33) instruct agents to emit ids matching `^[A-Z]{2,8}-\d{3,}$` (2-8 uppercase letters), but `skill/reference/report-schema.json` line 73 validates ids against the stricter `^[A-Z]{2,4}-[0-9]{3,}$` (only 2-4 letters). Any agent that follows its own prompt literally and picks a prefix of 5-8 letters (e.g. a prefix derived from a panel or lens name such as `SECURITY-001`, `DATABASE-001`) will produce an id the schema rejects.
findings.impact: Findings that are otherwise well-formed can fail report-schema validation purely because of an id-length mismatch between what agents are told is legal and what the schema accepts, causing silent drops or hard validation failures downstream.
findings.remediation: Unify the regex in one place (ideally report-schema.json as the single source of truth) and reference it verbatim from lens-sweep.md and panel-review.md, or widen the schema pattern to `^[A-Z]{2,8}-[0-9]{3,}$` to match what agents are actually told to produce.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Verified every cited line. /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/reference/report-schema.json:73 reads "id": {"type": "string", "pattern": "^[A-Z]{2,4}-[0-9]{3,}$"} inside properties.findings.items.properties. skill/agents/lens-sweep.md:28 and skill/agents/panel-review.md:33 both read '- id: ^[A-Z]{2,8}-\d{3,}$'. The divergence in the allowed prefix length (2-4 vs 2-8) is real and exactly as described; ids such as STRUCT-001 or SECURITY-001 satisfy the prompt contract but fail the schema pattern. This is not hypothetical: the repo's own test suite asserts STRUCT-001 must validate (tests/test_synthesize.py:1434-1439) and the rendered prompt goldens (tests/goldens/lens-sweep.rendered.txt:20, tests/goldens/panel-review.rendered.txt:26) carry the {2,8} form, so agents are in fact told to emit prefixes the schema rejects. Two caveats that do not change the verdict but temper the stated impact: (a) the claim says 'three fan-out agent prompts' yet only two exist with an id pattern — skill/agents/advisor.md and skill/agents/scout.md contain no id regex (grep for '^[A-Z]{' across skill/ returns only the two prompt files, report-schema.json, synthesize.py and tools/base.py); (b) the claimed 'silent drops or hard validation failures downstream' does not occur inside this repo, because nothing in skill/scripts/ imports jsonschema (grep for 'jsonschema' under skill/ returns no matches) and the only runtime id check, synthesize.py:723 via ID_RE at synthesize.py:454, uses the permissive {2,8} form. The exposure is therefore to external consumers that treat report-schema.json as the contract, plus the schema-vs-prompt inconsistency itself. Location, line number and both prompt references are accurate.

findings.title: Finding ID pattern constraint mismatch between schema and specification
findings.description: report-schema.json restricts finding IDs to pattern `^[A-Z]{2,4}-[0-9]{3,}$` (2-4 letter prefix) but lens-sweep.md and panel-review.md specify `^[A-Z]{2,8}-\d{3,}$` (2-8 letter prefix). Schema is more restrictive than the requirement.
findings.impact: Findings with 5-8 letter prefixes will fail schema validation even though they meet the specified format.
findings.remediation: Update report-schema.json line 73 to use pattern `^[A-Z]{2,8}-[0-9]{3,}$` to match the documented specification in lens-sweep.md and panel-review.md.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Independently verified the same three lines. report-schema.json:73 constrains finding ids to ^[A-Z]{2,4}-[0-9]{3,}$; skill/agents/lens-sweep.md:28 and skill/agents/panel-review.md:33 both specify ^[A-Z]{2,8}-\d{3,}$. The schema is strictly more restrictive than the prompt specification for prefixes of 5-8 uppercase letters, so a compliant agent finding such as STRUCT-001 (the very id namespace this claim itself uses) would fail schema validation. The impact sentence — 'findings with 5-8 letter prefixes will fail schema validation' — is true of anyone validating against report-schema.json, and the repo's runtime does not do that (no jsonschema import under skill/scripts/; the live check at synthesize.py:723 uses the widened ID_RE at synthesize.py:454). tests/test_schemas.py does validate findings against schema['properties']['findings']['items'] using jsonschema, but only for tool-adapter findings whose prefixes are all 2-3 letters (PA, NA, OS, ESS, CA, BK, SB, DC, BA, RS), so the mismatch is not caught by any existing test. The remediation (widen line 73 to ^[A-Z]{2,8}-[0-9]{3,}$) is the correct minimal fix and matches what synthesize.py already does. [0-9] vs \d is equivalent here and not a source of divergence.

findings.title: Scout prompt never populates several ScopeProfile fields, orphaning the facet feature
findings.description: `scope-profile-schema.json` defines `has_tests` (line 20), `size` (line 19), `facet` (line 8) and `facet_scope` (lines 24-27) on the ScopeProfile object, but `skill/agents/scout.md` never mentions any of these terms in its instructions (sections cover surfaces, risk, panels, lenses, depth, files, tools only). Separately, `skill/reference/code-review-groups.example.yml` demonstrates a live `facets` feature (lines 8-10, `Uploads`/`Pricing` keyword groups under the `Products` group) that maps directly onto ScopeProfile's `facet`/`facet_scope` fields, yet nothing in scout.md tells the scout how to detect or emit a facet, and the scout is separately required to decide test presence (for the `test` panel rule) without ever being told to record that decision in `has_tests`.
findings.impact: The `facet` grouping feature configured via code-review-groups.yml has no producer: the only agent that emits ScopeProfile (scout) is never instructed to read or set `facet`/`facet_scope`, so facet-scoped reviews likely degrade to unscoped ones silently. `has_tests` and `size` will also be perpetually empty/absent, weakening any downstream consumer that keys off them.
findings.remediation: Add explicit scout.md instructions for detecting the active facet (cross-referencing the group's `facets` config) and setting `facet`/`facet_scope`, and for recording `has_tests`/`size` alongside the panel-selection logic that already needs this information.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Verified directly. (1) `skill/reference/scope-profile-schema.json` defines `facet` (line 8), `size` (19), `has_tests` (20), and `facet_scope` (24-27). (2) I read all 83 lines of `skill/agents/scout.md` and grepped the whole repo: the strings `facet`, `facet_scope`, `has_tests`, and `size` appear nowhere in scout.md, and the rendered golden `tests/goldens/scout.rendered.txt` (the actual dispatched prompt, template body + tool-policy line) likewise omits them. So the sole ScopeProfile producer is never told to emit these fields. (3) Scout is in fact the sole producer: grep for `ScopeProfile` in skill/ yields only scout.md and the schema/SKILL.md/dispatch docstrings. (4) The facet feature is genuinely user-facing but has no producer or consumer: `skill/SKILL.md:31` documents `-g "Group[Facet]"`; `skill/scripts/orchestrator.py:202-207` parses the facet and `:459` echoes it into the result JSON; `load_catalog` (:281-305) parses the `facets:` keyword map from `code-review-groups.example.yml:8-10`; but the facet keywords are never used to filter files — `main` (:510-513) expands ALL of `catalog[name]['patterns']` regardless of facet, and `dispatch.build_plan` (:233-299) reads only `group`, `files`, `depth`, `panels`, `lenses`, `security_mode`, never `facet`/`facet_scope`. So a facet-scoped run silently reviews the whole group. (5) Decisive corroboration: the implementation plan `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-07-25-panopticon-kimi-port.md:209-212` specifies a `## Facet scoping` section for the scout prompt ('If a `facet` is supplied, populate `facet_scope` with the subset of files (and a one-line rationale) ... Resolve declared facet keywords') — that section was dropped from the shipped scout.md. Also confirmed: SKILL.md step 3 tells the orchestrating agent to append only 'the group's name, its file list ... and the `security_mode`' to the scout prompt, so the scout is not even told which facet is active. Minor overstatement in the claim: `has_tests`/`size` have no downstream consumers at all (grep finds `has_tests` only in the schema; `depth_planner.plan_lenses` uses only depth/panels/lenses), so their practical impact is dead schema surface rather than 'weakened consumers'. The core defect — orphaned facet feature and unpopulated schema fields — is real.

findings.title: Scout's default-lens cheat sheet omits the redteam panel it is told to schedule
findings.description: scout.md line 50 says: "When `security_mode` is `redteam`, schedule `redteam` instead of `security`." But the "Default lenses" list two lines later (lines 55-60) only enumerates `code`, `test`, `security`, `architecture`, and `database` — there is no `redteam: redteam` entry, even though `lenses.md` (lines 52-56) documents `redteam` as a first-class single-lens panel exactly analogous to `architecture: architecture` and `database: database`, and `report-schema.json`/`scope-profile-schema.json` both list `redteam` in their `panel` enums.
findings.impact: When a review runs in redteam mode — the mode a user explicitly chooses for heightened scrutiny — the scout has no documented default to fall back on for the `lenses.redteam` entry. Smaller/cheaper scout models (e.g. haiku, gpt-4o-mini per model-profiles.yml) that mechanically follow the enumerated cheat sheet may omit or mis-improvise the redteam lens's `spawn`/`priority`/`depth_threshold`, undermining the dedicated adversarial-chain review that redteam mode exists to provide.
findings.remediation: Add a `redteam: redteam` line to scout.md's "Default lenses" list (mirroring the architecture/database single-lens panels), and consider forcing `spawn: true` for redteam given its dedicated exploit-chain focus.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The textual defect is verified exactly as described. /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/agents/scout.md:50 instructs 'When `security_mode` is `redteam`, schedule `redteam` instead of `security`.' The immediately following 'Default lenses' cheat sheet (lines 55-60) enumerates only code, test, security, architecture, database — there is no `redteam: redteam` line. Meanwhile redteam is a first-class panel everywhere else: /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/prompts/lenses.md:52-56 defines the '## Red-team panel / ### redteam' block in the same single-lens shape as the architecture and database panels; scope-profile-schema.json:48 and report-schema.json:77 both include `redteam` in their panel enums; orchestrator.py:108-109 (compute_group_panels) actively emits the redteam panel in redteam mode. I also confirmed the scout receives ONLY the scout.md body plus an assignment stanza at runtime (see the real rendered prompt at .panopticon.prev-20260803/scout-prompts/._1.md, whose lines 47-52 reproduce the same five-entry list) — so the redteam lens mapping present in the design doc (docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-25-panopticon-kimi-port-design.md:63, '| redteam | redteam |') is NOT reachable by the scout at runtime. The claim's HIGH severity/impact is partly overstated, and I want the auditor to see the mitigation I traced: if the scout omits a `lenses.redteam` key, dispatch.py:249-253 still emits a panel_review agent for the redteam panel (the loop iterates `panels`, not `lenses`); `panel_lenses` resolves to [], depth_planner.plan_lenses returns [], and the prompt placeholder renders the literal fallback '- (all lenses)' (dispatch.py:274). panel-review.md:25 and :63 also carry redteam-specific instructions (security checklists, mandatory cvss + exploit_scenario). So redteam review is degraded, not lost: what is actually forfeited is the dedicated redteam lens_sweep agent (lens_sweep only spawns for named lenses with spawn:true) plus deterministic priority/depth_threshold. Real MEDIUM, not HIGH — but the documentation gap the claim names is unambiguously present.

findings.title: CWE catalog has an incomplete OWASP mapping and no architecture/CI-CD-specific entries
findings.description: `cwe-catalog.json`'s `cwe` table lists 34 CWE ids (lines 3-36), but the `cwe_owasp` mapping (lines 38-65) only covers 26 of them — CWE-125, CWE-787, CWE-476, CWE-416, CWE-190, CWE-362, CWE-400 and CWE-1333 have descriptions but no OWASP Top 10 mapping. Separately, the catalog contains no entries aligned with the Architecture panel's own stated scope in `lenses.md` (lines 42-46): CI/CD pipeline safety (`.github/workflows`), Dockerfile/container hygiene, k8s/helm manifests, or supply-chain integrity (e.g. nothing analogous to CWE-829 "Inclusion of Functionality from Untrusted Control Sphere" or CWE-1104 "Use of Unmaintained Third-Party Components").
findings.impact: Any lookup of `cwe_owasp[cwe_id]` for the 8 unmapped CWEs will silently return nothing, and architecture-panel findings about CI/CD or container hygiene — which this file group's own citations rule requires to carry cwe/owasp/cve — have no well-fitting catalog entry to cite, pushing reviewers toward loosely-fitting citations.
findings.remediation: Fill in the missing cwe_owasp entries (or explicitly document that memory-safety CWEs have no 2021 OWASP Top 10 analog), and add a small set of CI/CD/container/supply-chain CWEs (e.g. CWE-829, CWE-1104, CWE-494) to support the Architecture panel's stated scope.
references: skill/prompts/lenses.md:42-46 (architecture lens scope: CI/CD, Dockerfile, k8s/helm)
skill/scripts/citations.py:55-63 and :184-202 (off-catalog CWE -> verified False -> 'minimal' quality)

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Both halves of the claim hold up, and unlike the other mapping claim in this batch its enumeration is exact. Part one: `cwe` at skill/reference/cwe-catalog.json:3-36 has 34 ids; `cwe_owasp` at :38-65 has 26 entries (lines 39-64); the eight ids with a description but no OWASP mapping are precisely CWE-125, CWE-787, CWE-476, CWE-416, CWE-190, CWE-362, CWE-400, CWE-1333 — I checked each remaining id against the mapping block and confirmed CWE-732 (line 63) and CWE-276 (line 64) ARE mapped, matching this claim's count of 26/34. The stated behaviour, 'will silently return nothing', is exactly right: the sole consumer, `derive_owasp` at skill/scripts/citations.py:83-93, uses `catalog["cwe_owasp"].get(cid)` and drops the miss without any diagnostic. Part two: the catalog contains no CI/CD, container, or supply-chain CWE — no CWE-829, no CWE-1104, no CWE-494; the closest entries are CWE-502 (deserialization) and CWE-732/276 (permissions). That gap is measurable against skill/prompts/lenses.md:42-46, which scopes the architecture lens to CI/CD pipeline safety, Dockerfile/container hygiene, k8s/helm manifests and deployment risk. The claimed consequence is grounded in code, not just rhetoric: skill/agents/panel-review.md:58-61 requires each finding to carry at least one of cwe/owasp/cve, and `validate_cwe` (citations.py:55-63) returns `verified: False` for any agent-sourced id absent from the catalog, which `_compute_citation_quality` (citations.py:184-202) then scores 'minimal' rather than 'partial' — so an architecture finding citing the correct-but-off-catalog CWE-829 is penalised exactly as if it had cited nothing verifiable. I mark confidence LIKELY rather than CERTAIN because the eight unmapped ids are memory-safety/resource CWEs that have no genuine OWASP Top 10 2021 analog, so the 'gap' may be correct-by-omission; the claim's own remediation anticipates this by offering 'explicitly document that memory-safety CWEs have no 2021 OWASP Top 10 analog' as an alternative, and the second half (missing supply-chain entries) stands independently. Severity LOW is appropriate — nothing crashes, and CWE-829/1104 citations remain expressible, just unverified. The claim's attached citation CWE-1059 is not verifiable from this repo and I do not endorse it.

findings.title: cwe_owasp mapping's intentional sparseness (8 of 34 catalog CWEs unmapped) is undocumented
findings.description: The `cwe` object lists 34 CWE ids (lines 2-37), but `cwe_owasp` (lines 38-65) only maps 26 of them -- CWE-125, CWE-787, CWE-476, CWE-416, CWE-190, CWE-362, CWE-400, and CWE-1333 have no OWASP Top-10 entry. This is defensible (they are memory-safety/concurrency/ReDoS CWEs outside OWASP Top 10's web-app scope, and skill/scripts/citations.py's derive_owasp() tolerates the gap via `.get()`), but nothing in the file states the omission is deliberate.
findings.impact: Low -- no functional break today, since consumers use `.get()`. But a future contributor extending this catalog cannot tell 'no OWASP mapping exists for this CWE' apart from 'mapping was forgotten' without reading citations.py, reducing maintainability of a reference file meant to be hand-edited.
findings.remediation: Add a short note (e.g. in a README next to the catalog, since JSON has no native comments) stating that cwe_owasp intentionally covers only CWEs with an OWASP Top 10:2021 mapping.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Every factual assertion checks out. /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/reference/cwe-catalog.json lines 3-36 contain exactly 34 CWE ids; lines 39-64 of the cwe_owasp object contain exactly 26. Diffing the two sets, the unmapped ids are precisely the eight named in the claim: CWE-125, CWE-787, CWE-476, CWE-416, CWE-190, CWE-362, CWE-400, CWE-1333 (all memory-safety/concurrency/resource-consumption entries). The tolerance claim also holds: citations.py:87 does `mapped = catalog["cwe_owasp"].get(cid)` and only appends when truthy, so an unmapped CWE silently yields no OWASP tag rather than a KeyError; load_cwe_catalog (citations.py:48-52) additionally defaults each section to an empty map. Nothing in the JSON file itself signals intent (JSON has no comments) and there is no README in skill/reference/ (directory contains only code-review-groups.example.yml, cwe-catalog.json, scope-profile-schema.json, security-checklists.md, model-profiles.yml, report-schema.json). One partial mitigation the claim does not mention: DEVELOPMENT.md:40-41 describes the file as a '(curated CWE->OWASP map)', which hints the selection is deliberate, and DEVELOPMENT.md:51-53 documents the adjacent rule 'unlisted CWE -> kept but verified:false' for the `cwe` map. That is weaker than a statement about cwe_owasp coverage, so the documentation gap the claim describes is real, but it is squarely a LOW/style nit with no functional consequence, exactly as the claim itself states.

findings.title: No architecture-panel equivalent of security-checklists.md
findings.description: `panel-review.md` (lines 23-25) points security/redteam reviewers at `reference/security-checklists.md` for language-specific, cite-able patterns. The Architecture panel's lens description (`lenses.md` lines 42-46) is similarly concrete — CI/CD pipeline safety, Dockerfile/container hygiene, k8s/helm manifest review, dependency direction — but there is no corresponding `architecture-checklists.md` (or similar) in `skill/reference/` for this panel to draw on, unlike security's per-language checklists.
findings.impact: Architecture-panel reviews lack the same itemized, checklist-driven grounding that security reviews get, which is likely to make architecture findings less consistent across runs/models compared to the security panel's checklist-anchored output.
findings.remediation: Add a lightweight `reference/architecture-checklists.md` (GitHub Actions/workflow hygiene, Dockerfile hygiene, k8s/helm hygiene, dependency-direction heuristics) and reference it from panel-review.md the same way security-checklists.md is referenced.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Every factual assertion checks out. skill/agents/panel-review.md lines 23-25 contain a '## Security checklists' section pointing security/redteam panels at reference/security-checklists.md. skill/prompts/lenses.md lines 42-46 describe the architecture lens in equally concrete terms (repo layout, CI/CD pipeline safety in .github/workflows, Dockerfile/container hygiene, k8s/helm manifests, dependency direction, deployment risks). A full listing of skill/reference/ returns only code-review-groups.example.yml, cwe-catalog.json, scope-profile-schema.json, security-checklists.md, model-profiles.yml, report-schema.json — there is no architecture checklist file, and a repo-wide grep for 'checklist' finds no non-security checklist asset. The asymmetry is in fact slightly sharper than the claim states: the panel prompt renderer (skill/scripts/dispatch.py:274) injects only bare lens NAMES ('- architecture'), never the lenses.md description block, and nothing at runtime references skill/prompts/lenses.md at all (only DEVELOPMENT.md:43, tests/test_assets.py:13, and design docs do). So an architecture panel reviewer receives literally the word 'architecture' as its scope cue, whereas a security reviewer gets a pointer to per-language cite-able patterns. Verdict caveats: this is an enhancement/coverage-gap observation rather than a defect — nothing is broken, and the stated impact ('less consistent across runs/models') is a plausible prediction I could not measure from the repository. LOW severity is appropriate. I did not verify the CWE-1059 citation and make no claim about its applicability.

findings.title: cwe-catalog.json is missing CWE-16, CWE-778, CWE-693 needed by citations.py's category-derived CWE fallback
findings.description: skill/scripts/citations.py defines CATEGORY_CWE_OVERRIDES mapping category 'config' -> CWE-16, 'logging' -> CWE-778, and 'headers' -> CWE-693 (citations.py:16-29). Its _derive_cwe_from_category() helper (citations.py:177-181) only returns a derived CWE when `cid in catalog["cwe"]`. None of CWE-16, CWE-778, or CWE-693 appear anywhere in this catalog's `cwe` object (the 34 keys run from CWE-79 through CWE-1333, none of which is 16, 778, or 693), so the lookup silently returns None for those three categories.
findings.impact: Findings whose category is 'config', 'logging', or 'headers' and which lack an explicit CWE citation never receive the intended auto-derived CWE fallback. Their citation_quality is computed as 'minimal'/'none' instead of at least a derived CWE, weakening evidence quality for exactly the categories this override table was built to cover, with no error or warning surfaced anywhere.
findings.remediation: Add entries for CWE-16 (Configuration), CWE-778 (Insufficient Logging), and CWE-693 (Protection Mechanism Failure) to cwe-catalog.json's `cwe` object (and cwe_owasp where an OWASP Top-10 mapping applies), or repoint CATEGORY_CWE_OVERRIDES in citations.py at CWE IDs that already exist in the catalog.
references: skill/scripts/citations.py:177-181 (`if cid and cid in catalog["cwe"]` gate)
skill/scripts/synthesize.py:618, skill/scripts/synthesize.py:941 (load_cwe_catalog() with default path only)

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Every element of the claim checks out against the files. skill/scripts/citations.py:16-29 defines CATEGORY_CWE_OVERRIDES with `"config": "CWE-16"` (line 21), `"logging": "CWE-778"` (line 22), `"headers": "CWE-693"` (line 23). skill/scripts/citations.py:177-181 gates derivation on catalog membership: `if cid and cid in catalog["cwe"]: return {...}` else `return None`. I enumerated all 34 keys of the catalog's `cwe` object (skill/reference/cwe-catalog.json:3-36): 79, 89, 78, 77, 94, 95, 20, 22, 352, 434, 502, 918, 611, 287, 306, 862, 863, 269, 798, 522, 311, 327, 330, 200, 125, 787, 476, 416, 190, 362, 400, 732, 276, 1333. CWE-16, CWE-778 and CWE-693 are absent, so those three override rows are dead code — 9 of the 12 rows resolve, 3 never can. Glob for `**/cwe*.json` returns exactly one catalog, and both production call sites (skill/scripts/synthesize.py:618 and :941) invoke `load_cwe_catalog()` with no `path`, so no alternate catalog can supply the missing ids at runtime. The downstream consequence is real: in `enrich_citations` (citations.py:255-258) a finding with no explicit CWE gets `derived = None`, so `clean` keeps no `cwe`, and `_compute_citation_quality` (citations.py:184-202) falls through to 'minimal' (if some other citation subfield or top-level cvss exists) or 'none' (empty dict is falsy at line 186) — versus the 'minimal' + derived-CWE record the table was written to produce, as tests/test_citations.py:209-215 demonstrates for the working 'injection' row. The failure is silent: no stderr, no warning, and no test covers the config/logging/headers rows (test_citations.py exercises only 'injection' and 'sql_injection'). Two caveats that lower practical severity but not the claim's accuracy: (1) skill/agents/lens-sweep.md:32 sets `category: "{lens}"` and skill/agents/panel-review.md:36 says 'lens name or general', and no lens is named config/logging/headers (skill/prompts/lenses.md), so these rows may rarely be hit in practice — but the same is true of most working rows (auth, crypto, xss...), so the inconsistency is genuine either way; (2) CWE-16 and CWE-693 are MITRE category/pillar entries that are discouraged for direct mapping, so the correct fix may be to repoint CATEGORY_CWE_OVERRIDES rather than to add them — the claim's remediation already offers that alternative. The claim's own attached citation CWE-710 is unverifiable against this repo's catalog and I do not endorse it.

findings.title: scout.md never routes secrets_config-surfaced (or concurrency-surfaced) files to the security panel or a security lens
findings.description: scout.md:24 defines `secrets_config` as a detectable surface ('secrets, credentials, environment/config handling'), but neither the 'Surface -> security lens mapping' table (scout.md:30-35) nor the 'Panels' security-trigger rule (scout.md:46: `security if auth/crypto/money_pii/serialization/external_api/fs/templating/db_sql/http_web present`) lists `secrets_config`. `concurrency` (scout.md:19) is likewise never referenced by either section. This is confirmed by a real prior scout output: `.panopticon.prev-20260803/scout-._1.json` profiles surfaces `["architecture", "secrets_config"]` over files including Dockerfile, Dockerfile.fixtures, CODEOWNERS, and .github/workflows/security.yml, and correspondingly emits `panels: ["code", "architecture"]` -- no `security` panel, purely because secrets_config isn't a trigger.
findings.impact: Any file group that profiles as secrets/credential/config-handling (and doesn't independently trigger another security surface such as auth/crypto) silently skips security-panel review entirely, narrowing security coverage for exactly the surface category the tool defines as security-relevant. This is not hypothetical -- it happened in the corroborating scout run cited above.
findings.remediation: Add `secrets_config` to the security panel trigger list in the 'Panels' section and to the 'Surface -> security lens mapping' table (e.g. secrets_config -> known_vulns, novel). Decide whether `concurrency` should map to a lens (e.g. novel, for TOCTOU per lenses.md) since it is currently detected but consumed nowhere in scout.md.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Every element of this claim checks out against the file and the cited run artifact. (1) scout.md:24 does define `secrets_config` as a detectable surface ('secrets, credentials, environment/config handling'), and scope-profile-schema.json:15 accepts it in the surfaces enum. (2) The 'Surface -> security lens mapping' table at scout.md:30-35 maps db_sql, http_web, templating, auth, crypto, money_pii, serialization, external_api, fs, architecture, database — `secrets_config` and `concurrency` are both absent. (3) The security panel trigger at scout.md:46 reads 'security if auth/crypto/money_pii/serialization/external_api/fs/templating/db_sql/http_web present' — again neither `secrets_config` nor `concurrency` appears. So two of the thirteen declared surfaces are detected and then consumed by nothing in the routing sections; `concurrency` additionally does not appear in the Risk (line 39) or Depth (lines 71-73) rules, making it fully inert. (4) The corroborating artifact is real and I read it: .panopticon.prev-20260803/scout-._1.json emits surfaces ['architecture','secrets_config'] over CODEOWNERS, Dockerfile, Dockerfile.fixtures, pyproject.toml and four .github/workflows files including security.yml, and panels ['code','architecture'] with no security panel. (5) I chased this downstream to confirm it is not merely cosmetic: SKILL.md step 5 feeds the scout's ScopeProfile to dispatch.py, and dispatch.build_plan (dispatch.py:249) iterates `scope_profile['panels']`, so the scout's panel list is authoritative for fan-out. The resulting .panopticon.prev-20260803/dispatch-plan-._1.json contains only four entries — panels 'code' and 'architecture' — proving no security reviewer was ever dispatched over that CI/Dockerfile/CODEOWNERS group in a real run. Two caveats worth recording for the auditor: (a) orchestrator.compute_group_panels (orchestrator.py:99-111) unconditionally appends security (or redteam) to the discovery-stage plan, so the loss occurs specifically when the scout overrides it — the trigger list is what tells the scout it may drop security; (b) the claim's 'purely because secrets_config isn't a trigger' is an inference about the scout model's reasoning (the group was also docs-heavy and profiled risk 'low'), so the causal attribution is strong-but-inferred while the routing-rule gap named in the title is certain.

findings.title: model-profiles.yml's claude host entries omit max_context_size/max_output_size present on the other two hosts, with no comment explaining why
findings.description: The `kimi` (lines 2-18) and `openrouter` (lines 28-44) host blocks give every role a `model`, `max_context_size`, and `max_output_size`. The `claude` host block (lines 19-27) gives only `model` per role. skill/scripts/model_resolver.py's resolve_model() docstring states it 'Returns dict with at least {model, max_context_size, max_output_size}' (model_resolver.py:104), but for host='claude' it returns `host_defaults[role]` verbatim (model_resolver.py:118-122), i.e. just `{"model": "sonnet"}` etc. -- silently breaking that contract for host='claude'.
findings.impact: Currently the only caller (dispatch.py:261,286) forwards the whole dict without indexing max_context_size/max_output_size, so there is no active crash. But the asymmetric, undocumented shape is a latent trap for any future caller that assumes symmetry across hosts and reads those keys unconditionally, and it contradicts model_resolver.py's own docstring.
findings.remediation: Either add max_context_size/max_output_size defaults to the claude host block for structural consistency with kimi/openrouter, or add an inline comment in model-profiles.yml stating that Claude-host roles intentionally omit context/output caps (e.g. because the SDK manages them), and soften resolve_model()'s docstring to mark those keys optional.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: All structural facts verified against the files. model-profiles.yml: the kimi block (lines 2-18) and the openrouter block (lines 28-44) give every role model + max_context_size + max_output_size; the claude block (lines 19-27) gives only `model` per role (haiku/haiku/sonnet/opus). The file contains zero comments, so nothing explains the asymmetry. model_resolver.py:104 does say 'Returns dict with at least {"model": ..., "max_context_size": ..., "max_output_size": ...}', and lines 116-122 return `host_defaults[role]` verbatim when the role is present, so resolve_model('claude', 'panel_review') returns exactly {'model': 'sonnet'} -- the docstring's 'at least' contract is false for that host. The 'no active crash' assessment is also correct: the only production callers are dispatch.py:261 and dispatch.py:286, which stash the whole dict under the plan entry's 'model' key without indexing the size fields, and SKILL.md:49/:79 consume only `entry.model.model`. A repo-wide grep confirms max_output_size/max_context_size are read nowhere else except tests/test_model_resolver.py:17, which only asserts them for the kimi host. Two additions that strengthen rather than contradict the claim: the docstring is violated on three further paths, not just host='claude' -- the string-form CLI override (line 110), the plain-string env override (line 92, exercised by tests at test_model_resolver.py:35-39), and the unknown-host fallback `return {"model": None}` (line 71, exercised at test_model_resolver.py:26-28) -- and the hardcoded _CLAUDE_FALLBACK (lines 51-56) reproduces the same size-less shape, so remediation must cover the Python fallback table as well as the yml. LOW/style is the right severity.

findings.title: Monolithic main function violating single responsibility principle
findings.description: The main() function in synthesize.py (lines 823-976, 153 lines) performs multiple distinct responsibilities: CLI argument parsing, report building, finding aggregation, verdict processing, validation, and HTML/JSON artifact generation. This creates a thick orchestration layer that is difficult to test and refactor.
findings.impact: High cognitive complexity makes the function difficult to understand, test, and modify. Changes to one aspect require understanding the entire flow. Unit testing individual concerns is nearly impossible without significant refactoring.
findings.remediation: Decompose main() into smaller focused functions: parse_arguments(), load_and_prepare_findings(), build_and_validate_report(), emit_artifacts().
references: tests/test_synthesize.py (syn.main invoked with argv at 379, 422, 493, 977, 1004, 1294, 1320, 1352 and others)

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The described condition exists, though the cited line range is stale by 18 lines: main() is at skill/scripts/synthesize.py:841-994 (154 lines), not 823-976 (823 is inside write_report). The length and the responsibility list match what I read: argparse construction (843-877), a fully separate --compare mode with its own I/O and early return (879-905), groups.json loading (907-924), timestamp/output-path derivation (926-928), tools-dir warning + finding load + tool ingest (930-940), citation enrichment (941-943), severity filtering (944-946), the entire --emit-verify-queue pass-1 branch including stale-queue removal (948-968), verdict loading + build_report (970-977), validation/warning printing (978-983), and JSON/HTML/summary emission plus exit-code derivation (985-994). So the structural observation is accurate. Two material qualifications. First, the impact is overstated: every substantive concern is ALREADY extracted into module-level functions that the suite tests directly (load_findings, prepare_findings, build_report, validate_report, attach_schema_status, write_report, render_summary, derive_tool_policy_mode, _collect_models_used) — main() is a wiring layer, not a place where logic hides. Second, 'nearly impossible' to test is contradicted by the repository: tests/test_synthesize.py invokes syn.main([...]) with argv in at least 15 places (lines 379, 386, 422, 440, 493, 528, 563, 649, 764, 977, 1004, 1028, 1051, 1294, 1307, 1320, 1333, 1352), covering the compare branch, the verify-queue branch, verdict ingestion, severity filtering, and the gate exit code. Given that, this is a readability/cohesion observation about a CLI entrypoint, not a MEDIUM architectural defect; I would file it at LOW/INFO. The description itself is verified, so the claim stands as written minus the severity and the impact rationale.

findings.title: Mixed import styles in synthesize.py
findings.description: synthesize.py uses both 'import X as alias' and 'from X import Y' styles for importing from scripts modules. Lines 14 and 16-18 use 'import ... as', while line 15 uses 'from ... import'. This inconsistency makes the module's dependencies less clear and reduces readability.
findings.impact: Reduced code clarity and consistency. Makes it harder to track what external symbols are being used and their origins.
findings.remediation: Choose a single import style for scripts module imports and apply consistently.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Verified verbatim at /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/synthesize.py lines 14-18: line 14 `import scripts.citations as citations`, line 15 `from scripts.citations import load_cwe_catalog`, lines 16-18 `import scripts.evidence as evidence_mod` / `import scripts.html_report as html_report` / `import scripts.ingest_tools as ingest_tools`. The claim's description of which lines use which style is exactly right. The inconsistency is not merely cosmetic: lines 14 and 15 import the SAME module twice in two different styles, and both bindings are live — line 618 calls `catalog = load_cwe_catalog()` inside build_report while line 941 calls `catalog = citations.load_cwe_catalog()` inside main(). The same function is therefore invoked two different ways within one file. I checked for a legitimate reason for the redundant `from` import (e.g. tests monkeypatching `synthesize.load_cwe_catalog`) and found none: grepping /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/tests shows load_cwe_catalog referenced only as `cit.load_cwe_catalog()` in tests/test_citations.py, never through synthesize. So line 15 is redundant with line 14. Caveats on severity and citation: CONTRIBUTING.md documents no import-style rule, and the ruff config in pyproject.toml selects only E/F/W (no isort/`I` rules), so nothing enforces a style here — this is correctly rated LOW/cosmetic, not a defect. The attached CWE-1104 (Use of Unmaintained Third Party Components) is inapplicable to import-statement style; CWE-710 (Improper Adherence to Coding Standards) is the defensible class. findings.title: Panel-review lens-coverage fallback text conflates two opposite dispatch states
findings.description: In build_plan(), `non_spawned = [lens["name"] for lens in panel_lenses if lens["name"] not in spawned_set]` is empty in two semantically opposite situations: (a) the profile defines no lenses at all for this panel, where the panel reviewer genuinely must cover everything itself, or (b) the profile defines lenses but every one of them was spawned as a dedicated lens_sweep agent, where the panel reviewer should cover NONE of the mechanical lenses. Both cases render the same fallback string: `"\n".join(...) or "- (all lenses)"`. This is directly observable in this very run: scout-._5.json defines exactly one lens for the architecture panel which fully spawns at depth=standard, so dispatch-plan-._5.json has `"lenses": []` for the architecture panel_review entry, yet the rendered prompt says '- (all lenses)' — telling the reviewer to cover everything when a dedicated lens_sweep-architecture agent already ran. The same collision reproduces across this session's other dispatch plans (._1, ._4, ._6, ._7, ._10).
findings.impact: Panel reviewers are systematically told to 'cover all lenses' in exactly the case where a dedicated mechanical lens_sweep agent already covered them, causing redundant duplicate review work (wasted token budget, duplicate findings that then rely on dedupe/reinforce to reconcile) instead of being told to focus purely on holistic/cross-cutting concerns. Because this triggers for any panel whose lens set size is <= the depth's spawn limit, it is not a rare edge case but reproducible, always-on behavior for that configuration.
findings.remediation: Distinguish the two empty-non_spawned cases explicitly before building the fallback string: use '- (no additional lenses — all covered by dedicated lens sweep agents)' when panel_lenses is non-empty but non_spawned is empty, and reserve '- (all lenses)' only for the case where panel_lenses itself is empty.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Verified directly in code and in this repository's emitted artifacts. In /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/dispatch.py:251-253, `panel_lenses = scope_profile.get("lenses", {}).get(panel_name, [])` and `non_spawned = [lens["name"] for lens in panel_lenses if lens["name"] not in spawned_set]`; line 274 renders `"lenses": "\n".join("- %s" % n for n in non_spawned) or "- (all lenses)"`. `non_spawned == []` is produced by two distinct states and both collapse to the identical string: (a) panel_lenses itself empty — reachable, since the ScopeProfile schema (/Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/reference/scope-profile-schema.json:28-43) requires only that `lenses` be an object, with no per-panel key required, and the `.get(panel_name, [])` default silently supplies []; and (b) panel_lenses non-empty but fully consumed by depth_planner.plan_lenses (/Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/depth_planner.py:12-36), which spawns up to DEPTH_LIMIT (shallow 1 / standard 2 / deep 3) lenses. The claim's concrete example reproduces exactly: /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/.panopticon/scout-._5.json:84-91 defines exactly one architecture lens (name architecture, spawn true, depth_threshold shallow) at depth standard; /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/.panopticon/dispatch-plan-._5.json:298 has `"lenses": []` for the architecture panel_review while line 303+ dispatches a lens_sweep with `"lens": "architecture"`; and the rendered /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/.panopticon/prompts/._5-architecture-panel_review.md:13 says `- (all lenses)`. I independently grepped the current .panopticon/prompts directory and found the same collision in 10 panel_review prompts (._1-architecture, ._4-architecture, ._5-architecture, ._6-code, ._6-test, ._6-security, ._7-architecture, ._10-code, ._10-test, ._10-security). The contradiction is real at the prompt level because the template body (/Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/agents/panel-review.md:16,19-21) tells the reviewer to 'Cover all lenses assigned to this panel that are NOT being handled by dedicated lens sweep agents' and then lists '- (all lenses)' under 'Lenses assigned to this panel' — mutually contradictory instructions in the case where the correct answer is 'none of the mechanical lenses'. Note the impact is bounded: the plan's structured `lenses: []` field is correct, so only the natural-language prompt misleads; the harm is redundant review work / duplicate findings, not incorrect dispatch. The attached CWE-670 citation is a poor fit (this is prompt-text ambiguity, not always-incorrect control flow) and I do not endorse it; the finding stands on the code and artifacts alone.

findings.title: corroborated/corroborated_by are self-assertable by agents, unlike source/reinforced, allowing spoofed cross-panel verification
findings.description: AGENT_FORBIDDEN_FIELDS = ("source", "reinforced") strips only these two self-asserted trust fields from agent-authored finding JSON before synthesis (per the SEC-102 fix noted in the surrounding comment). It does not strip `corroborated` / `corroborated_by`, which drive the exact same class of trust decision: evidence.derive_evidence() (evidence.py lines ~64-69) returns evidence.status = 'corroborated' (with verified_by = the self-asserted panel list and a canned 'independently flagged' reasoning string) whenever finding.get('corroborated') is truthy — with no check that the finding actually passed through synthesize.cross_panel_corroboration(). That function only ever sets these keys on genuinely clustered multi-panel findings; it never clears or validates pre-existing values, so a finding arriving from an agent already carrying corroborated: true passes through untouched.
findings.impact: A single agent-sourced finding can unilaterally claim independent cross-panel corroboration it never received. Effects: (1) html_report._render_findings() only segregates needs_more_info/unverified into the collapsed Unverified section — 'corroborated' is not in that tuple, so the spoofed finding renders in the main verified tabs, appearing vetted; (2) evidence.triage_priority() gives corroborated CRITICAL/HIGH findings priority 0, so under a --max-verify cap a spoofed claim can push a genuine uncorroborated finding out of the advisor verify queue entirely. The one mitigating factor is that GATE_ELIGIBLE_DEFAULT does not include 'corroborated', so this does not by itself flip the CI gate to PASS — but it does materially corrupt report presentation and verification-queue fairness, the same threat model the source/reinforced fix was built to close.
findings.remediation: Add "corroborated" and "corroborated_by" to AGENT_FORBIDDEN_FIELDS in synthesize.py and have cross_panel_corroboration() be the sole writer of these keys, exactly as dedupe() is the sole writer of `reinforced`.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Every mechanical link in the chain checks out in the code. (1) synthesize.py:93 is exactly `AGENT_FORBIDDEN_FIELDS = ("source", "reinforced")`, and the strip loop at 125-129 pops only those two keys from each agent-authored finding dict; I grepped the whole repository for AGENT_FORBIDDEN_FIELDS and skill/scripts/synthesize.py is the only definition/use site, so there is no other sanitizer that removes `corroborated`. (2) evidence.py:64-69 returns `{"status": "corroborated", "verified_by": panels, "reasoning": "Nearby locus independently flagged by panels: ..."}` from a bare `if finding.get("corroborated")`, taking `verified_by` verbatim from the finding's own `corroborated_by` list — no provenance check that synthesize.cross_panel_corroboration() produced it. (3) cross_panel_corroboration() (synthesize.py:332-402) only ever assigns `m["corroborated"] = True` / `m["corroborated_by"] = list(panels)` at lines 380-381 inside the >=2-distinct-related-panels branch; there is no else-branch and no initialization pass, so a pre-existing self-asserted True on a finding that does not cluster survives untouched. dedupe() (229-317) likewise never touches these keys. (4) Presentation effect verified: html_report.py:611 `unverified_statuses = ("needs_more_info", "unverified")` and 612-615 segregate only those into the collapsed <details> 'Unverified findings' section, so a corroborated-status finding renders among the main cards. render_summary (synthesize.py:795) additionally prints a ' corroborated' marker straight off `f.get("corroborated")`, and evidence_stats (474-481) counts it. (5) Queue effect verified: evidence.triage_priority (81-83) computes `corroborated = bool(finding.get("corroborated") or finding.get("reinforced"))` and returns 0 for CRITICAL/HIGH, and build_verify_queue (107-113) sorts on that key and truncates at max_verify, so a forged priority-0 entry displaces a genuine priority-1 one. (6) The mitigating factor the claim itself concedes is also correct: evidence.py:17 GATE_ELIGIBLE_DEFAULT = {tool_confirmed, advisor_confirmed} excludes corroborated, so this does not by itself flip the gate. Corroboration is pipeline-owned by design — SKILL.md:123 describes it as 'multi-panel agreement' and no agent template instructs agents to emit it — which makes an agent-supplied value a spoof rather than a legitimate input. One precision caveat that does not change the verdict: derive_evidence's precedence (docstring at 37-38) means an applied advisor verdict overrides `corroborated`, so the *rendering* half of the impact materializes only when the spoofed finding is not answered by a verdict (single-pass runs with no --verdicts-dir, unanswered verdicts, or entries cut by --max-verify); the *queue-priority displacement* half is unconditional because triage runs before verdicts exist.

findings.title: Self-asserted corroborated/corroborated_by fields bypass agent-trust sanitization and forge cross-panel verification status
findings.description: `load_findings()` strips only `AGENT_FORBIDDEN_FIELDS = ("source", "reinforced")` (line 93; stripping loop at lines 125-129) from agent-authored finding JSON before it enters the pipeline. `corroborated` and `corroborated_by` — a field pair with the exact same trust-conferring character the code's own comment (lines 88-92) warns about — are not in that denylist. `evidence.derive_evidence()` (evidence.py:64-66) unconditionally trusts `finding.get("corroborated")`/`finding.get("corroborated_by")` when computing the authoritative `evidence.status`, and `evidence.triage_priority()` (evidence.py:81-84) gives a self-asserted `corroborated=true` the same priority boost as a genuine cross-panel match. The only code meant to set these fields, `synthesize.cross_panel_corroboration()` (synthesize.py:380-382), only ADDS the flag to findings that really do cluster with a different panel's finding within its 2-line window — it never clears a pre-existing self-asserted `true` on findings that fail to cluster. So a panel_review/lens_sweep agent's finding JSON that already carries `"corroborated": true` survives synthesis unchanged and is treated downstream as independently confirmed.
findings.impact: The forged status (a) inflates evidence_stats.corroborated and the human-facing corroborated marker in render_summary(), misrepresenting verification strength; (b) is used by triage_priority() to promote the finding to priority 0 in build_verify_queue() — the same tier as genuinely corroborated CRITICAL/HIGH findings. Under --max-verify N, a forged priority-0 entry can occupy an advisor-verification slot that would otherwise go to a real uncorroborated CRITICAL/HIGH finding (priority 1), which is then cut from the queue and left at evidence status unverified — outside GATE_ELIGIBLE_DEFAULT — so a genuine vulnerability can be excluded from grading/gate decisions. This directly violates the invariant evidence.py's own module docstring states: 'a reviewer cannot confirm its own finding.'
findings.remediation: Add "corroborated" and "corroborated_by" to AGENT_FORBIDDEN_FIELDS in synthesize.py so load_findings() strips them from every agent-authored payload before synthesis, identically to source/reinforced. Corroboration must then only ever be set by cross_panel_corroboration()'s own clustering pass, which already runs after stripping.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: I verified each cited line independently. synthesize.py:93 defines AGENT_FORBIDDEN_FIELDS as only ("source", "reinforced"); the stripping loop is at 125-129 inside load_findings (96-134) and pops nothing else; the comment at 88-92 states the trust rationale ('Fields that confer trust and must NEVER come from an agent-authored payload'), so `corroborated`/`corroborated_by` are omitted from a denylist whose stated purpose covers them. evidence.py:64-66 unconditionally trusts `finding.get("corroborated")` and echoes `finding.get("corroborated_by")` into evidence.verified_by; evidence.py:81-84 (triage_priority) gives self-asserted corroborated CRITICAL/HIGH the same priority 0 as a genuine cross-panel match. synthesize.py:380-382 inside cross_panel_corroboration is add-only: it sets the pair on clustered members and never clears or validates a pre-existing value, and neither dedupe() nor normalize_finding() nor aggregate_tool_findings() touches those keys. The full-pipeline path holds: main() -> load_findings (936) -> build_report (972) -> prepare_findings (617) -> build_verify_queue (619) -> derive_evidence (640), with the spoofed keys surviving end to end. The impact claims check out too: evidence_stats (synthesize.py:474-481) counts the forged 'corroborated' status; render_summary (795) prints the corroborated marker; build_verify_queue (evidence.py:107-113) sorts by triage_priority then truncates at max_verify, so a forged priority-0 entry consumes a slot and pushes a genuine uncorroborated CRITICAL/HIGH (priority 1) out of the queue; a cut finding then derives status 'unverified' (evidence.py:70), which is outside GATE_ELIGIBLE_DEFAULT (evidence.py:17), and build_report:646-648 filters grades/gate to gate-eligible findings only unless --gate-unverified — so the genuine finding really does drop out of grading and the gate. --max-verify is a live, documented flag (synthesize.py:873-875) and the repo's own docs record an earlier real starvation of SEC-102 by it. The stated invariant violation is quoted correctly from evidence.py's docstring at line 40 ('a reviewer cannot confirm its own finding'). Corroboration is pipeline-derived by design (SKILL.md:123; no agent template asks agents to emit it), so an agent-supplied value is illegitimate. Two precision notes that do not change the verdict: derive_evidence's precedence means an applied advisor verdict supersedes the forged 'corroborated' status, so the report-presentation half of the impact lands only when the finding goes unverified (no --verdicts-dir, unanswered verdict, or cut by --max-verify) while the queue-displacement half is unconditional; and of the claim's OWASP citations, A08 (Software and Data Integrity Failures) fits while A03 (Injection) does not — I did not endorse it.

discarded_claims.title: Asymmetric dispatch architecture across agent platforms
discarded_claims.description: The skill implements fundamentally different dispatch mechanisms per host platform: Claude Code uses parallel dispatch via Agent tool (first-class), Kimi Code uses AgentSwarm raw-prompt dispatch (supported), and other SKILL.md hosts fall back to sequential in-session dispatch (degraded). This creates different scalability and performance characteristics depending on the deployment platform.
discarded_claims.impact: Performance characteristics, parallelism availability, and execution model vary significantly by platform. A review that takes N seconds on Claude Code may take N*M seconds on other platforms. Scalability properties are platform-dependent.
discarded_claims.remediation: Document the host-specific dispatch models as architectural trade-offs. Consider extracting a dispatch-adapter interface to allow pluggable platform strategies, or provide clear performance documentation for each platform.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The factual description is accurate but it does not describe a defect, and the claim's own remediation is already satisfied by the very lines it cites as evidence. README.md:11-13 reads 'Claude Code — first-class: parallel fan-out via the Agent tool / Kimi Code CLI — supported: AgentSwarm raw-prompt dispatch / Other agents that read SKILL.md files — degraded: sequential dispatch, same prompts'. DEVELOPMENT.md:3-4 repeats it ('Claude Code first-class, Kimi Code supported, other SKILL.md hosts degraded-sequential'). skill/SKILL.md:71-87 ('## Host dispatch') spells out each mechanism and explicitly states the performance consequence for the fallback path: 'Other hosts — run the entries sequentially in-session with the same prompts; expect no parallelism.' The remediation asks to 'document the host-specific dispatch models as architectural trade-offs' — that documentation is exactly what the three cited references are. The second remediation half ('extract a dispatch-adapter interface to allow pluggable platform strategies') is also substantially implemented: skill/scripts/dispatch.py already parameterizes the plan by host (`--host claude|kimi|generic` at line 357-358, `build_plan(..., host=...)` at 215, `_detect_host()` at 179 documented as 'Fallback only', `_registration_dir(host, agents_dir)` at 201, `emit_host_agents(host, out_dir)` at 103), and skill/scripts/model_resolver.py resolves models per host — producing 'One plan, one prompt per reviewer' (SKILL.md:73) with only the execution verb differing. The residual asymmetry is a property of the host agent runtimes (whether Claude Code's Agent tool or Kimi's AgentSwarm offers parallel subagent fan-out), not of code in this repository; a prompt-format skill has no runtime control to abstract it away. The claim therefore restates a documented, deliberate, and externally-imposed constraint as an architectural finding, with no code path contradicted or improvable within this repo.

discarded_claims.title: Optional Docker container creates divergent code execution paths
discarded_claims.description: The Docker tool container is optional and auto-detected via docker_available() (lines 36-44). DEVELOPMENT.md line 54 states 'Tool container is optional and auto-detected; absent → clean fleet-only behavior'. The same codebase supports two execution modes with different evidence sources: with Docker/tools vs. without. This creates two distinct code paths that may not be equally tested.
discarded_claims.impact: Behavior diverges when Docker is available vs. unavailable. Some code paths may only be exercised when Docker is present. Users running on non-Docker systems may encounter untested behavior. Findings may vary between environments not due to code differences but infrastructure availability.
discarded_claims.remediation: Either: (1) Require Docker explicitly with clear error messaging, (2) Provide test coverage for both paths, or (3) Document which features are unavailable without Docker and provide graceful degradation with clear warnings.
references: tests/test_run_tools.py:9-24 (both detection outcomes tested) and :35-159 (Docker argv path tested via injected runner, no Docker needed)
skill/scripts/synthesize.py:930-938 with tests/test_synthesize.py:1720-1733 (tools-present and tools-absent both tested)

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The cited facts exist but the asserted defect does not. skill/scripts/run_tools.py:36-44 defines docker_available(); its only call site in this module is line 193 inside `if __name__ == "__main__"`, where absence produces `print("panopticon-tools image not available; skipping tool scan", file=sys.stderr); sys.exit(0)`. There is no second implementation of the scan — no host-side fallback is wired to the CLI (run_adapters, the only host-execution function, has no production caller). So the 'two distinct code paths' are: run the tools, or emit a warning and exit. That is a single documented degradation point, not divergent logic. The claim's specific impacts are contradicted: (1) 'some code paths may only be exercised when Docker is present' — every branch of run_tools() is unit-tested on a Docker-free machine via the injected `runner` seam (tests/test_run_tools.py:35-79, 101-159 cover exact argv, timeout, bad returncode, exception, NVD key propagation), and both outcomes of docker_available() are tested (:9-24); (2) the downstream 'with tools vs. without' split in synthesize.py:930-938 is tested in BOTH directions (tests/test_synthesize.py:764, 1720, 1722-1733); (3) the claim's own remediation option 3 is already implemented — DEVELOPMENT.md:54 lists it under 'Key design decisions (don't relitigate without reason)', SKILL.md:38/45 documents `--tools`/`--no-tools` and 'optional Docker container', and the stderr warning above is the clear degradation notice. CI (.github/workflows/security.yml:39-46) always pulls-or-builds the image, so the graded path is deterministic there. The one residually true observation is environment-dependent test strength in the adapter integration tests (tests/test_phase1_integration.py:20-21, tests/tools/test_ruby_integration.py:20-26 call skipTest when a fixture or tool binary is missing) — but that is about tool binaries/fixtures, not docker_available() at lines 36-44, and those tests skip loudly rather than silently changing behavior. The finding as located and framed is not supported.

discarded_claims.title: Pipeline phase coordination relies on JSON artifact contracts without versioning
discarded_claims.description: The orchestration pipeline (Discovery → Scout → Tools → Panels → Synthesis) uses JSON artifacts to pass data between phases (groups.json, scope-profile.json, dispatch-plan.json, findings-*.json, verify-queue.json). While the final CodeReviewReport has a versioned schema (report-schema.json), the intermediate phase artifacts have no versioning. Changes to these intermediate schemas could break phase-to-phase contracts.
discarded_claims.impact: Intermediate artifact schemas are not versioned, making evolution difficult. If an intermediate schema changes, old artifacts become incompatible. There is no clear way to handle schema migrations. Phase coupling is implicit through JSON structure rather than explicit contracts.
discarded_claims.remediation: Add schema versions to intermediate artifacts (groups.json, scope-profile.json, etc.). Document the schema for each intermediate artifact. Implement schema validation at phase boundaries.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The claim's load-bearing factual assertions are contradicted by the code. (1) It lists `verify-queue.json` among the unversioned intermediate artifacts, but `skill/scripts/evidence.py:123-130` writes it with an explicit `"version": "4.2.0"` field, and `DEVELOPMENT.md:85-89` makes that version a first-class release obligation ('Bump `SKILL.md` `metadata.version`, `synthesize.build_report`'s `meta.version`, and `evidence.write_verify_queue`'s payload `version` together'). (2) It asserts report-schema.json is the 'only versioned intermediate artifact' — the report is the pipeline's final output (`synthesize.py:682` sets `meta.version`), not an intermediate one, and as shown it is not the only versioned artifact. (3) It implies intermediate artifacts are undocumented ('Document the schema for each intermediate artifact'), but `skill/reference/scope-profile-schema.json` is a full draft-07 JSON Schema for the scout->dispatch boundary artifact, referenced normatively by the scout template (`skill/agents/scout.md:9`). (4) It asserts 'Phase coupling is implicit through JSON structure rather than explicit contracts' with no validation at phase boundaries; in fact `dispatch.py:311-351` (`render_advisor_prompts`) performs explicit fail-fast structural validation of the verify-queue at that boundary (object shape, `entries` list, per-entry shape, `queue_id` regex), `synthesize.py:716-755` (`validate_report`) validates the merged output, and `synthesize.py:48` normalizes/validates each incoming finding. What survives verification is a much narrower residue: `groups.json` (built by `orchestrator.build_result`, lines 455-467, and confirmed in the live artifact `.panopticon/groups.json` whose top-level keys are security_mode/mode/target/facet/groups/tests/counts), the dispatch plan (a bare JSON list, `dispatch.py:236-302`), and agent `findings-*.json` (contract in `skill/agents/panel-review.md`) carry no version field. That residue is not a defect with a demonstrable execution path: these are per-run scratch files under `.panopticon/`, regenerated from scratch by a single skill version within one run, and no code path reads an artifact produced by a different version (the archived `.panopticon.prev-20260803/` copies are never consumed). Rejecting the claim as written; an auditor who wants to keep a narrowed version should restate it as 'groups.json / dispatch-plan.json / findings-*.json lack the version field that verify-queue.json and the report already carry' — an internal-consistency nit, not the broad unversioned-contracts finding filed here.

discarded_claims.title: Project version mismatch across configuration sources
discarded_claims.description: pyproject.toml defines version as 3.0.0, but skill/SKILL.md (line 14), DEVELOPMENT.md (line 8), and actual code implementations use 4.2.0. This creates inconsistency in versioning across the codebase and affects generated User-Agent headers and report metadata.
discarded_claims.impact: Version discrepancy can cause confusion for users and automated systems relying on version checks. The outdated pyproject.toml version may be used incorrectly in build systems or package distribution.
discarded_claims.remediation: Update pyproject.toml line 3 to version = "4.2.0" to match the actual project version documented in DEVELOPMENT.md and embedded in skill/SKILL.md frontmatter and code.
references: /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/pyproject.toml:3 - version = "3.0.0"; file has no [build-system] table, so it is not buildable/distributable

/Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/DEVELOPMENT.md:85-89 - Versioning contract names only SKILL.md metadata.version, synthesize.build_report meta.version, and evidence.write_verify_queue payload version; pyproject.toml is not listed
/Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/citations.py:153 - headers={"User-Agent": "panopticon/3.0.0"} is a separate hardcoded literal, not derived from pyproject.toml
/Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/README.md:15-21,76 - install is by symlinking skill/ into the agent skills dir; no pip packaging path
/Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/docs/superpowers/2026-08-04-self-scan-report.json:953-956 - pre-existing, correctly scoped finding for the same drift

provenance.confirmation_reasoning:
The literal textual observation is true but every load-bearing part of the finding — its impact mechanism, its build/distribution risk, and its CRITICAL severity — is contradicted by the repository.

What is true: pyproject.toml line 3 is `version = "3.0.0"`; skill/SKILL.md line 14 is `version: "4.2.0"`; DEVELOPMENT.md line 8 is `**Current version: 4.2.0**`. That drift is real.

What is false:

(1) The claimed impact path does not exist. The finding asserts the mismatch 'affects generated User-Agent headers and report metadata.' Nothing in this repository ever reads pyproject.toml's version. I grepped for `tomllib`, `importlib.metadata`, `importlib_metadata`, and `pkg_resources` across the whole tree: zero matches. The only references to pyproject.toml in code are skill/scripts/tools/pip_audit.py:17,40 and skill/scripts/tools/osv_scanner.py:27, which treat it as a *scan-target dependency manifest* of the repo under review, not as panopticon's own version source. The User-Agent at skill/scripts/citations.py:153 (`headers={"User-Agent": "panopticon/3.0.0"}`) is an independent hardcoded string literal; changing pyproject.toml would not alter it. Likewise the report metadata at skill/scripts/synthesize.py:682 and skill/scripts/evidence.py:126 are independent hardcoded literals that already read "4.2.0" and are pinned by passing tests (tests/test_synthesize.py:1194 and :1479, tests/test_schema.py:170, tests/test_verify_queue.py:115). So report metadata is *not* affected — it is already correct.

(2) The claimed build/distribution risk cannot materialize. pyproject.toml is 28 lines and has no `[build-system]` table, no setuptools/hatchling/poetry backend, and no package discovery config — it is not buildable into a distribution at all. It carries `[project]` metadata plus `[tool.ruff]` lint config. README.md's Installation section and its repository-layout table state the install mechanism is symlinking the `skill/` directory into the agent's skills dir; there is no pip install of panopticon. No CI workflow builds or publishes a package (.github/workflows/ci.yml and security.yml only pip-install third-party tools like ruff/pytest/pyyaml).

(3) pyproject.toml is not a declared version source of truth. DEVELOPMENT.md lines 85-89 define the versioning contract explicitly: 'Bump `SKILL.md` `metadata.version`, `synthesize.build_report`'s `meta.version`, and `evidence.write_verify_queue`'s payload `version` together.' pyproject.toml is deliberately absent from that enumerated list. All three files the contract names are correctly at 4.2.0. By the project's own written policy there is no violation here.

(4) Severity is inflated by roughly four levels. Against skill/reference/report-schema.json's CRITICAL|HIGH|MEDIUM|LOW|INFO scale, a stale metadata string in a non-buildable, non-distributed config file with no runtime reader is INFO-grade cosmetic hygiene. It has no security, correctness, availability, or data-integrity consequence. The finding's own confidence field is POSSIBLE and citation_quality is 'none', which is inconsistent with a CRITICAL rating.

Note for the auditor: the same underlying drift is already tracked in this repo with correct scoping and correct causality — docs/superpowers/2026-08-04-self-scan-report.json lines 953-956 files it against citations.py's hardcoded User-Agent and explicitly notes pyproject was likely the copy source, and docs/superpowers/2026-08-04-run2-fixmes.md:121 records it as a known FIXME. If anything is retained here it should be a single INFO/LOW single-source-of-truth item covering pyproject.toml:3 and citations.py:153 (the two genuinely stale 3.0.0 literals), not a CRITICAL structural defect. I am rejecting the finding as filed, not the one-line observation inside it.

discarded_claims.title: Unversioned pip package installs enable known vulnerability injection
discarded_claims.description: Line 14 of Dockerfile installs Python packages (semgrep, bandit, bandit-sarif-formatter) without version pinning. Unversioned installs automatically pull the latest version at build time, which could include packages with known vulnerabilities that are patched in newer releases but not applied due to lack of version constraints.
discarded_claims.impact: The scanner image may contain known vulnerabilities in third-party dependencies. A vulnerable version of any installed package could be automatically pulled, potentially introducing CRITICAL/HIGH CVEs into the supply chain.
discarded_claims.remediation: Pin specific versions for all pip packages: `pip install --no-cache-dir semgrep==<VERSION> bandit==<VERSION> bandit-sarif-formatter==<VERSION>`. Use a locked requirements.txt file or specify versions explicitly to ensure reproducible, secure builds.
references: CWE-1104: Use of Unmaintained Third Party Components

provenance.confirmation_reasoning:
The literal observation is true but the finding as filed is not supportable, and its stated causal mechanism is inverted.

WHAT IS TRUE: /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/Dockerfile line 14 reads `RUN pip install --no-cache-dir semgrep bandit bandit-sarif-formatter` with no version specifiers, no `--require-hashes`, and no lockfile. The only requirements.txt in the repo is tests/fixtures/vulnerable-python/requirements.txt, a deliberately-vulnerable test fixture, not a build input. The image is published to ghcr.io as `:latest` by .github/workflows/docker-publish.yml and consumed by .github/workflows/security.yml, so build drift does reach a published artifact.

WHY THE CLAIM FAILS:

1. The mechanism is backwards. The description states unpinned installs 'could include packages with known vulnerabilities that are patched in newer releases but not applied due to lack of version constraints.' That describes PINNED, stale dependencies. An unpinned `pip install` resolves to the newest release on PyPI at build time, i.e. the MOST patched version available.
