discarded_claims.title: Unversioned cargo-audit installation enables known vulnerability injection
discarded_claims.description: Line 83 of Dockerfile installs cargo-audit without version pinning. This Rust security auditing tool will fetch the latest version, which may contain known vulnerabilities.
discarded_claims.impact: The Rust dependency scanner may contain known security vulnerabilities if an unpatched version is installed.
discarded_claims.remediation: Specify a pinned version: `RUN cargo install cargo-audit@<VERSION>`. See Dockerfile.fixtures line 20 for an example of properly versioned cargo-audit installation.
references: CWE-1104: Use of Unmaintained Third Party Components
Dockerfile:83 — RUN cargo install cargo-audit (unpinned; one of 8+ unpinned installs in the file)
Dockerfile:82,86 — curl|sh and curl|bash installs, higher supply-chain risk than line 83
Dockerfile.fixtures:20 — RUN cargo install cargo-audit --version 0.22.2 (the pinned instance that will go stale)
DEVELOPMENT.md:83 — documented monthly image rebuild cadence for scanner binaries and advisory DBs
DEVELOPMENT.md:54-56 — read-only, non-root, parse-not-execute design decision

provenance.confirmation_reasoning:
The literal code fact checks out, but the security reasoning built on it is inverted, and the claim as written does not describe a vulnerability.

VERIFIED FACTS: Dockerfile:83 is exactly `RUN cargo install cargo-audit` with no version pin. Dockerfile.fixtures:20 is exactly `RUN cargo install cargo-audit --version 0.22.2`. Both anchors the claim cites are accurate.

WHY IT IS REJECTED:

(1) The causal mechanism is backwards. The claim is filed under category `known_vulns` with CWE-1104 (Use of Unmaintained Third Party Components), and argues the unpinned install 'will fetch the latest version, which may contain known vulnerabilities.' Known vulnerabilities are by definition disclosed against specific versions and patched in later ones, so an unpinned install resolves to the release *least* likely to carry unpatched advisories. The proposed remediation — pin a version — is the pattern that causes an image to accumulate known-vulnerable components as the pin ages. The exemplar the claim holds up as correct (Dockerfile.fixtures:20, pinned at 0.22.2) is the instance that will actually go stale. DEVELOPMENT.md:83 documents this explicitly: 'adapter CODE is mounted from the checkout at run time (never stale), but the scanner BINARIES and their rule/advisory databases age with the image,' with a stated monthly rebuild cadence. Unpinned install is what makes that policy effective. The claim therefore recommends the change that worsens the exact risk it names.

(2) No known vulnerability is identified. The claim asserts cargo-audit 'may contain known security vulnerabilities' but names no CVE, no RUSTSEC advisory, and no affected version. Its only reference is a crates.io landing page. The claim's own metadata concedes this: `citation_quality: minimal`, `confirmation_status: UNVERIFIED`, and CWE-1104 carries `verified: false`. A `known_vulns` finding with no known vuln is not a finding.

(3) Location is arbitrary and the scoping inverts the risk ordering. Line 83 is one of at least eight unpinned installs in the same file: line 14 (pip semgrep/bandit), 17 (gem brakeman/bundler-audit), 21 (npm eslint), 24 (pip-audit), 43 (apt trivy), 57 (default-jdk/build-essential), 82 (`curl https://sh.rustup.rs | sh` with `--default-toolchain stable`), 86 (`curl https://dot.net/v1/dotnet-install.sh | bash --channel 8.0`). If unpinned installation were the vulnerability, this finding is both under-scoped (it is a file-level property) and mis-prioritized (it flags the mildest instance while ignoring two curl-pipe-shell installs).

Runtime posture further reduces exposure: Dockerfile:103-111 creates and switches to `USER scanner` (uid 1000), and skill/scripts/run_tools.py:131,165-166 mount the target read-only (`%s:/src:ro`). DEVELOPMENT.md:54-56 records the deliberate decision that scanners 'only parse code, never execute it. Mount stays read-only + non-root.'

That is a real but LOW-severity build-hygiene issue, it applies to the whole file rather than line 83, and the claim never articulates it. Reframed that way it could be refiled; as written — HIGH severity, `known_vulns`, CWE-1104, 'enables known vulnerability injection,' remediation 'pin a version' — it is wrong in mechanism, category, severity, and remediation direction.

Note on the `corroborated_by: [architecture, code, security]` metadata: I could not verify cross-panel corroboration from the repository, and corroboration among agents that share the same inverted premise would not make the premise correct.

discarded_claims.title: Incorrect GitHub Actions parameter for SARIF upload
discarded_claims.description: The security.yml workflow passes a directory path to the `sarif_file` parameter, but this parameter expects a single file path. The TOOLS_OUT variable (line 10) is set to .panopticon/tools directory containing multiple SARIF files, which should use the `sarif_directory` parameter instead.
discarded_claims.impact: The SARIF upload step will fail to upload findings to the GitHub Security tab because the parameter type is mismatched with the provided path. This prevents security findings from being visible in GitHub's security features.
discarded_claims.remediation: Change line 77 from `sarif_file: ${{ env.TOOLS_OUT }}` to `sarif_directory: ${{ env.TOOLS_OUT }}` to correctly indicate a directory containing SARIF files.
references: .github/workflows/security.yml:75-77 - `uses: github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v4` with `sarif_file: ${{ env.TOOLS_OUT }}`; the action's `sarif_file` input accepts a file OR a directory and defaults to the directory `../results`
.github/workflows/security.yml:10 - `TOOLS_OUT: .panopticon/tools` (directory holding multiple SARIF files, the supported case)
skill/scripts/run_tools.py:100-101 and :154-155 - writes `<tool>.sarif` for LEGACY_SARIF_TOOLS, `<tool>.json` for adapters, so the directory legitimately contains several SARIF files
.panopticon.prev-20260803/tools/ - committed prior run showing bandit.sarif, gitleaks.sarif, semgrep.sarif, trivy.sarif plus non-SARIF .json outputs
.github/workflows/security.yml:18 - `security-events: write` present, so upload permissions are correct

provenance.confirmation_reasoning:
The claim rests on two assertions about the `github/codeql-action/upload-sarif` action's input schema, and both are wrong. (1) `sarif_file` does NOT require a single file: its documented description is 'The SARIF file or directory of SARIF files to be uploaded to GitHub code scanning', and its default value is `../results` — a directory. Passing a directory is the action's normal, documented mode; when given a directory it collects the `*.sarif` files inside and uploads them as one batch. (2) There is no `sarif_directory` input on `upload-sarif` at all (the `sarif_directory`-style concept belongs to `codeql-action/analyze`'s `output`). Applying the proposed remediation would therefore make things worse, not better: Actions would emit 'Unexpected input(s) sarif_directory', `sarif_file` would silently fall back to the default `../results`, which does not exist in this checkout, and the upload step would hard-fail.

Repository facts I verified rather than assumed: `.github/workflows/security.yml:10` sets `TOOLS_OUT: .panopticon/tools`; line 50 creates it; line 51 fills it via `skill/scripts/run_tools.py`. `run_tools.py:100-101` and `:154-155` write `<tool>.sarif` for tools in `LEGACY_SARIF_TOOLS` and `<tool>.json` otherwise, so the directory legitimately holds several SARIF files — confirmed by the committed prior run at `.panopticon.prev-20260803/tools/` (bandit.sarif, gitleaks.sarif, semgrep.sarif, trivy.sarif alongside eslint-security.json, osv-scanner.json, pip-audit.json). A directory of multiple SARIF files is precisely the case `sarif_file` is designed for; a single-file parameter could not express it. The job also grants `security-events: write` (line 18), so the upload is otherwise correctly configured. The non-`.sarif` JSON files in the directory are ignored by the action's extension filter, so their presence is not a defect either.

The claim's stated impact ('the upload step will fail because the parameter type is mismatched') is contradicted by the action's contract. Grepping the whole repo shows this is the only `upload-sarif` usage and there is no vendored action definition, so the schema point is settled from the action's published contract (default `../results`) rather than from a repo file; that external fact is unambiguous and well-established, hence CERTAIN.

One adjacent, genuinely-possible issue that is NOT this claim and does not rescue it: because the step runs with `if: always()` and adapters emit `.json`, a run in which every legacy SARIF tool is skipped would leave zero `.sarif` files and `upload-sarif` would error with 'No SARIF files found to upload'. That is a robustness nit about emptiness, not a parameter-type mismatch, and its fix is `continue-on-error`/a guard, not `sarif_directory`.

discarded_claims.title: OS Command Injection via Unquoted Shell Variable
discarded_claims.description: Unquoted ARG variable in git clone command. If RAILS_GOAT_REF contains shell metacharacters (e.g., '; rm -rf /'), the docker build --build-arg RAILS_GOAT_REF='main; rm -rf /' would execute arbitrary commands during image build.
discarded_claims.impact: Arbitrary command execution during Docker image build if an attacker controls build arguments.
discarded_claims.remediation: Quote the variable: git clone --depth 1 --branch "${RAILS_GOAT_REF}" https://github.com/OWASP/railsgoat.git

cwe.name: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command ('OS Command Injection')

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The line is quoted correctly by the claim -- Dockerfile.fixtures:26 is `RUN git clone --depth 1 --branch ${RAILS_GOAT_REF} https://github.com/OWASP/railsgoat.git`, unquoted -- but the exploitation mechanism the claim asserts does not work, and there is no attacker-controlled path to the variable. (1) Mechanism: `RUN` in shell form is not one of the instructions on which the Dockerfile parser performs variable substitution (that list is ADD, COPY, ENV, EXPOSE, FROM, LABEL, STOPSIGNAL, USER, VOLUME, WORKDIR, ONBUILD). ARG values are exported into the environment of the `/bin/sh -c` process instead, so `${RAILS_GOAT_REF}` is a POSIX parameter expansion evaluated by the shell after the command line has already been parsed. Results of parameter expansion undergo field splitting and pathname expansion only -- they are never re-parsed for control operators. The claim's own PoC, `--build-arg RAILS_GOAT_REF='main; rm -rf /'`, therefore splits into the argv words `main;` `rm` `-rf` `/` and is handed to git clone, which fails with a usage error (too many arguments); `rm -rf /` is never executed as a command. The consequence of the missing quotes here is word splitting/globbing, i.e. a broken build, not OS command injection. (2) Trust boundary: nothing in this repository ever supplies that build arg. skill/scripts/run_fixture_tests.py:38-44 `build_image()` runs `docker build -f <dockerfile> -t <tag> <root>` with no `--build-arg` at all; a repo-wide grep for `build-arg` and for `RAILS_GOAT_REF` finds hits only in Dockerfile.fixtures itself and in the design/plan docs; and no GitHub workflow builds Dockerfile.fixtures (docker-publish.yml builds ./Dockerfile, security.yml builds panopticon-tools). The only way to set this value is for a human to type it into their own `docker build` invocation, at which point they already have arbitrary execution on that host -- no privilege boundary is crossed, which is why build args are not treated as a security boundary. The nearest genuine residual is git argument injection (a value like `main --config=...` would split into extra options consumed by git clone), but that is a different weakness from the one claimed, requires the same already-privileged actor, and does not reach command execution over the https transport used here. Adding quotes is still correct hygiene; the MEDIUM command-injection framing is not supportable.

discarded_claims.title: Unversioned gem package installs enable known vulnerability injection
discarded_claims.description: Line 17-18 of Dockerfile installs Ruby gems (brakeman, bundler-audit) without version pinning. Unversioned gem installs will fetch the latest available version, which may contain known vulnerabilities or breaking changes.
discarded_claims.impact: The scanner image may contain known vulnerabilities in Ruby security scanning tools. Known CVEs in brakeman or bundler-audit could be automatically included in the build.

references: CWE-1104: Use of Unmaintained Third Party Components

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The literal code observation is accurate: /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/Dockerfile line 17 reads `RUN gem install --no-document brakeman bundler-audit` with no version constraint (line 18 is `bundle-audit update`, a build-time fetch of the ruby-advisory-db data, not a gem install). But the finding as filed — HIGH severity, known_vulns lens, 'enables known vulnerability injection', impact 'Known CVEs in brakeman or bundler-audit could be automatically included' — is not supported. (1) The mechanism is inverted: an unpinned `gem install` resolves to the newest published release, which for an actively maintained tool is the most-patched version. Pinning is what freezes a build on a known-vulnerable version; floating is what escapes it. The claim would be coherent as an argument for pinning-plus-monitoring, but not as 'unpinned therefore known CVE'. (2) No CVE is named. The known_vulns lens is defined in skill/prompts/lenses.md as 'OWASP Top 10, CWE Top 25, dependency CVEs, known-bad API usage'; a dependency-CVE finding at HIGH needs an advisory affecting a version actually resolved at build time, and none is offered. (3) The cited CWE-1104 (Use of Unmaintained Third Party Components) is inapposite — brakeman and bundler-audit are actively maintained, and always-latest resolution is the opposite of consuming unmaintained components. (4) The impact framing is not supported by how the image runs: these gems are build-time developer tooling in a scanner image that executes as unprivileged `USER scanner` (Dockerfile line 110) against a read-only bind mount (`-v <target>:/src:ro`, skill/scripts/run_tools.py lines 131 and 165-166); no exploit path from a hypothetically vulnerable brakeman to attacker impact is shown. (5) The claim also slices arbitrarily: line 14 (`pip install semgrep bandit bandit-sarif-formatter`) and line 83 (`cargo install cargo-audit`) are equally unpinned and unflagged, while the materially stronger supply-chain exposures in the same file — lines 82 and 86, which pipe remotely fetched installer scripts into `sh`/`bash` — are not raised at all. There IS a real, smaller issue underneath: unpinned installs make the ghcr-published image non-reproducible (.github/workflows/docker-publish.yml pushes `latest` and sha tags) and leave a window for a compromised or typosquatted upstream release. That is a build-integrity/reproducibility concern (CWE-1357/CWE-829, OWASP A08:2021), appropriately LOW, and best filed once at file scope — the repo already demonstrates the fix pattern with ARG-pinned gitleaks/gosec/osv-scanner/SpotBugs/dependency-check and `cargo install cargo-audit --version 0.22.2` in Dockerfile.fixtures line 20. Rejecting the finding as characterized, not the underlying hygiene observation.

discarded_claims.impact: The fixtures testing image may contain known vulnerabilities in pytest or its dependencies, affecting test infrastructure security.

references: CWE-1104: Use of Unmaintained Third Party Components
Dockerfile.fixtures:1 (image declared vulnerable-by-design), :16 (curl|bash), :26,:32 (mutable main clone refs), :48 (cited line), :54-55 (local test use only)
docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-02-local-scanner-fixture-suite-design.md:19-22 (local-only, independent of CI gates, not merge-blocking)

provenance.confirmation_reasoning:
The literal textual anchor is accurate: Dockerfile.fixtures line 48 is exactly `RUN pip install --no-cache-dir pytest`, with no version pin. Everything built on top of that fact, however, is unsupported, and the claim as filed (HIGH severity, security panel, known_vulns lens) does not survive inspection on four independent grounds.

(1) The causal mechanism is inverted. An unpinned `pip install pytest` against the default PyPI index resolves to the LATEST release — by construction the most-patched version available at build time. Pinning is what freezes a build on a known-vulnerable version; not pinning is what floats it forward. The description's premise ('could pull a version with known vulnerabilities') and the title ('enables known vulnerability injection') describe the opposite of how the cited line behaves. The genuine risk of an unpinned install is non-reproducibility and exposure to a future compromised upstream release — a supply-chain/build-hygiene concern, not a 'known vulnerability' one. The lens assignment (known_vulns) is therefore wrong for the defect actually present.

(2) The CWE is misapplied and self-contradicting. CWE-1104 is 'Use of Unmaintained Third Party Components.' pytest is actively maintained, and nothing at line 48 pins it to an unmaintained version. Worse, the claim's own remediation ('Pin pytest to a specific version') is the action that would create CWE-1104 exposure over time, not remove it. The claim carries `verified: false` on this citation and `citation_quality: minimal`, consistent with the mapping being generated rather than derived.

(3) No vulnerable artifact is identified. No CVE is cited, and none is verifiable from the repository — there is no lockfile, no SBOM, and no recorded resolved pytest version anywhere in the tree (only `pyproject.toml`, which declares no dependencies at all, and `tests/fixtures/vulnerable-python/requirements.txt`, which is unrelated fixture content). A known_vulns finding with no known vuln is not a finding.

(4) The severity is indefensible given how this image is scoped and used. Dockerfile.fixtures line 1 declares it 'vulnerable-by-design applications for scanner validation'; lines 26/29/32 deliberately clone OWASP RailsGoat, WebGoat, and AspGoat, and line 41 copies a hand-rolled crate whose stated purpose (per the design spec) is 'known-vulnerable dependencies and deliberate source-level flaws.' Lines 54-55 state the trust posture explicitly: 'intended for local test use only.' The design spec at docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-02-local-scanner-fixture-suite-design.md:19-22 confirms it is local-only, 'independent of CI gates,' and 'user-triggered, not a merge-blocking gate.' I verified this against .github/workflows/ci.yml, which contains no `docker build` step at all — the image is never built or published by CI. Rating 'the fixtures image may contain known vulnerabilities' as HIGH, in an image whose entire raison d'etre is to contain known vulnerabilities, is a scope error.

Consistency check also undercuts the claim's selectivity. If unpinned/unverified acquisition were the concern, the same file contains strictly more consequential instances that the finding does not mention: line 16 `curl -sfL https://dot.net/v1/dotnet-install.sh | bash -s -- --channel 8.0` (curl-pipe-to-shell with no checksum or signature verification), lines 26 and 32 `git clone --depth 1 --branch main` of third-party repos (mutable ref — build content changes silently between rebuilds), and lines 9-13 (unpinned apt packages plus `gem install bundler`). The base Dockerfile is the same: lines 14, 24, and 83 install semgrep/bandit/pip-audit/cargo-audit unpinned, and even CI itself runs `pip install pytest ruff pyyaml jsonschema` unpinned (.github/workflows/ci.yml:39). Line 48 is the least consequential instance of a repo-wide convention, singled out and escalated.

Disposition: reject at HIGH/known_vulns. There is a legitimate residual worth at most an INFO/LOW hygiene note under build reproducibility — and if it is refiled, it should cover the curl-pipe-bash at line 16 and the mutable `main` clone refs first, since those dominate the pytest pin by a wide margin. Note the claim's own metadata already signals weakness: confidence POSSIBLE, confirmation_status UNVERIFIED, citation_quality minimal.

An unpinned `pip install pytest` against the default PyPI index resolves to the LATEST release — by construction the most-patched version available at build time. Pinning is what freezes a build on a known-vulnerable version; not pinning is what floats it forward. The description's premise ('could pull a version with known vulnerabilities') and the title ('enables known vulnerability injection') describe the opposite of how the cited line behaves. The genuine risk of an unpinned install is non-reproducibility and exposure to a future compromised upstream release — a supply-chain/build-hygiene concern, not a 'known vulnerability' one. The lens assignment (known_vulns) is therefore wrong for the defect actually present.

(2) The CWE is misapplied and self-contradicting. CWE-1104 is 'Use of Unmaintained Third Party Components.' pytest is actively maintained, and nothing at line 48 pins it to an unmaintained version. Worse, the claim's own remediation ('Pin pytest to a specific version') is the action that would create CWE-1104 exposure over time, not remove it. The claim carries `verified: false` on this citation and `citation_quality: minimal`, consistent with the mapping being generated rather than derived.

(3) No vulnerable artifact is identified. No CVE is cited, and none is verifiable from the repository — there is no lockfile, no SBOM, and no recorded resolved pytest version anywhere in the tree (only `pyproject.toml`, which declares no dependencies at all, and `tests/fixtures/vulnerable-python/requirements.txt`, which is unrelated fixture content). A known_vulns finding with no known vuln is not a finding.

(4) The severity is indefensible given how this image is scoped and used. Dockerfile.fixtures line 1 declares it 'vulnerable-by-design applications for scanner validation'; lines 26/29/32 deliberately clone OWASP RailsGoat, WebGoat, and AspGoat, and line 41 copies a hand-rolled crate whose stated purpose (per the design spec) is 'known-vulnerable dependencies and deliberate source-level flaws.' Lines 54-55 state the trust posture explicitly: 'intended for local test use only.' The design spec at docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-02-local-scanner-fixture-suite-design.md:19-22 confirms it is local-only, 'independent of CI gates,' and 'user-triggered, not a merge-blocking gate.' I verified this against .github/workflows/ci.yml, which contains no `docker build` step at all — the image is never built or published by CI. Rating 'the fixtures image may contain known vulnerabilities' as HIGH, in an image whose entire raison d'etre is to contain known vulnerabilities, is a scope error.

Consistency check also undercuts the claim's selectivity. If unpinned/unverified acquisition were the concern, the same file contains strictly more consequential instances that the finding does not mention: line 16 `curl -sfL https://dot.net/v1/dotnet-install.sh | bash -s -- --channel 8.0` (curl-pipe-to-shell with no checksum or signature verification), lines 26 and 32 `git clone --depth 1 --branch main` of third-party repos (mutable ref — build content changes silently between rebuilds), and lines 9-13 (unpinned apt packages plus `gem install bundler`). The base Dockerfile is the same: lines 14, 24, and 83 install semgrep/bandit/pip-audit/cargo-audit unpinned, and even CI itself runs `pip install pytest ruff pyyaml jsonschema` unpinned (.github/workflows/ci.yml:39). Line 48 is the least consequential instance of a repo-wide convention, singled out and escalated.

Disposition: reject at HIGH/known_vulns. There is a legitimate residual worth at most an INFO/LOW hygiene note under build reproducibility — and if it is refiled, it should cover the curl-pipe-bash at line 16 and the mutable `main` clone refs first, since those dominate the pytest pin by a wide margin. Note the claim's own metadata already signals weakness: confidence POSSIBLE, confirmation_status UNVERIFIED, citation_quality minimal.

discarded_claims.title: Base Docker image uses version tag without digest, allowing known vulnerabilities in base layers
discarded_claims.description: Line 4 specifies `FROM python:3.12-slim` without a content digest (SHA256). While the version tag ensures a specific release, the underlying base image layers can be updated by the Docker registry, potentially pulling layers with known vulnerabilities without explicit control.
discarded_claims.impact: Over time, pulling the image could result in base layers containing known vulnerabilities (glibc, openssl, etc.) that were patched after the image tag was created but are included in updated pulls of the same tag.
discarded_claims.remediation: Use a pinned digest: `FROM python:3.12-slim@sha256:HASH` to ensure bit-for-bit reproducible builds with no possibility of pulling updated vulnerable layers. Example: `FROM python:3.12-slim@sha256:abc123...`

provenance.confirmation_reasoning:
The code observation is accurate — Dockerfile:4 is literally `FROM python:3.12-slim` with no `@sha256:` digest — but the claim's stated impact mechanism is inverted, and that mechanism is the only thing that makes this a MEDIUM security finding rather than a build-hygiene preference.

The claim asserts that an unpinned tag means 'pulling the image could result in base layers containing known vulnerabilities ... that were patched after the image tag was created but are included in updated pulls of the same tag.' That is backwards. `python:3.12-slim` is a rolling tag that upstream rebuilds against current Debian security updates; a fresh pull of the tag yields *newer, more patched* base layers. Pinning a bare digest is what freezes the build on the base layers as they existed at pin time, and absent automated digest bumping (there is no Renovate/Dependabot config in this repo) a digest pin would monotonically accumulate the exact unpatched glibc/openssl CVEs the claim worries about. The proposed remediation would make the stated impact more likely, not less.

The repository also documents the floating tag as an intentional freshness decision, not an oversight: DEVELOPMENT.md:83 states the panopticon-tools image is rebuilt on a monthly cadence precisely because 'the scanner BINARIES and their rule/advisory databases age with the image.' The secondary benefit the claim offers — 'bit-for-bit reproducible builds' — is not achievable by a base-image digest here anyway, since the same Dockerfile installs floating-latest versions throughout: `pip install semgrep bandit bandit-sarif-formatter` (line 14), `gem install brakeman bundler-audit` (line 17), `npm install -g eslint ...` (line 21), `pip install pip-audit` (line 24), `cargo install cargo-audit` (line 83), plus `curl | sh` installs of rustup (line 82) and the .NET SDK (line 86). Digest-pinning line 4 alone changes nothing about reproducibility.

The citation is also wrong: CWE-426 (Untrusted Search Path) has no relationship to base-image tag pinning. Finally, .github/workflows/docker-publish.yml:62-67 already emits a signed build-provenance attestation with the pushed image digest, which addresses the substitution-tracking concern that a digest pin would otherwise serve. Residual legitimate content: unpinned base tags do mean two builds of the same commit are not identical, which is worth an INFO-level note about adopting digest pinning *paired with automated bumping* — but the finding as written is not supportable at MEDIUM.

discarded_claims.title: Multiple imports on single line
discarded_claims.description: Line 4 has multiple imports separated by commas: `import sys, os`. PEP 8 requires each import on a separate line.
discarded_claims.impact: Violates PEP 8 style guidelines and reduces code readability
discarded_claims.remediation: Separate the imports: `import sys` and `import os` on individual lines

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The literal observation is accurate — tests/tools/test_base.py line 4 is exactly `import sys, os` — but the normative claim ('violates style guidelines', actionable) is contradicted by the repository's own enforced lint policy. /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/pyproject.toml lines 22-24 configure ruff with `select = ["E", "F", "W"]` and `ignore = ["E401", "E501", "E701", "E702"]`. E401 IS the pycodestyle rule 'multiple imports on one line' — the project has explicitly and deliberately opted out of precisely this check, alongside line-length and multiple-statements-on-one-line. This is not an oversight in a single file: the same comma-import form appears in tests/test_ingest_tools.py:1 (`import contextlib, io, os, sys, json, tempfile, unittest`), tests/test_run_tools.py:2 (`import json, os, sys, tempfile, unittest`), and .github/apply-labels.sh:22 (`import re, sys`), and it is the form used throughout the project's own design docs under docs/superpowers/plans/. A style finding whose sole basis is a rule the target project's linter configuration explicitly disables is a false positive against that project's standard; PEP 8's own preface defers to project consistency. Nothing in the codebase would flag this, and 'fixing' it would diverge from the surrounding convention. Rejecting on the normative claim, not on the existence of the line — an auditor re-filing this would need a new basis (e.g. a proposal to remove E401 from the ignore list repo-wide), not a per-file style defect.

discarded_claims.title: Test with inverted logic and meaningless assertion
discarded_claims.description: The test checks if cargo is available, and if so, raises SkipTest. This logic is backwards - the test should execute when cargo is available. Additionally, line 16 contains a meaningless 'self.assertTrue(True)' assertion that always passes and wastes test resources.
discarded_claims.impact: Test does not properly validate behavior when cargo is not available. The meaningless assertion makes the test less maintainable and wastes execution time.
discarded_claims.remediation: Remove the SkipTest when cargo is available, or refactor to test actual behavior. Remove the 'self.assertTrue(True)' statement as it serves no verification purpose.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Rejected on the claim's defining thesis. The claim states the skip guard is 'backwards - the test should execute when cargo is available.' The code contradicts that reading. The method is named test_cargo_audit_skips_without_rust — its declared subject is the no-Rust-toolchain host — and the skip message at tests/tools/test_rust_cs_integration.py:15 spells out the design explicitly: 'cargo is available; run full fixture test instead'. That referenced full fixture test exists and is the exact mirror image: tests/tools/test_rust_integration.py:15-17 opens with `if not shutil.which("cargo"): self.skipTest("cargo not installed")` and then drives the real vulnerable-rust fixture through is_applicable/invoke/parse. The two guards are deliberately complementary so that exactly one of the pair runs on any given host; inverting the one in test_rust_cs_integration.py, as the remediation proposes, would duplicate the cargo-available path already covered in test_rust_integration.py and would delete the only branch the file was written to occupy. The plan of record confirms the intent (docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-01-scanner-ecosystem-expansion.md:1144-1155, 'Expected: PASS or SKIP'). So 'inverted logic' is not supported. Two further errors: the impact line blames the SkipTest for the missing validation, but the actual reason the without-cargo behavior is unvalidated is the empty body, not the guard; and 'wastes test resources / wastes execution time' is not credible for a single no-op assertion. What IS accurate in this claim is the narrow secondary observation that line 16 is `self.assertTrue(True)` and asserts nothing — I verified that independently and it stands on its own. But that observation is the claim's incidental half; the titular defect, the analysis behind it, and the primary remediation are all contradicted by the code, so this claim as filed should not be actioned.

discarded_claims.title: Path Traversal via Unvalidated FIXTURE_ROOT Environment Variable
discarded_claims.description: FIXTURE_ROOT is read from environment without validation and directly used in os.path.join(). An attacker with control over the FIXTURE_ROOT environment variable can use path traversal sequences (e.g., '../../../../etc') to access files outside the intended fixtures directory.
discarded_claims.impact: Allows arbitrary filesystem access during test execution, potentially exposing sensitive files or causing unauthorized file operations.
discarded_claims.remediation: Validate and normalize FIXTURE_ROOT against a whitelist of allowed paths, or use os.path.abspath() and verify the result starts with the expected base directory.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The code does not support the claim on three independent grounds. (1) No traversal primitive exists. tests/tools/test_csharp_integration.py:8-10 reads FIXTURE_ROOT as the *base* with a fallback, and line 15 joins a hardcoded literal onto it: `os.path.join(FIXTURE_ROOT, 'AspGoat')`. The classic traversal pattern is an untrusted *component* joined onto a trusted base; here the base itself is the configuration knob and the component is a constant. '../../../../etc' in FIXTURE_ROOT yields nothing an operator could not achieve by simply setting FIXTURE_ROOT=/etc — there is no escape from a boundary because no boundary was asserted. os.path.abspath()/prefix-check remediation would break the feature, not fix a hole. (2) The threat model is inverted. FIXTURE_ROOT is a designed, documented deployment knob, not attacker-reachable input: Dockerfile.fixtures:51 sets `ENV FIXTURE_ROOT=/opt/panopticon-fixtures`, skill/scripts/run_fixture_tests.py:81 passes `-e FIXTURE_ROOT=/opt/panopticon-fixtures` to docker run so the read-only-mounted tests can find the vendored corpora, and docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-02-local-scanner-fixture-suite.md:850 records it as intended ('FIXTURE_ROOT is always read from os.environ with a fallback'). An actor who can set the environment of the pytest process already has code execution as that user; the env var grants no privilege they lack. The same pattern appears in test_java_integration.py:8, test_ruby_integration.py:8, test_rust_integration.py:9. (3) The claimed impact ('arbitrary filesystem access... unauthorized file operations') is not reachable. The test guards in order: line 16 skips unless the roslyn-secguard adapter is registered; line 19-20 `os.path.isdir(target)` skips unless FIXTURE_ROOT/AspGoat is a directory; line 21-22 skips unless `adapter.is_applicable(target)`, which per skill/scripts/tools/roslyn_secguard.py:26-31 requires a top-level .csproj or .sln. Only then does invoke() run, and it copies the tree into tempfile.mkdtemp() and rmtree's it in a finally block, writing nothing to the target. The strongest real consequence is that a pre-existing malicious .csproj would be built by `dotnet build` (MSBuild target execution) — but reaching that requires the adversary to both plant that project and set the env var, i.e. capabilities that already subsume the alleged gain. HIGH severity on a test-only file is unsupportable. CWE-426 (Untrusted Search Path) is also miscited: this is not an executable/library search path.

discarded_claims.title: Hardcoded Docker Container Paths in Test Fixtures
discarded_claims.description: Test fixture at line 20 contains hardcoded path '/src/tests/fixtures/vulnerable-python/requirements.txt' from Docker container environment. This reveals build/container infrastructure details and could leak information about the test execution environment.
discarded_claims.impact: Information disclosure about build environment structure and Docker configuration. Test fixtures containing real environment paths may inadvertently expose infrastructure details.
discarded_claims.remediation: Use relative paths or symbolic paths that don't reveal container infrastructure. Strip mount prefixes from production code paths before using in test fixtures.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The `/src` prefix is not infrastructure to be disclosed — it is a fixed, already-published constant of this repo, and the fixture that contains it exists precisely so a regression test can assert it gets stripped. Three independent lines of evidence: (1) `/src` is documented in the repo's own public files — Dockerfile:3 (`docker run --rm -v "$PWD":/src:ro panopticon-tools`), Dockerfile:111 (`WORKDIR /src`), skill/scripts/run_tools.py:131 and :165 (`"-v", "%s:/src:ro" % os.path.abspath(target)`), and DEVELOPMENT.md:204-205, 223. A test fixture cannot 'leak' a value that production source and the README-tier docs state outright, and the value is identical for every user since it is a hardcoded mount point, not a host path. (2) Production code is built around it: skill/scripts/tools/sarif_utils.py:38-51 `_norm_uri` exists to strip `/src/`, and skill/scripts/tools/osv_scanner.py:52 routes `source.path` through it. (3) The fixture is load-bearing: tests/tools/test_osv_scanner.py:97-101 (`test_source_path_mount_prefix_stripped`) asserts no finding's `location.file` starts with `/src`, and tests/tools/test_osv_scanner.py:75-76 asserts the normalized value `tests/fixtures/vulnerable-python/requirements.txt`. Both assertions become vacuous if the prefix is removed from the input. The comment at tests/tools/test_osv_scanner.py:11-16 warns 'Do NOT replace this with a hand-invented shape — a fictional fixture previously masked a parser that dropped 100% of real findings', and DEVELOPMENT.md:223 records that same historical bug ('Ingest fixtures don't match real tool SARIF (no `file:///src/` uri...): replace with golden real-tool SARIF — would have caught the `/src/` bug'). The claim's remediation ('strip mount prefixes ... before using in test fixtures') would therefore reintroduce a known 100%-finding-loss regression in exchange for zero security benefit. There is no secret, credential, host path, or user-specific data in the fixture. CWE-200 and OWASP A01:2021 (Broken Access Control) are both inapplicable — nothing is exposed to an unauthorized actor and no access-control decision is involved.

discarded_claims.title: Unvalidated Path Manipulation in sys.path.insert
discarded_claims.description: sys.path.insert uses os.path.join with relative path traversal without validation. If an attacker can manipulate the file structure or working directory, this could lead to importing unintended modules from arbitrary locations.
discarded_claims.impact: Potential for loading malicious modules during test execution if directory structure is compromised or working directory is controlled by attacker.
discarded_claims.remediation: Use absolute paths or validate that the constructed path resolves to the expected location before adding to sys.path.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The cited line is `sys.path.insert(0, os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), os.pardir, os.pardir, "skill"))` in tests/tools/test_base.py:6. The claim's premise — that this depends on relative path traversal from an attacker-influenceable working directory — is false for this repository. (1) The path element is derived entirely from `__file__`, not from CWD, argv, environment, or any external input. pyproject.toml sets `requires-python = ">=3.11"` and .github/workflows/ci.yml tests only 3.11/3.12/3.13; on every supported interpreter `__file__` is absolute (both for `__main__` since 3.9 and for pytest-imported modules, since pytest inserts absolute rootdir entries). `os.pardir` components are just `..` segments appended to an absolute prefix, so the resolved entry is deterministically <repo>/skill regardless of CWD. (2) There is no untrusted search-path element to speak of: `skill/` contains only SKILL.md plus the subdirectories prompts/, reference/, scripts/, agents/ — no top-level .py modules — so the position-0 insertion cannot shadow a stdlib module either. (3) The only stated attack path, 'if an attacker can manipulate the file structure', presupposes write access to the checked-out repo tree, which already implies arbitrary code execution via the test files themselves; it is not a distinct vulnerability. CWE-426/CWE-427 both require a search-path element influenced by untrusted input, which is absent here. (4) The pattern is the project-wide idiom, present identically in ~15 other test files (tests/test_run_tools.py:3, tests/test_schema.py:6, tests/tools/test_cargo_audit.py:7, etc.) and in production code (skill/scripts/tools/base.py:9, skill/scripts/_run_adapter.py:10); singling out one test file as a MEDIUM security finding is arbitrary. Also note this is test-only code that is never executed in the shipped skill runtime. At most this is a packaging/style nit (use a conftest.py or a real package), not a security defect.

discarded_claims.title: Inconsistent subprocess mocking pattern across test suite
discarded_claims.description: This test uses 'patch.object(subprocess, "run")' (line 52), while other test files use 'mock.patch("scripts.tools.base.subprocess.run")'. This inconsistency in mocking strategies could lead to subtle bugs where tests verify different behavioral contracts.
discarded_claims.impact: Inconsistent mock implementations may mask integration issues and make test maintenance harder. Different mocking patterns may not capture the same call signatures.
discarded_claims.remediation: Standardize on using mock.patch with the full module path throughout the test suite to ensure consistent verification of subprocess interactions.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The surface observation is literally true: /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/tests/tools/test_legacy_sarif.py:52 and :66 use `with patch.object(subprocess, "run") as mock_run:` while tests/tools/test_base.py:49,56,67,76,86, test_pip_audit.py:110,124, test_npm_audit.py:95, test_osv_scanner.py:123, test_cargo_audit.py:48, test_bundler_audit.py:49, test_brakeman.py:55 and test_eslint_security.py:138,154 all use `mock.patch("scripts.tools.base.subprocess.run", ...)`. But the claim's substance — that these are different mocking strategies that 'verify different behavioral contracts', 'may mask integration issues', and 'may not capture the same call signatures' — is contradicted by what the two forms actually do. `mock.patch("scripts.tools.base.subprocess.run")` splits on the last dot: it imports `scripts.tools.base`, getattrs `subprocess` (which IS the singleton stdlib module object, per `import subprocess` at skill/scripts/tools/base.py:6), and sets `run` on it. `patch.object(subprocess, "run")` in the test file resolves the same singleton module object from sys.modules and sets the same attribute. Both are therefore the identical global patch of `subprocess.run`, and `run_tool` (base.py:72) does an attribute lookup at call time (`res = subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, timeout=timeout, **kwargs)`), so both interception points are byte-for-byte the same. I verified the legacy_sarif tests do observe the real call signature this way: test_invoke_runs_tool_command asserts cwd is None and the target is in argv, and test_invoke_runs_gosec_in_target_directory asserts cwd == '/go/project' — these only pass because the patch reaches base.run_tool. There is no divergent contract, no unsignatured call, no masked integration path. What remains is a cosmetic import/spelling difference, which is precisely the LOW-severity STY-003 in this same batch; as a MEDIUM test_design defect resting on a false mechanism, TD-003 does not hold. (The one genuine stylistic difference in these tests — auto-MagicMock with `return_value` vs. a hand-written `fake_run` callable — is not what the claim asserts, and both remain valid ways to assert on call_args.)

discarded_claims.title: TestRunTool class defined after if __name__ == '__main__' block
discarded_claims.description: The TestRunTool class (line 44) is defined after the `if __name__ == '__main__':` block (lines 40-41). This placement prevents proper test discovery when tests are run as a module, as test runners will stop collecting tests after the if __name__ block.
discarded_claims.impact: Test discovery may fail depending on how tests are executed; TestRunTool tests may not be discovered or executed in all test runner configurations.
discarded_claims.remediation: Move the if __name__ == '__main__' block to the end of the file, after all TestCase classes are defined.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The positional fact is accurate: `if __name__ == "__main__": unittest.main()` sits at tests/tools/test_base.py:40-41 and `class TestRunTool(unittest.TestCase)` follows at line 44-89. But the load-bearing assertion — 'prevents proper test discovery when tests are run as a module, as test runners will stop collecting tests after the if __name__ block' — is contradicted by Python semantics and by this repo's actual runner. An `if` statement does not terminate module execution; when the module is imported (pytest, `python -m unittest`), `__name__` is the module name, the guard evaluates False, execution continues, and TestRunTool is defined and collected normally. This repo runs tests exactly that way in all three documented paths: .github/workflows/ci.yml:41, README.md:92 and CONTRIBUTING.md:13 all invoke `python -m pytest tests/ -q`. There is no pytest config in pyproject.toml overriding default collection, and no tests/__init__.py or tests/tools/__init__.py, so pytest imports the file as a plain module and collects both unittest.TestCase subclasses. The 'run as a module' path the claim names is precisely the path that works. A narrower, different defect does exist: under direct script execution (`python tests/tools/test_base.py`) `unittest.main()` runs at line 41 with only TestBase in the module namespace and then calls sys.exit() (exit=True is the default), so lines 44-89 never execute and the five F-CAL-1 run_tool regression tests are silently skipped. That is a real but narrow organizational defect exercised by no path in this repository — not a HIGH-severity test-discovery failure, and not the mechanism described. The CWE-1104 citation (unmaintained third-party components) is unrelated to file-ordering in a test module and is marked unverified in the claim itself.

discarded_claims.title: test_rust_cs_integration.py performs no genuine fixture-based integration test despite its name and location alongside test_ruby_integration.py/test_java_integration.py
discarded_claims.description: test_ruby_integration.py and test_java_integration.py both follow the same pattern: look up a vendored vulnerable fixture (railsgoat/WebGoat) via FIXTURE_ROOT, skip if absent, otherwise actually invoke the real adapter and assert it produces findings against real vulnerable code. test_csharp_integration.py follows the identical pattern for AspGoat/roslyn-secguard. test_rust_cs_integration.py's single test, `test_cargo_audit_skips_without_rust`, does neither: it only asserts `ADAPTERS["cargo-audit"] is not None`, then either raises `unittest.SkipTest` (if `cargo` is on PATH) or falls through to a no-op `assertTrue(True)` (if it isn't) — in neither branch does it check out/build a real vulnerable Cargo.lock fixture, invoke cargo-audit, or assert on findings. It also does not reference a FIXTURE_ROOT vulnerable-Rust project the way the other integration files do, and provides no C# ("_cs") coverage at all despite the filename (that coverage lives entirely in the separate test_csharp_integration.py).
discarded_claims.impact: Unlike railsgoat/WebGoat/AspGoat, there is no vendored vulnerable-Rust fixture exercised anywhere in the suite, so cargo-audit's real end-to-end behavior (invoke() against an actual Cargo.lock with a known RUSTSEC advisory, followed by parse()) is never verified against ground truth — only against the hand-written CARGO_AUDIT_SAMPLE mock in test_cargo_audit.py. A regression that breaks the real cargo-audit CLI integration (flag changes, output-shape drift) would go undetected by this file in either of its two execution branches.
discarded_claims.remediation: Either add a genuine fixture-based integration test (vendored vulnerable Rust project + real cargo-audit invocation + assertion on findings, matching test_ruby_integration.py's pattern) or rename/fold this file to make clear it is only a registry smoke-check, not Rust/C# integration coverage.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The claim's description of the file is accurate, but its load-bearing impact assertion is factually contradicted by the repository, so the finding as filed does not stand. Accurate part: /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/tests/tools/test_rust_cs_integration.py is 17 lines whose only test asserts `assertIsNotNone(adapter)`, then raises SkipTest if `shutil.which('cargo')` else `assertTrue(True)` — a registry smoke check that never invokes a fixture, and contains no C# coverage. False part (the impact): the claim states 'there is no vendored vulnerable-Rust fixture exercised anywhere in the suite' and that cargo-audit end-to-end behavior is 'only [verified] against the hand-written CARGO_AUDIT_SAMPLE mock in test_cargo_audit.py'. A separate file, /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/tests/tools/test_rust_integration.py, does exactly the fixture-based integration test the claim says is missing: `test_cargo_audit_finds_rustsec_advisories` resolves `os.path.join(FIXTURE_ROOT, 'vulnerable-rust')` (line 18), guards on cargo/adapter/is_applicable, calls `adapter.invoke(target)` and `adapter.parse(raw, 'g1')`, and asserts both non-empty findings and `any('RUSTSEC-' in str(f.get('citations')) for f in findings)` (lines 26-34) — a stronger assertion than the ruby/csharp integration tests it is compared against. discarded_claims.title: Inconsistent finding object schema across findings array
discarded_claims.description: Findings in the self-scan-report.json have missing/inconsistent fields. Some findings include 'source_role' (e.g., BN-001 at line 1520), others lack it entirely (e.g., STRUCT-001 at line 579). Similarly, 'lens' field present in some (STRUCT-001, line 582) but absent in many others (RUN-001). 'depth' field appears in some findings (STRUCT-001, line 598) but not consistently across all findings.
discarded_claims.impact: Schema inconsistency makes it difficult to process findings uniformly; tools relying on field presence must defensively check each finding, increasing complexity and error surface.
discarded_claims.remediation: Establish a canonical finding schema and normalize all findings to include required fields (with null values if missing data), ensuring consistent structure across the entire findings array.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning:
Every specific example the claim offers is exactly inverted from what the file contains.

- 'others lack it [source_role] entirely (e.g., STRUCT-001 at line 579)' — false. STRUCT-001 begins at line 579 and carries `"source_role": "lens_sweep"` at line 597.
- "'lens' field present in some (STRUCT-001, line 582) but absent in many others (RUN-001)" — false. RUN-001 carries `"lens": "correctness"` at line 345.
- 'Some findings include source_role (e.g., BN-001 at line 1520)' — false. BN-001 starts at line 1514 and has *no* source_role; line 1520 is `"source": "tool:bandit"`. BN-001 is one of the findings that lacks the field.

So the claim's three anchors point at the opposite of what it asserts. The real distribution, which I counted: the `findings` array spans lines 340-3643 and holds 72 findings (`discarded_claims` starts at 3644). Of those, 47 carry `"source": "tool:..."` and 25 do not. All 25 agent findings have `source_role` and `depth`; zero of the 47 tool findings do. `lens` is present on 15 — the 25 agent findings minus the 10 whose `source_role` is `panel_review` (lines 688, 1047, 1091, 1136, 1180, 1224, 1268, 1371, 1426, 1482). The partition is exact and semantically meaningful, not ragged: a static-analysis tool finding has no lens, no source_role and no review depth, and a panel review has no lens.

The framing of accidental schema drift is also contradicted by the code. `/Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/reference/report-schema.json` is the canonical finding schema the remediation asks for; it requires only `id, title, severity, confidence, panel, category, evidence` (line 71) and declares `lens` (78), `source_role` (80) and `depth` (81) as optional properties. And `normalize_finding` in `/Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/synthesize.py` deliberately *removes* the key rather than emitting a null:

    lens = f.get("lens")
    if lens:
        f["lens"] = str(lens)
    else:
        f.pop("lens", None)

So the omission is an intentional, schema-sanctioned design choice, not an unnormalized artifact. The claim's remediation ('establish a canonical finding schema') is already satisfied. Rejected: the asserted evidence is false, and the residual kernel of truth is by design and documented.

discarded_claims.title: Section structure inconsistency in prose-heavy list
discarded_claims.description: The 'Fixed this round' section (lines 18-54) mixes numbered list items with embedded paragraph explanations. Items 1-8 use numbered list format with inline prose, creating inconsistent hierarchy. Contrast with 'Original FIXME list' (lines 73-106) which uses sub-headings with dashes. No consistent pattern for depth-2 structure.
discarded_claims.impact: Readers must adapt parsing strategy per section; structured document consumers (Markdown parsers expecting consistent nesting) may misinterpret the outline.
discarded_claims.remediation: Standardize on one pattern: either numbered sub-headings (## Fixed this round / ### 1. Description) or consistent bullet-paragraph pairing, applied uniformly across all sections.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning:
I read the entire file (107 lines). Every load-bearing assertion in the claim is contradicted by the document.

(1) 'Contrast with Original FIXME list (lines 73-106) which uses sub-headings with dashes' — false. A grep for `^#{1,6} ` returns exactly five headings in the whole file: line 1 (`#`), and lines 7, 18, 55, 73 (all `##`). There is not a single `###` sub-heading anywhere. Lines 75-101 are a flat unordered list of seven items, each shaped `- **F-CAL-N: label** — prose`.

(2) 'Items 1-8 use numbered list format with inline prose, creating inconsistent hierarchy' — the eight items at lines 20-53 are in fact rigidly uniform: every one is `N. **Bold summary** — prose`, with wrapped continuation lines belonging to the same list item. There are no paragraph blocks embedded between or inside the numbered items. The two sections therefore use the *same* item shape (bold lead-in, em-dash, prose); they differ only in ordered vs. unordered marker, which is semantically appropriate (an enumeration of eight fixes vs. a set of labeled F-CAL-1..7 items).

(3) 'No consistent pattern for depth-2 structure' — depth-2 is consistent: all four body sections are `##`, and three of them contain a flat item list with bold lead-ins. The `## FIXME resolution` section (55-71) is prose, which is a normal and unambiguous Markdown construct.

(4) The stated impact — 'Markdown parsers expecting consistent nesting may misinterpret the outline' — has no mechanism. A document outline derives from headings, and the headings here are uniform `##`. An ordered list in one section and an unordered list in another is valid CommonMark and produces no nesting ambiguity for any parser.

I also checked for a project style rule that the file could be violating: there is no markdownlint config anywhere in the repo (glob `**/.markdownlint*` returns nothing), so there is no documented convention being breached either.

The claim's cited line ranges are approximately right, but the structural facts it asserts at those lines are not present in the file.

discarded_claims.title: Provenance object field structure varies across findings
discarded_claims.description: The 'provenance' object structure is inconsistent: some findings (STRUCT-001, line 600+) include all fields (discovered_by, expanded_by, confirmed_by, model, model_version, confirmation_status, confirmation_reasoning); others (RUN-001, line 360) lack 'model_version' or have inconsistent null usage. Fields like 'expanded_by' may be null in some but completely absent in others.
discarded_claims.impact: Code processing provenance fields must account for missing keys; no single schema documents the complete expected structure, requiring defensive programming.
discarded_claims.remediation: Ensure every finding's provenance object includes all defined fields, using null for empty values rather than omitting keys. Document the complete provenance schema in report-schema.json.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning:
The claim's premise is directly falsifiable by counting keys, and it fails.

The file contains 73 `provenance` objects (72 in `findings`, 1 in `discarded_claims`). Grepping each sub-key returns 73 occurrences for every one of the seven fields: `discovered_by` 73, `expanded_by` 73, `confirmed_by` 73, `model` 73 (75 total matches for `"model":` including two in meta.models_used), `model_version` 73, `confirmation_status` 73, `confirmation_reasoning` 73. Not one provenance object is missing a field.

The named counterexample is wrong in particular: the claim says 'others (RUN-001, line 360) lack model_version'. I read lines 360-368. RUN-001's provenance is complete and includes `"model_version": "4.5"` at line 365. Likewise 'expanded_by may be null in some but completely absent in others' — it is present in all 73, always spelled explicitly as `"expanded_by": null` where empty (e.g. lines 362, 1529, 1571).

This uniformity is produced deliberately: `/Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/provenance.py` has both constructors — `tool_provenance()` (lines 5-14) and `agent_provenance()` (lines 17-27) — emit the identical seven-key dict literal with explicit `None` values, which is precisely the discipline the claim's remediation prescribes.

The only real variance is additive, and in the opposite direction from the claim: four findings carry an eighth key `confirmed_by_model`, set by `/Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/evidence.py:237` (`prov["confirmed_by_model"] = verdict["model"]`) on advisor-confirmed findings, e.g. STRUCT-001 at line 607. That key is not undocumented — `/Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/reference/report-schema.json` line 127 declares `"confirmed_by_model": { "type": ["string", "null"] }` inside the provenance object, so the claim's second remediation ('Document the complete provenance schema in report-schema.json') is also already done. Consumers read it defensively-by-choice via `prov.get("confirmed_by_model")` in synthesize.py:196, which is the correct handling of an optional enrichment key, not a symptom of schema drift.

discarded_claims.title: Planned Phase-5 Panopticon integration reuses the static-scan fixture pattern for a corpus that fundamentally needs a running multi-service stack
discarded_claims.description: BursarBuddy's Phase 5 states Panopticon-side integration will be 'a `git clone` in `Dockerfile.fixtures` plus a `manifest.json` entry, so one artifact serves both adapter validation and fleet calibration' — reusing the exact mechanism defined in local-scanner-fixture-suite-design.md for RailsGoat/WebGoat/AspGoat/vulnerable-rust. But that design explicitly scopes out 'Running the target applications (these are static-analysis fixtures only)' and 'Dynamic testing or DAST against the fixtures' (Out of Scope section). BursarBuddy's own Proof Harness, by contrast, requires `docker-compose` bringing up Next.js, Postgres, a Python FastAPI service, and a fake LLM provider, with proofs running as an external client against the live stack — a categorically different operational shape (multi-service, network-listening, stateful) than 'clone a repo directory and hand it to a SAST adapter.'
discarded_claims.impact: The two design documents describe the same future integration point with incompatible assumptions about what 'the fixture' is (a static source tree vs. a live multi-container application). If Phase 5 is implemented by literally following both specs as written, the git-clone/manifest.json mechanism will not, by itself, produce anything the BursarBuddy proof harness or the fleet-calibration scoring model can exercise.
discarded_claims.remediation: When Phase 5 is scoped, explicitly reconcile the two mechanisms — e.g., extend Dockerfile.fixtures (or a sibling image) to also bring up BursarBuddy's docker-compose stack, or treat BursarBuddy calibration as a distinct harness invocation from the static scanner-fixture suite despite sharing a manifest format.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The claim's individual quotations are accurate, but the inference drawn from them is contradicted by the BursarBuddy spec's own architecture, which explicitly separates the live-stack proof harness from the static Panopticon integration. The quotations verify: bursarbuddy spec L252 does describe Phase-5 Panopticon integration as 'a `git clone` in `Dockerfile.fixtures` plus a `manifest.json` entry, so one artifact serves both adapter validation and fleet calibration'; L187 does specify `docker-compose` bringing up Next.js, seeded Postgres, the Python AI service, and a fake LLM provider with proofs as an external client; and local-scanner-fixture-suite-design.md L209-210 does scope out 'Running the target applications (these are static-analysis fixtures only)' and 'Dynamic testing or DAST against the fixtures'. What defeats the claim is the sentence that introduces the mechanism. L13 reads in full: 'A separate, private harness scores the fleet against a ground-truth answer key. Eventually — in Phase 5, not at the outset — Panopticon also consumes it the way it consumes RailsGoat, via a `git clone` in `Dockerfile.fixtures` and a `manifest.json` entry.' The proof harness is designated 'separate' and 'private' in the same breath as the Dockerfile.fixtures mechanism — the spec never asks Panopticon's fixture image to run it. That separation is reinforced structurally: L83 places the 'exploit suite, decoy registry, scoring harness, mutator, CI gates' in the private `bursarbuddy-key` repo; L85 states 'CI gates live in the private repo, which checks out the public app and runs proofs against it'; L174 states the four invariants are 'enforced by the private repo's CI'. The docker-compose runtime is therefore private-repo CI infrastructure, not a Panopticon fixture requirement. The claim's second limb — that a static clone produces nothing 'the fleet-calibration scoring model can exercise' — is also unsupported. Every metric at L218-222 (evidence calibration against `evidence.status`, recall by difficulty, precision against decoys, complementarity on `scanner_visible`, severity calibration) is computed by comparing Panopticon's emitted findings to key entries, and key entries are anchored to static loci (L131-134 `file`/`lines`/`symbol`, invariant 4 at L179 'Every `locus` resolves to a real file and line'). Panopticon is a source reviewer; a cloned source tree is precisely its required input. L230 confirms the shape: 'Scoring harness v0 runs Panopticon and emits a precision/recall figure.' Finally, the claim's framing that 'the two design documents describe the same future integration point' does not hold: a repo-wide case-insensitive grep for bursarbuddy returns five files and local-scanner-fixture-suite-design.md is not among them — that spec predates BursarBuddy and never contemplates it, so its Out-of-Scope list bounds its own harness rather than contradicting a spec it does not reference. Two residual notes for the auditor. No BursarBuddy implementation plan exists (docs/superpowers/plans/ contains no bursarbuddy entry, and L258 defers each phase to its own plan), so this concerns unscoped future work either way. And there is a narrow kernel the claim gestures at without establishing: if BursarBuddy's Next.js/Prisma/FastAPI tree is added to Dockerfile.fixtures, the existing dependency-preparation steps (Dockerfile.fixtures L35-37 handle bundle/mvnw/dotnet only) would need npm/pip equivalents for SCA adapters to have a resolved dependency graph. That is an ordinary build-step gap, not the categorical static-vs-live incompatibility the claim asserts, and it is not what the claim describes.

discarded_claims.title: Frontmatter `arguments` list covers only 4 of roughly 13 documented CLI flags
discarded_claims.description: SKILL.md's frontmatter declares `arguments: [target, mode, security, out]`. Per host-portability-research.md Section 1, on Kimi Code `arguments` is a real mechanism ('Named parameters ... accessible via `$<name>` placeholders in the body'), not inert metadata. The 'Modes' section (lines 27-35) and 'Global flags' section (lines 37-38) of the same file document far more surface: `-f/--file`, `-d/--directory`, `-g/--group`, `-c/--changes`, `--pr`, `-e/--explore`, `--full`, `--fail-on`, `--severity`, `--tools`, `--no-tools`, `--epss`, `--gate-unverified`, `--max-verify` — none of which appear in the declared `arguments` array.
discarded_claims.impact: On Kimi Code specifically (where this field is functional per the project's own research), most of the flags described in the skill body may not be recognized as named parameters the way `target`/`mode`/`security`/`out` are, creating a host-dependent behavioral gap between what the prose documents and what the frontmatter contract actually exposes. On Claude Code the field is inert (frontmatter beyond name/description is ignored), so the mismatch is silent there but live on Kimi.
discarded_claims.remediation: Either declare the full flag surface in `arguments` (if Kimi's parameter mechanism is meant to expose all of them) or clarify in the spec/README why only four are declared (e.g., if the rest are meant to be parsed from free-form prompt text rather than as named arguments) so the two hosts' behavior is intentional rather than incidental.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The literal observation is true — skill/SKILL.md lines 6-10 declare `arguments: [target, mode, security, out]` while the Modes (lines 27-35) and Global flags (line 38) sections document many more flags — but the defect thesis (a 'host-dependent behavioral gap' live on Kimi) is contradicted by the repository. (1) The claim's own cited authority, docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-03-host-portability-research.md:35, defines the mechanism narrowly: `arguments` = 'Named parameters (array or space-separated string), accessible via `$<name>` placeholders in the body'. Its only documented effect is placeholder substitution. (2) skill/SKILL.md contains no `$<name>` placeholders at all — a grep for `\$\{?(target|mode|security|out)\b` across all markdown in the repo returned no matches. So the four declared arguments are substituted nowhere; declared and undeclared flags behave identically on Kimi, and there is no differential the claim's impact depends on. (3) `arguments` is not a flag registry, so 'covers only 4 of roughly 13 documented CLI flags' is a category mismatch: `target` and `mode` are generic parameters that abstract over the mode flags (-f/-d/-g/-c/--pr/-e select a *mode* applied to a *target*), and `security`/`out` map to `--security`/`--out`. The four names were deliberately specified this way in the design plan (docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-01-multi-model-reviewer-dispatch.md:1319-1339 prescribes this exact frontmatter block), so it is an intentional design choice, not an incidental omission. (4) Nothing in the repo consumes the field: greps across *.py and tests/ for `arguments` found no parser or test, and skill/scripts/dispatch.py's `parse_template_frontmatter` operates on agents/*.md templates, not SKILL.md. The same research doc (line 275) notes these Kimi keys are a host dialect other runtimes ignore. Residual unknown for the auditor: the repo cannot establish whether the Kimi runtime does anything with `arguments` beyond `$<name>` substitution (e.g. rejecting or ignoring undeclared named parameters); that would require Kimi Code runtime behavior outside this repository. But on the mechanism this project itself documents, the claimed gap cannot occur.

discarded_claims.title: Finding format specification omits required 'confidence' field
discarded_claims.description: The lens-sweep.md finding format (lines 26-36) does not specify the 'confidence' field, which is required by report-schema.json (line 71). Same issue in panel-review.md (lines 31-40). This will cause schema validation failures when findings are aggregated.
discarded_claims.impact: Findings emitted by lens_sweep and panel_review agents will fail JSON schema validation during report aggregation, causing pipeline failures or incomplete results.
discarded_claims.remediation: Add 'confidence' field (enum: CERTAIN|LIKELY|POSSIBLE|NOTE) to finding format specification in both lens-sweep.md and panel-review.md. Require agents to populate this field.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The observable half of the claim is true: skill/agents/lens-sweep.md lines 26-36 and skill/agents/panel-review.md lines 31-40 do not list a `confidence` field, while skill/reference/report-schema.json line 71 lists confidence in the findings `required` array. I also confirmed empirically that lens_sweep agents do omit it — .panopticon.prev-20260803/findings-._5-code-lens_sweep-structure.json contains 9 findings with zero `confidence` keys, and findings-._5-security-lens_sweep-injection.json has zero occurrences of the string. But the claim's actual assertion — that this 'will cause schema validation failures when findings are aggregated', causing 'pipeline failures or incomplete results' — is contradicted by the aggregation code. Every finding that reaches validation passes through synthesize.normalize_finding first: agent findings via load_findings (skill/scripts/synthesize.py:130, called from main at line 936) and tool findings via line 940. normalize_finding lines 51-56 read `conf = str(f.get('confidence','')).upper()` and, when it is not in CONFIDENCES, assign `f['confidence'] = VERDICT_TO_CONFIDENCE.get(verdict, 'POSSIBLE')` — so confidence is always populated before validate_report runs at line 978. This defaulting is deliberate and tested: tests/test_synthesize.py:34-36 (`test_unlabeled_defaults_possible`) and line 77 assert POSSIBLE for a finding loaded with no confidence. Further, validation is advisory by design — attach_schema_status (synthesize.py:708-713) only records a count and the docstring states 'a run never aborts'. So the claimed failure path cannot execute. Residual true observation worth refiling at LOW as a docs/epistemics gap, not HIGH: because no reviewer spec asks for confidence, lens_sweep findings are silently stamped POSSIBLE by the pipeline, which sits awkwardly against the invariant documented at synthesize.py:340-341 ('confidence is left untouched — it is the reviewer's self-assessment, never the pipeline's'). Panel_review models sometimes emit it voluntarily (findings-._5-code-panel_review.json line 18 has LIKELY), making the axis model-dependent rather than broken.

discarded_claims.title: Missing coordination mechanism between lens_sweep and panel_review agents
discarded_claims.description: panel-review.md line 16 states: 'Cover all lenses assigned to this panel that are NOT being handled by dedicated lens sweep agents.' However, no interface, protocol, or mechanism is documented for panel_review to determine which lenses are already handled by lens_sweep, creating potential for duplicate findings or missed coverage.
discarded_claims.impact: Lens coverage is unpredictable—either duplicate findings from both agents or gaps where both assume the other handles a lens. Report aggregation becomes ambiguous about finding source and completeness.
discarded_claims.remediation: Define a coordination interface: (1) document how panel_review queries which lenses have spawn:true from scout output, (2) specify exclusion logic (e.g., skip lenses listed in scope profile with spawn:true), (3) provide explicit deduplication rules in report aggregation phase.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The coordination mechanism the claim says is missing exists and is deterministic — it is computed by the orchestrator, not left to the agent to discover. skill/scripts/dispatch.py build_plan lines 249-277: for each panel it calls depth_planner.plan_lenses(scope_profile, panel_name) to get the spawned set, computes `non_spawned = [lens['name'] for lens in panel_lenses if lens['name'] not in spawned_set]` (line 253), stores it on the plan entry as `lenses` (line 267), and renders it into the panel-review prompt at line 274 as `'\n'.join('- %s' % n for n in non_spawned)`. That rendered list lands at skill/agents/panel-review.md line 21 (`{lenses}`) under the heading '## Lenses assigned to this panel' — i.e. the panel reviewer is handed exactly the non-spawned lens list, so it never has to 'determine which lenses are already handled'. depth_planner.plan_lenses (skill/scripts/depth_planner.py:12-36) implements the spawn:true + depth_threshold + priority + cap selection the claim's remediation item (1) asks for. The exclusion is verified by tests/test_dispatch.py:68-88 (test_panel_review_includes_non_spawned_lenses: three security lenses, two spawn, and the panel entry gets exactly ['novel']) and by the committed golden tests/goldens/panel-review.rendered.txt lines 11-14, which shows the security panel prompt listing only known_vulns and novel. Remediation item (3), deduplication at aggregation, also already exists: synthesize.dedupe (skill/scripts/synthesize.py:229-317) plus the cross-panel corroboration pass at lines 334-402. One narrower, genuinely real defect sits nearby but is NOT what this claim asserts: dispatch.py line 274 falls back to the string '- (all lenses)' whenever non_spawned is empty, which conflates 'the profile listed no lenses' with 'every lens was spawned as a sweep'. That second case is observable in the prior run — .panopticon.prev-20260803/dispatch-plan-._1.json dispatched both an architecture panel_review and an architecture lens_sweep for the same single lens, and .panopticon.prev-20260803/prompts/02-._1-architecture.md line 13 shows the panel reviewer was told '- (all lenses)'. That is a one-line fallback bug (already noted in docs/superpowers/2026-08-04-self-scan-report.json around line 232), not the absence of a coordination interface.

discarded_claims.title: Report schema requires confidence/evidence but no fan-out prompt emits them
discarded_claims.description: `report-schema.json` line 71 marks `confidence` and `evidence` as required properties of every finding object (`evidence.status` is itself required, line 106-118). Neither `skill/agents/lens-sweep.md` (Finding format, lines 26-36) nor `skill/agents/panel-review.md` (Finding format, lines 31-40) instructs the generating agent to produce a `confidence` or `evidence` field — both only ask for `provenance` and `citations`. `advisor.md` does emit a `confidence` value (line 33) but that is on its separate verdict object, not on the finding itself.
discarded_claims.impact: The raw JSON that lens-sweep/panel-review agents are told to produce is, by their own specification, incomplete relative to what report-schema.json requires. Unless an out-of-scope synthesis stage derives `confidence`/`evidence` from `provenance`/advisor verdicts (not documented anywhere in this file set), the final report either fails schema validation or ships with unspecified defaults for these fields.
discarded_claims.remediation: Either document (in this reference set) how confidence/evidence are synthesized from provenance/citations downstream, or add explicit instructions to lens-sweep.md and panel-review.md for how the agent should populate confidence and an initial evidence.status.
references: skill/scripts/synthesize.py:640 (build_report assigns evidence to every finding)

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The claim's surface observation is accurate — report-schema.json:71 does require `confidence` and `evidence` on every finding, and neither lens-sweep.md (Finding format, lines 26-36) nor panel-review.md (lines 31-40) instructs the agent to emit them. But the claim's stated impact is falsified by the pipeline. The schema describes the SYNTHESIZED CodeReviewReport, not the raw agent fan-out payload, and skill/scripts/synthesize.py deterministically populates both required fields for every finding: normalize_finding() lines 51-56 sets `f['confidence']` from an explicit value, else a verdict mapping, else the default 'POSSIBLE' (so it is never absent and never unspecified); build_report() line 640 sets `f['evidence'] = evidence_mod.derive_evidence(f, matched.get(id(f)))` for every finding in the list, and derive_evidence() (skill/scripts/evidence.py:34-71) always returns a dict containing a `status` key — every branch (tool_confirmed, reinforced, advisor verdict, corroborated, and the terminal fallback at line 70) returns a status, so evidence.status is total. synthesize.validate_report() lines 731-737 additionally hard-errors on a bad confidence or a bad evidence.status, so a report missing them cannot pass. tests/test_schema.py:117 ('test_actual_build_report_output_validates_against_schema') runs real build_report output through jsonschema.validate against this exact schema file, empirically settling that the produced report does validate. The omission from the fan-out prompts is also deliberate rather than an oversight: evidence.py's derive_evidence docstring states 'Self-asserted provenance.confirmation_status is deliberately ignored — a reviewer cannot confirm its own finding', and synthesize.py:88-93 (AGENT_FORBIDDEN_FIELDS) strips agent-supplied trust fields for the same reason — letting a reviewer self-declare its own evidence status would defeat the verification axis. Finally the claim's remediation ('document how confidence/evidence are synthesized') is already satisfied outside the reviewer's narrow file slice: skill/SKILL.md lines 115-128 document the two-axis severity x evidence.status model and enumerate every evidence status. No schema-validation failure and no unspecified defaults occur on any path I could trace.
