discarded_claims.title: Incomplete CWE to OWASP category mapping in reference catalog
discarded_claims.description: The cwe_owasp object is missing mappings for 10 CWE entries that are defined in the cwe object: CWE-125, CWE-787, CWE-476, CWE-416, CWE-190, CWE-362, CWE-400, CWE-732, CWE-276, and CWE-1333. These entries have definitions but no OWASP Top 10 category assignment.
discarded_claims.impact: Reference lookups for unmapped CWE codes will fail or return incomplete data. Tools or processes relying on complete cwe_owasp mappings will have gaps for these 10 CWE codes.
discarded_claims.remediation: Add OWASP Top 10 category mappings for all 10 missing CWE entries in the cwe_owasp object to achieve completeness and consistency with the cwe catalog.
references: skill/reference/cwe-catalog.json:3-36 (34 cwe keys; claim cites 27-36 only)

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The claim's central enumeration is factually wrong and its stated impact is contradicted by the consuming code. I read the whole catalog. The `cwe` object (lines 3-36) holds 34 keys; the `cwe_owasp` object (lines 39-64) holds 26. The set difference is EIGHT ids, not ten: CWE-125, CWE-787, CWE-476, CWE-416, CWE-190, CWE-362, CWE-400, CWE-1333. The claim names CWE-732 and CWE-276 as unmapped, but both are explicitly mapped in the file: line 63 `"CWE-732": "A01:2021-Broken Access Control"` and line 64 `"CWE-276": "A05:2021-Security Misconfiguration"`. The error looks like an artifact of reading only the cited window `27-36` (which is exactly the 10 `cwe` entries from CWE-125 to CWE-1333) and never checking the tail of `cwe_owasp`. Acting on the remediation as written ('Add ... mappings for all 10 missing CWE entries') would produce duplicate keys for CWE-732 and CWE-276. The impact statement is also unsupported: the only consumer of this map is `derive_owasp()` in skill/scripts/citations.py:83-93, which does `catalog["cwe_owasp"].get(cid)` and skips a miss — nothing 'fails', and `load_cwe_catalog()` (citations.py:37-52) even degrades an entirely absent catalog to empty dicts by design, with a regression test locking that behavior in (tests/test_citations.py:18-29). A narrower, true statement does exist (8 memory-safety/resource CWEs carry no OWASP Top 10 2021 mapping, arguably because the 2021 list has no analog for them), but that is not the claim filed here, and the claim as written cannot be handed to a fixer.

discarded_claims.title: Invalid enum value in confirmation_status schema field
discarded_claims.description: The confirmation_status enum at line 130 includes value 'TOOL' which is not produced by any agent. lens-sweep.md and panel-review.md specify only 'UNVERIFIED', while advisor.md produces 'CONFIRMED', 'REJECTED', or 'NEEDS_MORE_INFO'. The enum should be: ["UNVERIFIED", "CONFIRMED", "REJECTED", "NEEDS_MORE_INFO"], not include 'TOOL'.
discarded_claims.impact: Enum validation allows invalid values that contradict the actual agent implementations, creating confusion about valid confirmation status values.
discarded_claims.remediation: Update the confirmation_status enum at line 130 to remove 'TOOL' and use only: ["UNVERIFIED", "CONFIRMED", "REJECTED", "NEEDS_MORE_INFO"].

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The claim asserts that 'TOOL' in the confirmation_status enum (report-schema.json:130) 'is not produced by any agent' and should be removed. This is contradicted directly by the repository. skill/scripts/provenance.py:5-14 defines tool_provenance(), which returns exactly `"confirmation_status": "TOOL"` at line 12. That function is not dead code — it is the provenance constructor for every static-analysis adapter finding. skill/scripts/tools/base.py:10 imports tool_provenance and base.py:18-21 wraps it as attach_tool_provenance(), which sets finding['provenance'] = tool_provenance(...). attach_tool_provenance is called by every Phase 1 adapter: eslint_security.py:85, pip_audit.py:79, bundler_audit.py:61, dependency_check.py:100, brakeman.py:92, roslyn_secguard.py:139, cargo_audit.py:101, osv_scanner.py:104, spotbugs.py:75, npm_audit.py:51 and :86. The legacy SARIF path reaches it independently via skill/scripts/tools/sarif_utils.py:12 and :110, which calls tool_provenance(tool_name, reasoning=res.get('ruleId')) directly. The value is also pinned by tests: tests/test_provenance.py:14 asserts p['confirmation_status'] == 'TOOL', and tests/tools/test_base.py:32 and tests/tools/test_legacy_sarif.py:39 cover the same attachment. The claim's error is one of scope: it enumerated only the three agent markdown prompts (lens-sweep.md, panel-review.md, advisor.md) and concluded no producer exists, missing the entire tool-sourced ingestion path. 'TOOL' is the correct and necessary fifth enum member — removing it as the remediation instructs would break schema validation for every adapter-emitted finding.

discarded_claims.description: File is named with `.example.yml` suffix but the header comment states 'Lives in the TARGET repo under .panopticon/' and describes it as the actual groups.yml file. This creates ambiguity about whether this is a template/example or an actual output artifact.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The quoted text is accurate but does not support the claimed ambiguity or impact. `skill/reference/code-review-groups.example.yml:1-2` reads '# .panopticon/groups.yml — learned by `panopticon -e`, hand-editable.' / '# Lives in the TARGET repo under .panopticon/ (gitignored by default).' That second line is precisely the disambiguator: it tells the reader the real artifact lives in the TARGET repo, i.e. NOT at this path, which is inside panopticon's own `skill/reference/` asset directory (siblings: cwe-catalog.json, report-schema.json, scope-profile-schema.json, security-checklists.md, model-profiles.yml — all reference material). Combined with the `.example.yml` suffix, the file does not present itself as a runtime artifact; the header names the format and destination it exemplifies. The claimed impact has no mechanism: I grepped the repo for `code-review-groups` / `groups.example` — nothing reads, copies, or installs this file. `orchestrator.load_catalog` (`skill/scripts/orchestrator.py:281-305`) reads only `os.path.join(repo, '.panopticon', 'groups.yml')` in the target repo, so this example can never be picked up as live config, and there is no copy step a user could get wrong. Repo docs treat it consistently as a reference asset (`DEVELOPMENT.md:41`, `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-25-panopticon-kimi-port-design.md:177` lists it in the reference/ tree). At most this is a cosmetic wording preference (adding the word 'example' to line 1); it is not misleading documentation and produces no configuration risk.

discarded_claims.title: Global mutable singleton state without thread safety
discarded_claims.description: The module uses a module-level global `_PROFILES` variable (line 35) with a singleton pattern via `_profiles()` (lines 38-42). This introduces implicit global state that is not thread-safe and makes concurrent invocations problematic.
discarded_claims.impact: Concurrent calls to resolve_model() may experience race conditions when the global _PROFILES is being modified. Unit testing becomes difficult due to shared state between tests.
discarded_claims.remediation: Refactor to eliminate module-level mutable state. Consider dependency injection of profiles or lazy initialization within a thread-safe context manager.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The code description is accurate but the alleged defect and its impact are contradicted by the repository. (1) Lines 35-42 do contain `_PROFILES = None` plus a lazy `_profiles()` memoizer using `global`. That much is real. (2) The claimed race path cannot execute: there is no concurrency anywhere in this codebase. A repo-wide grep of all *.py for `import threading`, `from threading`, `ThreadPool`, `concurrent.futures`, `multiprocessing`, `asyncio`, `Thread(` returned zero matches, and there is no web/async framework (the only flask/django/fastapi hits are literal strings in test fixture data at tests/test_schemas.py:187-193 and tests/test_synthesize.py:224). Every script is a one-shot CLI entry point (`if __name__ == "__main__"` + argparse in dispatch.py:441, orchestrator.py:572, synthesize.py:997, run_tools.py:184, model_resolver.py:133). pyproject.toml declares no [project.scripts], no build-system, and no library export -- it is a skill package, not a hosted service. The only production caller is dispatch.py:261 and dispatch.py:286, inside a synchronous `for panel_name in ...` loop in build_plan(). Cross-process invocation via subprocess (run_tools.py, orchestrator.py, run_fixture_tests.py) gives each process its own interpreter and its own `_PROFILES`, so no sharing occurs. (3) The specific impact wording -- 'race conditions when the global _PROFILES is being modified' -- describes a state that does not exist. `_PROFILES` has exactly two assignment sites in the entire codebase (model_resolver.py:35 initial None, model_resolver.py:41 one-time init); it is never modified after initialization. Even if threads were introduced, this is the textbook benign lazy-init race: `_load_profiles()` is a pure, side-effect-free YAML read, so a duplicated call yields an equivalent dict, name binding is atomic, and last-write-wins produces a correct result. It is the same risk profile as functools.cache. There is no torn state, no partial construction, and no invariant to violate. (4) The testability half of the impact is empirically false: tests/test_model_resolver.py:79 and :83 patch the singleton cleanly with `with patch.object(mr, "_PROFILES", {})`, which auto-restores; the suite exercises both the populated and empty-profile paths without order dependence. Testing is demonstrably not difficult. A HIGH-severity architecture finding is not supportable here. Incidental observation, outside this claim's scope and not a basis for the verdict: model_resolver.py:121 (`return cfg`) and role_config() return the cached sub-dict by reference rather than a copy, so a caller that mutated a returned config would poison the process-wide cache. No current caller mutates it -- dispatch.py only embeds the dict into the plan and json.dumps it -- so this is a latent aliasing/encapsulation nit, not a thread-safety issue, and it is not what ARCH-001 alleges. discarded_claims.title: Tight coupling between synthesize and domain modules
discarded_claims.description: synthesize.py imports four domain modules (citations, evidence_mod, html_report, ingest_tools) as hard dependencies (lines 14-18). These modules are directly used throughout main(), creating tight coupling that inhibits independent evolution of subsystems.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The literal observation is true — synthesize.py lines 14-18 import scripts.citations (plus load_cwe_catalog), scripts.evidence as evidence_mod, scripts.html_report, and scripts.ingest_tools, and all four are used (ingest_tools.ingest_dir at line 938, citations.load_cwe_catalog/enrich_citations at 941-942 and 618/638, html_report.write_html at 903 and 990, evidence_mod throughout build_report at 619-648). The direction is entry-point -> leaf modules, i.e. correct layering, not mutual/tight coupling. discarded_claims.title: sys.path manipulation undermines module installability
discarded_claims.description: Multiple scripts manipulate sys.path to enable local imports (line 10 in _run_adapter.py, line 13 in synthesize.py, line 11 in run_tools.py, line 9 in dispatch.py). This pattern prevents the code from being cleanly installed as a package and relies on execution context.
discarded_claims.impact: The codebase cannot be installed via standard Python packaging tools. Brittle when run from different directories. Makes containerization and deployment more complex. IDE tooling struggles with import resolution.
discarded_claims.remediation: Convert the project to a proper Python package with pyproject.toml. Use relative imports or add the package to PYTHONPATH during installation. Remove all sys.path.insert() calls.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The raw code observation is accurate — `sys.path.insert` appears at exactly the cited lines (_run_adapter.py:10, dispatch.py:9, run_tools.py:11, synthesize.py:13, plus two more the claim missed: skill/scripts/tools/base.py:9 and skill/scripts/tools/sarif_utils.py:11). But every stated impact is contradicted by the repository. (1) 'Brittle when run from different directories / relies on execution context' is backwards: all six inserts are anchored on `os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))`, which is the standard CWD-independent form. There is no dependence on cwd or on how the interpreter was invoked. (2) 'Makes containerization and deployment more complex' is contradicted by /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/Dockerfile lines 53-54, which do `COPY skill/scripts /opt/panopticon/scripts` and `ENV PYTHONPATH=/opt/panopticon`; containerization already works, and inside the image the inserts are harmless no-ops that re-add an already-resolvable path. (3) 'sys.path manipulation prevents the code from being cleanly installed as a package' is a false causal attribution. An installed package would still execute these lines successfully (they would append the package's own parent directory, e.g. under site-packages) — they block nothing. What actually makes the repo non-pip-installable is unrelated: pyproject.toml has a [project] table but no [build-system] section and no packages/discovery configuration. The claim never mentions that, and removing the sys.path calls would not fix it. (4) The inserts are load-bearing given the project's documented design, not incidental: skill/scripts has no __init__.py (PEP 420 namespace package) and skill/scripts/tools/__init__.py uses absolute imports (`from scripts.tools.pip_audit import PipAuditAdapter`), so `skill/` must be on sys.path for `from scripts.tools import ADAPTERS` to resolve when a script under skill/scripts is executed directly — which is exactly the documented invocation model (README.md lines 30, 50, 107: `python3 skill/scripts/dispatch.py`, `python skill/scripts/run_tools.py`). README.md lines 19-51 and 76 and DEVELOPMENT.md line 21 state the distribution model explicitly: `skill/` is symlinked into an agent's skills directory, and design docs repeatedly constrain the code to stdlib-only with zero new Python dependencies. 'Install as a pip package' is therefore a non-goal the claim assumes without evidence. The only defensible residue is stylistic duplication of a six-line path shim, which does not support a MEDIUM architecture defect.

discarded_claims.title: Fragile sys.path manipulation at module import time
discarded_claims.description: sys.path manipulation occurs at module level before subsequent imports (_run_adapter.py line 10, dispatch.py line 9, run_tools.py line 11, synthesize.py line 13). This pattern is duplicated across 4 files and relies on sys.path.insert succeeding silently. If insertion fails or sys is unavailable, the subsequent 'from scripts.tools import ADAPTERS' statements will fail with confusing ImportError messages.
discarded_claims.impact: Fragile import mechanism could mask real errors and make debugging difficult. Duplicate code creates maintenance burden. Not idempotent if modules are re-imported.
discarded_claims.remediation: Centralize sys.path manipulation in a single module initialization function or use proper package structure with __init__.py files. Alternatively, configure PYTHONPATH at the execution level rather than module level.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The locations are real (sys.path.insert at _run_adapter.py:10, dispatch.py:9, run_tools.py:11, synthesize.py:13, and also tools/base.py:9 and tools/sarif_utils.py:11), but the fragility mechanism the claim rests on cannot occur. (1) 'relies on sys.path.insert succeeding silently. If insertion fails or sys is unavailable...' — `sys.path` is a plain list and `list.insert` has no failure mode short of MemoryError; `sys` is a built-in module compiled into the interpreter, so `import sys` cannot fail while Python is running. The described path to a 'confusing ImportError' does not exist. (2) 'Not idempotent if modules are re-imported' — module bodies do not re-execute on re-import (sys.modules caching), and even a duplicated sys.path entry is semantically inert. (3) 'could mask real errors' — no supporting code; the inserts add a fixed, __file__-derived directory and swallow nothing. (4) The pattern is load-bearing rather than gratuitous: skill/scripts has no __init__.py (PEP 420 namespace package) and skill/scripts/tools/__init__.py imports absolutely (`from scripts.tools.pip_audit import PipAuditAdapter`), so `skill/` must be on sys.path for `from scripts.tools import ADAPTERS` (_run_adapter.py:12, run_tools.py:12-13) to resolve under the documented direct-script invocation (README.md lines 30, 50, 107). Removing the shim without restructuring would break execution. (5) The CWE-427 citation does not apply: the inserted element is derived from `os.path.abspath(__file__)`, not from cwd, PYTHONPATH, or any untrusted input, and it is inserted at index 0 so it takes precedence rather than being shadowed. In the container, cwd (/src, the untrusted mounted target) is not on sys.path for direct script execution, so there is no search-path hijack surface. The one accurate residue is that a 4-6 line path shim is copy-pasted across six source files (and ~36 test files) — a minor duplication nit, not a MEDIUM structural defect, and the claim's own asserted failure modes for it are not real.

discarded_claims.title: Template management scattered across multiple functions
discarded_claims.description: Agent template management is dispersed: load_template() (lines 70-76), emit_host_agents() (lines 103-141), render_prompt() (lines 151-176). No TemplateManager abstraction exists. Templates are treated as file I/O operations rather than as managed resources.
discarded_claims.impact: Template paths are hard-coded in multiple places. Difficult to change template storage mechanism. Testing template logic requires file system access. No caching or memoization of parsed templates.
discarded_claims.remediation: Introduce a TemplateManager class that encapsulates template loading, parsing, rendering, and caching. Make it injectable into dispatch functions.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The claim's descriptive surface is true (load_template at 70-76, emit_host_agents at 103-141, render_prompt at 151-176; there is no TemplateManager class), but every load-bearing harm it asserts is contradicted by the code. (1) 'Template paths are hard-coded in multiple places' is false: grep for TEMPLATE_DIR across the repo returns exactly one definition (dispatch.py:14) and exactly one consumer (load_template, lines 72 and 74); the only other occurrences are tests. Both emit_host_agents (line 117) and render_prompt (line 162) reach templates solely through load_template. (2) 'Difficult to change template storage mechanism' is false for the same reason — load_template is a single I/O chokepoint; swapping file I/O for package resources is a one-function change. (3) 'Testing template logic requires file system access' is false: parse_template_frontmatter takes text, not a path, and tests/test_agent_templates.py:42 calls it with a bare string; tests/test_dispatch.py:151 redirects storage with mock.patch.object(dispatch, 'TEMPLATE_DIR', ...). The module already implements the separation the remediation asks for, just functionally rather than as a class: pure parser (21-67) -> single loader (70-76) -> consumers (emit/render). The only sub-assertion that holds is 'no caching or memoization' — build_plan does re-read panel-review.md/lens-sweep.md once per plan entry (lines 269, 293) — but that is a handful of small reads in a short-lived CLI process, not an architectural defect. One real (unclaimed) nit I did find: the role->file-stem mapping is duplicated between ROLE_FILES (line 81) and AGENT_NAME (line 193), and build_plan renders via AGENT_NAME[...] + '.md' rather than ROLE_FILES; that is the actual small duplication here, and it is not what the claim describes. Rejecting because the claim is a style preference (class over module) whose stated justifications the code contradicts.

discarded_claims.title: Tuple size mismatch breaks deduplication logic in model collection
discarded_claims.description: The function collects unique (model, role) pairs into a set using 2-tuples as keys (line 188: key = (model, role)). However, when processing advisor confirmations, a 3-tuple is added (line 198: advisor_key = (confirmed_by_model, None, "advisor")). Since Python tuples of different lengths are never equal, the 3-tuple will never match existing 2-tuples in the set, breaking the deduplication logic entirely.
discarded_claims.impact: Duplicate advisor entries with the same model may be added to the output list, causing incorrect model/role reporting in CodeReviewReport metadata.
discarded_claims.remediation: Change line 198 to use a 2-tuple consistent with the deduplication scheme: advisor_key = (confirmed_by_model, "advisor").
references: skill/scripts/synthesize.py:189-190 (the `continue` that makes the advisor block unreachable for repeat agent keys)

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The literal observation is right (line 188 builds a 2-tuple `key = (model, role)`; line 198 builds a 3-tuple `advisor_key = (confirmed_by_model, None, "advisor")`, a leftover from the model/version/role scheme still described in the docstring at line 170), but the asserted consequence does not hold and the asserted impact is not reachable. The `seen` set holds two disjoint key namespaces: 2-tuples are only ever produced by the agent branch and 3-tuples only ever by the advisor branch, so they cannot collide and there is nothing for the shapes to shadow. Crucially, advisor dedup still works: every advisor key has the identical shape `(model, None, 'advisor')`, so a second finding carrying the same provenance.confirmed_by_model hits `if advisor_key not in seen` and is correctly skipped. Deduplication is therefore not 'broken entirely'. For the claimed duplicate to appear in `out`, an agent-authored finding would have to carry provenance.discovered_by == 'agent:advisor' (so _role_from_discovered_by returns 'advisor' at synthesize.py:159-166) with the same model string as a verdict's model — and no such path exists: advisors never author findings files, they author verdict files, and evidence.apply_verdict (skill/scripts/evidence.py:224-243) writes only prov['confirmed_by'] = 'agent:advisor' and prov['confirmed_by_model'], never discovered_by. The only producers of discovered_by are provenance.tool_provenance ('tool:<name>', model=None, skipped at line 183) and provenance.agent_provenance, driven by the panel_review and lens_sweep templates (skill/agents/panel-review.md:46, skill/agents/lens-sweep.md:42); there is no advisor findings template. Separately, while verifying this I found a real but DIFFERENT defect in the same block that the claim does not describe and whose direction is the opposite of the claimed impact: the advisor block at lines 196-201 sits after the `if key in seen: continue` guard at 189-190, so when a second finding repeats an already-seen (model, role) agent pair its confirmed_by_model is never collected and the advisor is silently OMITTED from meta.models_used (under-reporting, not duplication). Rejecting the claim as filed; the suggested 2-tuple edit is harmless tidying but fixes nothing observable, whereas hoisting the confirmed_by_model handling above the `continue` would fix a genuine omission.

discarded_claims.title: Inconsistent sys.path manipulation depth in dispatch.py
discarded_claims.description: dispatch.py adds only the current directory to sys.path (one os.path.dirname call), while all peer files (_run_adapter.py, run_tools.py, synthesize.py) add the parent directory (two os.path.dirname calls). This inconsistency could cause fragility if dispatch.py is later refactored to depend on scripts.* imports.
discarded_claims.impact: Inconsistent module import patterns can lead to import failures or confusion when the code structure changes or is maintained by others.
discarded_claims.remediation: Align sys.path manipulation in dispatch.py line 9 to use os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(...)) consistently with peer modules, or document why the different depth is intentional.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The surface observation is literally true but the claimed defect is contradicted by the code, and the proposed remediation would break a currently-exercised import path. Verified line contents: /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/dispatch.py:9 `sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))` (one dirname -> skill/scripts) versus run_tools.py:11, synthesize.py:13 and _run_adapter.py:10, which all use two dirnames (-> skill/). The depths differ because the import styles differ, and each is exactly correct for its own file: dispatch.py:10-11 imports bare sibling modules (`import depth_planner`, `import model_resolver`), which requires skill/scripts on sys.path; the peers import package-qualified names (run_tools.py:12-13 `from scripts.tools import ADAPTERS`, synthesize.py:14-18 `import scripts.citations` etc., _run_adapter.py:12 `from scripts.tools import ADAPTERS`), which requires skill/ on sys.path. Neither depth would satisfy the other file's imports, so there is no latent import failure to trigger. Concretely, the claim's remediation ('Align sys.path manipulation in dispatch.py line 9 to use os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(...))') would regress a real path: /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/tests/test_synthesize.py:1086 does `import scripts.dispatch as dispatch` (skill/ on path via test_synthesize.py:9, namespace packages — there is no __init__.py under skill/ or skill/scripts/, only skill/scripts/tools/__init__.py). Under that import, sys.path[0] is the tests directory, not skill/scripts, so dispatch.py:9 is the load-bearing entry that makes `import depth_planner` resolve; changing it to skill/ would raise ModuleNotFoundError for depth_planner in that test. The genuine (and much smaller) inconsistency in the repo is the bare-vs-package import convention, not the path depth, and fixing that means changing the imports, not the dirname count. The attached CWE-99 (Improper Control of Resource Identifiers) is inapplicable — no untrusted input reaches sys.path here; the inserted value is derived solely from __file__. Rejected as a MEDIUM structural defect; at most it is an INFO-level convention note.

discarded_claims.title: Untested error handling in _run_adapter.main()
discarded_claims.description: _run_adapter.py has no unit tests. The main() function (lines 15-34) contains three critical exception handlers (KeyError on line 20, generic Exception on lines 25 and 31) that catch adapter failures. These error paths are exercised only if an adapter fails at runtime, with no test coverage for the recovery behavior.
discarded_claims.impact: Adapter failures during tool invocation may not degrade gracefully as intended, potentially causing unhandled exceptions or incorrect exit codes in production.
discarded_claims.remediation: Add unit tests for _run_adapter.py covering: (1) missing adapter KeyError handling, (2) adapter.invoke() exception handling, (3) stdout.buffer.write() exception handling, (4) success/failure exit codes.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The claim's central premise — '_run_adapter.py has no unit tests' — is false. Unit tests for `main()` exist in /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/tests/test_run_tools.py, which does `import scripts._run_adapter as ra` (line 5) and defines class `TestRunAdapterHelper` (lines 172-209) with three tests that call `ra.main(...)` directly: (1) `test_main_runs_named_adapter_and_returns_rc` (lines 173-192) registers a fake adapter into `ra.ADAPTERS`, swaps `sys.stdout` for a fake with a BytesIO `buffer`, and asserts both the return code and that the adapter's raw bytes were written — this covers the success path, the exit code, and the `sys.stdout.buffer.write` call on line 30; (2) `test_main_skips_unregistered_adapter` (lines 194-196) calls `ra.main([..., 'not-a-real-adapter', ...])` and asserts rc == 0 — this is precisely the KeyError handler on lines 20-22; (3) `test_main_skips_adapter_that_crashes` (lines 198-209) registers an adapter whose `invoke()` raises RuntimeError and asserts rc == 0 — this is precisely the generic Exception handler on lines 25-28. Two of the three cited handlers and the exit-code behavior are therefore directly covered. The scanner appears to have looked only for a file named tests/test_run_adapter.py; the tests live alongside the run_tools tests. Residual truth worth noting but not sufficient to sustain a HIGH coverage finding: the third handler (the `sys.stdout.buffer.write` failure branch, lines 29-33) has no test, and no test exercises a non-zero `rc` pass-through from a successful adapter. That is a narrow, LOW/INFO-grade gap, not 'no unit tests' or 'no test coverage for the recovery behavior'.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The claim's factual premise — 'test_dispatch.py does not include tests verifying that placeholder values containing {...} literal syntax pass through correctly and don't interfere with sentinel replacement' — is directly contradicted by the file. tests/test_dispatch.py:229-233 is `test_brace_safety_value_containing_placeholder_syntax`, which sets `mapping['file_list'] = 'weird-{depth}-name.py'` (a value containing another live placeholder token, the hardest case for the two-step sentinel scheme) and asserts `self.assertIn('weird-{depth}-name.py', p)` — i.e. it verifies the value survives literally and is not re-substituted. A second test covers the same property on the advisor path: tests/test_dispatch.py:294-305 renders a verify-queue entry whose finding description is 'raw query with {code_context} text' and asserts `self.assertIn('{code_context}', text)` with the comment 'brace-safe: survives', confirming brace syntax inside a JSON-serialized value passes through render_prompt intact. The complementary direction is also covered at lines 217-219, which asserts no known mapping token survives unresolved in the rendered output. The claim's hypothetical failure mode is additionally not reachable as described: PLACEHOLDER_RE (dispatch.py:79) is `\{([a-z_]+)\}`, so a value like {'model':'x'} contains no matchable token, and detection runs against `body` only (dispatch.py:163), never against substituted values. discarded_claims.title: LegacySarifAdapter violates ToolAdapter protocol structure
discarded_claims.description: LegacySarifAdapter uses __init__(name) parameter and @property prefix instead of class attributes. ToolAdapter protocol (base.py:51-62) requires name and prefix as class attributes, not instance or property attributes.
discarded_claims.impact: Inconsistent adapter structure breaks protocol contract, complicating adapter registration and instantiation patterns in __init__.py.
discarded_claims.remediation: Convert to class attribute pattern: `name = 'legacy-sarif'` and `prefix = 'TL'` at class level, eliminating __init__ and @property.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The code facts are as described (legacy_sarif.py:31-32 sets `self.name` in `__init__`; lines 34-36 define `prefix` as a read-only @property), but the claim's central assertion is wrong on Python semantics and its impact/remediation are contradicted by the code. (1) `ToolAdapter` at base.py:51-62 is a `typing.Protocol` with bare annotations `name: str` / `prefix: str`. Under PEP 544 structural typing, protocol variable members are satisfied by instance attributes assigned in `__init__` — they do NOT require class attributes. So `self.name = name` is fully conformant; the claim's premise ('requires ... class attributes, not instance ... attributes') is false. (2) The only defensible kernel is the narrow mypy rule that a read-only property does not satisfy a settable protocol variable — but that is unenforceable here: I grepped the whole repo and `ToolAdapter` appears exactly once, at its definition (base.py:51). It is used as no annotation anywhere, is not @runtime_checkable, and there is no isinstance check. pyproject.toml configures only ruff (select E,F,W) and .github/workflows/ci.yml runs only `ruff check` plus pytest — no mypy/pyright anywhere. There is therefore no static or runtime path on which this 'violation' can produce an error. (3) The claimed impact ('complicating adapter registration and instantiation patterns in __init__.py') is inverted: __init__.py:19-24 deliberately instantiates the one class six times, `LegacySarifAdapter('semgrep')`, `('bandit')`, `('trivy')`, `('gitleaks')`, `('gosec')`, `('eslint')`. The parameterized constructor IS the registration mechanism. (4) The proposed remediation would break the code outright: `invoke()` dispatches on `TOOL_CMD[self.name]` (line 43-45) and `parse()`/`prefix` resolve `su.PREFIX.get(self.name, 'TL')` against sarif_utils.py:16-17 (`{'semgrep': 'SG', 'trivy': 'TR', ...}`). Hardcoding `name = 'legacy-sarif'` / `prefix = 'TL'` would make every invocation raise NotImplementedError, make every finding id use the wrong prefix, and make the positional-arg calls in __init__.py raise TypeError; tests/tools/test_legacy_sarif.py:28,50,65,76,82,88 assert exactly the constructor-arg and derived-prefix behavior the remediation removes. A structure claim whose mechanism is factually wrong and whose fix breaks working, tested behavior does not stand.

So `self.name = name` is fully conformant; the claim's premise ('requires ... class attributes, not instance ... attributes') is false. (2) The only defensible kernel is the narrow mypy rule that a read-only property does not satisfy a settable protocol variable — but that is unenforceable here: I grepped the whole repo and `ToolAdapter` appears exactly once, at its definition (base.py:51). It is used as no annotation anywhere, is not @runtime_checkable, and there is no isinstance check. pyproject.toml configures only ruff (select E,F,W) and .github/workflows/ci.yml runs only `ruff check` plus pytest — no mypy/pyright anywhere. There is therefore no static or runtime path on which this 'violation' can produce an error. (3) The claimed impact ('complicating adapter registration and instantiation patterns in __init__.py') is inverted: __init__.py:19-24 deliberately instantiates the one class six times, `LegacySarifAdapter('semgrep')`, `('bandit')`, `('trivy')`, `('gitleaks')`, `('gosec')`, `('eslint')`. The parameterized constructor IS the registration mechanism. (4) The proposed remediation would break the code outright: `invoke()` dispatches on `TOOL_CMD[self.name]` (line 43-45) and `parse()`/`prefix` resolve `su.PREFIX.get(self.name, 'TL')` against sarif_utils.py:16-17 (`{'semgrep': 'SG', 'trivy': 'TR', ...}`). Hardcoding `name = 'legacy-sarif'` / `prefix = 'TL'` would make every invocation raise NotImplementedError, make every finding id use the wrong prefix, and make the positional-arg calls in __init__.py raise TypeError; tests/tools/test_legacy_sarif.py:28,50,65,76,82,88 assert exactly the constructor-arg and derived-prefix behavior the remediation removes. A structure claim whose mechanism is factually wrong and whose fix breaks working, tested behavior does not stand.

discarded_claims.title: Unsafe sys.path Manipulation
discarded_claims.description: sys.path.insert(0, ...) modifies the module search path at module import time. While the path is hardcoded relative to __file__, this pattern could allow arbitrary module loading if path sources were untrusted.
discarded_claims.impact: If the script location or parent directories were writable by untrusted users, arbitrary modules could be loaded. Current implementation uses hardcoded relative paths which mitigates this risk.
discarded_claims.remediation: Use relative imports or configure PYTHONPATH appropriately instead of modifying sys.path at runtime. Consider using importlib for more controlled imports.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The line exists as cited — base.py:9 is `sys.path.insert(0, os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), os.pardir, os.pardir))`, followed at line 10 by `from scripts.provenance import tool_provenance`. But the claim describes no executable attack path, and it concedes as much in its own impact text ('Current implementation uses hardcoded relative paths which mitigates this risk'). CWE-426 (Untrusted Search Path) requires a search-path element that an attacker can influence across a trust boundary; nothing here qualifies. (a) The inserted element is derived solely from `__file__`, never from argv, env, cwd, or scan-target input — I grepped the tools package and the scanned-target path is only ever passed to subprocesses via `run_tool(..., cwd=...)` (verified by tests/tools/test_base.py:84-89, `rec.assert_called_once_with(["t"], capture_output=True, timeout=7, cwd="/x", env={"A": "1"})`), which changes the child process's cwd, not the parent interpreter's sys.path. (b) pyproject.toml pins `requires-python = ">=3.11"`, where `__file__` is always absolute, so the unnormalized `os.pardir` segments cannot resolve relative to an attacker-influenced cwd — the one variant of this pattern that would be genuinely dangerous. (c) The resolved directory is the skill root `skill/`, which per a full glob of `skill/**/*.py` contains no top-level `.py` modules at all (only SKILL.md and the `scripts/` package), so inserting at index 0 shadows nothing in the stdlib. (d) Most decisively, any attacker with write access to that directory can simply edit base.py itself, so no privilege boundary is crossed by the sys.path insert. This is also the repo-wide convention, appearing in skill/scripts/run_tools.py:11, synthesize.py:13, _run_adapter.py:10, dispatch.py:9, and tools/sarif_utils.py:11. One genuine but unrelated nit I noticed while verifying: line 10's post-insert import would trip ruff E402 under the configured `select = ["E","F","W"]` (E402 is not in the ignore list), and base.py/sarif_utils.py omit the `os.path.abspath()` wrapper the four other call sites use — a consistency issue, not the security claim made here. Verdict is REJECTED as a vulnerability; confidence LIKELY rather than CERTAIN only because the deployed install layout of the skill directory is not determinable from the repo.

discarded_claims.title: Line exceeds maximum length with complex nested ternary operator
discarded_claims.description: Line 66 contains a nested ternary conditional expression that spans approximately 107 characters, exceeding PEP 8's 79-character guideline and the common 99-character compromise limit. The line is: `severity = "CRITICAL" if score >= 9 else "HIGH" if score >= 7 else "MEDIUM" if score >= 4 else "LOW"`
discarded_claims.impact: Long lines are harder to read and maintain, violating PEP 8 style guidelines.
discarded_claims.remediation: Refactor the nested ternary into a more readable structure, such as an if-elif-else block or a lookup mapping.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The line exists, but the rule it is measured against does not apply in this repository, and the measurement itself is wrong. /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/pyproject.toml lines 18-24 configure the project's only linter: `[tool.ruff] line-length = 100` with `[tool.ruff.lint] select = ["E", "F", "W"]` and `ignore = ["E401", "E501", "E701", "E702"]`. E501 is line-too-long — the project has explicitly and deliberately disabled line-length enforcement, and E701/E702 (multiple statements on one line) too. .github/workflows/ci.yml line 23 runs `python -m ruff check skill/scripts/ tests/` as the gating lint job, so line 66 produces no violation in the authoritative check. This is a settled convention, not an oversight: a `^.{101,}$` grep across skill/scripts finds 67 over-100-character lines in 19 files, including 8 in cargo_audit.py alone and 23 in html_report.py. The claim also appeals to 'the common 99-character compromise limit', which is not this project's limit (100), and PEP 8's 79 characters, which the project overrode. Separately, the character count is inaccurate: line 66 is 116 characters (it matches `^.{115,}$`), not the claimed ~107. The claim additionally cites only line 66 while line 70 is the byte-identical expression at deeper indentation (120 chars) — so even the located extent is incomplete. I do not dispute that the duplicated nested ternary at lines 66 and 70 is less readable than the alternative, and the repo itself demonstrates the cleaner form in skill/scripts/tools/osv_scanner.py lines 9-17 (`_cvss_bucket` as an if-chain, reused at line 73), so extracting a shared helper would be a legitimate refactor. But that is a duplication/readability nit, not the line-length violation this claim asserts; as filed against a config that ignores E501, the finding is invalid.

discarded_claims.title: String Concatenation in Command Argument Construction
discarded_claims.description: Command argument is constructed using string concatenation: "-p:ErrorLog=" + sarif + ",version=2.1". While sarif is derived from tempfile.mkdtemp() and is trusted, this pattern is vulnerable to injection attacks if the path source were ever compromised.
discarded_claims.impact: If sarif path contained special characters or were attacker-controlled, command injection could occur. Current implementation mitigates this by using trusted path source.
discarded_claims.remediation: Use proper argument construction with list indexing or f-strings with proper escaping. Avoid string concatenation for building command arguments.

cwe.name: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command ('OS Command Injection')

provenance.confirmation_reasoning:
The claimed vulnerability class (CWE-78 OS command injection) cannot occur on this path, and the proposed remediation would change nothing.

1. No shell is involved. Line 64 of skill/scripts/tools/roslyn_secguard.py builds one element of a Python list `cmd`, which is passed to `run_tool(cmd, timeout=600)`. run_tool (skill/scripts/tools/base.py:72) calls `subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, timeout=timeout, **kwargs)` with no `shell` argument, and roslyn_secguard passes no kwargs. A repo-wide grep for `shell\s*=\s*True` finds zero occurrences in executable code — the only hits are a checklist item in skill/reference/security-checklists.md:28 and stored scan-report JSON. With shell=False and a list argv, each element is delivered verbatim as a single argv entry via execve; shell metacharacters have no meaning. There is no command to inject into.

2. The value is not attacker-controlled. `sarif = os.path.join(tmp, "out.sarif")` where `tmp = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="roslyn-")` (lines 53, 60). The scanned target path never reaches this string; it only reaches `tmp_target` (a separate argv element) and shutil.copytree.

3. The remediation is self-refuting. `"-p:ErrorLog=" + sarif + ",version=2.1"` and `f"-p:ErrorLog={sarif},version=2.1"` compile to the same string with the same characters and the same lack of escaping. Recommending f-strings 'with proper escaping' as a security control for argv-list construction reflects a misunderstanding; the claim's own impact text concedes the current code 'mitigates this'.

The only residual, non-security concern is MSBuild property parsing: since ErrorLog uses a comma to separate the version qualifier, a temp path containing a comma would confuse msbuild's own property parser. That is a robustness edge case in a process-controlled path, not injection, and f-strings would not fix it either. The underlying stylistic observation is separately captured by STY-005; judged as a security finding under CWE-78/A03, this one is rejected.

discarded_claims.title: Awkward line break in conditional expression
discarded_claims.description: Lines 88-89 split a ternary conditional across lines in an awkward way: the first operand ends on line 88, and the `or` operator is placed at the start of line 89. This breaks the readability of the conditional chain: `"description": vuln.get("summary") or (vuln.get(...))[:500]`
discarded_claims.impact: The visual flow of the conditional is interrupted, making it harder to parse the intent of the code.
discarded_claims.remediation: Restructure the conditional to keep the operator with the first operand, or split the expression differently to maintain visual flow.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The literal code observation is accurate: /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/tools/osv_scanner.py line 88 is `"description": vuln.get("summary")` and line 89 begins with `or (vuln.get("details") or "No description provided.")[:500],` at the same 24-space indent as line 88 (verified by anchored regex `^ {24}or \(vuln\.get\("details"\)` matching line 89). But every judgment the claim builds on that observation is wrong. (1) It is not a ternary conditional — there is no if/else; it is a two-operand `or` short-circuit fallback. (2) The claim's own reference, PEP 8 'Should a line break before or after a binary operator?', explicitly recommends the Knuth style of breaking BEFORE the binary operator, which is exactly what this code does; the remediation ('keep the operator with the first operand') would move the code away from the cited standard, not toward it. (3) The style is locally consistent, which is the other thing PEP 8 asks for: the same break-before-operator form appears at skill/scripts/evidence.py:48, skill/scripts/synthesize.py:660-661 and skill/scripts/evidence.py:194. (4) The repo's configured linter cannot flag it: pyproject.toml sets ruff with select = ["E","F","W"], ignore = ["E401","E501","E701","E702"]; ruff implements no W503/W504 equivalent, and the continuation line is legally indented relative to the opening `{` on line 78, so no E12x rule applies either. There is no defect here, not even an INFO-level one, and acting on the remediation would degrade conformance. (Note, out of scope for this claim: the `[:500]` truncation applies only to the `details` fallback and not to `summary` — a behavioral asymmetry, not a formatting one.)

discarded_claims.title: XML External Entity (XXE) Injection in XML Parsing
discarded_claims.description: ET.fromstring() is called without disabling external entity processing. This is a known vulnerable pattern that could allow XXE attacks if the XML source is compromised.
discarded_claims.impact: An attacker who can control the spotbugs XML output could exploit this to read files or perform SSRF attacks through external entity expansion.
discarded_claims.remediation: Use defusedxml library or explicitly disable external entity processing via XMLParser with resolve_entities=False and load_external_dtd=False.

cwe.name: Improper Restriction of XML External Entity Reference

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The call site is real (/Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/tools/spotbugs.py:45, `root = ET.fromstring(text)`), but the specific mechanism and impact this claim asserts cannot execute. (a) Parser behavior: `xml.etree.ElementTree` does not process external entities. CPython's XMLParser installs no ExternalEntityRefHandler and does not enable parameter-entity parsing, so `<!ENTITY x SYSTEM "file:///etc/passwd">` + `&x;` yields `ParseError: undefined entity` rather than file contents, and external DTD subsets are never fetched. Python's own 'XML vulnerabilities' table and defusedxml's matrix both classify etree as safe for 'external entity expansion' and 'DTD retrieval' (only billion-laughs/quadratic-blowup remain, which is a DoS, not the file-read/SSRF impact claimed here). (b) The remediation is also inapplicable to the code as written: `resolve_entities=False` / `load_external_dtd=False` are lxml `XMLParser` parameters, not options of `xml.etree.ElementTree.XMLParser` — evidence the claim was pattern-matched rather than checked against this parser. (c) Input control: the claim's precondition is 'an attacker who can control the spotbugs XML output'. I traced the only consumer — `ingest_dir` (skill/scripts/ingest_tools.py:55-79) reads `.panopticon/tools/*.json` written by run_tools.py from the container's spotbugs stdout (run_tools.py:156-176) with the target mounted `:ro`. Analyzed-code strings enter that XML only as escaped attribute/text content, after the root element, where no DTD can be declared. I found no path in the repository where a third party controls the bytes reaching line 45. Rejecting the XXE (file read / SSRF) claim specifically; the unrelated, weaker entity-expansion-DoS/hygiene aspect of this line is addressed on its own merits under the separate claim.

discarded_claims.description: sys.path.insert(0, ...) modifies the module search path at module import time. While the path is hardcoded relative to __file__, this pattern is a known anti-pattern that could allow arbitrary module loading if path sources were untrusted.
discarded_claims.impact: If the script location or parent directories were writable by untrusted users, arbitrary modules could be loaded. Current implementation uses hardcoded relative paths which mitigates this risk.
discarded_claims.remediation: Use relative imports or configure PYTHONPATH appropriately instead of modifying sys.path at runtime. Consider using importlib for more controlled imports.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The line exists as quoted — /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/tools/sarif_utils.py line 11 is `sys.path.insert(0, os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), os.pardir, os.pardir))` followed by `from scripts.provenance import tool_provenance` — but the security claim it carries does not hold. (1) The inserted element is derived solely from the module's own `__file__` (resolving to the `skill/` directory, two levels up from `skill/scripts/tools/`); no environment variable, CLI argument, cwd, or any other attacker-influenceable input contributes to it, which is what CWE-426 (untrusted search path) requires. (2) The stated precondition is self-defeating: an attacker who can write to `skill/` or `skill/scripts/tools/` can simply edit sarif_utils.py itself, so no privilege or trust boundary is crossed by the sys.path insert — it grants no capability the attacker does not already have. The claim's own impact text concedes this ('Current implementation uses hardcoded relative paths which mitigates this risk'). (3) I checked for the one concrete hazard this pattern can create — stdlib shadowing from inserting at index 0 — and it does not apply: the inserted `skill/` directory contains no top-level .py modules (Glob 'skill/*' returns only SKILL.md; the only package there is skill/scripts with skill/scripts/tools/__init__.py), so nothing in it can shadow a stdlib module. (4) The pattern is the repo-wide import convention, not an outlier: skill/scripts/tools/base.py line 9 is byte-identical, and ~30 test modules use the same construct (e.g. tests/test_ingest_tools.py line 2, tests/tools/test_base.py line 6). At most this is a packaging/style nit (the project is not pip-installable, hence the shim); it is not a known_vulns security finding and the CWE-426 citation is unsupported.

discarded_claims.title: Unguarded XML Parsing Causes Crash on Malformed Output
discarded_claims.description: SpotBugsAdapter.parse() calls ET.fromstring() without exception handling. If SpotBugs produces malformed XML output (due to corruption, truncation, or tool crash), the adapter crashes instead of gracefully degrading or logging an error.
discarded_claims.impact: Tool failures or malformed output cause the entire adapter to crash, resulting in missing security analysis and potential false negatives in scan coverage.
discarded_claims.remediation: Wrap ET.fromstring() in try-except block to catch xml.etree.ElementTree.ParseError and return empty findings list with appropriate logging.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The literal code observation is accurate but the claimed impact is contradicted by the caller. spotbugs.py:45 does call `root = ET.fromstring(text)` with no local try/except, so an xml.etree.ElementTree.ParseError would propagate out of parse(). However, the only production caller of any adapter's parse() is ingest_dir() in skill/scripts/ingest_tools.py:78-82, which is `try: parsed = adapter.parse(raw, group)` / `except Exception as e:  # noqa: BLE001 - tolerant by design` / `print("ingest error %s: %s" % (path, e), file=sys.stderr); continue`. ET.ParseError subclasses SyntaxError, which subclasses Exception, so it is caught. The loop then continues to the next tool-output file. I grepped all `.parse(` call sites repo-wide: the only non-test caller is ingest_tools.py:79; skill/scripts/synthesize.py:939 reaches parse only through ingest_dir. So the claimed outcome -- 'the entire adapter crashes' causing a broken scan -- does not materialize; the observed behavior is already exactly what the remediation asks for (skip, log to stderr, produce no findings from that file), only with the handler one frame up. The proposed fix would change nothing except the wording of the log line, and would not recover any findings from truncated XML. The house convention is consistent: roslyn_secguard.py:110 calls json.loads() equally unguarded, and ingest_dir's docstring (lines 40-49) documents 'Files without a registered adapter or that fail to parse are skipped with a stderr diagnostic.' HIGH severity is unsupported -- there is no security consequence, and the degradation path is deliberate and tested (tests/tools/test_spotbugs.py:41-43 covers the empty-input early return at spotbugs.py:43-44). Residual nit only: parse() is not independently robust if a future caller invokes it without a guard, which is a style preference, not a HIGH security finding.

discarded_claims.title: Unfiltered Stderr Output May Leak Sensitive Information
discarded_claims.description: run_tool() outputs up to 1000 bytes of tool stderr to sys.stderr without sanitization when a tool exits with an unexpected code. Tool stderr may contain secrets, API keys, file paths, or other sensitive information from failed tool invocations.
discarded_claims.impact: Sensitive information from scanner failures could be leaked to CI/CD logs, monitoring systems, or other consumers of stderr output.
discarded_claims.remediation: Sanitize stderr output before printing, redact common secret patterns (API keys, passwords), or use a configurable verbosity level to disable diagnostic output in sensitive environments.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The mechanical description is accurate — `skill/scripts/tools/base.py` lines 74-77 print `(res.stderr or b'')[-1000:]` decoded and unsanitized to sys.stderr when the return code is outside ok_codes — but the claimed impact path ('leaked to CI/CD logs') does not execute, and no sensitive-data source is demonstrated. (1) Exposure: on the CI path (`.github/workflows/security.yml` line 51 -> `skill/scripts/run_tools.py`), adapters are never run in-process; they are dispatched into the Docker container via `_run_adapter.py` (run_tools.py lines 156-176), and that subprocess is invoked with `stderr=subprocess.PIPE`. The captured `res.stderr` is then DISCARDED in the adapter branch — on a bad exit it prints only `'adapter %s exited %s; skipping' % (tool, res.returncode)` (line 172), with no stderr excerpt. So run_tool's excerpt is written to container stderr and swallowed; it never reaches the GitHub Actions log. The only in-process host caller of adapter.invoke() is `run_adapters()` (run_tools.py lines 94-112), which grep shows is referenced nowhere outside tests/test_run_tools.py:97. (2) Sensitive data: the sole credential the pipeline handles is NVD_API_KEY, and it is passed only as an environment variable (`docker.extend(['-e', 'NVD_API_KEY'])`, run_tools.py line 158; `dependency_check.py` line 25 only reads `bool(os.environ.get('NVD_API_KEY'))` and never places it on argv), so it is not in the command line that a failing tool would echo. Also note run_tool prints only `cmd[0]`, not the full argv, so target paths/flags are not emitted by this code. (3) The behavior is a deliberate, documented, tested feature: the docstring cites F-CAL-1, `docs/superpowers/2026-08-03-calibration-fixmes.md` lines 75-78 records that discarding stderr made failures undiagnosable, and tests/tools/test_base.py lines 44-82 pin the excerpt, its 1000-byte cap, and the no-log-on-rc-1 behavior. The finding is a generic 'stderr may contain secrets' hypothesis with no identified secret and a blocked exposure path. Worth flagging for the auditor as adjacent-but-uncited: `skill/scripts/run_tools.py` lines 136-140 (the legacy TOOL_CMD branch) DOES print a 500-byte unsanitized tool-stderr excerpt to the host stderr, which on CI does land in the Actions log. If the reviewer intended that sink, it should be re-filed against that location — but it is a different code site than the one cited, and the same lack of a demonstrated secret applies (GitHub also masks registered secrets in logs).

discarded_claims.title: Brittle Path Substitution Pattern in Tool Command Construction
discarded_claims.description: LegacySarifAdapter.invoke() uses exact string equality to substitute '/src' with the target path in tool commands. If a tool command contains a path variant (e.g., '/src/', '/src/path' prefix), the substitution silently fails and the tool runs against the wrong path or fails to find files.
discarded_claims.impact: Security scanners might not run against intended targets or fail silently, creating a false sense of coverage when analysis is incomplete or skipped.
discarded_claims.remediation: Use robust path manipulation (os.path substitution or regex with proper escaping) and validate that the target path appears in the final command before execution.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The cited line is `cmd = [target if arg == "/src" else arg for arg in TOOL_CMD[self.name]]` (skill/scripts/tools/legacy_sarif.py:45). I enumerated the entire TOOL_CMD table it operates on (same file, lines 17-24): every entry that needs the target passes '/src' as a standalone argv element — semgrep ['semgrep','scan','--config','auto','--sarif','--quiet','/src'], gitleaks ['--source','/src',...], trivy ['trivy','fs','--format','sarif','/src'], bandit ['bandit','-q','-r','/src','-f','sarif']. gosec is the sole entry with no '/src' and it is deliberately handled by cwd=target (line 47), documented and covered by tests/tools/test_legacy_sarif.py:64-73 which asserts cwd=='/go/project' and that '/src' is absent from argv. There is no '/src/' or '/src/path' variant anywhere in the table, and TOOL_CMD is never mutated or extended — it is only read by skill/scripts/run_tools.py:127 (docker path, where the literal '/src' is correct because the target is bind-mounted at /src per line 131) and by tests. So the failure mode the claim describes has no executable path; it is a hypothetical about a future table entry, not a defect in the code as written. The 'silently fails' premise is also wrong: if a scanner were handed a nonexistent '/src', run_tool (skill/scripts/tools/base.py:64-78) prints a stderr excerpt on any exit code outside (0,1), and run_tools.py:104-105 / _run_adapter.py:25-28 log 'exited N; skipping'. CWE-426 (Untrusted Search Path) does not describe this pattern either — the argv is a hard-coded constant, not attacker-influenced.

discarded_claims.title: Unvalidated Directory Copy Operation Before Analysis
discarded_claims.description: RoslynSecGuardAdapter.invoke() copies the entire target directory using shutil.copytree() without validating success before proceeding to build analysis. If the copy fails (permission errors, disk space, symlinks), the exception is silently caught in the finally block and the build proceeds against an incomplete or missing directory.
discarded_claims.impact: Analysis may run against incomplete project state, potentially missing security issues or producing false negatives.
discarded_claims.remediation: Validate that copytree() succeeded and that key files exist before proceeding with the build step. Log or raise exceptions on copy failures.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The claim's stated mechanism is contradicted by Python semantics and by the actual code. roslyn_secguard.py:53-72 is `tmp = tempfile.mkdtemp(...)` / `try:` (lines 55-70, including copytree at 58 and the dotnet build at 61-66) / `finally: shutil.rmtree(tmp, ignore_errors=True)`. A `finally` block does not catch exceptions -- it only runs cleanup and then lets the exception propagate. There is no `except` clause anywhere in invoke(). So if shutil.copytree() raises (PermissionError, OSError/disk-full, or shutil.Error for dangling symlinks / per-file failures, which copytree aggregates and raises at the end of the walk), control leaves invoke() immediately: lines 60-70 (`dotnet build`, SARIF read) are NEVER reached. The claimed outcome 'the build proceeds against an incomplete or missing directory' cannot execute. The claim that the failure is 'silently caught' is also wrong in the opposite direction -- the propagated exception is caught and logged by both production callers: skill/scripts/_run_adapter.py:25-28 prints `adapter {name} crashed: {exc}; skipping` plus a full traceback.print_exc() to stderr, and skill/scripts/run_tools.py:110-111 prints `adapter {name} failed: {e}; skipping`. The only `ignore_errors=True` in the function is on the rmtree cleanup of the throwaway temp dir, which is not the copy and cannot mask a copy failure. tests/tools/test_roslyn_secguard.py:99-139 (test_invoke_builds_in_temp_copy) confirms the intended control flow: the build command is only constructed after copytree returns. The remediation ('validate copytree succeeded before proceeding') describes a guard that Python's exception propagation already provides. No residual defect found at the cited line.

discarded_claims.title: Unguarded JSON Parsing in CargoAuditAdapter Causes Crash
discarded_claims.description: CargoAuditAdapter.parse() calls json.loads() without exception handling. If cargo audit produces malformed or truncated JSON output, the adapter crashes instead of gracefully handling the error.
discarded_claims.impact: Cargo audit failures or corrupted output cause the entire adapter to crash, resulting in missing Rust dependency vulnerability analysis.
discarded_claims.remediation: Wrap json.loads() in try-except block to catch json.JSONDecodeError and return empty findings list with logging.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The literal observation is true — `skill/scripts/tools/cargo_audit.py` line 55 is `data = json.loads(raw.decode('utf-8', errors='replace'))` with no try/except — but the claimed consequence ('the adapter crashes', HIGH severity) is contradicted by the only production caller. I grepped every `.parse(` call site in the repo: outside tests and docs, the sole caller is `skill/scripts/ingest_tools.py` line 79, and it is wrapped: `try: parsed = adapter.parse(raw, group) / except Exception as e:  # noqa: BLE001 - tolerant by design / print('ingest error %s: %s' % (path, e), file=sys.stderr); continue` (lines 78-82). A JSONDecodeError therefore produces a stderr diagnostic and a skipped file — precisely the 'return empty findings list with logging' behavior the remediation asks for — and never propagates. This is a documented invariant, not an accident: DEVELOPMENT.md line 57-58 states 'Tolerant by design: ... skip/log malformed input, never abort the run', and it is regression-tested — tests/test_ingest_tools.py line 31-38 writes a literal `{not json` file and asserts the sibling findings still ingest with no raise, and lines 60-66 do the same for structural garbage. ingest_dir also pre-trims non-JSON stdout prefixes (lines 68-77), removing the most common cause of malformed adapter output. Additionally, cargo_audit is in no way an outlier: unguarded `json.loads` at the top of `parse()` is the uniform pattern across npm_audit.py:21, osv_scanner.py:48, pip_audit.py:50, eslint_security.py:55, brakeman.py:63, dependency_check.py:57, roslyn_secguard.py:110 and legacy_sarif.py:53, so singling out cargo_audit at HIGH is unjustified. The residual true statement — a corrupt cargo-audit output file yields zero Rust findings for that run — is the intended graceful degradation, is announced on stderr, and at most supports a LOW/INFO note, not HIGH.

discarded_claims.description: Multiple adapter parse() methods (pip_audit, npm_audit, cargo_audit, eslint_security, dependency_check, roslyn_secguard, osv_scanner, brakeman) call json.loads() directly without exception handling. Tests do not verify behavior when malformed JSON is received.
discarded_claims.impact: Invalid tool output will crash adapters with unhandled JSONDecodeError, causing entire scan to fail silently without diagnostics.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The claim's narrow observation is true but its material premise — the stated impact that justifies HIGH severity — is contradicted by the code. Verified true part: a grep of skill/scripts/tools shows every named adapter calls `json.loads(raw.decode(...))` as the first statement of `parse()` with no local try/except (cargo_audit.py:55, npm_audit.py:21, roslyn_secguard.py:110, osv_scanner.py:48, brakeman.py:63, eslint_security.py:55, dependency_check.py:57, pip_audit.py:50; legacy_sarif.py:53 likewise), and no adapter unit test in tests/tools/ feeds syntactically invalid JSON to `parse()` (the closest, test_osv_scanner.py:133 `test_parse_tolerates_malformed_entries`, uses structurally-garbage but valid JSON). Contradicted part: the sole production caller of `adapter.parse()` in the entire skill/ tree is `ingest_dir` at /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/ingest_tools.py lines 78-82, which is explicitly tolerant by design: `try: parsed = adapter.parse(raw, group) / except Exception as e: print("ingest error %s: %s" % (path, e), file=sys.stderr); continue`. discarded_claims.title: Test isolation issue in roslyn_secguard invoke test
discarded_claims.description: test_roslyn_secguard.py test_invoke_builds_in_temp_copy() (lines 99-139) directly patches module-level functions (tools_base.subprocess.run, rs.shutil.copytree) and restores them in a finally block. This manual restoration approach is fragile and could cause test order dependencies.
discarded_claims.impact: Tests may pass or fail depending on execution order. If test fails before restoration, subsequent tests could use the patched version. Modern mock context managers would prevent this.
discarded_claims.remediation: Refactor to use mock.patch() context managers or @patch decorators instead of direct module manipulation with manual restoration.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning:
The claim's description of the mechanics is accurate, but the impact it asserts is contradicted by the code. tests/tools/test_roslyn_secguard.py:99-139 does exactly what the claim says structurally: it captures `old_run = tools_base.subprocess.run` (line 111) and `old_copytree = rs.shutil.copytree` (112), assigns fakes (123-124), and restores both in a `finally` (131-133).

The defect the claim alleges does not exist. Both assignments occur INSIDE the `try` that begins at line 113, and the originals are captured BEFORE it. Python's try/finally therefore guarantees restoration on any exception path, including a failing `self.assertEqual` inside the block — assertion failures raise, and `finally` still runs. The claim's stated impact, 'If test fails before restoration, subsequent tests could use the patched version,' is false for this construct. Correspondingly there is no test-order dependency: no ordering of tests can observe the fakes, because they are unwound before control leaves the method. The test is in fact carefully written — the assertions at lines 135-139 deliberately sit AFTER the finally, so they execute against restored module state.

The implied contrast with `mock.patch()` also does not hold in this repo. `tools_base.subprocess` is the stdlib module object imported at skill/scripts/tools/base.py:6, so `tools_base.subprocess.run = fake_run` mutates the shared `subprocess` module globally. The sibling tests' `mock.patch('scripts.tools.base.subprocess.run', ...)` (e.g. tests/tools/test_pip_audit.py:110,124) resolves to that same global module attribute and mutates it identically. The two approaches have the same isolation blast radius; mock.patch differs only in that restoration is automatic rather than hand-written. So the recommended refactor is a readability/consistency preference, not a fix for any behavioural isolation problem.

I reject the finding as stated. A rewritten claim scoped purely to style consistency ('hand-rolled patching where the rest of the suite uses mock.patch') would be defensible, but the asserted impact — cross-test leakage and order-dependent pass/fail — is not supported by the code. The cited CWE-1117 (Callable with Insufficient Behavioral Summary) is unrelated to test patching and I could not substantiate it. One caveat on confidence: I did not execute the suite, and my reasoning assumes standard sequential unittest execution; I found no parallel-test runner configuration that would create a concurrent window during which the globally-patched `subprocess.run` could be observed by another test.

discarded_claims.title: Unregistered Tool Output Formats Silently Skip
discarded_claims.description: Files without a registered adapter are skipped with diagnostic logging to stderr, but the architecture provides no enforcement mechanism to ensure all tool output formats are registered. This can mask tool output that should be ingested if format registration is incomplete.
discarded_claims.impact: Tool output may be silently dropped if adapter registration is missing or incomplete, reducing visibility of security findings without explicit error.
discarded_claims.remediation: Implement explicit adapter registry validation at startup or configuration time; consider failing fast on unknown tool formats during ingest initialization rather than per-file.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Two independent parts of the claim fail. (1) 'Silently skip' is false: skill/scripts/ingest_tools.py:59-61 emits `print("ingest skip %s: no adapter registered" % path, file=sys.stderr)` before `continue`, and the cited test (tests/test_ingest_tools.py:40-50) exists precisely to pin that diagnostic (`assertIn("no adapter registered", stderr.getvalue())`). DEVELOPMENT.md:146 records this as an already-shipped remediation of the older 'silently dropped' bug (DEVELOPMENT.md:197). (2) The claimed failure mode - 'tool output may be dropped if adapter registration is missing or incomplete' - cannot arise from the pipeline, because the producer derives filenames from the same registry the consumer reads. skill/scripts/run_tools.py:100-101 (`out_path = os.path.join(out_dir, f"{name}.{ext}")` where `name` is an ADAPTERS key), :129 (`"%s.sarif" % tool` where `tool` is a TOOL_CMD key) and :152-155 (`adapter = ADAPTERS.get(tool)`) all name output after the registry key, and ingest_dir re-derives that key via `os.path.splitext(os.path.basename(path))[0]` (ingest_tools.py:57). I cross-checked the key sets: every TOOL_CMD key {semgrep, gitleaks, trivy, bandit, gosec} is present in ADAPTERS (skill/scripts/tools/__init__.py:14-31), and PHASE1_ADAPTERS/PHASE2_ADAPTERS are subsets of ADAPTERS keys. So the 'no adapter registered' branch only fires for files a human dropped into the directory by hand - for which there is by definition no parser, making skip-with-diagnostic the only available behavior. The proposed remediation ('failing fast on unknown tool formats') would additionally contradict the repository's explicit, documented design decision (DEVELOPMENT.md:57-58, 'Tolerant by design ... never abort the run') and would abort on any unrelated .json file present in the tools directory. What remains is at most a wish for a startup registry self-check, which is not the stated impact.

discarded_claims.title: Generic Host Model Resolution Returns None
discarded_claims.description: Model resolver returns None for generic/unknown hosts (line 27-28). Dispatch plan still includes entries for generic host (test_dispatch.py:418-420) despite model being None. Downstream code may fail if it assumes a model is always present.
discarded_claims.impact: Potential runtime failures or incorrect behavior if downstream agents/dispatch logic requires a model to be non-None. Creates ambiguity about whether generic host is fully supported.
discarded_claims.remediation: Either ensure generic host has defined default models or explicitly exclude generic host from dispatch plans; make the architecture decision clear via validation.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning:
The observed behavior is real but it is an explicit, documented architectural decision with an explicit consumer contract, and the hypothesized failure has no instance in the repository.

The null is deliberate and self-documenting: skill/scripts/model_resolver.py `_hardcoded_fallback()` lines 59-71 carries the docstring "Unknown hosts resolve to model=None, meaning 'inherit the session's model' — never silently assume kimi." docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-03-claude-code-port-design.md line 123 states the same decision: "`generic` host resolves every role to `{\"model\": null}` = inherit the session's model — the safe default for unknown hosts (including Codex)."

The consumer contract handles null explicitly. skill/SKILL.md line 79 tells the orchestrator to dispatch unenforced entries "with the model named by `entry.model.model` (omit when null)", and line 86 covers this host class directly: "Other hosts — run the entries sequentially in-session with the same prompts." So generic host is fully supported by design, not ambiguous.

The "downstream code may fail" hypothesis has no realized instance. I grepped every .py for consumers of the plan's model field: the only Python reader of dispatch-plan JSON is `derive_tool_policy_mode()` at skill/scripts/synthesize.py:491-511, which touches only `e.get("enforced")`. skill/scripts/orchestrator.py contains no occurrence of "model" at all. `max_context_size`/`max_output_size` are consumed by nothing outside model-profiles.yml and one test assertion. The `model` field's only consumer is the orchestrating agent following SKILL.md, which is instructed to omit it when null. Note also that the same `{"model": None}` shape reaches consumers today for any dict-valued profile entry, since the claude block of skill/reference/model-profiles.yml (lines 19-27) already omits the size keys, so partial model dicts are the norm, not a generic-host anomaly.

tests/test_dispatch.py:417-420 (`test_generic_host_never_enforced_by_default`) does not show a defect: it asserts that generic-host entries exist and are unenforced, which is the intended behavior per `_registration_dir()` (dispatch.py:201-206 — no default registration dir for non-claude hosts). The cited CWE-248 (Uncaught Exception) has no bearing; no exception path is involved.

discarded_claims.title: Path Traversal Validation Incomplete
discarded_claims.description: Path expansion only checks for and excludes "../" style path traversals (line 143). Does not address alternative traversal techniques: Windows-style "..\", encoded variants (%2e%2e), or symbolic link attacks that could escape repo boundaries.

discarded_claims.remediation: Use canonicalize path resolution (os.path.realpath after normalization) to resolve all path forms to canonical representation, then verify resolved path is within repo; test against Windows and encoded variants.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The claim asserts that path expansion 'only checks for and excludes "../" style path traversals' and recommends canonicalizing with os.path.realpath and verifying containment. discarded_claims.title: HTML Escaping Strategy Inconsistently Applied
discarded_claims.description: Test explicitly checks that title is escaped once to prevent double-escaping (line 80-81). This suggests that escaping strategy is field-specific rather than architectural. No evidence other fields follow consistent single-pass escaping, creating risk of inconsistent HTML encoding across report fields.
discarded_claims.impact: Inconsistent HTML escaping across different report fields could result in some fields being double-escaped (displaying escape sequences) or under-escaped (XSS vulnerability), depending on field-specific handling.
discarded_claims.remediation: Define architectural escaping rule: either all fields use single-pass escaping with a clear architecture documenting why, or implement post-rendering normalization; test all text fields for both double-escaping and XSS.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The claim's factual premise about the test is correct (tests/test_html_report.py:76-81 does assert `<title>Panopticon — <script></title>` and `assertNotIn('&lt;')`), but its inference is contradicted by the renderer. skill/scripts/html_report.py has exactly one escaping primitive, `_escape(value) -> html.escape(str(value))` (line 172-174), and it is applied exactly once at every text interpolation site: `_html_doc` title (line 184), `_render_header` target/review_type/timestamp/security_mode/grade/risk/gate (lines 334-345), `_render_card` description/impact/remediation (line 509), title/id/panel/category/confidence (lines 549-553), refs (line 514), cvss/exploit_scenario (521-523), citation chips (529-540), `_render_bar_chart` labels (line 424), `_render_heatmap` path/tooltip (598-599), `_render_dashboard` grades/group names/top issues (452-462), `_render_compare_summary`/`_render_compare_dashboard` (360-376). I found no site where a value is escaped twice, and no site where a text value reaches the document unescaped. The `where` variable in `_render_card` (line 490) is pre-escaped once and then interpolated raw, which is the correct single-pass pattern, not a second pass. So 'escaping strategy is field-specific rather than architectural' and 'no evidence other fields follow consistent single-pass escaping' are both false as stated; the title test is an ordinary regression test for a past double-escape bug (render() builds the title raw at line 693/701 and _html_doc escapes it once), not evidence of per-field strategy. Separate observation the claim does NOT make and which does not rescue it: CSS *class tokens* are sanitized by three different ad-hoc mechanisms — `_severity_class`/`_panel_class` use an isalnum filter (lines 292-306), `_render_provenance` uses a regex (line 315), and `_render_citation_quality` (line 327) interpolates `cit-{quality}` into a single-quoted class attribute with NO sanitization at all. In the normal pipeline that token is always overwritten by `citations.enrich_citations` (skill/scripts/citations.py:226/261/269) with one of full/partial/minimal/none, so it is latent rather than live; regardless, it is an attribute-token sanitization gap, not the text-field double/under-escaping inconsistency this claim asserts, and the claim's remediation ('test all text fields for double-escaping and XSS') would not surface it.
