discarded_claims.title: Tool Finding Verdict Handling Not Architecturally Enforced
discarded_claims.description: Test documents that 'Tool findings never enter the queue; if a verdict is passed anyway, tool_confirmed still wins' (line 52-54). This indicates tool findings can receive verdicts (which violates the rule) but defensive code ignores them. Architecture relies on code discipline rather than structural prevention.
discarded_claims.impact: Tool findings might receive inappropriate verdicts upstream in the pipeline. Without structural enforcement, bugs could cause tool verdicts to be incorrectly applied and then silently ignored, hiding the upstream error.
discarded_claims.remediation: Structurally prevent tool findings from entering verdict pipeline (e.g., separate queue types); add integrity checks to verify tool findings are verdict-free; document architectural constraint explicitly.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The claim asserts that the tool-finding/verdict rule is enforced only by 'code discipline' and defensive ignoring, with no structural prevention. The code contradicts this at three layers. (1) Structural queue filter: /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/evidence.py:107-108 builds the verify queue as `agentic = [(i, f) for i, f in enumerate(findings) if not is_tool_sourced(f) and not f.get('reinforced')]` — tool-sourced and reinforced findings are excluded from the queue by construction, not by convention. (2) Structural verdict routing: in /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/synthesize.py:619-640, verdicts are matched by queue_id against queue entries only; apply_verdict is called solely on entry['finding'], and derive_evidence receives `matched.get(id(f))`, a dict keyed by the object identity of queued findings. A tool finding is never in that dict, so it can never receive a verdict through the pipeline. Aggregation and dedupe (lines 616-617) run before queue construction, so a finding cannot become tool-sourced after being queued, and apply_verdict (evidence.py:224-243) never sets `source`. (3) Anti-forgery at load: synthesize.py:89-93 defines AGENT_FORBIDDEN_FIELDS = ('source', 'reinforced'), stripped from agent-authored findings files, so an agent cannot self-declare tool provenance to escape the queue (regression-tested in tests/test_synthesize.py:1494-1521). The claimed failure mode of silently hiding an upstream error is also wrong: a verdict file with no matching queue entry produces an explicit stderr warning naming the queue_id (synthesize.py:633-636), covered by test_unknown_queue_id_verdict_ignored (tests/test_synthesize.py:1223). The cited comment in tests/test_evidence.py:52-57 is documenting exactly that invariant plus a defense-in-depth precedence rule inside derive_evidence, which is a unit-level function being called directly with a hand-constructed verdict — not evidence that the pipeline routes verdicts to tool findings. The invariant itself is directly regression-tested in /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/tests/test_verify_queue.py:36-41 (test_tools_excluded_agentic_included) and :94-103 (test_reinforced_agentic_finding_excluded). The claim's CWE-1025 citation is unverified and does not bear on the verdict.

discarded_claims.title: Circular Import Avoidance Via Shared Utilities Pattern
discarded_claims.description: Test verifies that legacy adapter and ingest_tools module avoid circular imports by sharing SARIF utilities in a separate module (line 159-160 comment). This is a defensive architectural pattern that works but indicates tight coupling between legacy and new adapter systems.
discarded_claims.impact: While the current pattern prevents circular imports, it creates tight coupling where both adapter systems must coordinate on shared utility location. Future refactoring of adapter architecture is constrained by this dependency.
discarded_claims.remediation: Consider longer-term refactoring: use proper plugin architecture with adapter registry pattern instead of shared utility imports; decouple legacy adapter from new adapter system through abstraction.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The descriptive half checks out - skill/scripts/tools/sarif_utils.py:1-4 states verbatim 'This module exists to break the circular import between scripts.ingest_tools and scripts.tools.legacy_sarif', and the cited test pins it. But the asserted defect (tight coupling that constrains future refactoring) is contradicted by the actual dependency graph. I grepped every import in skill/scripts/tools/*: no module under scripts.tools imports scripts.ingest_tools. The edges are one-directional into a leaf: scripts.ingest_tools -> scripts.tools.sarif_utils (ingest_tools.py:13) and scripts.tools.legacy_sarif -> scripts.tools.sarif_utils (legacy_sarif.py:5). That is an acyclic hub, i.e. the textbook resolution of a cycle by extracting shared code to a common leaf module - a reduction in coupling, not evidence of it. The claim's own remediation is already implemented: skill/scripts/tools/__init__.py:14-31 is an adapter registry (ADAPTERS) and skill/scripts/tools/base.py:51-62 defines a `ToolAdapter` Protocol with is_applicable/invoke/parse that every adapter satisfies, including LegacySarifAdapter; DEVELOPMENT.md:66-72 documents the plugin-registration procedure. Legacy tools are not a separate 'system' - they are ordinary ADAPTERS entries (`LegacySarifAdapter("semgrep")` etc.). The only residual wart I could substantiate is ingest_tools.py:13-37 re-exporting the sarif_utils helpers for back-compat, which the claim does not raise. No actionable defect at the cited location.

discarded_claims.title: Late imports within test method suggests inconsistent sys.path setup
discarded_claims.description: test_ingest_tools.py imports 'scripts.tools.legacy_sarif' and 'scripts.tools.sarif_utils' within a test method (lines 161-162) rather than at module level. This pattern is unusual and suggests the sys.path setup may not be working reliably for all import variations at the module level.
discarded_claims.impact: Late imports indicate potential fragility in module import system. This workaround pattern may mask underlying structural issues with sys.path configuration and creates maintenance burden.
discarded_claims.remediation: Move imports to module level after sys.path.insert() call. If module-level import fails, investigate and fix the sys.path configuration to support all import patterns consistently.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The observable fact (imports at tests/test_ingest_tools.py:161-162 sit inside a test method) is true, but the claim's substance - that this indicates the sys.path setup does not work reliably for module-level imports - is contradicted by the same file and by a sibling test. tests/test_ingest_tools.py:2-3 already performs `sys.path.insert(0, .../skill)` followed by a module-level `import scripts.ingest_tools as it`, which succeeds; there is no fallback or try/except around it. That module-level import transitively loads exactly the two modules imported late: skill/scripts/ingest_tools.py:13 does `from scripts.tools.sarif_utils import (...)` at module scope, which forces execution of skill/scripts/tools/__init__.py, which at line 6 does `from scripts.tools.legacy_sarif import LegacySarifAdapter`. So both `scripts.tools.legacy_sarif` and `scripts.tools.sarif_utils` are already in sys.modules before any test body runs; lines 161-162 merely bind local names to already-loaded modules and cannot be a sys.path workaround. Independently, tests/tools/test_legacy_sarif.py:8-10 uses the identical sys.path idiom and imports `scripts.tools.legacy_sarif` and `scripts.tools.ADAPTERS` at module level without issue. The in-method placement is ordinary scoping for a test whose subject IS the import relationship (it asserts `it.sarif_to_findings is su.sarif_to_findings`). The CWE-426 (Untrusted Search Path) citation is inapposite to a local import in a test. No fragility, no maintenance burden beyond style preference; not a MEDIUM structural defect.

discarded_claims.title: Environment variable pollution without proper test isolation
discarded_claims.description: Lines 34-39 and 42-49 modify os.environ directly within test methods without using setUp/tearDown or context managers for isolation. The tests set PANOPTICON_MODEL_ADVISOR and rely on try/finally blocks for cleanup, but this approach can interfere with parallel test execution and leaves global state modifications during test execution.
discarded_claims.impact: Test isolation is compromised. If an exception occurs before the finally block completes, the environment variable may not be cleaned up, affecting subsequent tests.
discarded_claims.remediation: Use mock.patch.dict(os.environ, {...}) context manager or implement setUp/tearDown methods to ensure environment variables are properly isolated and cleaned up.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning:
Both stated impacts are contradicted by the code and the project's test configuration.

(1) "If an exception occurs before the finally block completes, the environment variable may not be cleaned up" — this is backwards. tests/test_model_resolver.py lines 34-39 and 41-49 wrap the assertion in `try:` / `finally: del os.environ["PANOPTICON_MODEL_ADVISOR"]`. A `finally` block is precisely the construct that runs when the body raises (including on assertion failure), so an exception cannot skip the cleanup. The only escape hatches are hard process termination, which no test-isolation idiom survives either.

(2) "can interfere with parallel test execution" — the project runs tests serially: .github/workflows/ci.yml line 41 is `python -m pytest tests/ -q`, and the installed deps (line 39: pytest, ruff, pyyaml, jsonschema) include no pytest-xdist or other parallel plugin; /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/pyproject.toml has no [tool.pytest] config enabling parallelism. Even under xdist, workers are separate processes with separate os.environ copies.

(3) The proposed remediation is semantically equivalent to the existing code. `mock.patch.dict(os.environ, ...)` also mutates the real os.environ for the duration of the block and restores it in a finally — it does not avoid "global state modifications during test execution," which is the claim's stated defect.

discarded_claims.title: Ambiguous assertTrue usage with confusing assertion semantics
discarded_claims.description: Lines 16-17 use self.assertTrue(meta['name'], role_file) and self.assertTrue(meta['description'], role_file). This passes dict values for truthiness testing but then uses role_file as the message parameter, making the intent unclear. The assertion checks if dict values are truthy (non-empty strings) rather than explicitly checking for existence or specific content.
discarded_claims.impact: Test assertions lack clarity about what is being validated. If a value is an empty string, the test fails but the error message doesn't explain what value was tested.
discarded_claims.remediation: Use explicit assertions: self.assertIsNotNone(meta['name']) or self.assertTrue(meta['name'], f'name missing in {role_file}') to make intent clear.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Lines 16-17 of tests/test_agent_templates.py are `self.assertTrue(meta['name'], role_file)` / `self.assertTrue(meta['description'], role_file)`. The second positional argument of `unittest.TestCase.assertTrue(expr, msg=None)` is the documented `msg` parameter, not an ambiguity: on failure unittest emits `False is not true : scout.md`, which does identify the offending template. The claim's stated impact — 'the error message doesn't explain what value was tested' — is therefore contradicted by the code and by unittest semantics; the traceback additionally pins the exact assertion line. The pattern is a deliberate, file-wide convention, not an accident: the same `msg=role_file` trailing argument is used on assertIn (lines 18-19), assertNotIn (lines 20-21, 27-28) and assertEqual (lines 35-38), where no truthiness ambiguity is even possible. The proposed remediation is also self-defeating: `assertIsNotNone(meta['name'])` is strictly weaker (an empty string would pass), and the alternative offered (`assertTrue(meta['name'], f'name missing in {role_file}')`) is the identical construct with a slightly wordier message. That leaves only a cosmetic message-verbosity nit, which does not support MEDIUM severity. Separately, and NOT what the claim alleges: these two assertions are actually vacuous, because skill/scripts/dispatch.py lines 61-63 already raise ValueError when `name` or `description` is falsy (`for required in ('name','description'): if not meta.get(required): raise ValueError(...)`), so load_template can never return a falsy name/description. If a finding is wanted here, that redundancy is the accurate one; the claim as written describes a defect that does not exist.

discarded_claims.title: Overly complex test fixture builder with conditional branching
discarded_claims.description: The _compare_finding helper method (lines 266-302) builds test objects with complex conditional logic based on level and issue parameters. It has nested if statements (lines 281, 287) that modify the base dict with different data depending on parameter combinations. This makes it difficult to understand what combinations are valid and what the output will contain.
discarded_claims.impact: Test maintenance is difficult. It's unclear what data combinations the method produces, making it hard to understand what each test that uses this fixture is actually testing.
discarded_claims.remediation: Simplify by creating separate factory methods for different complexity levels or use pytest parameterization to make data variations explicit.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: I read tests/test_html_report.py:266-302. The helper exists as described, but the claim's specific evidence is wrong. Lines 281 (`if level in ("medium", "complex"):`) and 287 (`if level == "complex":`) are two SEQUENTIAL if-statements at the same indentation level inside the method body — they are not nested, and neither contains the other. The method is a progressive-enrichment fixture builder: a base dict, then one additive `update` for medium/complex, then one additive `update` for complex. Total branching is two ifs plus two ternaries on `issue` (lines 270, 274); cyclomatic complexity is roughly 5, and most of the 37 lines are a flat dict literal. It carries a docstring stating its purpose ('Build a finding of the requested complexity for compare scenarios'). The claim that it is 'unclear what combinations are valid' is contradicted by the single call site: test_compare_scenario_matrix (lines 310-354) enumerates the valid levels explicitly in `for level in ("simple", "medium", "complex")` and passes only issue="sqli"/"xss", with `subTest(level=..., scenario=...)` labelling each combination. The tests using it assert on delta counts via _assert_delta_counts, so what is being tested (compare fingerprint/delta behaviour holding across payload richness) is explicit and independent of which optional fields the fixture adds. The only real (and trivial) smell I found is one the claim does not raise: the `variant` parameter (line 266, default "base") is never overridden by any caller, so it is effectively dead and only ever produces ids of the form SEC-base-<level>-<issue>. That does not support a MEDIUM 'overly complex' finding.

discarded_claims.title: Type mismatch: line_start is string instead of integer
discarded_claims.description: In test_reinforce_across_type_and_category_mismatch, the second finding's line_start is a string "151" (line 225), while the first finding uses integer 151 (line 222). The schema and all other tests expect line_start to be an integer. This type inconsistency will cause failures when the findings are processed by code expecting numeric line numbers.
discarded_claims.impact: Test data with incorrect type will not match schema validation and may cause unexpected behavior when dedupe or other processing functions attempt numeric operations on line_start.
discarded_claims.remediation: Change line 225 from "line_start":"151" to "line_start":151 to match the integer type used in line 222 and throughout the rest of the test suite.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The literal string is real: tests/test_synthesize.py:225 has "line_start":"151" while the paired finding at line 222 uses integer 151. It is the only string-valued line_start anywhere in the repo (grep for 'line_start\"?\\s*:\\s*\"' across the tree returns exactly that one line). But every claimed consequence is contradicted by the code under test. skill/scripts/synthesize.py:222-226 defines `_norm_line(v)` which does `int(v)` inside a try/except (TypeError, ValueError), and dedupe() at line 248 keys the locus map on `_norm_line(loc.get("line_start"))`, gating on `isinstance(line, int)` at line 249. So "151" normalizes to 151, both findings land in the same ('webapp.py', 151) bucket, the cluster is exactly-two with one tool- and one agent-sourced member (lines 261-268), and the test's assertions (len(out)==1, out[0]['reinforced']) hold. The test passes as written and in fact provides the only regression coverage for the `_norm_line` string-coercion path -- deleting `_norm_line` would make this test fail (the string finding would fall to `passthrough` and len(out) would be 2). The 'schema validation' impact does not materialize either: this test calls syn.dedupe() directly and never touches syn.validate_report() or skill/reference/report-schema.json (which does declare line_start as integer at lines 87 and 178); there is no conftest.py under tests/ applying any global validation. Additionally the surviving finding here is the HIGH/LIKELY agent finding SE-001, which carries the integer 151, so even the merged output holds an int. No numeric operation is performed on the raw string anywhere in the path (line_end handling at synthesize.py:385-386 also goes through _norm_line). The claim describes a cosmetic inconsistency in test fixture data as a correctness defect with failures that cannot occur. The cited CWE-1025 (Comparison Using Wrong Factors) is not apt and was unverified by the reporter.

discarded_claims.title: Hard-coded absolute fixture paths in manifest.json
discarded_claims.description: The manifest.json defines fixture paths as absolute paths like `/opt/panopticon-fixtures/railsgoat` instead of relative or environment-configurable paths. This breaks portability: fixtures cannot be used on different systems or in different deployment environments.
discarded_claims.impact: Fixtures are not portable across development, CI, and deployment environments. The fixture paths are tightly coupled to a specific system layout, making the test suite difficult to run in different contexts.
discarded_claims.remediation: Use relative paths from a base fixtures directory, or make paths configurable via environment variables. For example: `${FIXTURES_DIR}/railsgoat` or a computed relative path.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The surface observation is true — manifest.json lines 7/14/21/28 hold absolute paths under /opt/panopticon-fixtures — but the claimed impact ('fixtures cannot be used on different systems', 'tightly coupled to a specific system layout', 'test suite difficult to run in different contexts') is contradicted by how those values are consumed. Two separate consumption paths exist and neither is a host path. First, the `path` field is read in exactly one place: check_fixtures() in /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/run_fixture_tests.py:49-57, which injects the values into `docker run --rm <tag> sh -c 'if [ -d "<path>" ] ...'` — i.e. they are paths *inside the container image*, whose layout is fixed by Dockerfile.fixtures (`WORKDIR /opt/panopticon-fixtures`, line 22; `ENV FIXTURE_ROOT=/opt/panopticon-fixtures`, line 51). A container-internal path is by definition identical on every host, so it cannot break cross-system portability. Second, the actual test suite never reads manifest.json at all for locating fixtures: tests/tools/test_ruby_integration.py:8-15, test_java_integration.py:8-15, test_csharp_integration.py:8-15 and test_rust_integration.py:9-18 each do `FIXTURE_ROOT = os.environ.get('FIXTURE_ROOT', os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), '..', 'fixtures'))` and join the fixture name onto it. That is precisely the environment-configurable-with-relative-fallback mechanism the remediation asks for, and it already exists; the tests skip cleanly (`self.skipTest('... fixture not vendored')`) when the directory is absent, so running them outside the image is supported. What genuinely remains is a small duplication nit — the `/opt/panopticon-fixtures` prefix is spelled out in manifest.json, Dockerfile.fixtures:22/51, and run_fixture_tests.py:81 — but that is a DRY observation with no portability consequence, not the defect described. Note also that the suggested `${FIXTURES_DIR}/railsgoat` remediation would make things worse here, since check_fixtures interpolates the path straight into a `sh -c` string with no quoting/escaping, so making the value externally variable would add injection surface rather than remove coupling.

discarded_claims.title: Code Injection via eval() with User Input
discarded_claims.description: User-supplied command-line arguments are directly passed to eval() without sanitization. An attacker can execute arbitrary JavaScript code by providing malicious input via process.argv.
discarded_claims.impact: Complete code execution compromise. An attacker can execute arbitrary code with the privileges of the Node.js process.
discarded_claims.remediation: Remove eval() entirely. Use safer alternatives such as the Function constructor with validated input, a domain-specific language, or architecture changes to avoid dynamic code execution.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The two-line file is verbatim as described (`const userInput = process.argv[2];` / `eval(userInput);`), and CWE-95 is the correct mapping for that pattern in isolation. But this is not application code -- it is an intentionally vulnerable test fixture whose sole purpose is to be the positive-detection input for the eslint-security adapter. tests/test_phase1_integration.py:80-93 (test_eslint_security_finds_eval) points the adapter at tests/fixtures/insecure-js and asserts findings are produced; the test runs eslint statically over the file and never executes it with node. The fixture is documented as such in docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-01-static-analysis-phase1-design.md:169 ('insecure-js/ -- JS files triggering eslint-plugin-security rules') and docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-01-static-analysis-phase1.md:48. The directory contains only app.js -- no package.json, no entrypoint, no bin -- so it is not installable, not shipped, and has no reachable execution path; process.argv[2] is never populated by anything in this repo. Decisively, the project already classifies findings from this exact path as scan noise and has a first-class mechanism to suppress them: .github/workflows/security.yml:60-63 calls `it.ingest_dir(..., exclude_globs=['tests/fixtures/*'])` under the comment 'Fixture exclusion is the standard ingest mechanism (F-CAL-2)', ingest_tools.py:44-49 documents it ('intentionally vulnerable apps under tests/fixtures/ dominate self-scans otherwise'), and tests/test_ingest_tools.py:217-228 regression-tests exclusion using this very file path. discarded_claims.title: Known vulnerability in lodash 4.17.20 (CVE-2021-23337)
discarded_claims.description: Lodash version 4.17.20 contains a known prototype pollution vulnerability (CVE-2021-23337). Affected versions are before 4.17.21.
discarded_claims.impact: Prototype pollution attacks can lead to property injection, allowing attackers to modify object properties and potentially achieve remote code execution or bypass authentication mechanisms.
discarded_claims.remediation: Upgrade lodash to version 4.17.21 or later.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The version string is real (line 5 of the cited file is `"lodash": "4.17.20"`, mirrored in package-lock.json), and CVE-2021-23337 does affect lodash <4.17.21. But the claim treats a purpose-built, never-installed test fixture as a live dependency vulnerability, and its remediation would break a passing test. Three independent lines of evidence: (1) INTENT IS DOCUMENTED. /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-01-static-analysis-phase1-design.md:168 specifies `vulnerable-node/` as '`package.json` + `package-lock.json` with a known vulnerable package', and the implementation plan at plans/2026-08-01-static-analysis-phase1.md:486-513 dictates the exact byte content of both files, lodash 4.17.20 included. The vulnerable version IS the fixture. (2) THE REMEDIATION BREAKS A TEST. /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/tests/test_phase1_integration.py:28-41 (`test_npm_audit_finds_lodash_vulnerability`) points npm-audit at this directory and asserts `self.assertTrue(findings, "expected npm-audit findings for lodash")`. Upgrading to 4.17.21 as the claim instructs makes that assertion fail. (3) NO EXECUTION PATH. The package is never installed: there is no node_modules, Dockerfile.fixtures builds only vulnerable-rust (line 41-42) and never runs npm install, .github/dependabot.yml monitors only pip/actions/docker at `/`, and the adapter's own command is `["npm", "audit", "--json", "--prefix", target]` (skill/scripts/tools/npm_audit.py:17), which reads the lockfile without installing. No lodash code exists in this repo, let alone executes. The repo already implements the correct suppression: .github/workflows/security.yml:62-63 calls `it.ingest_dir(..., exclude_globs=['tests/fixtures/*'])` with the comment 'Fixture exclusion is the standard ingest mechanism (F-CAL-2)'. This finding exists only because the AGENT path lacks that exclusion while the TOOL path has it -- a gap already filed by the maintainers as FIXME-4 ('No agent-side fixture exclusion', docs/superpowers/2026-08-04-run2-fixmes.md:48-59). SECONDARY DEFECT: the claim mischaracterizes the CVE. CVE-2021-23337 is command injection via `lodash.template`, not prototype pollution; the repo's own OSV fixture at tests/test_phase1_integration.py:54-57 labels GHSA-35jh-r3h4-6jhm/CVE-2021-23337 'Command Injection in lodash'. The cited CWE-1321 (prototype pollution) and the stated impact are therefore wrong even on the CVE's own terms.

discarded_claims.title: Known vulnerability in requests 2.25.1 (CVE-2023-32681)
discarded_claims.description: The requests library version 2.25.1 contains a known vulnerability (CVE-2023-32681 / PYSEC-2023-1). This version is vulnerable to session fixation attacks when using custom cookies.
discarded_claims.impact: Attackers may be able to perform session fixation attacks, potentially hijacking user sessions or bypassing authentication controls.
discarded_claims.remediation: Upgrade requests to version 2.31.0 or later.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The cited line is real (requirements.txt line 1 is `requests==2.25.1`) and the version does fall in CVE-2023-32681's affected range, but the claim is rejected on two independent grounds: it describes the wrong vulnerability, and it flags a deliberate fixture as a live exposure. WRONG VULNERABILITY: the claim states 2.25.1 'is vulnerable to session fixation attacks when using custom cookies' and cites CWE-384 (Session Fixation). The repo's own osv-scanner artifact contradicts this -- /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/.panopticon.prev-20260803/tools/osv-scanner.json:1792-1800 records `"id": "GHSA-j8r2-6x86-q33q"`, `"aliases": ["CVE-2023-32681", "PYSEC-2023-74"]`, `"summary": "Unintended leak of Proxy-Authorization header in requests"`. That is credential leakage to a redirect target (information exposure), not session fixation. The claim's alias 'PYSEC-2023-1' is also wrong; the real alias is PYSEC-2023-74. So the CVE id and the version range are right, but the description, impact and CWE are fabricated around them. FIXTURE, NOT EXPOSURE: docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-01-static-analysis-phase1-design.md:167 specifies `vulnerable-python/` as 'requirements.txt with a known vulnerable package', and plans/2026-08-01-static-analysis-phase1.md:352-356 dictates the exact content `requests==2.25.1`. tests/test_phase1_integration.py:13-26 (`test_pip_audit_finds_requests_cve`) points pip-audit at this directory and asserts `any("CVE-" in str(f.get("citations")) for f in findings)`; the claim's remediation (upgrade to 2.31.0) would break it. The package is never installed into any environment: pip-audit runs `["pip-audit", "--format=json", "--desc=on", "--requirement", req]` (skill/scripts/tools/pip_audit.py:31-42), which resolves metadata rather than installing; Dockerfile.fixtures never pip-installs it; .github/dependabot.yml scopes its pip ecosystem to `/`, not tests/fixtures. The intended suppression already exists on the tool path -- .github/workflows/security.yml:62-63 passes `exclude_globs=['tests/fixtures/*']` to `ingest_dir` -- and its absence on the agent path is the maintainers' own FIXME-4 (docs/superpowers/2026-08-04-run2-fixmes.md:48-59). On the `corroborated_by: [security, test]` flag: agreement between two lens sweeps that both scanned the fixture tree without exclusion is correlated error from a shared blind spot, not independent evidence of real exposure.

discarded_claims.title: Dangerous eval() with user input (CWE-95)
discarded_claims.description: Direct use of eval() function with user-controlled input from process.argv. This is a known pattern for arbitrary code execution vulnerabilities (CWE-95).
discarded_claims.impact: Attackers can inject and execute arbitrary JavaScript code, leading to complete system compromise, data exfiltration, or lateral movement.
discarded_claims.remediation: Remove eval() usage entirely. Use safer alternatives such as JSON.parse() for data parsing, or sandboxed execution environments if dynamic code evaluation is absolutely necessary.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The literal pattern is present -- /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/tests/fixtures/insecure-js/app.js is exactly two lines: `const userInput = process.argv[2];` then `eval(userInput);`. But the claim's substance (arbitrary code execution, system compromise, 'remove eval() entirely') is contradicted by how the file exists in this repo. (1) The file is a purpose-built calibration fixture for the eslint-plugin-security adapter. docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-01-static-analysis-phase1-design.md:169 specifies `insecure-js/ -- JS files triggering eslint-plugin-security rules`, and docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-01-static-analysis-phase1.md:821-828 dictates this exact two-line content verbatim as 'Step 4: Create fixture'. (2) Nothing executes it. I grepped the whole repo for references (`insecure-js`, `app.js`, `node .`, `npm start`): the only live consumer is tests/test_phase1_integration.py:80-93 `test_eslint_security_finds_eval`, which passes the *directory* to `ADAPTERS['eslint-security'].invoke()`. That adapter (skill/scripts/tools/eslint_security.py:36-52) runs `eslint --no-config-lookup ... --format json <target>` -- a static lint, never `node`. There is no package.json, no entrypoint, and no import/require of the file anywhere; tests/tools/test_eslint_security.py uses synthetic JSON and a tempdir, not this file. The claimed exploit path (attacker supplies process.argv[2] to a running process) has no invoker in this repository. (3) The prescribed remediation would actively break a passing test: removing the eval is precisely what test_eslint_security_finds_eval asserts eslint detects ('expected eslint-security findings for eval usage'). (4) The repo already classes this file as intentional noise: ingest_tools.ingest_dir's `exclude_globs` (F-CAL-2, skill/scripts/ingest_tools.py:40-50) exists because 'intentionally vulnerable apps under tests/fixtures/ dominate self-scans otherwise', and .github/workflows/security.yml:62-63 drops findings under `tests/fixtures/*` from the CI gate -- the same eslint hit on this same file is visible in .panopticon.prev-20260803/tools/eslint-security.json and is excluded by that mechanism. Rejected as a defect; at most it is an informational note that a deliberately-vulnerable fixture exists.

discarded_claims.title: Test guarding secret propagation to Docker only checks the key NAME is present in argv, not that the VALUE is absent -- a future regression that leaks the secret into process arguments would pass
discarded_claims.description: `test_run_tools_propagates_nvd_api_key_when_set` sets `os.environ['NVD_API_KEY'] = 'secret-key'` and asserts only `self.assertIn('-e', calls[0])` and `self.assertIn('NVD_API_KEY', calls[0])`. It never asserts that the literal secret value ('secret-key') is absent from the constructed docker argv. The current production implementation (`skill/scripts/run_tools.py` line 157-158: `docker.extend(['-e', 'NVD_API_KEY'])`) is correct -- it passes only the variable name and lets Docker inherit the value from the parent process's environment, which does not expose the value via `ps`/process listing. However this test provides no safety net against a future edit that instead does `docker.extend(['-e', 'NVD_API_KEY=%s' % os.environ['NVD_API_KEY']])`, which would embed the raw secret in the process argument list (visible to any co-resident user via `ps aux`, and frequently captured verbatim in CI job logs when commands are echoed) -- and this test would still pass because 'NVD_API_KEY' remains a substring of the embedded assignment.
discarded_claims.impact: No live vulnerability today (verified the current implementation passes only the variable name), but a real security-relevant regression in how a secret reaches a subprocess would go undetected by this test suite, since the assertion is a weak substring match rather than checking exact-argument equality or explicitly asserting the secret value's absence.
discarded_claims.remediation: Strengthen the assertion to check that `calls[0]` contains the exact argument `'NVD_API_KEY'` (not an assignment form) and additionally assert `'secret-key' not in calls[0]` (or `not any('secret-key' in str(a) for a in calls[0])`) so a regression that embeds the value in argv fails the test.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning:
The claim's factual premises about the production code are correct, but its central technical mechanism is wrong, and that mechanism is the entire basis of the finding.

Verified premises: tests/test_run_tools.py:141-159 does set os.environ['NVD_API_KEY'] = 'secret-key' and asserts only `self.assertIn('-e', calls[0])` and `self.assertIn('NVD_API_KEY', calls[0])`. skill/scripts/run_tools.py:157-158 is `if os.environ.get("NVD_API_KEY"): docker.extend(["-e", "NVD_API_KEY"])`, i.e. name-only passthrough, which is the safe form. The test does exercise that branch: 'dependency-check' is absent from TOOL_CMD in skill/scripts/tools/legacy_sarif.py (which contains only semgrep/gitleaks/trivy/bandit/gosec) and present in ADAPTERS via skill/scripts/tools/__init__.py:28, so run_tools takes the Phase-1 adapter path where the -e flag is built.

Where the claim fails: it asserts the check is 'a weak substring match' and that a regression to `docker.extend(['-e', 'NVD_API_KEY=%s' % os.environ['NVD_API_KEY']])` 'would still pass because NVD_API_KEY remains a substring of the embedded assignment.' That is false. `calls[0]` is the `docker` argv **list** (the runner stub does `calls.append(cmd)` at line 145, and `cmd` is the list built at run_tools.py:156-167). unittest's assertIn evaluates `member in container`; for a list container this is element-wise equality, not substring matching. `'NVD_API_KEY' in ['docker','run','--rm','-e','NVD_API_KEY=secret-key', ...]` evaluates to False, so the exact regression the claim describes would FAIL this test, not pass it. The assertion is already the exact-argument equality check the remediation asks for.

The suggested extra assertion (`'secret-key' not in calls[0]`) would likewise be an element-membership check and would add nothing over the existing one for the described regression. Only a contrived double-injection (keeping a bare 'NVD_API_KEY' element while also adding an assignment element) would evade the current test, which is not the scenario claimed. Since the claim reports no live vulnerability and its sole asserted test-gap mechanism is contradicted by the code, this is rejected.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The claim's conclusion — 'dead fixture data; unclear whether fixture should be used, archived, or removed' — is false. tests/fixtures/manifest.json has a single, explicit, well-documented consumer: /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/run_fixture_tests.py declares `MANIFEST = REPO_ROOT / 'tests' / 'fixtures' / 'manifest.json'` (line 13), loads and hard-fails on it in load_manifest() (lines 91-99, `sys.exit(1)` if missing or malformed), enumerates `manifest['fixtures']` for the run banner (lines 113-117), and feeds the entries into check_fixtures() (line 125) to report PRESENT/MISSING per fixture inside the image. Its purpose is also documented in DEVELOPMENT.md:74-83 ('Local scanner fixture suite') and in docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-02-local-scanner-fixture-suite-design.md:172 ('the test runner uses it to report which fixtures were found/missing'). discarded_claims.description: Lines 186 and 195 in test_run_tools.py use hardcoded '/tmp/target' instead of tempfile.TemporaryDirectory(). This violates test isolation principles and creates side-effect risk.
discarded_claims.impact: Tests may fail unpredictably if /tmp/target exists or is modified by external processes; multiple test runs could interfere with each other.
discarded_claims.remediation: Replace hardcoded '/tmp/target' with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() context manager, consistent with the pattern used throughout the rest of the test suite (see lines 41, 50, 61, etc.).

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The claim's premise — that '/tmp/target' is used as a real filesystem path — is contradicted by the code. Lines 186/195/206 pass '/tmp/target' as argv[2] to `ra.main`, which is `skill/scripts/_run_adapter.py:main`. That function does `target = argv[2] if len(argv) > 2 else '/src'` and then only forwards `target` to `adapter.invoke(target)`. It never opens, stats, creates, or writes the path. At line 186 the injected `FakeAdapter.invoke(self, target)` ignores its argument entirely and returns `(b'{"ok":true}', 0)`. At line 195 the name 'not-a-real-adapter' misses the `ADAPTERS` dict, so `main` hits the `except KeyError` branch and returns 0 before `target` is ever used. So no file is created and no file is read: the claimed impact (tests failing if /tmp/target exists or is modified externally; cross-run interference; side effects) cannot occur, and CWE-377 (insecure temporary file creation) does not apply since no temporary file is created. The remediation's appeal to consistency is also wrong: lines 41, 50, 61 use `tempfile.TemporaryDirectory()` because those tests exercise `rt.run_tools`, which really does write `out_dir` to disk — a different situation. Furthermore, an inert '/tmp/...' placeholder string is the deliberate, repo-wide convention for mock-backed adapter tests: `/tmp/fake` appears the same way in tests/tools/test_pip_audit.py, test_npm_audit.py, test_brakeman.py, test_cargo_audit.py, test_bundler_audit.py, test_osv_scanner.py, test_eslint_security.py, test_spotbugs.py, and tests/test_dispatch.py ('/tmp/x'), always with the subprocess layer mocked. Wrapping these in TemporaryDirectory would add ceremony without changing behavior.

discarded_claims.title: Test function defined outside unittest.TestCase class
discarded_claims.description: Line 257 in test_schemas.py defines test_multi_model_fields_in_schemas() as a bare function rather than a method within a TestCase class. This breaks standard unittest discovery patterns and could be missed by test runners.
discarded_claims.impact: Test discovery tools and CI/CD pipelines may fail to run this test; it is likely missed during routine test execution.
discarded_claims.remediation: Convert the bare function into a proper method by creating a new TestCase class (e.g., class TestMultiModelFields(unittest.TestCase)) and placing the function as a test method within it.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The structural observation is accurate — tests/test_schemas.py:257 does define `test_multi_model_fields_in_schemas()` as a module-level function rather than a TestCase method, and it is the only such function in the whole suite (grep for '^def test_' across tests/ returns exactly this one hit). But the claimed impact is false for this repository. The project runs pytest, not unittest discovery: .github/workflows/ci.yml:41 is `python -m pytest tests/ -q`, CONTRIBUTING.md:13 and README.md:92 give the same command, and DEVELOPMENT.md:72 uses pytest as well. `python -m unittest` / `unittest discover` appears nowhere in the repo. pytest's default `python_functions = test*` collects bare module-level test functions, and nothing overrides that default here: there is no conftest.py anywhere in the tree (glob for **/conftest.py returns nothing), no pytest.ini, setup.cfg, or tox.ini, and pyproject.toml contains no [tool.pytest.ini_options] section — only [project] and ruff config. So the function is collected and executed on every CI run across the 3.11/3.12/3.13 matrix. It is also a live, meaningful test rather than dead code: I verified its assertions hold against skill/reference/scope-profile-schema.json, which defines 'files' (line 22), 'depth' (line 23), and lens item 'priority' (line 38) and 'depth_threshold' (line 39). The only real caveat is narrow and not what the claim asserts: `unittest.main()` at line 274 means invoking the file directly as `python tests/test_schemas.py` would skip this one function. That is a cosmetic inconsistency worth noting, not a MEDIUM/LOW correctness or coverage defect, and CWE-1104 (use of unmaintained third-party components) is unrelated to the issue described.
